blocks.html: Two tiny Latin parts open a whole family of words. bene- means well (you know it from benefit), and mal- means badly (you know it from malfunction). Put one in front of another part and you get a word for good will or for ill will.
bene- = well, good. mal- = badly, bad. A bene- word usually points to kindness or help; a mal- word points to harm, illness or trouble.
Each card has a picture and a memory hook: a sound-alike that acts out the meaning. Say the hook out loud, look at the picture, then read the sentences to see the word at work.

entry.def: kind and wishing good for others
entry.ex: The {benevolent} neighbor shoveled every driveway on the street after the storm.
entry.ctx: Though the old shopkeeper looked stern, the town knew him to be {benevolent}; every winter he quietly paid the heating bills of families who could not.
entry.etym: From Latin benevolens, “wishing well”: bene (well) + volens (wishing).

mn.text: Every Saturday, Ben volunteers at the bread table; a man who gives his time to help others is {benevolent}.

scene.alt: Ben, in an apron, hands out free bread to happy children.

entry.def: a person who gives money or help to a person or cause
entry.ex: An unnamed {benefactor} paid for the new playground.
entry.ctx: The museum could never have bought the painting on its own; a {benefactor} who loved art covered the whole cost and asked only that the public be allowed to see it.
entry.etym: From Latin benefactor, “one who does good”: bene (well) + facere (to do).

mn.cue: the owner of the BENEFIT FACTORY
mn.text: Picture a factory that makes good things for other people: its owner, the {benefactor}, is the one who gives.

scene.alt: A gentleman in a top hat gives a bag of money; a woman cheers beside a sign for a new library.

entry.def: helpful; producing good results
entry.ex: Reading aloud every evening proved {beneficial} to her spelling.
entry.ctx: The new bus route proved {beneficial} to the whole neighborhood: workers reached their jobs faster, and the shops near each stop saw more customers.

roots.means: having to do with (an adjective ending)

entry.etym: From Latin beneficium, “a kindness, a favor”: bene (well) + facere (to do).

mn.text: A fish that sweeps the sea floor clean helps every creature around it; its work is {beneficial}.

scene.alt: A smiling fish sweeps the sea floor clean with a broom.

entry.def: gentle and kind; also, not harmful
entry.ex: Despite his size, the farm’s old horse was {benign} and let the children brush his mane.
entry.ctx: The rumor about the new rule sounded alarming, but the change turned out to be {benign}: it did nothing except change the color of the hall passes.
entry.etym: From Latin benignus, “kindly, good-natured,” from bene (well).
entry.note: Doctors use benign for a growth that is not harmful; the opposite is malignant.

mn.cue: BE NINE: a big dog named Nine
mn.text: The family dog, Nine, is huge, but he is {benign}: he lets the kitten nap on his back.

scene.alt: A huge dog named Nine stands calmly while a kitten naps on his back.

entry.def: a person who receives a benefit, such as money left in a will
entry.ex: Lila was the {beneficiary} of her grandfather’s garden and all his tools.
entry.ctx: When the old sailor died, his will named the town library as the {beneficiary} of his whole collection of maps, so anyone can now come and study them.
entry.etym: From Latin beneficiarius, “one who receives a favor,” from beneficium, a kindness.

mn.cue: the one who gets the FISH
mn.text: The fisherman gives; the boy who gets the fish is the bene-FISH-iary. The {beneficiary} is the one who receives.

scene.alt: A fisherman gives a fish to a delighted boy; the giver is labeled gives, the boy gets.

entry.def: wishing harm to others
entry.ex: In the old story, a {malevolent} sorcerer cast a spell of endless winter on the valley.
entry.ctx: The villain’s grin was not friendly but {malevolent}; he was already planning how to ruin the festival for everyone in town.
entry.etym: From Latin malevolens, “wishing ill”: male (badly) + volens (wishing).

mn.text: An evil villain sneaks through the mall wishing bad luck on every shopper: he is {malevolent}.

cast.think: I wish them all bad luck!

scene.alt: A caped villain sneaks through a store, wishing everyone bad luck; a girl looks worried.

entry.def: meaning to hurt someone on purpose
entry.ex: Spreading a {malicious} rumor can hurt a person’s friendships for years.
entry.ctx: The broken window was no accident; the footprints and the thrown rock showed that the damage was {malicious}.
entry.etym: From Latin malitia, “badness, ill will,” from malus (bad).

mn.text: Sneaky Mal pours salt into the baker’s delicious pie on purpose; spoiling it just to hurt her is {malicious}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man pours salt into a pie while the baker is not looking.

entry.def: an illness, or a deep-rooted problem
entry.ex: Boredom is a common {malady} on long car trips.
entry.ctx: The town’s real {malady} was not its empty storefronts but its loss of hope; once neighbors began working together, the shops slowly filled again.
entry.etym: From Old French maladie, from malade, “sick,” from Latin male habitus, “in poor condition.”

mn.text: Poor Granny Mae is the lady with the bad cold; her {malady} keeps her in bed.

scene.alt: An old lady lies in bed with a bad cold, sneezing.

entry.def: to say harmful and untrue things about someone
entry.ex: It is unfair to {malign} a teammate who is not there to answer.
entry.ctx: Rather than bake better bread, the rival shop tried to {malign} its new neighbor, telling customers false stories about its kitchen.
entry.etym: From Latin malignus, “ill-natured,” the opposite of benignus.
entry.note: Malign is also an adjective meaning evil or harmful (a malign influence), but it is most often a verb.

mn.text: A mean line about someone that is not true: whispering “Dev cheats!” is a way to {malign} him.

labels.text: MAL LINE = a lie that hurts

scene.alt: A sneaky teen whispers a false rumor about Dev, who looks hurt.

entry.def: a person who is always dissatisfied and complaining
entry.ex: Even on a perfect beach day, the {malcontent} found something to grumble about.
entry.ctx: Most of the crew liked the new schedule, but one {malcontent} complained about it at every meeting and refused even to try it.
entry.etym: From French malcontent, “ill content”: mal (badly) + content (satisfied).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus is never content, not even at the beach: he is a {malcontent}.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather complains on a lovely beach while his wife enjoys the sun.

blocks.cap: Words built on bene- (well, good).

blocks.name: vo-roots
blocks.cap: Words built on mal- (badly, bad).

blocks.html: Learners mix up benefactor (the giver) and beneficiary (the receiver), and take malign for an adjective only; it is most often a verb: to speak ill of someone.

meaning
mal- word
meaning
blocks.cap: Pairs that share a second part: bene- and mal- flip the meaning.

blocks.html: Keep the giver and the receiver straight: a benefactor gives and a beneficiary receives. The ending -or names the one who does something, as in actor and donor.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some people notice when others are hurting and do something about it. Others notice and shrug, or even make things worse. English has a rich set of words for both kinds of heart, and good writers choose among them carefully: a considerate neighbor and a magnanimous rival are kind in different ways, and a callous boss is cruel in a different way from a vindictive one.

Warm hearts: compassionate (feels for others’ pain), considerate (thinks of others), altruistic (helps with no reward), humane (merciful), magnanimous (generous to a rival), solicitous (anxiously caring). Cold hearts: callous (unfeeling), ruthless (pitiless), vindictive (wants revenge), spiteful (mean out of petty ill will).

entry.def: feeling for others who suffer and wanting to help them
entry.ex: The {compassionate} nurse held the frightened boy’s hand until his parents arrived.
entry.ctx: Instead of laughing when the runner tripped, the {compassionate} crowd went silent, and two of her rivals stopped to help her to her feet.
entry.etym: From Latin compati, “to suffer with”: com (with) + pati (to suffer).

mn.text: Maya’s heart works like a compass: it always points her toward whoever is hurting. She is {compassionate}.

scene.alt: A teenage girl kneels beside a crying boy on the playground and offers him a bandage.

entry.def: careful not to hurt, bother or inconvenience others
entry.ex: It was {considerate} of Omar to call ahead and say he would be late.
entry.ctx: The upstairs neighbors were unusually {considerate}: knowing the baby napped at noon, they always waited until two o’clock to vacuum.

mn.text: Before Jonah bangs his drum, he stops to consider it: is the baby asleep? Thinking of others first makes him {considerate}.

scene.alt: A teenage boy sets down his drum and shushes because his baby brother is napping.

entry.def: helping others with no thought of reward for oneself
entry.ex: The {altruistic} teen spent her summer teaching little kids to swim for free.
entry.ctx: Her reasons for volunteering were purely {altruistic}: she asked for no pay, no thanks and no mention of her name in the newsletter.
entry.etym: From French altruisme, built on Italian altrui, “of others,” from Latin alter, “other.”

mn.text: Al shovels every neighbor’s walk and waves away their money. Al truly helps for nothing in return: he is {altruistic}.

scene.alt: A man named Al, holding a snow shovel, waves away the coins an old woman offers him.

entry.def: kind and merciful; causing no needless pain
entry.ex: The shelter found a {humane} way to catch the stray cats without hurting them.
entry.ctx: The old rules let farm animals be kept in cramped cages, but the new law is more {humane}: every animal must have room to move, fresh water and shelter.
entry.etym: From Latin humanus, “human”; humane began as another spelling of human and came to mean kind and gentle.
entry.note: Humane (hyoo-MAYN) means kind and merciful; human (HYOO-mun) means a person, or having to do with people.

mn.text: Add an E to human for Extra kindness: Ada’s {humane} trap catches the mouse without a scratch, and she lets it go in the garden.

scene.alt: A woman kneels in a garden and lets a mouse run free from a box trap.

entry.def: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival
entry.ex: In a {magnanimous} gesture, the champion invited the runner-up to share the stage.
entry.ctx: After winning the chess final, Ada was {magnanimous}: instead of gloating, she praised her opponent’s bold opening and offered to practice with him.
entry.etym: From Latin magnanimus, “great-souled”: magnus (great) + animus (mind, soul).

mn.text: Dev wins the race, then lifts the trophy with the runner-up and cheers for him too. A heart that big toward a rival is {magnanimous}.

scene.alt: The winner of a race offers to share his trophy with the surprised runner-up.

entry.def: eagerly caring about someone’s comfort and well-being
entry.ex: The {solicitous} host kept asking whether everyone had enough to eat.
entry.ctx: Grandpa had only a mild cold, but Lila was so {solicitous} that she brought him tea, tucked in his blanket and checked on him every ten minutes.
entry.etym: From Latin sollicitus, “anxious, troubled.”

mn.text: “So, list us your needs: tea? a pillow? another blanket?” Lila fusses over Granny Mae’s sniffle. She is {solicitous}.

scene.alt: A girl offers tea to her grandmother on the sofa and asks what else she needs.

entry.def: unfeeling toward other people’s pain or trouble
entry.ex: Laughing at the boy who dropped his lunch tray was a {callous} thing to do.
entry.ctx: The landlord’s answer to the flooded families was {callous}: he said their ruined furniture was not his problem and went back to his lunch.
entry.etym: From Latin callosus, “hard-skinned,” from callum, hard skin.
entry.note: Callous (unfeeling) sounds just like callus, the patch of hard skin a hand gets from hard work.

mn.text: A callus is hard skin that feels nothing. Rex walks past the crying girl without a glance, as if his heart had a callus: he is {callous}.

scene.alt: A man walks away without caring while a girl cries over her dropped ice cream.

entry.def: showing no pity; willing to hurt others to get one’s way
entry.ex: Lin is a {ruthless} checkers player who never lets anyone take back a move.
entry.ctx: The new owner was {ruthless}: he closed the beloved bakery, let every worker go without warning and never once looked back.
entry.etym: From the old word ruth, “pity,” + -less: without pity.

mn.text: Ruth is an old word for pity. The cartoon king who takes the farmers’ very last pears has no ruth at all: he is {ruthless}.

scene.alt: A cartoon king points and orders that a sad farmer’s last basket of fruit be taken.

entry.def: wanting revenge; set on paying someone back
entry.ex: After losing at checkers, my {vindictive} cousin hid the winner’s shoes.
entry.ctx: Most fans forgave the referee’s honest mistake, but one {vindictive} fan spent the whole season writing letters demanding that he be fired.
entry.etym: From Latin vindicta, “revenge.”

mn.text: Vin keeps a whole dictionary of everyone who ever wronged him, and he plans to pay back every one. Vin is {vindictive}.

scene.alt: A man named Vin reads a book of grudges and plans his payback.

entry.def: mean on purpose, out of petty ill will
entry.ex: The {spiteful} cat stared right at me and pushed my cup off the table.
entry.ctx: Jealous that her brother got the bigger room, she did something {spiteful}: she hid his favorite cap where he would not find it for weeks.
entry.etym: From spite, a shortening of despite, which once meant scorn.

mn.text: Dinner was late, so Mittens looks Felix in the eye and slowly pushes his cup off the table: a {spiteful} cat.

scene.alt: A sneaky cat on a table pushes a cup off the edge while its owner gasps.

blocks.html: humane (kind) is not human; callous (unfeeling) is not callus (hard skin). magnanimous is about a big heart, not a big size.

head: warm word
cold opposite
the difference
rows: feels another’s pain / feels nothing for it
forgives a rival / wants to pay a rival back
spares needless pain / shows no pity
careful not to bother others / bothers others on purpose
blocks.cap: Four kind words and the cruel words that mirror them.

blocks.html: Two sound-alike traps: humane (hyoo-MAYN, kind) is not human (a person), and callous (unfeeling) is not callus (a patch of hard skin). And magnanimous is about a big heart, never a big size.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Manners are the small ways we show other people that they matter: a greeting, a careful word, a secret kept. This topic’s words describe people by their manners, from the gracious to the gruff. Notice how many of the rude words are about how something is said (too short, too rough, too mean) rather than how loud it is.

Polite: courteous (respectful), tactful (spares feelings), discreet (keeps things private), urbane (polished and at ease), suave (smoothly charming). Rude: boorish (rough and loud), brusque (abrupt), curt (rudely brief), uncouth (without manners), churlish (mean and ungracious).

entry.def: polite and respectful toward others
entry.ex: The {courteous} bus driver waited for the running boy and greeted him with a smile.
entry.ctx: Even when the customer began to shout, the clerk stayed {courteous}, thanking him for his patience and calmly offering to fix the order.
entry.etym: From Old French corteis, “having manners fit for a royal court.”

mn.cue: manners fit for a royal COURT
mn.text: Sami bows to the queen and says, “Good morning, Your Majesty.” Manners fit for a royal court are {courteous}.

scene.alt: A boy bows politely to a smiling queen in her throne room.

entry.def: careful to say things without hurting anyone’s feelings
entry.ex: Felix gave a {tactful} answer when his aunt asked whether he liked her very orange sweater.
entry.ctx: Rather than calling the essay boring, the teacher was {tactful}: she praised its strong opening and suggested ways to make the middle livelier.
entry.etym: From tact, which comes from Latin tactus, “touch.”

mn.text: Tact comes from the Latin for touch. Aunt Greta asks if Felix likes her bright orange sweater, and he answers with a light touch: “It’s so cheerful!” He is {tactful}.

scene.alt: A woman in a loud orange dress asks her nephew if he likes it, and he answers kindly.

entry.def: careful in what one says or does, especially in keeping secrets
entry.ex: Be {discreet} about the surprise party; Grandma notices everything.
entry.ctx: The nurse was always {discreet}: she never mentioned a patient’s name outside the clinic, not even at home with her own family.
entry.etym: From Latin discretus, “separated,” from discernere, “to tell apart”: a discreet person can tell what to say from what to keep.
entry.note: Discreet (careful, private) is not discrete (separate, distinct). Both come from the same Latin word but have gone separate ways.

mn.text: Zoe whispers her news, and Kai zips his lips: “This secret stays with me.” He never tells a soul. Kai is {discreet}.

scene.alt: A girl whispers a secret to a boy, who puts a finger to his lips; a padlock floats beside him.

entry.def: polished, courteous and at ease in any social setting
entry.ex: The {urbane} host remembered every guest’s name and made each one feel welcome.
entry.ctx: Though he had grown up on a remote ranch, Marcus became an {urbane} diplomat, as comfortable at a formal dinner as at a cattle auction.
entry.etym: From Latin urbanus, “of the city,” from urbs, city; city manners were thought to be polished.
entry.note: Urban (of the city) and urbane (polished in manner) share the Latin urbs, city, but urbane is about manners, not places.

mn.text: At the museum gala, Victor greets each guest by name, bows, and tells just the right joke. His manners are city-polished: he is {urbane}.

scene.alt: A gentleman in a top hat bows gracefully to welcome a guest at a museum party.

entry.def: charming, confident and smooth in manner
entry.ex: The {suave} magician bowed, winked and pulled a rose from behind his hat.
entry.ctx: Her brother tried to look {suave} at the dance, but the effect was spoiled when he tripped over his own feet and spilled punch down his shirt.
entry.etym: From Latin suavis, “agreeable, sweet.”
entry.note: Suave is often praise, but it can hint that the charm is a little too smooth to trust.

mn.text: Spell it out: Smooth, Unruffled, At ease, Very charming, Elegant. Jamal glides across the stage in his bow tie and never misses a step: he is {suave}.

scene.alt: A man in a bow tie and sunglasses dances smoothly in a spotlight on stage.

entry.def: rough, loud and bad-mannered
entry.ex: His {boorish} habit of talking with his mouth full annoyed everyone at the table.
entry.ctx: The other guests were chatting quietly, so his {boorish} behavior stood out: he shouted across the room, put his feet on a chair and grabbed the last rolls.

mn.cue: a BOAR at the dinner table
mn.text: Picture a wild boar at a dinner party: snorting, grabbing, crumbs everywhere. Rex eats just like one. He is {boorish}.

labels.text: BOOR = a BOAR at the table

scene.alt: A rude man gobbles pizza and shouts for more beside a piggy; an old woman looks disgusted.

entry.def: abrupt and short in speech or manner
entry.ex: The busy clerk gave a {brusque} nod and turned to the next customer.
entry.ctx: Usually warm and chatty, the coach was {brusque} that morning: he said “Laps. Now.” and walked off before anyone could ask a question.
entry.etym: From French brusque, “lively, fierce,” from Italian brusco, “sour.”

mn.text: Nell asks a hurrying man for directions, and he brushes her off with one word, “Busy,” and keeps walking. A brush-off that quick is {brusque}.

scene.alt: At a train station, a hurrying man brushes off a woman asking for directions.

entry.def: rudely brief
entry.ex: Her {curt} reply, “No,” ended the conversation.
entry.ctx: I wrote a long, friendly letter asking for help, but the reply was {curt}: just two words, “Not possible,” and not even a signature.
entry.etym: From Latin curtus, “cut short.”

mn.text: Zoe starts to show the banker her whole plan for a lemonade stand, and he cuts her short: “No.” A reply cut that short is {curt}.

scene.alt: A girl holds up her plan to show a banker, who crosses his arms and says only no.

entry.def: lacking good manners or refinement
entry.ex: Talking loudly on the phone all through the movie was {uncouth}.
entry.ctx: In the old story, the {uncouth} giant wiped his hands on the tablecloth and stomped across the clean floor in muddy boots, to the queen’s horror.
entry.etym: From Old English uncuth, “unknown, strange”: un (not) + cuth (known).

mn.text: It rhymes: the youth with no manners is uncouth. Jonah stomps into the quiet library in muddy boots, yelling for his friend. He is {uncouth}.

scene.alt: A muddy teenager shouts in a quiet library while a reader glares at him.

entry.def: rude and mean-spirited; ungracious
entry.ex: It would be {churlish} to refuse a gift from a friend who saved for months to buy it.
entry.ctx: After the neighbors spent all day fixing his fence, it was {churlish} of him to complain that they had painted it the wrong shade of white.

mn.text: Ivy gives Uncle Marcus a scarf she knitted herself, and he hurls it back with a grunt: “Itchy.” Hurling back a kind gift is {churlish}.

scene.alt: A grumpy man tosses back a gift from a girl, who is sad.

blocks.html: discreet (careful, private) is not discrete (separate). brusque and curt are about too few words, not loud ones.

head: word
what is wrong (or right) with the manner
rows: abrupt: few words, no warmth, a hurry to be done
rudely brief: the shortness itself is the insult
rough and loud: no care for anyone around
unpolished: never learned the manners at all
mean and ungracious: answering kindness with rudeness
polished and at ease: the opposite of uncouth
blocks.cap: The rude words are not interchangeable: each one names a different fault.

blocks.html: discreet (careful, good at keeping secrets) and discrete (separate: “three discrete steps”) sound the same. Remember: a discreet friend keeps the secret; in discrete the t separates the two e’s.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some people say a great deal in a few words; others use a great many words to say very little. This topic gathers the words for both. Half praise economy (concise, succinct, pithy), a few describe people who simply talk very little (laconic, taciturn), and the rest describe a flood of talk (verbose, garrulous, voluble).

Few words, well chosen: concise, succinct, pithy, brevity. Few words, maybe too few: terse, laconic, taciturn. Many words: verbose (in speech or writing), garrulous (chatter about little things), voluble (fast, fluent, eager talk).

entry.def: giving all the needed information in few words
entry.ex: Her {concise} note said everything: “Pizza in the oven. Back at six.”
entry.ctx: The first draft rambled on for ten pages, but the final report was {concise}: two pages that covered every key finding without a wasted word.
entry.etym: From Latin concisus, “cut short,” from concidere: con (thoroughly) + caedere (to cut).

mn.text: Zoe’s report ran three pages, so she cut it to size: one tight paragraph that still says it all. Now it is {concise}.

scene.alt: A girl proudly holds up one short page, the long drafts in the trash, while a woman claps.

entry.def: brief and clear; said in few words
entry.ex: When the coach asked what went wrong, Lin gave a {succinct} answer: “We stopped passing.”
entry.ctx: The museum’s labels are {succinct}: each one tells you what the object is, how old it is and why it matters, all in a single sentence.
entry.etym: From Latin succinctus, “tucked up, belted,” as a traveler belts up a long robe to move quickly.
entry.note: Say both c’s: suk-SINKT, like “success” at the start.

mn.cue: suk-SINKT: SINK it in one shot
mn.text: Kai sinks the ball in the bucket with one clean toss: no extra bounces, no wasted moves. A {succinct} answer is like that: it makes its point in one shot.

scene.alt: A boy cheers as his ball drops straight into a bucket in one clean toss.

entry.def: brief, sometimes to the point of seeming rude
entry.ex: The {terse} text, “K,” left Jamal wondering whether his sister was upset.
entry.ctx: Grandma usually writes long, chatty letters, so her {terse} postcard, “Arrived. Raining. Love, G,” made the whole family laugh.
entry.etym: From Latin tersus, “wiped clean, polished”: a terse sentence has every extra word wiped away.

mn.text: Chef Omar keeps his lips pursed while he cooks and answers every question with one word: “Busy.” “Later.” “No.” His answers are {terse}.

cast.say: What’s for dinner? Can I help? Is it…

scene.alt: A chatty boy asks a cook many questions; the cook answers with one word.

entry.def: using very few words
entry.ex: The {laconic} rancher answered every question with “Yep” or “Nope.”
entry.ctx: Though the reporters asked long questions about her record-breaking climb, the {laconic} mountaineer said only, “It was cold.”

roots.means: Laconia, the land around ancient Sparta

entry.etym: From Greek Lakonikos, “of Laconia,” the region of ancient Sparta, whose speakers were known for short replies.

mn.text: Asked how his long, long trip across the desert went, the rancher says only, “Fine.” He lacks words to spare: he is {laconic}.

cast.say: So, how was the long trip across the whole desert?

scene.alt: A man asks a long question; the cowboy answers with a single word.

entry.def: short but full of meaning
entry.ex: Grandpa’s {pithy} advice fit on a sticky note: “Measure twice, cut once.”
entry.ctx: The speech was long and dull, but its closing line was {pithy}: “Start small, start now.” People were still quoting it weeks later.
entry.etym: From pith, the soft core of a plant stem; the pith of an idea is its core.

mn.cue: PIT-HY: a tiny PIT, a whole tree
mn.text: A tiny peach pit holds a whole tree inside it. A {pithy} saying is the same: a few words with a big idea packed in.

scene.alt: An old professor holds up a tiny fruit beside a big fruit tree: small seed, big tree.

entry.def: shortness, especially in speech or writing
entry.ex: The {brevity} of the speech delighted the hungry dinner guests.
entry.ctx: Teachers praised her essay for its {brevity}: where others wrote ten pages, she made the same points clearly in three.
entry.etym: From Latin brevitas, from brevis, “short,” the same root as brief and abbreviate.

mn.text: Nobody calls little Theodore by his whole name; he is just Theo. Brev- means brief, and {brevity} is the art of keeping it short.

scene.alt: A grandmother waves to a toddler; a sign shows the long name Theodore shortened to Theo.

entry.def: using more words than are needed
entry.ex: The {verbose} instructions took three pages to explain how to plug in a lamp.
entry.ctx: His answer was so {verbose} that by the time he finally reached his point, half the class had forgotten the question.
entry.etym: From Latin verbosus, “full of words,” from verbum, word.

mn.cue: VERB-HOSE: a fire hose of words
mn.text: Ask the lawyer a yes-or-no question, and words gush out like water from a fire hose: “Firstly, secondly, furthermore…” He is {verbose}.

scene.alt: A lawyer talks on and on as papers fly, and the judge falls asleep.

entry.def: talking too much, especially about unimportant things
entry.ex: Our {garrulous} seatmate told us about every one of her eleven cats.
entry.ctx: The {garrulous} barber kept up a stream of chatter about the weather, his nephew’s soccer team and the price of eggs, hardly pausing to breathe.
entry.etym: From Latin garrulus, “chattering,” from garrire, “to chatter.”

mn.text: Once Grandpa Gus starts talking, he runs on and on: the weather, his knees, the fish he almost caught. Gus is {garrulous}.

cast.say: And another thing! And then! And also…

scene.alt: A grandfather talks on and on while the boy listening falls asleep.

entry.def: quiet by habit; saying very little
entry.ex: Her {taciturn} uncle spoke perhaps ten words during the whole holiday dinner.
entry.ctx: In class Dev was {taciturn}, rarely raising his hand or chatting, yet his notebooks were full of sharp ideas and funny drawings.
entry.etym: From Latin taciturnus, from tacitus, “silent,” the root of tacit.

mn.cue: TACIT TURN: his turn, and silence
mn.text: Around the campfire everyone takes a turn telling a story. When it is Omar’s turn, he just smiles and pokes the fire. He is {taciturn}.

scene.alt: At a campfire a woman says it is Omar’s turn to tell a story; he just sits quietly.

entry.def: talking easily, quickly and at length
entry.ex: The {voluble} tour guide chatted happily all the way up the mountain.
entry.ctx: Shy in a big crowd, Rosa became {voluble} with close friends, talking fast and happily for hours about books, music and her plans.
entry.etym: From Latin volubilis, “rolling, flowing,” from volvere, “to roll”: words roll easily off a voluble tongue.

mn.text: Lila and Maya talk like a volleyball game: words fly fast, bounce right back and never hit the ground. Both girls are {voluble}.

scene.alt: Two girls on the beach chatter fast while a ball flies between them.

blocks.html: laconic and taciturn are close: a laconic person speaks briefly; a taciturn person seldom speaks at all. succinct is pronounced suk-SINKT.

blocks.cap: Brevity can be a gift or a chill; many words can be warm or wearing.

blocks.html: laconic and taciturn are close cousins. A laconic person answers, but very briefly (“Fine.”). A taciturn person tends not to talk at all and may seem unfriendly. And succinct is said suk-SINKT: both c’s count.

blocks.html: “Happy” is a fine word, but it does a lot of jobs. Is the happiness loud or quiet? Sudden or steady? Earned by a victory, or simply part of someone’s nature? The ten words in this topic each name a different kind of joy, and choosing the right one lets a reader hear the cheering, see the bouncing or feel the calm hope.

A burst of joy: elated (thrilled by good news), jubilant (joy at a win), ecstatic and euphoric (overwhelming happiness). A happy nature: buoyant (bounces back), blithe (carefree, maybe too carefree), ebullient and exuberant (bubbling with energy), sanguine (hopeful). The sound of it: mirth (laughter and fun).

entry.def: very happy and excited about something good
entry.ex: Maya was {elated} when the letter said she had made the team.
entry.ctx: After months of rejection letters, the young writer was {elated}: a magazine had finally accepted her story and planned to print it in the spring issue.
entry.etym: From Latin elatus, “lifted up,” a form of efferre, “to carry out, to raise.”

mn.cue: e-LAY-ted: she LAID a golden egg!
mn.text: Henrietta the hen has just laid a golden egg, and she flaps and clucks with joy. She is {elated}.

scene.alt: A joyful hen stands by the golden egg she has just laid while a boy cheers.

entry.def: joyful and triumphant, especially after a success
entry.ex: The {jubilant} fans poured onto the field after the final whistle.
entry.ctx: The mood in the gym was {jubilant}: the team had just won its first championship in forty years, and nobody wanted to go home.
entry.etym: From Latin jubilare, “to shout for joy.”

mn.cue: JUBIL-ANTS: the Ants won the cup!
mn.text: The Ants, the smallest team in the league, just won the cup, and every player is leaping and cheering. They are {jubilant}.

scene.alt: Three players on a team called the Ants leap and cheer, holding up a trophy.

entry.def: overwhelmingly happy and excited
entry.ex: The puppy was {ecstatic} to see its family come home after a week away.
entry.ctx: Lila had expected socks for her birthday, so when she unwrapped a telescope, she was {ecstatic}, shrieking and hugging everyone in the room.
entry.etym: From Greek ekstatikos, from ekstasis, “standing outside oneself”: ek (out) + histanai (to place, to stand).

mn.text: Ivy is so happy about her new puppy that she crackles like static electricity: she jumps, squeals and sparks with joy. She is {ecstatic}.

scene.alt: A girl leaps with joy, sparks flying, as a puppy jumps up to greet her.

entry.def: intensely happy and excited
entry.ex: The {euphoric} climbers hugged and took pictures on the summit.
entry.ctx: Crossing the finish line of her first marathon, Tia felt {euphoric}: the ache in her legs vanished, and she laughed and cried at the same time.
entry.etym: From Greek euphoria, “well-being,” from euphoros, “bearing well”: eu (well) + pherein (to bear).

mn.text: Tia finishes her first marathon and feels so light with joy that she could float off into the sky like a UFO. She is {euphoric}.

scene.alt: A runner with a medal floats up among the clouds, glowing with happiness.

entry.def: cheerful and hopeful; also, able to float
entry.ex: Despite the rain, the campers stayed {buoyant}, singing all the way back to their cabins.
entry.ctx: The team had lost its first three games, yet the players remained {buoyant}, joking at practice and sure that their luck was about to turn.
entry.etym: Probably from Spanish boyante, “floating,” from boya, buoy.

mn.cue: BUOY-ant: bobs up like a BUOY
mn.text: A wave knocks Sven’s hat into the sea, and he just laughs and bobs along like a buoy. His spirits always float back up: he is {buoyant}.

scene.alt: A man in a rowboat laughs as the wind blows his hat away; a life ring bobs nearby.

entry.def: cheerful and carefree, sometimes carelessly so
entry.ex: Humming a {blithe} tune, Zoe skipped down the lane to the pond.
entry.ctx: His {blithe} attitude toward deadlines worried his teammates; he whistled and joked while the project sat unfinished the night before it was due.
entry.etym: From Old English blithe, “joyful,” related to bliss.
entry.note: Blithe can be praise (a blithe spirit) or blame (a blithe disregard for the rules): carefree cheer in the wrong place is carelessness.

mn.text: Pip skips home whistling, blissful and light as a feather, without a care in the world, not even for the storm cloud right behind him. He is {blithe}.

scene.alt: A boy skips and whistles happily, not noticing a rain cloud behind him.

entry.def: bubbling over with cheerful energy
entry.ex: The {ebullient} host greeted every guest with a hug and a joke.
entry.ctx: Usually quiet, Professor Edwin became {ebullient} whenever someone asked about dinosaurs, waving his arms and talking faster than anyone could take notes.
entry.etym: From Latin ebullire, “to boil up”: e (out) + bullire (to bubble, to boil).

mn.text: Like a pot bubbling over, Zoe can’t hold in her joy at her first A: she jumps, laughs and hugs the whole class. She is {ebullient}.

scene.alt: A girl leaps for joy with her graded paper while a classmate claps.

entry.def: full of energy, excitement and joy
entry.ex: The {exuberant} puppy raced around the yard, leaping at every leaf.
entry.ctx: The concert hall was usually hushed, but tonight the crowd was {exuberant}, clapping along, dancing in the aisles and calling for one more song.
entry.etym: From Latin exuberare, “to be abundantly fruitful,” from uber, “fertile.”

mn.cue: ex-ZOO-ber-ant: a ZOO bursting with joy
mn.text: The keeper rolls in a birthday cake, and the whole zoo bursts with joy: the monkey leaps, the parrot sings, the elephant sprays a happy fountain. The animals are {exuberant}.

scene.alt: An elephant, a leaping monkey and a singing parrot celebrate around a birthday cake.

entry.def: laughter, fun and amusement
entry.ex: The puppet show filled the library with {mirth}.
entry.ctx: The meeting had been tense, but when the principal’s puppy trotted in wearing a party hat, the room dissolved into {mirth}; even the grumpiest teacher laughed.
entry.etym: From Old English myrgth, related to merry.

mn.text: At Theo’s birthday party, the puppy steals the party hat and wears it, and the whole room bursts into laughter. Birthdays bring {mirth}.

scene.alt: Children in party hats laugh as a puppy wears a hat at a birthday party.

entry.def: hopeful and confident about the future
entry.ex: Despite the gray sky, Dad was {sanguine} about our chances for a beach day.
entry.ctx: The rest of the crew doubted the old boat would ever float again, but Sven remained {sanguine}, sure that a little paint and patience would have her sailing by summer.
entry.etym: From Latin sanguineus, “of blood”; doctors of the Middle Ages believed a hopeful, cheerful temper came from plenty of blood.

mn.text: The sky is gray, but Jamal wears a sun grin and packs the beach umbrella anyway: “It’ll clear up by noon!” He is {sanguine}.

scene.alt: Under a gray cloud, a grinning man in sunglasses points to the sun peeking out.

blocks.html: blithe can be a criticism: a blithe disregard for danger is carelessness. sanguine comes from the Latin for blood, but in English it means hopeful.

blocks.cap: Kinds of happiness: a moment, a nature or a hope.

blocks.html: sanguine comes from the Latin word for blood, but in English it means hopeful. blithe can be a warning: a blithe disregard for danger is carelessness, not cheer.

blocks.html: How do we know what we know? Scientists, judges, detectives and careful readers all use the same small set of words for testing ideas: you start with a hypothesis or a premise, gather empirical evidence, see whether others corroborate it, and decide whether the result is conclusive. These words turn up constantly in the science and history passages of reading tests.

Starting points: hypothesis (an idea to test), premise (a statement you reason from). Kinds of evidence: empirical (observed, measured), anecdotal (stories). Backing it up: corroborate, substantiate, validate. Reaching an answer: deduce (reason it out), extrapolate (extend beyond the data), conclusive (settles it).

entry.def: based on observation or experiment, not on theory alone
entry.ex: Sami gathered {empirical} evidence by timing how long each paper airplane stayed in the air.
entry.ctx: The claim sounded convincing, but it had no {empirical} support: no one had ever tested it, measured anything or watched it happen.
entry.etym: From Greek empeirikos, “experienced,” from empeiria, “experience.”

mn.text: Don’t just guess how many seeds will sprout: peer at them, count them, write it down. Knowledge you get by peering and testing is {empirical}.

scene.alt: A girl in a lab coat peers through a magnifying glass at sprouting plants.

entry.def: based on personal stories rather than careful study
entry.ex: The only proof that the shortcut was faster was {anecdotal}: Dev said it felt quicker.
entry.ctx: Several fishermen swore that the biggest trout bit only on rainy days, but the evidence was merely {anecdotal}; no one had ever kept a careful record of the catches.
entry.etym: From Greek anekdota, “things not published”: an (not) + ekdotos (given out); an anecdote began as a private, untold story.

mn.text: Annie swears her lucky socks win every game. Her only proof is Annie’s tale about last Saturday, not a count of wins and losses. Her evidence is {anecdotal}.

scene.alt: A girl holds up her lucky sock and tells a story, while a scientist wonders where the data is.

entry.def: to confirm or support with more evidence
entry.ex: Two neighbors {corroborated} the boy’s story about the runaway goat.
entry.ctx: At first only one hiker reported seeing the rare owl, but photos from three other hikers soon {corroborated} her account.
entry.etym: From Latin corroborare, “to strengthen”: cor (thoroughly) + roborare (to make strong), from robur, oak, strength.

mn.cue: co-ROB: a CO-REPORT backs it up
mn.text: “The goat ate my sock!” says Kai. “I saw it too!” says Maya, pointing at the sock in the goat’s mouth. Her second report helps {corroborate} his story.

scene.alt: A boy says a goat ate his sock, and a girl points at the goat and says she saw it too.

entry.def: to support a claim with proof
entry.ex: Can you {substantiate} your claim that the cafeteria pizza is getting smaller?
entry.ctx: The scientist’s bold theory was exciting, but she could not yet {substantiate} it; until her experiments produced solid data, other researchers stayed doubtful.
entry.etym: From substance, Latin substantia, “that which stands under”: the solid stuff beneath a thing.

mn.cue: SUB-STAN-tiate: solid ground to STAND on
mn.text: A claim needs something solid to stand on. Dev backs up “The pizza shrank!” with a ruler and last month’s photo. Now he can {substantiate} it.

scene.alt: A boy measures a pizza with a ruler to prove it has shrunk, next to a photo from last month.

entry.def: to check or prove that something is sound or correct
entry.ex: The lab ran the test three more times to {validate} the surprising result.
entry.ctx: The new trail map looked accurate, but the rangers wanted to {validate} it before printing it, so they walked every path with a compass and the old survey.
entry.etym: From Latin validus, “strong,” from valere, “to be strong, to be worth.”

mn.text: The conductor checks Nell’s ticket against the schedule and stamps it VALID. To check that something is sound and correct is to {validate} it.

scene.alt: A train conductor holds up a passenger’s ticket marked valid with a check mark.

entry.def: settling a question beyond doubt
entry.ex: The muddy paw prints on the sofa were {conclusive}: the dog had been inside.
entry.ctx: Earlier studies had only hinted at the answer, but this one was {conclusive}: it tested thousands of samples and left no room for doubt.
entry.etym: From Latin concludere, “to close up”: con (thoroughly) + claudere (to shut).

mn.cue: con-CLUE-sive: the CLUE that closes the case
mn.text: Muddy paw prints lead from the door straight to the dog asleep on the sofa: the last clue that closes the case. The evidence is {conclusive}.

scene.alt: A boy detective with a magnifying glass follows muddy prints to a sleeping dog on the sofa.

entry.def: a statement assumed true and used as a starting point for reasoning
entry.ex: The whole plan rested on one {premise}: that the store would still be open at nine.
entry.ctx: Her conclusion followed logically, but it was built on a false {premise}; she had assumed the bridge was open, and it had been closed for repairs all week.
entry.etym: From Latin praemissa, “sent before”: prae (before) + mittere (to send); a premise is put first, before the conclusion.
entry.note: In the plural, premises can also mean a building and its grounds: “No dogs on the premises.”

mn.cue: PRE-MISE: the block that goes FIRST
mn.text: An argument is a tower of blocks, and the {premise} is the block at the bottom: set down first, before anything is built on it. If it is wobbly, the whole tower falls.

scene.alt: A professor points to a stack of boxes; the bottom one is labeled premise and the top one conclusion.

entry.def: to reach a conclusion by reasoning from facts
entry.ex: From the crumbs on his shirt, Mom {deduced} who had eaten the last cookie.
entry.ctx: No one told the detective where the thief had gone, but she {deduced} it from the clues: wet footprints, an open window and a missing umbrella.
entry.etym: From Latin deducere, “to lead down”: de (down, from) + ducere (to lead); reasoning leads you from the facts to the answer.

mn.text: The bread is gone, and one duck has crumbs all over its beak. Zoe didn’t see it happen, but she can {deduce} who ate it.

scene.alt: A girl with an empty bread bag points at the duck with crumbs on its beak.

entry.def: to use known facts or trends to predict what lies beyond them
entry.ex: From three weeks of growth, Lin {extrapolated} that her sunflower would top the fence by August.
entry.ctx: The town had grown by about a hundred people a year for a decade, so planners {extrapolated} from that trend to estimate how many classrooms they would need in ten years.
entry.etym: Formed from extra (beyond) and the ending of interpolate, “to fill in between known points.”

mn.cue: EXTRA-polate: draw the line EXTRA far
mn.text: Lin’s sunflower grew a foot each week, so she draws the line extra far, past what she has measured: “By August it will beat the fence!” To predict that way is to {extrapolate}.

cast.think: By August: TALLER than the fence!

scene.alt: A woman with a ruler imagines her sunflower growing taller than the fence by August.

entry.def: a proposed explanation that can be tested
entry.ex: Kai’s {hypothesis} was that plants given music would grow taller.
entry.ctx: Every test so far had matched her {hypothesis}, but the scientist kept experimenting, knowing that one careful result could still prove her idea wrong.
entry.etym: From Greek hypothesis, “a foundation, a supposition”: hypo (under) + thesis (a placing).
entry.note: The plural is hypotheses (hye-POTH-uh-seez).

mn.cue: HYPO = UNDER: an idea put UNDER a test
mn.text: Kai guesses that music helps plants grow, so he plays songs to one plant and not to the other. A guess that you put under a test is a {hypothesis}.

scene.alt: A boy wonders whether music helps plants grow, testing a plant beside a radio against one without.

blocks.html: anecdotal evidence is real stories, but too few or too unrepresentative to prove a pattern. extrapolate reaches beyond the data; interpolate fills in between data points.

word
example

A second class gets the same result.
So the music made the difference.
A year of music would double their height?
Many careful tests agree; no doubt remains.
blocks.cap: The words of a fair test, in order.

blocks.html: Anecdotal evidence is real (the stories happened), but there are too few stories, or they are too hand-picked, to prove a pattern. Extrapolate reaches beyond the data you have; interpolate fills in between data points you already have.

blocks.html: Some things are here and gone: a rainbow, a firefly’s glow, a train passing through town. Others seem to last forever: a stone statue, a deep friendship, a stain that will not wash out. This topic gathers the words writers use for how long things last, and for whether they can change at all.

Here and gone: ephemeral (a very short life), transient and transitory (passing, temporary), fleeting (over in a flash), evanescent (fading from sight). Here to stay: enduring (lasting long), perpetual (never stopping), indelible (cannot be erased). Change: mutable (can change), immutable (cannot).

entry.def: lasting a very short time
entry.ex: The rainbow was {ephemeral}, gone before Lila could find her camera.
entry.ctx: Fame online is often {ephemeral}: a video that millions watch on Monday may be forgotten by Friday.
entry.etym: From Greek ephemeros, “lasting only a day”: epi (for) + hemera (day).

mn.cue: a snowman in the noon sun
mn.text: Pip’s snowman stood proud at breakfast; by lunch it was a puddle and a carrot. Its life was {ephemeral}.

scene.alt: A snowman melts into a puddle in the hot sun while a boy in a scarf looks on, dismayed.

entry.def: lasting only a short time; staying only briefly
entry.ex: The {transient} storm soaked the picnic and moved on within ten minutes.
entry.ctx: Most of the town’s summer crowd is {transient}: visitors arrive in June, rent a cottage for a week or two and are gone by September.
entry.etym: From Latin transire, “to go across, to pass by”: trans (across) + ire (to go).
entry.note: As a noun, a transient is a person who is only passing through a place.

mn.text: The express train roars through the mountain valley, toots once and is gone. Its visit is {transient}: here for a moment, then away.

scene.alt: A boy waves as a train speeds through a mountain valley without stopping.

entry.def: passing very quickly
entry.ex: Kai caught a {fleeting} glimpse of the fox before it vanished into the trees.
entry.ctx: The sun appeared for only a {fleeting} moment between the clouds, just long enough for the hikers to see the valley below.
entry.etym: From the old verb fleet, “to glide away swiftly.”

mn.cue: FLEE-ting: it FLEES before you look
mn.text: Kai turns, and the fox flees into the trees: one flash of orange tail, and it is gone. His look at it was {fleeting}.

scene.alt: A boy points as a fox dashes away into the forest.

entry.def: not permanent; lasting only for a time
entry.ex: Her disappointment was {transitory}; by dinner she was laughing again.
entry.ctx: The town’s gold-rush wealth proved {transitory}: within ten years the mines were empty and most of the grand hotels had closed.
entry.etym: From Latin transitorius, “passing,” from transire, “to go across.”

mn.cue: TRANSIT-ory: life at a bus stop
mn.text: Nobody stays long at a bus stop: people wait a few minutes, then ride away in transit. A stay that short is {transitory}.

scene.alt: People hurry onto a bus that is about to leave the bus stop.

entry.def: quickly fading from sight or memory
entry.ex: The {evanescent} glow of the fireflies flickered across the meadow.
entry.ctx: Like breath on a cold window, her smile was {evanescent}: it appeared for an instant and faded before anyone could be sure they had seen it.
entry.etym: From Latin evanescere, “to vanish”: e (out) + vanescere (to fade away), from vanus, empty.

mn.cue: e-VANISH-ent: blink, and it is gone
mn.text: Each firefly glows for a moment, then vanishes into the dark before Zoe can point to it. Their light is {evanescent}.

scene.alt: At night a girl with a jar looks for fireflies whose glows fade in and out.

entry.def: lasting a long time
entry.ex: Their {enduring} friendship began in kindergarten and is still going strong.
entry.ctx: Many songs are popular for a single summer, but this lullaby has proved {enduring}: parents have sung it to their babies for more than two hundred years.
entry.etym: From Latin indurare, “to make hard,” from durus, hard, the root of durable.

mn.text: The great stone pyramid has stood through thousands of years of sun and sandstorms, and visitors still come to see it. It is {enduring}.

scene.alt: An old professor points to a great stone pyramid that has stood for thousands of years.

entry.def: never ending or changing; constant
entry.ex: The {perpetual} drip of the leaky faucet kept Felix awake all night.
entry.ctx: Living beside the waterfall meant {perpetual} noise: day and night, summer and winter, the roar never stopped.
entry.etym: From Latin perpetuus, “continuing throughout.”

mn.cue: per-PET-ual: a PET whose tail never stops
mn.text: Biscuit the dog wags his tail morning, noon and night; even in his sleep it thumps. His wagging is {perpetual}.

labels.text: per-PET-ual: a PET that never stops

scene.alt: A happy dog wags its tail nonstop while its owner laughs.

entry.def: impossible to erase, remove or forget
entry.ex: Theo drew on the wall with {indelible} marker, and no amount of scrubbing helped.
entry.ctx: Meeting the astronauts left an {indelible} impression on Maya; twenty years later, she could still recall every word they said.
entry.etym: From Latin indelebilis: in (not) + delere (to wipe out), the root of delete.

mn.text: Theo’s marker drawing won’t wash off the wall, no matter how hard Dad scrubs: you can’t delete it. The ink is {indelible}.

scene.alt: A dad scrubs hard at marker on the wall while his toddler proudly holds up the marker.

entry.def: able or likely to change
entry.ex: Spring weather is {mutable}: sunshine at noon, hail by three.
entry.ctx: The rules of the backyard game proved {mutable}; each new player who joined suggested a change, and soon nobody remembered how it had started.
entry.etym: From Latin mutabilis, from mutare, “to change.”

mn.text: The octopus turns red, then blue, then sandy brown to match whatever it touches. A creature that changes that easily is {mutable}.

scene.alt: An octopus changes from red to blue.

entry.def: never changing; unable to be changed
entry.ex: For Grandma, Sunday dinner at five o’clock was an {immutable} rule.
entry.ctx: Fashions and slang change every few years, but some things are {immutable}: the sun still rises in the east, just as it did a thousand years ago.
entry.etym: From Latin immutabilis: im (not) + mutabilis (changeable).

mn.text: Sun, snow, rain or wind, the old stone statue in the square keeps the very same pose year after year. It is {immutable}.

scene.alt: A stone statue stands unchanged while sun, snow and rain come and go around it.

blocks.html: ephemeral things don't last, but that does not make them unimportant. indelible ink cannot be erased; an indelible memory cannot be forgotten.

flavor

blocks.cap: Words for time: how long something lasts, and how.

blocks.html: Short-lived does not mean unimportant: an ephemeral moment (a sunset, a first snowfall) can leave an indelible memory. And mutable/immutable are about change, not time: an immutable law could be brand-new.

blocks.html: There are many ways to make things better. You can ease a pain without curing it, fix a mistake completely, add a finishing touch to something already good, or bring something tired back to life. Each of these ten verbs names one of those ways, and test passages love to ask which one fits.

Make a bad thing less bad: ameliorate, alleviate, mitigate. Fix it: remedy, rectify. Make a good thing better: enhance, refine, bolster (support). Bring back the life: rejuvenate (make young again), revive (make live again).

entry.def: to make a bad situation better
entry.ex: New streetlights helped {ameliorate} the problem of dark, lonely corners.
entry.ctx: The new bus route did not end the town’s traffic problem, but it did {ameliorate} it: commutes that once took an hour now took forty minutes.
entry.etym: From Latin melior, “better,” by way of French améliorer, “to improve.”

mn.cue: A MEAL-iorate: a MEAL makes it better
mn.text: Grandpa Gus is cold, tired and cranky after shoveling, until Nell brings him a hot bowl of soup. A good meal can {ameliorate} a gloomy afternoon.

scene.alt: A woman brings hot soup to a cold grandfather on a snowy bench, and he brightens up.

entry.def: to make pain or trouble easier to bear
entry.ex: An extra checkout lane helped {alleviate} the long lines at the store.
entry.ctx: The volunteers could not end the drought, but they could {alleviate} its effects: they trucked in fresh water and shared it with every farm in the valley.
entry.etym: From Latin alleviare, “to lighten”: ad (to) + levis (light).

mn.text: Kai staggers under a heavy crate until Sven lifts it onto his own broad shoulders. Taking some of the weight is a way to {alleviate} a burden.

scene.alt: A big man lifts a heavy crate off a tired boy’s hands.

entry.def: to make less severe or harmful
entry.ex: Planting trees along the river helped {mitigate} the spring floods.
entry.ctx: The hikers could not stop the storm, but they could {mitigate} its dangers: they waited it out in a sturdy shelter and kept their extra clothes dry.
entry.etym: From Latin mitigare, “to soften,” from mitis, mild, gentle.
entry.note: Don’t confuse mitigate (to lessen) with militate (to work against: “The rain militated against a picnic”).

mn.cue: MITT-igate: a big MITT softens the blow
mn.text: A fast ball stings a bare hand, but a thick padded mitt softens the catch. The mitt helps {mitigate} the sting.

scene.alt: A player reaches up with a big padded mitt to catch a fast ball.

entry.def: to fix or correct something that is wrong
entry.ex: The mechanic {remedied} the squeak with a single drop of oil.
entry.ctx: When the library learned that its ramp was too steep for wheelchairs, it moved quickly to {remedy} the problem, building a gentler ramp within a month.
entry.etym: From Latin remedium, “a cure,” from mederi, “to heal,” the root of medical.
entry.note: Remedy is also a noun: a cure or a fix (“a remedy for boredom”).

mn.text: The wagon wheel squeaks and wobbles until Grandpa Gus mends it with a wrench and a drop of oil. To mend what’s wrong is to {remedy} it.

scene.alt: A grandfather kneels to fix a wagon wheel with a wrench while a girl cheers.

entry.def: to put right; to correct
entry.ex: The store {rectified} its mistake by refunding the extra charge.
entry.ctx: The newspaper had printed the wrong date for the concert, so the next morning it {rectified} the error with a notice on the front page.
entry.etym: From Latin rectificare, “to make right”: rectus (straight, right) + facere (to make).

mn.text: The family photo hangs crooked, so Priya nudges it until every corner is square, like a rectangle. To set something straight is to {rectify} it.

scene.alt: A woman straightens a crooked picture frame on the wall.

entry.def: to improve the quality, value or appeal of
entry.ex: A pinch of salt will {enhance} the sweetness of the caramel.
entry.ctx: The old photographs were faded and blurry, so the museum used careful scanning to {enhance} them; now visitors can read the shop signs in the background.
entry.etym: From Old French enhaucier, “to raise,” based on Latin altus, high.

mn.cue: en-HANS: Hans adds the cherry on top
mn.text: The sundae is already good, but Hans adds whipped cream and a cherry on top. Little touches like that {enhance} it.

scene.alt: A shopkeeper named Hans holds up an ice cream with a cherry on top for a delighted girl.

entry.def: to support or strengthen
entry.ex: Winning the first game {bolstered} the team’s confidence.
entry.ctx: Her argument was weak on its own, so she {bolstered} it with three surveys and a letter from the town engineer.
entry.etym: From bolster, an old word for a long, firm pillow used to prop things up.

mn.cue: a BOLSTER is a propping PILLOW
mn.text: Granny Mae keeps slumping on the bed until Rosa props her up with a long, firm pillow called a bolster. To prop up and support something is to {bolster} it.

scene.alt: A teenager props her grandmother up in bed with a big firm pillow.

entry.def: to make young, fresh or lively again
entry.ex: A week at the lake {rejuvenated} the whole family.
entry.ctx: The tired old park was {rejuvenated} by the neighbors’ hard work: they planted flowers, painted the benches and fixed the fountain.
entry.etym: From re (again) + Latin juvenis (young), the root of juvenile.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus borrows Pip’s skateboard and rolls down the sidewalk laughing like a ten-year-old. The ride seems to {rejuvenate} him.

scene.alt: A grandfather in a helmet rides a skateboard, laughing like a kid, as his grandson cheers.

entry.def: to bring back to life, strength or use
entry.ex: A bucket of water {revived} the wilted tomato plants.
entry.ctx: The old folk dance had nearly been forgotten, but a group of students {revived} it, learning the steps from their grandparents and performing it at the spring fair.
entry.etym: From Latin revivere, “to live again”: re (again) + vivere (to live).

mn.text: The droopy flowers perk right up after Ivy gives them a long drink: they live again! Water can {revive} a wilted plant.

scene.alt: A girl waters a drooping flower, and it stands up tall and bright again.

entry.def: to improve by making small changes; also, to purify
entry.ex: Lila {refined} her essay through five careful drafts.
entry.ctx: The first robot could barely roll across the floor, but the team kept {refining} the design, adjusting a gear here and a sensor there, until it won the contest.
entry.etym: From re (again) + fine in its old sense, “to make pure.”

mn.text: Dev’s robot rolls, but it wobbles. He tightens one gear, then another, making it a little finer each time. Little by little, he will {refine} it.

scene.alt: A teen kneels and adjusts a small robot with a wrench, improving it bit by bit.

blocks.html: Groups agree and disagree in many different ways. A vote can be unanimous or face a lone dissent; a family can live in accord or in discord; a quarrel can be polite or acrimonious. Several of these words are built from the same Latin pieces: sent (feel, think), cord (heart) and con- (together) against dis- (apart).

Coming together: consensus (general agreement), unanimous (everyone agrees), concur (to agree), accord (harmony), coalesce (to merge into one). Pulling apart: dissent (disagreement with the majority), discord (lack of harmony), acrimonious (bitter), divisive (splitting people), controversy (a long public dispute).

entry.def: general agreement among a group
entry.ex: After a long debate, the club reached a {consensus}: pizza on Fridays.
entry.ctx: The scientists had argued for years, but a {consensus} slowly formed: nearly all of them came to accept that the bones belonged to a new species.
entry.etym: From Latin consensus, “agreement,” from consentire: con (together) + sentire (to feel, to think).
entry.note: Consensus already means general agreement, so “general consensus” says the same thing twice.

mn.cue: CON-SENSE-us: we all SENSE the same
mn.text: The class votes on a name for the new bunny, and almost every hand goes up for “Clover.” When nearly everyone senses the same, the group has a {consensus}.

scene.alt: Children raise their hands together to agree on a name for the class bunny.

entry.def: agreed on by everyone
entry.ex: The vote was {unanimous}: all twelve players wanted the blue jerseys.
entry.ctx: Usually the judges argue for hours, but this year their decision was {unanimous}; every one of them chose the same cherry pie as the winner.
entry.etym: From Latin unanimus, “of one mind”: unus (one) + animus (mind).

mn.text: Nana Mae, Nana Lou and Grandpa Gus judge the pie contest, and all three hold up a perfect 10 for the cherry pie. Every vote the same: the decision is {unanimous}.

scene.alt: Three grandparent judges all hold up a score of 10 for a cherry pie.

entry.def: to agree
entry.ex: Both coaches {concurred} that the game should wait until the storm passed.
entry.ctx: I thought the movie was far too long, and my sister {concurred}; she had fallen asleep twice before the ending.
entry.etym: From Latin concurrere, “to run together”: con (together) + currere (to run).

mn.text: Two dogs spot the same ball and race for it side by side, of one mind. When two people’s thoughts run together like that, they {concur}.

scene.alt: Two dogs run side by side toward the same ball on the beach.

entry.def: agreement; harmony
entry.ex: The neighbors reached an {accord} about where to build the shared fence.
entry.ctx: For years the two villages quarreled over the river, but the new {accord} let each draw water on alternate days, and the arguments finally stopped.
entry.etym: From Latin ad (to) + cor, cordis (heart): hearts brought together.
entry.note: Of your own accord means freely, without being asked: “She cleaned her room of her own accord.”

mn.text: Lin plays three notes at once on the piano, and they sound lovely together: a chord. People who get along in harmony like that are in {accord}.

scene.alt: A woman plays a pleasant chord on the piano while a couple listens happily.

entry.def: to come together to form one whole
entry.ex: Tiny raindrops {coalesced} into one fat drop at the edge of the roof.
entry.ctx: At first the volunteers worked in scattered groups, but over the summer they {coalesced} into one well-organized team with a single plan.
entry.etym: From Latin coalescere, “to grow together”: co (together) + alescere (to grow up).

mn.text: Dozens of little fish swim closer and closer until they move like one big fish. When separate parts join into a single whole, they {coalesce}.

scene.alt: Many small fish swim close together to form one big fish shape, and two more join them.

entry.def: disagreement with an official or majority view
entry.ex: Only one hand went up in {dissent} when the class voted for the zoo trip.
entry.ctx: The proposal passed easily, but not without {dissent}: two members of the committee wrote a long letter explaining why they thought it was a mistake.
entry.etym: From Latin dissentire, “to differ in feeling”: dis (apart) + sentire (to feel, to think).
entry.note: Dissent (disagreement) sounds just like descent (a way down).

mn.cue: DIS-SENT: one vote SENT the other way
mn.text: Every hand goes up for the new rule except Marcus’s; he sends his vote the other way and says why. His “no” is a {dissent}.

scene.alt: At a meeting, three people raise their hands in favor while one man crosses his arms and votes no.

entry.def: disagreement; a lack of harmony
entry.ex: A quarrel over the last pancake brought {discord} to the breakfast table.
entry.ctx: The band sounded wonderful in rehearsal, but {discord} among its members, who argued over every song, broke it up before its first concert.
entry.etym: From Latin discordia, from discors, “disagreeing”: dis (apart) + cor (heart).

mn.text: Kai strums one song on the guitar while Lila plays a different one on the violin, and the dog howls. Sounds that clash, like people who clash, are in {discord}.

scene.alt: A boy with a guitar and a girl with a violin play different tunes while a dog howls between them.

entry.def: angry and bitter in tone
entry.ex: The {acrimonious} argument over the parking space lasted twenty minutes.
entry.ctx: What began as a friendly debate about the town fountain turned {acrimonious}: neighbors shouted, slammed doors and stopped speaking to each other for weeks.
entry.etym: From acrimony, Latin acrimonia, “sharpness,” from acer, sharp, sour.

mn.cue: ACRI = ACID: a sour, bitter fight
mn.text: The two lemonade sellers argue over the best corner until their words turn as sour as acid. Their quarrel is {acrimonious}.

scene.alt: Two lemonade sellers point and shout bitterly at each other.

entry.def: causing disagreement or splitting people into sides
entry.ex: Pineapple on pizza is a surprisingly {divisive} topic in our family.
entry.ctx: The plan to close the old library proved {divisive}, splitting the town into two angry camps that argued about it at every meeting.
entry.etym: From Latin divisus, “divided,” from dividere, “to divide.”

mn.text: Put a pineapple pizza on the table, and the family splits in two: half cheer, half groan. A topic that divides people is {divisive}.

scene.alt: A pineapple pizza splits a table: one man cheers, a woman recoils.

entry.def: a long public disagreement
entry.ex: The new school mascot stirred up a {controversy} on the letters page of the local paper.
entry.ctx: The painting caused a {controversy} when it was unveiled: some critics called it a masterpiece, others called it a mess, and the arguments filled the papers for months.
entry.etym: From Latin controversia, “a dispute,” from controversus, “turned against”: contra (against) + versus (turned).

mn.text: At the museum, half the crowd loves the new painting and half calls it a mess, and the argument goes on for weeks in public. Views turned against each other make a {controversy}.

scene.alt: Two museum visitors hold up opposite signs, love and mess, on either side of a new painting.

blocks.html: consensus means general agreement, so "general consensus" says it twice. dissent (disagreement) is not descent (going down).

blocks.html: Two more are built the same way: unanimous is un (one) + anim (mind): of one mind. Concur is con (together) + cur (run): minds that run together.
Consensus already means general agreement, so “general consensus” is padding; just say consensus. And dissent (disagreement) is not descent (a way down): dis + sent, to feel apart.

blocks.html: Writers often need to say how much of something there is, and “a lot” and “not much” wear out fast. This topic gives you five ways to say plenty and five ways to say too little, from the everyday (abundant, scant) to the formal (plethora, paucity).

Plenty: abundant (more than enough), copious (in large amounts), myriad (countless), plethora (too many), profuse (pouring out). Too little: sparse (thinly scattered), scant (barely enough), meager (skimpy), dearth (a shortage), paucity (a very small amount).

entry.def: existing in large amounts; more than enough
entry.ex: Blackberries were {abundant} along the creek that summer.
entry.ctx: Water is scarce in the desert, but in the rain forest it is {abundant}: it drips from the leaves, fills the rivers and soaks the ground every afternoon.
entry.etym: From Latin abundare, “to overflow,” literally to flow over in waves: ab (off) + unda (wave).

mn.text: The baker made so many buns that they cover every shelf and table, and he does a happy bun dance. Buns are {abundant}.

scene.alt: A baker dances among piles and piles of fresh buns.

entry.def: plentiful; in large amounts
entry.ex: Sami took {copious} notes on the museum tour, filling half his notebook.
entry.ctx: The garden needed little watering that year, thanks to {copious} rain that fell almost every afternoon from April through June.
entry.etym: From Latin copiosus, from copia, “plenty,” as in cornucopia, the horn of plenty.

mn.text: Sami copies down every word the guide says, page after page after page. His notes are {copious}.

scene.alt: A boy scribbles page after page of notes while a professor keeps talking.

entry.def: countless; extremely many
entry.ex: On a clear night in the desert, {myriad} stars fill the sky.
entry.ctx: The coral reef was home to {myriad} creatures: bright fish, waving sea fans, darting shrimp and more kinds of life than the divers could count.
entry.etym: From Greek myrias, “ten thousand,” which came to mean a number too great to count.
entry.note: Myriad works as an adjective (myriad stars) or a noun (a myriad of stars); both are standard.

mn.text: Lila tries to count the stars above the campsite and gives up after ten thousand. There are {myriad} stars.

scene.alt: A girl sits under the night sky trying to count countless stars.

entry.def: too many; a great excess
entry.ex: The new phone came with a {plethora} of settings that no one ever used.
entry.ctx: Faced with a {plethora} of choices, forty kinds of cereal lining one long aisle, Grandpa simply gave up and went home with oatmeal.
entry.etym: From Greek plethore, “fullness,” from plethein, “to be full.”

mn.text: Theo asked for one balloon and got sixty, so many that his toes leave the ground. Sixty is a {plethora} of balloons.

scene.alt: A toddler holding far too many balloons floats off the ground while his mother reaches for him.

entry.note: Careful writers use plethora for too many, an excess; in everyday speech it often just means a lot.

entry.def: pouring out in great amounts
entry.ex: The roses grew in {profuse} clusters, spilling over the fence onto the sidewalk.
entry.ctx: Embarrassed that he had forgotten her birthday, Dev was {profuse} in his apologies; he said sorry a dozen times and baked her a cake the next morning.
entry.etym: From Latin profusus, “poured out,” from profundere: pro (forth) + fundere (to pour).

mn.text: Dev knocks over the juice, and apologies pour out of him: “Sorry! So sorry! I’m so, so sorry!” His apologies are {profuse}.

cast.say: Sorry! So sorry! So, so sorry!

scene.alt: A teen who spilled juice pours out apologies while his friend laughs.

entry.def: thinly scattered; few and far between
entry.ex: The desert’s {sparse} bushes offered little shade.
entry.ctx: The audience was {sparse}: only a dozen people sat scattered across a theater built for five hundred.
entry.etym: From Latin sparsus, “scattered,” from spargere, “to scatter.”

mn.text: On the night of the big storm, nearly every seat at Jonah’s concert is spare; just two fans sit far apart. The crowd is {sparse}.

scene.alt: A teen sings on stage to an almost empty theater, with only two fans far apart.

entry.def: barely enough; very little
entry.ex: The recipe calls for a {scant} teaspoon of salt.
entry.ctx: With {scant} evidence and no witnesses, the detective had little choice but to close the file and wait for new clues.
entry.etym: From Old Norse skamt, “short.”

mn.text: Zoe shakes the cereal box and gets five flakes and some dust. You can’t call that breakfast: the cereal is {scant}.

scene.alt: A girl shakes an almost empty cereal box over her bowl and gets only a few flakes.

entry.def: too small in amount or quality; skimpy
entry.ex: The hikers shared a {meager} lunch of two pears and a granola bar.
entry.ctx: Her first paycheck was {meager}, barely enough for bus fare and lunches, but she was proud of every dollar she had earned.
entry.etym: From Old French maigre, “thin,” from Latin macer, thin.
entry.note: The British spelling is meagre.

mn.text: The cat stares at the three tiny crumbs in its bowl and growls, “Me? Grrr! That’s all?” Its dinner is {meager}.

scene.alt: A cat glares and growls at a nearly empty food bowl.

entry.def: a lack or shortage
entry.ex: There is a {dearth} of good pizza places in our small town.
entry.ctx: Because of a {dearth} of rain, the river shrank to a trickle, and the farmers had to haul water to their fields in buckets.
entry.etym: From Middle English derthe, from dear in its old sense of “costly”: when something runs short, it grows dear.

mn.text: No rain for months, and the field is nothing but dry, cracked earth. The dry earth shows a {dearth} of rain.

scene.alt: Under a blazing sun, a farmer holds up an empty bucket beside wilted plants.

entry.def: a very small amount; scarcity
entry.ex: The report’s {paucity} of facts made it hard to believe.
entry.ctx: Scientists know little about the giant deep-sea squid because of a {paucity} of evidence: only a handful have ever been photographed alive.
entry.etym: From Latin paucitas, from paucus, “few.”

mn.text: Paw City built a giant dog park, and on opening day just one dog showed up. With so few paws, the park suffers a {paucity} of dogs.

scene.alt: A lonely dog sits by itself in a big, empty dog park.

blocks.html: plethora first meant too many; today it often means a great many. myriad can be an adjective (myriad stars) or a noun (a myriad of stars).

blocks.html: Plethora once meant only too many; today it often just means a great many, though careful writers keep a hint of excess. Myriad can be an adjective (myriad stars) or a noun (a myriad of stars).
