blocks.html: Three Latin roots run through this topic. cred means believe (you know it from credit and incredible), fid means trust or faith (as in confident), and ver means true (as in very, which first meant “truly”). Spot one of them, and you have a strong clue to the meaning.
cred = believe: credible, incredulous, credulous, credence. fid = trust: fidelity, confidant, diffident. ver = true: veracity, verify, verdict.
Watch the endings: -ible (able to be) makes credible, “able to be believed”; -ulous (inclined to) makes credulous, “inclined to believe,” too easily.

entry.def: believable; worthy of trust
entry.ex: Dev’s excuse was hardly {credible}: a dog ate his homework, and he has no dog.
entry.ctx: The story seemed far-fetched at first, but it became {credible} once three hikers who had never met described the same strange lights over the lake.
entry.etym: From Latin credibilis, from credere, “to believe.”

mn.cue: CRED-ible: can you give it CREDIT?
mn.text: Dev says the dog ate his homework, but Dev has no dog. His teacher gives the story no credit at all: it isn’t {credible}.

scene.alt: A boy claims his dog ate his homework while his teacher, who knows he has no dog, doubts him.

entry.def: unwilling or unable to believe something
entry.ex: Maya gave an {incredulous} laugh when her little brother said he had cleaned his room.
entry.ctx: When the waiter announced that their meal was free, the diners were {incredulous}; they asked him three times whether he was joking.
entry.etym: From Latin incredulus: in (not) + credulus (believing).
entry.note: A story can be incredible (hard to believe); the person hearing it is incredulous (not believing).

mn.text: Kai says he cleaned his room, but Maya can see socks on the floor and books on the bed. Her raised eyebrows are {incredulous}.

scene.alt: A boy claims his messy room is clean while his sister stares in disbelief.

entry.def: too ready to believe things; easily fooled
entry.ex: The {credulous} tourist paid ten dollars for a “real” moon rock.
entry.ctx: Only the most {credulous} readers believed the website’s claim that a single bean could make a person fly.
entry.etym: From Latin credulus, “trusting,” from credere, “to believe.”

mn.text: Rex sells young Lou a “flying potion,” and Lou pays him on the spot without a single question. Lou believes anything: he is {credulous}.

scene.alt: A sneaky seller offers a so-called flying potion to a starry-eyed young man who hands over his coins.

entry.def: belief or acceptance that something is true
entry.ex: Nobody gave much {credence} to the rumor that school would close for a month.
entry.ctx: At first the scientists gave little {credence} to the farmer’s report of a strange new bird, but his clear photographs soon changed their minds.
entry.etym: From Latin credentia, from credere, “to believe.”
entry.note: We usually give or lend credence: “Her careful notes lent credence to her story.”

mn.cue: CRED-ence: give it CREDIT, believe it
mn.text: Nobody believed Ivy’s story about a fox family in the park, until she showed her photos. The pictures lend {credence} to her story.

scene.alt: A girl holds up her camera to prove her fox story, and her grandfather is convinced.

entry.def: faithfulness and loyalty; also, accuracy
entry.ex: The old dog’s {fidelity} was famous: he waited at the gate every afternoon for his boy.
entry.ctx: The translation was praised for its {fidelity}: it kept not only every meaning of the original poem but even its rhythm and rhymes.
entry.etym: From Latin fidelitas, from fidelis, “faithful,” from fides, faith.
entry.note: High-fidelity (hi-fi) sound is sound that is faithful to the original.

mn.cue: FIDO-lity: loyal as a dog named FIDO
mn.text: Every afternoon at three, Fido waits at the gate for Sami to come home from school, rain or shine. Fido’s {fidelity} never wavers.

scene.alt: A loyal dog waits at the garden gate as his boy runs home from school.

entry.def: a trusted friend you can share secrets with
entry.ex: Grandpa was Rosa’s {confidant}; she told him things she told no one else.
entry.ctx: The young queen trusted few people at court, but her old nurse was her {confidant}, the one person who heard all her worries and never repeated a word.
entry.etym: From French confident, from Latin confidere, “to trust fully”: con (thoroughly) + fidere (to trust).
entry.note: A confidant (a person you trust; sometimes spelled confidante for a woman) is not confident (sure of yourself).

mn.cue: CONFIDE-ANT: the one you CONFIDE in
mn.text: Rosa confides her biggest worries to Grandpa Gus on the park bench, and he never tells a soul. The person you confide in is your {confidant}.

scene.alt: A teenager whispers a worry to her grandfather on a bench by the river.

entry.def: shy and lacking confidence in oneself
entry.ex: The {diffident} new student spoke so softly that the teacher asked her to repeat her name.
entry.ctx: Though she was the best singer in the choir, Lin was {diffident} about her talent and always asked someone else to take the solo.
entry.etym: From Latin diffidere, “to distrust”: dis (not) + fidere (to trust); a diffident person does not trust herself.

mn.text: Lin sings beautifully, but she hides behind the curtain and lets someone else take the solo. She is the opposite of confident: {diffident}.

scene.alt: A shy woman hides her face instead of stepping up to the microphone while a friend urges her on.

entry.def: truthfulness; accuracy
entry.ex: No one doubted the {veracity} of Nana’s story; she had the photos to prove it.
entry.ctx: The reporter checked every quotation with the person who had said it, because the {veracity} of her article mattered more to her than being first.
entry.etym: From Latin verax, “truthful,” from verus, true.
entry.note: Don’t confuse veracity (truthfulness) with voracity (a huge appetite).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus swears he caught a fish as long as his arm, and this time the photo proves every word. The {veracity} of his story is beyond doubt.

scene.alt: A grandfather holds up a huge fish while a woman snaps a photo to prove his story is true.

entry.def: to check or prove that something is true
entry.ex: Please {verify} your address before you click send.
entry.ctx: The museum would not display the old letter until experts could {verify} that it had been written in 1776, not copied a century later.
entry.etym: From Latin verificare, “to make true,” from verus, true.

mn.cue: VER-ify: make sure it’s VERY true
mn.text: Before she buys the old coin, Ada studies it under her magnifying glass, front and back. She wants to {verify} that it is real gold.

scene.alt: A woman examines a gold coin through a magnifying glass to check that it is real.

entry.def: a decision or judgment, especially a jury’s
entry.ex: After one bite, Grandpa gave his {verdict}: the best chili he had ever tasted.
entry.ctx: After two days of listening to witnesses, the jury returned its {verdict}: not guilty on every charge.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin veredictum, “truly said”: vere (truly) + dictum (said).

mn.text: In the case of the missing cake, the jury says what it truly believes: “Not guilty!” The dog wags happily at the {verdict}.

scene.alt: In a courtroom a juror announces “Not guilty!” and the dog on trial wags happily.

blocks.html: Honesty comes in flavors. A candid friend admits mistakes; a frank one tells you what you would rather not hear; a sincere one means every word. Dishonesty has flavors too: the devious person sneaks around the rules, the duplicitous one plays both sides, and the disingenuous one pretends to be more innocent than he is.

Honest: candid (open), frank (blunt), sincere (meant), forthright (speaks up directly), integrity (honesty all the way through), guileless (innocent, no tricks). Dishonest: deceitful (lying), devious (sneaky), duplicitous (two-faced), disingenuous (falsely innocent).

entry.def: open and honest in what one says
entry.ex: In a {candid} interview, the coach admitted the team had played badly.
entry.ctx: Rather than make excuses, Pip was {candid}: he told his mother exactly how the vase had broken and offered to pay for a new one from his allowance.
entry.etym: From Latin candidus, “white, pure,” related to candle: a candid answer has nothing hidden in the shadows.
entry.note: A candid photo is an unposed one, taken without the subject getting ready.

mn.cue: CAN + DID: I CAN tell what I DID
mn.text: “I did it. I broke the vase,” says Pip, before anyone even asks. He can tell what he did: he is {candid}.

cast.say: I did it. I broke the vase.

scene.alt: A boy openly admits to his surprised mother that he broke the vase.

entry.def: direct and honest, even when it is uncomfortable
entry.ex: Dad was {frank} with us: the car needed repairs, and the trip would have to wait.
entry.ctx: Most guests politely praised the soup, but Grandma was {frank}: she said it needed salt, pepper and about an hour more on the stove.
entry.etym: From Old French franc, “free”: a frank speaker feels free to say what she thinks.

mn.text: Nana Lou tastes the soup and gives it to you straight as a plank: “Needs salt. Lots of salt.” No sugarcoating: she is {frank}.

scene.alt: A grandmother tastes the cook’s soup and bluntly says it needs salt.

entry.def: meaning what one says; free of pretense
entry.ex: Her apology was {sincere}; she had tears in her eyes.
entry.ctx: Unlike the salesman’s rehearsed compliments, the boy’s thank-you note was {sincere}: he had written it himself, misspellings and all, because he loved the gift.
entry.etym: From Latin sincerus, “pure, clean, whole.”

mn.cue: sin-SEER: you can SEE he means it
mn.text: Theo hands Mom a crumpled crayon card that says “I LUV U,” and she can see he means every word. His card is {sincere}.

labels.text: sin-SEER: you SEE he means it

scene.alt: A toddler hands his kneeling mother a homemade card, and she is moved.

entry.def: direct and outspoken; saying plainly what one thinks
entry.ex: The {forthright} referee explained exactly why the goal did not count.
entry.ctx: Instead of hinting that the budget was a problem, the treasurer was {forthright}: she stood up at the meeting and said the club would run out of money by June.
entry.etym: From Old English forthriht, “straight forward”: forth (forward) + riht (straight).

mn.cue: FORTH-RIGHT: steps FORTH, says it RIGHT
mn.text: When Rex cuts into the ticket line, Maya steps forth and says it right out: “That’s not fair. The line starts back there.” She is {forthright}.

scene.alt: A teen girl steps forward and tells a line-cutter plainly to go to the back.

entry.def: the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles
entry.ex: A person of {integrity} keeps a promise even when no one would ever find out.
entry.ctx: When the cashier handed her twenty dollars too much in change, Rosa showed her {integrity}: she walked back across the parking lot to return it.
entry.etym: From Latin integritas, “wholeness,” from integer, whole: the same word as the integer of math.

mn.text: Like a whole number, Rosa is honest all the way through: she finds a wallet full of cash and returns every dollar to its owner. She has {integrity}.

scene.alt: A teenager returns a lost wallet to its delighted owner on a city street.

entry.def: trying to make others believe what is false
entry.ex: The {deceitful} player pretended to be hurt so the referee would call a foul.
entry.ctx: The ad looked friendly, but it was {deceitful}: tiny print at the bottom revealed that the “free” game cost ten dollars a month.
entry.etym: From deceit, Old French deceite, from Latin decipere, “to catch, to trap.”

mn.cue: de-SEE-tful: you SEE what isn’t there
mn.text: Rex paints a plain rock gold and tells the tourists it is pirate treasure. Making people see what isn’t there is {deceitful}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man in a pirate hat paints a rock gold and claims it is real treasure.

entry.def: sly and tricky in getting one’s way
entry.ex: The cat came up with a {devious} plan to reach the fish tank.
entry.ctx: Rather than ask for a later bedtime, the {devious} twins quietly set every clock in the house back an hour.
entry.etym: From Latin devius, “off the road”: de (away from) + via (way).

mn.text: Instead of asking for a later bedtime, Pip and Ivy take the sneaky road: they tiptoe in and turn the clock back an hour. That trick is {devious}.

scene.alt: Two sneaky kids tiptoe to the bedroom clock and turn it back.

entry.def: two-faced; saying one thing and doing another
entry.ex: The {duplicitous} spy smiled at both sides while secretly working for neither.
entry.ctx: The knight seemed loyal to the king, but he was {duplicitous}: by day he guarded the castle, and by night he sent messages to the king’s enemies.
entry.etym: From duplicity, Latin duplicitas, “doubleness,” from duplex, double.

mn.text: Rex smiles at the queen, “I’m your loyal knight!”, then turns around and whispers plans to the dragon. Two faces, like a duplicate: he is {duplicitous}.

scene.alt: The same knight appears twice: bowing loyally to the queen, and whispering plans to a dragon.

entry.def: insincere; pretending to be more innocent or less informed than one is
entry.ex: It was {disingenuous} of Dev to ask “What cookies?” with chocolate on his chin.
entry.ctx: The company’s claim that it had “no idea” its toys were breaking was {disingenuous}; its own engineers had warned about the problem a year earlier.
entry.etym: From dis (not) + ingenuous, “innocent, frank,” from Latin ingenuus, “freeborn, noble.”
entry.note: Disingenuous is not the opposite of ingenious (clever); it is the opposite of ingenuous (innocent, frank).

mn.text: “What cookies?” asks Dev, wide-eyed, with chocolate all over his chin and an empty jar behind him. Pretending to be innocent like that is {disingenuous}.

scene.alt: A boy with crumbs on his face shrugs innocently beside an empty cookie jar while his mother frowns.

entry.def: innocent and without tricks; open and honest
entry.ex: The puppy’s {guileless} eyes made it impossible to stay angry.
entry.ctx: Unlike the sly older players, the new girl was {guileless}: she told everyone her strategy before the game and was surprised when they used it against her.
entry.etym: From guile, “sly trickery,” + -less: without tricks.

mn.text: Theo plays cards holding his hand face out so everyone can see it: no tricks, no secrets, no bluffing. He is {guileless}.

scene.alt: A toddler happily shows everyone his cards while his grandfather laughs.

blocks.html: disingenuous is not the opposite of ingenious; it means insincere, often pretending innocence. candid means open and honest, as in a candid answer or a candid (unposed) photo.

head: honest word
what it adds
rows: means what is said; no pretending
no tricks at all, sometimes too trusting
blocks.cap: Shades of honesty.

blocks.html: Three look-alikes: ingenious means clever; ingenuous means innocent and frank; disingenuous means falsely innocent. A disingenuous person pretends to be ingenuous.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: How much do you want to do something? English has a whole scale of words for it, from the burning eagerness of an ardent fan to the foot-dragging of a reluctant helper. Several of the eager words come from Latin words for heat: ardent from “burn,” fervent from “boil.”

Eager: zealous (devoted to a cause), ardent and fervent (burning, glowing with feeling), avid (eager for more), keen (eager; also sharp), alacrity (cheerful speed, a noun). Unwilling: reluctant (hesitant), loath (unwilling), averse (opposed, turned away), grudging (given unwillingly).

entry.def: full of eager devotion to a cause or task
entry.ex: The {zealous} volunteers cleaned the whole beach before breakfast.
entry.ctx: Most of the club recycled when it was convenient, but Omar was {zealous} about it: he sorted every scrap, rinsed every can and reminded everyone else to do the same.
entry.etym: From zeal, from Greek zelos, “eagerness, fervor.”

mn.cue: ZEAL-ous: full of ZEAL, A to Z
mn.text: Omar sorts every can, bottle and scrap of paper into the right bin and cheers each one in. His zeal for recycling makes him {zealous}.

scene.alt: A man in a headband eagerly sorts bottles into recycling bins.

entry.def: passionate and enthusiastic
entry.ex: Grandma is an {ardent} baseball fan; she has not missed a home game in forty years.
entry.ctx: Though his friends had lost interest in comic books, Jamal remained an {ardent} collector, hunting through yard sales every weekend for missing issues.
entry.etym: From Latin ardere, “to burn.”

mn.text: Granny Mae has cheered for the home team for forty years, and her love still burns hot: cap, flag and a voice you can hear in the parking lot. She is an {ardent} fan.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a cap waves a flag and cheers her team with burning enthusiasm.

entry.def: showing strong, warm feeling
entry.ex: Lila made a {fervent} wish as she blew out the candles.
entry.ctx: The crowd’s applause was {fervent}: people stood, cheered and stamped their feet until the band came back for one more song.
entry.etym: From Latin fervere, “to boil, to glow.”

mn.text: Lila squeezes her eyes shut and wishes so hard over her birthday candles that she glows as if she had a fever. Her wish is {fervent}.

scene.alt: A girl squeezes her eyes shut and wishes with all her heart over her birthday cake.

entry.def: very eager and enthusiastic
entry.ex: Zoe is an {avid} reader who finishes a book every two days.
entry.ctx: Even in the rain, the {avid} bird-watchers stayed out on the marsh for hours, binoculars raised, hoping to glimpse the rare heron.
entry.etym: From Latin avidus, “eager, greedy,” from avere, “to crave.”

mn.text: The moment the new book arrives, Zoe grabs it: “I have to have it!” She has read it twice by Sunday. She is an {avid} reader.

labels.text: AV-id: I have to HAVE it!

scene.alt: A girl hugs a new book eagerly beside a tall pile of books she has already read.

entry.def: eager and enthusiastic; also, sharp
entry.ex: Dev was {keen} to try the new climbing wall.
entry.ctx: The owl’s {keen} eyesight let it spot a mouse moving in the grass from the top of a tall pine, far across the dark field.
entry.etym: From Old English cene, “bold, brave.”
entry.note: Keen has two common senses: eager (keen to help) and sharp (a keen knife, keen eyes, a keen mind).

mn.text: Dev, the keen teen, is first in line at the climbing rock, helmet on, an hour before it opens. He is {keen} to climb.

scene.alt: A teen in a climbing helmet bounces with eagerness at the foot of a climbing rock.

entry.def: cheerful readiness and speed
entry.ex: When Mom asked who wanted ice cream, the kids answered with {alacrity}.
entry.ctx: Kai usually dragged his feet at chore time, but when Grandpa asked for help building a treehouse, he agreed with {alacrity}, grabbing a hammer before Grandpa had finished asking.
entry.etym: From Latin alacritas, from alacer, “lively, brisk.”

mn.text: When Grandpa asks who wants to help build the treehouse, Kai springs off the couch like an acrobat: “Me! Now!” He answers with {alacrity}.

scene.alt: A boy springs up eagerly from the sofa when his grandfather holds up a hammer.

entry.def: unwilling and hesitant
entry.ex: The {reluctant} puppy had to be carried into the bath.
entry.ctx: Ivy was {reluctant} to jump off the high dive: she climbed the ladder twice, peered over the edge, and climbed back down both times.
entry.etym: From Latin reluctari, “to struggle against”: re (against) + luctari (to struggle).

mn.cue: re-LUCK-tant: no LUCK getting him to go
mn.text: Maya tugs Kai toward the dance floor, but he leans back with all his weight: no luck. He is {reluctant} to dance.

scene.alt: A girl tugs a boy toward the dance floor while he leans back, unwilling.

entry.def: unwilling; reluctant
entry.ex: Grandpa was {loath} to sell the old truck he had driven for forty years.
entry.ctx: Though the job paid well, Nell was {loath} to take it, because it meant moving far from the friends and the garden she loved.
entry.etym: From Old English lath, “hostile, hateful,” the same source as loathe.
entry.note: Loath (unwilling) is an adjective; loathe (to hate) is a verb. “I am loath to go,” but “I loathe cold soup.”

mn.cue: a SLOTH is LOATH to let go
mn.text: Time to climb down? The sloth hugs its cozy branch and won’t budge an inch. A sloth is always {loath} to let go.

scene.alt: A sleepy sloth clings to its branch and refuses to come down while a girl calls it.

entry.def: strongly opposed or unwilling
entry.ex: Our cat is {averse} to baths.
entry.ctx: Though usually {averse} to risk, the careful banker surprised everyone by leaving his job to open a surf shop.
entry.etym: From Latin aversus, “turned away”: ab (away) + vertere (to turn).
entry.note: Averse (unwilling, usually followed by to) is not adverse (harmful): “averse to risk,” but “adverse weather.”

mn.text: Show Mittens the washtub, and she turns her whole body away, nose in the air. She is {averse} to baths.

scene.alt: A cat turns its back on a washtub of water while a woman holds up soap.

entry.def: given or done unwillingly
entry.ex: Kai gave a {grudging} apology to his sister, staring at his shoes the whole time.
entry.ctx: Though the critic had disliked the director’s earlier films, he offered {grudging} praise for this one, admitting that its final scene was beautiful.
entry.etym: From grudge, from an old verb meaning “to grumble, to complain.”

mn.text: Mom says Kai must share, so he hands his sister half of his fudge with a scowl and a long sigh. His sharing is {grudging}.

scene.alt: A grumpy boy hands half his fudge to his happy sister.

blocks.html: loath (unwilling, an adjective) is not loathe (to hate, a verb). averse (unwilling) is not adverse (harmful).

its flavor
unwilling word
its flavor
blocks.cap: The scale of wanting.

blocks.html: Two sound-alike traps: loath (unwilling, an adjective) and loathe (to hate, a verb); averse (unwilling) and adverse (harmful, unfavorable). You are averse to risk; the weather is adverse.

blocks.html: Praise can be a quiet word of thanks or a stadium roaring your name. These ten words cover the range: formal praise (commend), loud public praise (acclaim, laud, extol), honors you can hold (accolade, tribute), deep lifelong respect (revere, venerate), lifting someone up (exalt) and praise that goes too far (adulation).

To praise: commend (formally), laud and extol (highly, enthusiastically), exalt (raise high). Praise you receive: acclaim (public applause), accolade (an award or honor), tribute (a gift or act of respect), adulation (too much admiration). Deep respect: revere, venerate.

entry.def: to praise formally or officially
entry.ex: The principal {commended} the students who organized the food drive.
entry.ctx: Instead of scolding the lifeguard for leaving her chair, the manager {commended} her: she had left it only to help a tired swimmer out of the deep end.
entry.etym: From Latin commendare, “to entrust, to recommend”: com (thoroughly) + mandare (to entrust, to order).

mn.text: Kai mends the broken garden fence all by himself, and the principal hands him a certificate in front of the whole school. To praise someone formally like that is to {commend} him.

scene.alt: A principal hands a certificate to a proud boy who mended the garden fence.

entry.def: enthusiastic public praise
entry.ex: Her first novel won wide {acclaim}.
entry.ctx: The young violinist’s concert earned instant {acclaim}: the audience rose to its feet, and the next morning every newspaper in the city praised her.
entry.etym: From Latin acclamare, “to shout at”: ad (to) + clamare (to shout).

mn.text: Rosa plays her last note, and the whole hall rises, clapping and calling out “Bravo!” That storm of public praise is {acclaim}.

scene.alt: A violinist bows on stage while the audience claps and cheers.

entry.def: to praise highly
entry.ex: Critics {lauded} the new bridge as a work of art.
entry.ctx: Though the inventor had been mocked for years, the scientists who once doubted him now {lauded} his work, calling it the most important discovery of the decade.
entry.etym: From Latin laudare, “to praise,” from laus, praise.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus reads Pip’s poem and praises it so loud the whole street can hear: “Best poem ever written!” To praise that highly is to {laud}.

scene.alt: A grandfather loudly praises his grandson’s poem while the boy blushes.

entry.def: to praise enthusiastically
entry.ex: Nana never stops {extolling} the virtues of a good night’s sleep.
entry.ctx: In every speech, the coach {extolled} her team’s hard work, praising the players’ early-morning practices even more than their victories.
entry.etym: From Latin extollere, “to lift up”: ex (out, up) + tollere (to raise).

mn.text: After the beach volleyball final, the team lifts Rosa onto their shoulders and sings her praises. To lift someone up with praise is to {extol} her.

scene.alt: Two teammates lift a cheering girl high onto their shoulders on the beach.

entry.def: an award, honor or expression of praise
entry.ex: The firefighter received the town’s highest {accolade} for bravery.
entry.ctx: Winning the science fair was nice, but the {accolade} Maya treasured most was a handwritten note from the judge calling her experiment the cleverest she had ever seen.
entry.etym: From French accolade, “an embrace around the neck,” once part of the ceremony of making a knight.

mn.text: The judge hangs a gold medal around Dev’s neck for his science project. Col means neck, and an {accolade} is an honor like that.

scene.alt: A boy stands on a podium with a gold medal around his neck while a woman claps.

entry.def: an act, statement or gift that shows respect or admiration
entry.ex: The concert was a {tribute} to the town’s beloved music teacher.
entry.ctx: When the old lighthouse keeper retired, the villagers paid him {tribute}: they renamed the harbor road in his honor and painted his portrait on the post office wall.
entry.etym: From Latin tributum, “a payment,” from tribuere, “to assign, to pay.”
entry.note: Long ago, tribute also meant a payment that one ruler forced another to make.

mn.cue: TREE-bute: a TREE planted in her honor
mn.text: When Ms. Ada retires, her students plant an oak in the schoolyard with a sign: “For Ms. Ada, who taught us to wonder.” The tree is a {tribute} to her.

labels.text: TREE-bute: a tree in her honor

scene.alt: Students plant a young tree with a sign in honor of their retiring teacher, who beams.

entry.def: to feel deep respect and admiration for
entry.ex: The young players {revere} their coach, who once played for the national team.
entry.ctx: Though the old doctor had retired long ago, the townspeople still {revered} her, for she had cared for three generations of their families and never turned anyone away.
entry.etym: From Latin revereri: re (thoroughly) + vereri (to stand in awe of). This ver is not the ver (true) of verify.

mn.cue: re-VEER: every eye VEERS toward her
mn.text: When Coach Tia walks onto the field, every player’s eyes veer toward her with awe: she once played for the national team. They {revere} her.

labels.text: re-VEER: all eyes turn to her

scene.alt: Three young players gaze in admiration at their coach, a former national team player.

entry.def: to regard with deep respect, often for age or wisdom
entry.ex: The villagers {venerate} the ancient oak that has shaded their square for five hundred years.
entry.ctx: The young chefs {venerated} Granny Mae: at ninety, she had cooked in the same kitchen for seventy years, and half the recipes in the town’s cookbook began with hers.
entry.etym: From Latin venerari, “to honor, to adore.”

mn.cue: ven-ERA-te: honored from an old ERA
mn.text: Every spring the town gathers under the five-hundred-year-old oak, a survivor from a long-ago era, and leaves flowers at its roots. The townspeople {venerate} it.

scene.alt: People bow and bring flowers to an ancient oak tree.

entry.def: to raise high in rank, power or praise
entry.ex: The old legends {exalt} the village baker who fed everyone through the long winter.
entry.ctx: Rather than take credit herself, the director {exalted} the quiet helpers in her speech, calling the stagehands the true stars of the show.
entry.etym: From Latin exaltare, “to raise high”: ex (up) + altus (high), as in altitude.
entry.note: Exalt (to raise up, to praise) is not exult (to rejoice): you exalt a hero; you exult in a victory.

mn.text: The village lifts its brave baker onto the tallest platform in the square, as high as the rooftops. To raise someone high in honor is to {exalt} her.

scene.alt: A baker in a sash stands high on a platform while villagers cheer below.

entry.def: excessive praise or admiration
entry.ex: The young singer was overwhelmed by the {adulation} of her fans.
entry.ctx: After his famous goal, the striker basked in the {adulation} of the crowd, though his coach reminded him that the cheering would fade if he stopped practicing.
entry.etym: From Latin adulari, “to fawn upon,” a word first used of dogs wagging their tails at their masters.

mn.text: The fans scream, wave signs and toss flowers, adding praise upon praise until the young singer can barely be seen. That flood of admiration is {adulation}.

scene.alt: Screaming fans toss flowers and wave signs at a startled young singer.

blocks.html: exalt (praise, raise up) is not exult (rejoice). adulation goes beyond admiration toward flattery.

head: word
part of speech
the kind of praise
blocks.cap: Who is praising, and how much?

blocks.html: exalt (raise up, praise) and exult (rejoice) differ by one letter. The fans exult in the win; the poem exalts the hero. And adulation goes beyond admiration: it is praise piled so high that it starts to feel like flattery.

blocks.html: Sadness has as many shades as happiness. Some sadness is a passing disappointment (crestfallen); some is a deep, lasting mood (melancholy); some is hopeless (despondent) or lonely (forlorn), and some mixes sorrow with sweetness (wistful, poignant). Choosing the right one tells a reader exactly how a character feels.

Moods: melancholy (deep sadness, a noun), somber (dark and serious), morose (sullen and gloomy), lugubrious (over-the-top mournful). After a loss: despondent (no hope), forlorn (lonely, abandoned), crestfallen (disappointed), disconsolate (beyond comfort). Tender sadness: wistful (longing), poignant (deeply moving).

entry.def: a deep, lasting sadness
entry.ex: A gentle {melancholy} settled over the house after the last guests drove away.
entry.ctx: The song’s cheerful tune hid a deep {melancholy}: its words told of a sailor who never came home.
entry.etym: From Greek melankholia, “black bile”: doctors long ago blamed lasting sadness on too much black bile in the body.
entry.note: Melancholy is also an adjective: a melancholy song.

mn.text: Ever since his melon ball rolled into the river, the old collie lies by the window and sighs all day. Poor melon-collie: he is full of {melancholy}.

scene.alt: A sad old dog lies by the window beside a melon, sighing.

entry.def: dark and gloomy; serious
entry.ex: The {somber} gray sky matched our mood on the last day of vacation.
entry.ctx: The usually noisy classroom was {somber} that morning; the students spoke in low voices after hearing that their favorite teacher was moving away.
entry.etym: From French sombre, “dark.”
entry.note: The British spelling is sombre.

mn.text: Clouds bar the sun, the sky turns gray, and the picnic goes quiet and serious. With the sun barred, the mood is {somber}.

scene.alt: Two people stand quietly at a gray picnic as clouds cover the sun.

entry.def: in low spirits from loss of hope
entry.ex: After the third rejection letter, Felix was {despondent}.
entry.ctx: The team was {despondent} after losing the final by a single point, and for days afterward no one could bear to talk about the game.
entry.etym: From Latin despondere, “to give up, to lose heart”: de (away) + spondere (to promise).

mn.cue: de-SPOND-ent: no hope by the POND
mn.text: Felix has fished the pond all day without a single nibble, and now he slumps on the bank, all hope gone. He is {despondent}.

scene.alt: A man slumps on a pond bank after catching nothing, while a fish leaps behind him.

entry.def: sad and lonely; abandoned
entry.ex: A {forlorn} teddy bear sat in the rain beside the empty swing.
entry.ctx: After the carnival packed up and drove away, the field looked {forlorn}: just trampled grass, a torn ticket and one lonely balloon caught in a fence.
entry.etym: From Old English forloren, “lost, ruined.”

mn.text: Everyone has gone home from the playground, and one little teddy bear sits all alone on the bench in the rain. It looks {forlorn}.

scene.alt: A lonely teddy bear sits on an empty playground bench in the rain.

entry.def: sullen, gloomy and bad-tempered
entry.ex: The {morose} goalie barely spoke during the long bus ride home.
entry.ctx: Usually cheerful, Uncle Marcus turned {morose} whenever it rained: he sat in his armchair, scowling, and answered every question with a grunt.
entry.etym: From Latin morosus, “peevish, hard to please.”

mn.cue: MO-ROSE: no ROSE can cheer him
mn.text: Lin brings Marcus a rose to cheer him up, and he only scowls and grunts. No rose can brighten his sullen mood: he is {morose}.

scene.alt: A scowling man under a little rain cloud ignores the rose a woman offers him.

entry.def: deeply moving; stirring sadness or tender regret
entry.ex: Grandpa’s {poignant} letter to his younger self made the whole family cry.
entry.ctx: The film’s last scene was {poignant}: the two friends, now old men, met again at the very station where they had said goodbye sixty years before.
entry.etym: From Old French poignant, “pricking,” from Latin pungere, “to prick,” the root of pungent.
entry.note: Say POIN-yunt: the g is silent.

mn.cue: POIGN-ant: POINTS straight at the heart
mn.text: Two old friends meet again on the platform where they said goodbye sixty years before, and the moment points straight at your heart. It is {poignant}.

scene.alt: Two old friends hug and cry on a station platform after sixty years apart.

entry.def: disappointed and downcast
entry.ex: Kai was {crestfallen} when the trip to the lake was canceled.
entry.ctx: Sami had practiced his speech for weeks, so he was {crestfallen} when the assembly was called off at the last minute.

roots.means: the comb or plume on top of the head

entry.etym: From crest, the comb on a bird’s head or the plume on a helmet, + fallen: the word pictures a drooping crest.

mn.text: Rocky the rooster loses the crowing contest, and his proud red comb flops down over one eye. He is {crestfallen}.

scene.alt: A sad rooster droops after losing, while the winning rooster stands proudly by a trophy.

entry.def: so sad that nothing can comfort
entry.ex: The {disconsolate} toddler cried for an hour after his balloon floated away.
entry.ctx: Friends brought cards, cookies and funny movies, but Ivy remained {disconsolate}; nothing could make up for her best friend moving across the country.
entry.etym: From Latin disconsolatus: dis (not) + consolatus (comforted).

mn.text: Theo’s balloon floats away, and nothing helps: not a hug, not a cookie, not even a new balloon. He cannot be consoled; he is {disconsolate}.

scene.alt: A toddler cries as his balloon floats away; his grandmother’s cookie does not help.

entry.def: sadly longing for something past or out of reach
entry.ex: Grandma gave a {wistful} smile as she looked through her old dance photos.
entry.ctx: Watching his friends ride off to summer camp, Pip grew {wistful}; he had loved camp, but this year his family could not afford to send him.

mn.text: Granny Mae turns the pages of her old dance photos, smiling but a little sad, wishing she could dance like that once more. Her smile is {wistful}.

scene.alt: A grandmother smiles a little sadly as she looks through an old photo album.

entry.def: mournful, often in an exaggerated way
entry.ex: The hound gave a {lugubrious} howl whenever the family left the house.
entry.ctx: The actor played the old butler in a {lugubrious} voice so slow and gloomy that the audience, instead of crying, burst out laughing.
entry.etym: From Latin lugubris, “mournful,” from lugere, “to mourn.”

mn.cue: lu-GOO-brious: a howl as slow as GOO
mn.text: Every time the car pulls away, Biscuit the hound lets out a howl as slow and droopy as goo: “Aroooooo.” It is over the top, and it is {lugubrious}.

scene.alt: A droopy dog howls mournfully as the family car drives away.

blocks.html: poignant is pronounced POIN-yunt; it can describe a tender memory as well as a sad one. morose suggests sullen bad temper, not only sadness.

head: word
the kind of sadness
rows: moving: sad and tender at once
blocks.cap: Shades of sadness, from a moment to a mood.

blocks.html: poignant is said POIN-yunt (the g is silent), and it can describe a tender, happy-sad memory, not only a sad one. morose adds bad temper to gloom; a morose person is sulking, not just sad.

blocks.html: Between “I know” and “I have no idea” lies a lot of ground, and careful thinkers have words for every step of it. You can presume without proof, speculate with no evidence at all, find a claim plausible or dubious, hold a conviction firmly, or stay skeptical until you see the facts. These words fill the science and history passages of every reading test.

Believing: conviction (a firm belief), tenet (a principle a group holds), presume (take as true without proof), dogmatic (sure, and closed to evidence). Weighing: plausible (seems likely), speculate (guess without evidence). Doubting: skeptical (wants proof), dubious (doubtful, or shady), cynical (distrusts people’s motives), fallacy (a mistaken belief or bad reasoning).

entry.def: doubting; not easily convinced
entry.ex: Dad was {skeptical} when the ad promised a car that would never need a single repair.
entry.ctx: The salesman swore the vacuum could clean a whole house in five minutes, but Nana remained {skeptical} and asked to see it work on her own carpet first.
entry.etym: From Greek skeptikos, “inquiring,” from skeptesthai, “to look at, to examine.”

mn.text: Rex claims his round rock is a dinosaur egg, so Ada pulls out her magnifying glass and looks very closely before believing a word. She is {skeptical}.

scene.alt: A scientist examines a so-called dinosaur egg through a magnifying glass before believing it.

entry.def: doubtful; also, possibly dishonest
entry.ex: Ivy was {dubious} about her brother’s promise to clean the kitchen by himself.
entry.ctx: The deal sounded too good to be true, and it came from a company with a {dubious} record: three of its last four products had been recalled.
entry.etym: From Latin dubius, “doubtful, wavering.”
entry.note: Dubious can describe a doubting person (“I’m dubious”) or a thing that deserves doubt (“a dubious claim”).

mn.text: A sign promises shoes that let you fly for five dollars. Grandpa Gus squints at it, full of doubt, and the seller looks shady too. Gus is {dubious}.

scene.alt: A grandfather squints doubtfully at a shady seller offering “flying shoes.”

entry.def: seeming reasonable or likely
entry.ex: Zoe’s excuse was {plausible}: the bus really had broken down that morning.
entry.ctx: The detective’s theory was {plausible}, since it explained both the muddy boots and the open window, but she still needed proof before she could be sure.
entry.etym: From Latin plausibilis, “deserving applause,” from plaudere, “to applaud.”

mn.text: Zoe says she is late because the bus broke down, and there it sits, steaming at the corner. Her excuse earns a nod and a clap: it is {plausible}.

scene.alt: A girl points to a broken-down, smoking bus as her excuse, and her teacher accepts it.

entry.def: a firmly held belief; also, a finding of guilt in court
entry.ex: Nell spoke with {conviction} about saving the old oak trees.
entry.ctx: Though everyone laughed at her plan, Tia held to her {conviction} that the empty lot could become a garden, and by summer it was full of tomatoes.
entry.etym: From Latin convictio, from convincere, “to overcome, to prove”: con (thoroughly) + vincere (to conquer).
entry.note: In a courtroom, a conviction is a finding of guilt: “The conviction was overturned on appeal.”

mn.cue: con-VICT-ion: a belief that WINS you
mn.text: Everyone laughs at Tia’s plan to turn the empty lot into a garden, but she plants her flag and won’t budge. She speaks with {conviction}.

scene.alt: A determined woman plants a flag in an empty lot she believes will become a garden.

entry.def: a principle or belief held as true by a group
entry.ex: A basic {tenet} of the hiking club is to leave no trash behind.
entry.ctx: Fair play was the central {tenet} of the soccer league: every child got equal time on the field, no matter the score.
entry.etym: From Latin tenet, “he holds,” from tenere, “to hold”: a tenet is a belief a group holds.
entry.note: A tenet (a principle) is not a tenant (someone who rents a home).

mn.cue: TEN = HOLD: a belief the club HOLDS
mn.text: The hiking club’s sign lists the beliefs its members hold to, and number one is “Leave no trash.” Each rule they hold is a {tenet}.

scene.alt: Two hikers carry out their trash beside a club sign whose first rule is leave no trash.

entry.def: insisting one’s opinions are true without considering evidence
entry.ex: Our {dogmatic} neighbor insists there is only one right way to mow a lawn.
entry.ctx: Good scientists change their minds when new evidence appears, but the {dogmatic} professor refused even to look at the results that contradicted his theory.
entry.etym: From Greek dogma, “opinion, belief,” from dokein, “to seem, to think.”

mn.cue: DOG + MAT: a dog that won’t budge
mn.text: Rufus has decided that the doormat is his, and no treat, toy or argument will move him an inch. Stuck to an opinion like a dog on its mat is {dogmatic}.

scene.alt: A stubborn dog refuses to leave its mat even when a boy offers a bone.

entry.def: to suppose something is true without proof
entry.ex: I {presume} you’ve already eaten, since there are crumbs on your shirt.
entry.ctx: Seeing the wet umbrellas by the door, Dad {presumed} it was raining, but he stepped outside into bright sunshine; the umbrellas had only been left there to dry.
entry.etym: From Latin praesumere, “to take beforehand”: prae (before) + sumere (to take).

mn.cue: PRE-SUME: take it as true BEFORE checking
mn.text: Omar sees wet umbrellas by the door and pops his own open before stepping out, into blazing sunshine. He did not check; he chose to {presume}.

scene.alt: A man holds an open umbrella under a bright, cloudless sun, looking puzzled.

entry.def: to form ideas or theories without firm evidence
entry.ex: Fans {speculated} about who would win the baking contest.
entry.ctx: With no letters or diaries to go on, historians can only {speculate} about why the village was abandoned: perhaps a flood, perhaps a sickness, perhaps a better harvest elsewhere.
entry.etym: From Latin speculari, “to watch, to look out,” from specere, “to look.”

mn.cue: SPEC-ulate: look and guess, no peeking
mn.text: The kids stare at the big wrapped box and guess: a bike? a puppy? a robot? With no way to peek inside, all they can do is {speculate}.

scene.alt: Two children stare at a big wrapped present, guessing what is inside.

entry.def: a mistaken belief, or a flaw in reasoning
entry.ex: “Everyone I know likes pizza, so everyone in the world must like pizza” is a {fallacy}.
entry.ctx: His argument rested on a {fallacy}: just because the rooster crows before sunrise does not mean that the rooster makes the sun come up.
entry.etym: From Latin fallacia, “deceit,” from fallere, “to deceive,” the root of false.

mn.text: The rooster crows, the sun comes up, and he proudly believes his crowing made it rise. That reasoning falls apart: it is a {fallacy}.

scene.alt: A proud rooster crows and claims credit for the rising sun.

entry.def: believing that people act only out of self-interest
entry.ex: The {cynical} shopper assumed the free samples must be some kind of trick.
entry.ctx: When the new neighbor offered to help paint his fence, Victor was {cynical}: he assumed she must want something in return, though she only wanted to be friendly.
entry.etym: From Greek kynikos, “doglike,” the name given to the Cynics, ancient Greek thinkers who scorned wealth, comfort and custom.

mn.text: Nell brings her new neighbor a pie, and Victor squints: “What’s the catch? What do you want?” He thinks every kindness hides a selfish reason. Victor is {cynical}.

scene.alt: A friendly woman offers a pie, and a suspicious man wonders what she really wants.

blocks.html: tenet (a principle) is not tenant (a renter). skeptical is doubt about claims; cynical is distrust of people's motives.

head: doubting word
what it doubts
rows: either; or the thing itself is shady
blocks.cap: A skeptic doubts what people say; a cynic doubts why they say it.

blocks.html: tenet (a principle) and tenant (a renter) sound alike but differ: both come from ten, hold. A tenet is a belief a group holds; a tenant holds a lease. And to presume is to take something as true before checking (pre-), while to speculate is to guess with no real evidence at all.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Weather, moods, prices and people can all change without warning, and English has a word for each kind of change. Some describe things that swing unpredictably (erratic, volatile, fluctuate); some describe people whose moods or loyalties shift (capricious, fickle, mercurial); and some describe acting without stopping to think (impulsive, impetuous, spontaneous).

Changing moods and loyalties: capricious (on a whim), fickle (loyalty that shifts), mercurial (quick mood swings). Unpredictable things: erratic (irregular), volatile (ready to blow up), fluctuate (to rise and fall), vacillate (to waver between choices). Acting without planning: impulsive and impetuous (rash), spontaneous (natural, unplanned, often a good thing).

entry.def: changing suddenly and without reason
entry.ex: The {capricious} weather switched from sunshine to hail three times in one afternoon.
entry.ctx: The king was {capricious}: one day he rewarded his cook with gold, and the next, for no reason anyone could see, he banished him from the kitchen.
entry.etym: From Italian capriccio, “a sudden whim.”

mn.cue: a goat on a whim: this way, then that
mn.text: The little goat leaps left, then right, then left again, for no reason at all: just a whim. Its leaping is {capricious}.

scene.alt: A goat leaps one way, then the other, for no reason at all.

entry.def: changing loyalties or feelings often
entry.ex: The {fickle} cat loved me on Monday and ignored me by Tuesday.
entry.ctx: Fans can be {fickle}: they cheered the young pitcher all spring, then booed him the moment he lost two games in a row.
entry.etym: From Old English ficol, “deceitful, crafty.”

mn.cue: a FICKLE NICKEL: flips like a coin
mn.text: Ivy picks her best friend by flipping a nickel: heads it’s Zoe, tails it’s Lila, and tomorrow she flips again. Loyalty that flips like a coin is {fickle}.

scene.alt: A girl flips a coin to choose her best friend while two friends look confused.

entry.def: not regular or predictable
entry.ex: The old car’s {erratic} engine coughed, roared and then went silent.
entry.ctx: Lin’s sleep became {erratic} during exam week: some nights she slept three hours, some nights eleven, and she never went to bed at the same time twice.
entry.etym: From Latin erraticus, “wandering,” from errare, “to wander, to stray,” the root of error.

mn.text: The pet rat zigzags across the floor, left, right, back, around the sofa, so no one can guess where it will go next. Its path is {erratic}.

scene.alt: A pet rat zigzags across the floor while a man tries to follow it.

entry.def: likely to change suddenly, often for the worse
entry.ex: The {volatile} stock market rose sharply in the morning and fell by afternoon.
entry.ctx: The mood at the meeting was {volatile}: one careless word, and the calm discussion could explode into shouting.
entry.etym: From Latin volatilis, “flying,” from volare, “to fly”: a volatile liquid quickly flies off into the air.

mn.cue: VOL-atile: a VOLCANO ready to blow
mn.text: Dev’s science-fair volcano rumbles and fizzes, and no one knows when it will blow. Anything ready to erupt or change suddenly is {volatile}.

scene.alt: A model volcano fizzes and smokes on a table while two students jump back.

entry.def: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
entry.ex: The {mercurial} chef was laughing one minute and shouting the next.
entry.ctx: Working for the {mercurial} director was exhausting: she praised a scene warmly in the morning and called the same scene a disaster that afternoon.
entry.etym: From Latin mercurialis, “of Mercury,” the swift messenger of Roman myth; the quick, slippery liquid metal mercury carries the same name.

mn.text: Chef Victor laughs at a joke, roars at a dropped spoon, then hums happily, all in one minute. His moods slip and dart like quick, silvery mercury: he is {mercurial}.

scene.alt: A chef swings from laughing to shouting to humming while a boy watches, dizzy.

entry.def: acting suddenly without thinking first
entry.ex: In an {impulsive} moment, Jonah dyed his hair green the night before school photos.
entry.ctx: Ivy’s purchase was {impulsive}: she saw the giant teddy bear at the checkout and bought it without a single thought about where it would fit in her tiny room.
entry.etym: From Latin impulsus, “a push,” from impellere, “to push on”: im (on) + pellere (to drive).

mn.text: Ivy spots a giant teddy bear at the checkout and buys it in one heartbeat, without a thought about where it will fit. Her purchase is {impulsive}.

scene.alt: A girl hugs a giant teddy bear she bought on the spot while the cashier wonders where it will fit.

entry.def: acting quickly and rashly, without thought
entry.ex: The {impetuous} knight charged across the river without checking how deep it was.
entry.ctx: Dev’s {impetuous} decision to quit the team after one bad game surprised everyone, and by the next morning he was asking the coach to let him back.
entry.etym: From Latin impetuosus, from impetus, “a rush, an attack.”

mn.text: Dev races down the dock and leaps into the lake without checking how cold it is. Splash! Brrr! His headlong leap was {impetuous}.

scene.alt: A teen leaps headlong off the dock into a chilly lake without checking first.

entry.def: happening naturally, without planning
entry.ex: The crowd broke into {spontaneous} applause when the puppy crossed the finish line.
entry.ctx: Nothing about the party was planned: it was {spontaneous}, starting when one neighbor brought out a guitar and others drifted over with snacks and folding chairs.
entry.etym: From Latin sponte, “of one’s own accord, freely.”

mn.text: One neighbor starts strumming a guitar on her steps, and soon the whole street is dancing, with no plan at all. The party is {spontaneous}.

scene.alt: A neighbor plays guitar and others start dancing in the street, unplanned.

entry.def: to waver back and forth between choices
entry.ex: Kai {vacillated} between chocolate and vanilla until the shop closed.
entry.ctx: For weeks Ada {vacillated} about the job offer: one day she was packing boxes for the move, and the next she was telling friends she would stay.
entry.etym: From Latin vacillare, “to sway, to totter.”

mn.text: Kai stares at the menu: vanilla? chocolate? vanilla? He sways back and forth so long that the shop closes. To waver like that is to {vacillate}.

scene.alt: A boy wavers between a vanilla cone and a chocolate cone.

entry.def: to rise and fall irregularly
entry.ex: The price of strawberries {fluctuates} with the seasons.
entry.ctx: Desert temperatures {fluctuate} wildly: an afternoon can top 100 degrees, and the same night can drop close to freezing.
entry.etym: From Latin fluctuare, “to move like a wave,” from fluctus, a wave.

mn.text: The little boat rides the waves up, down, up, down, never level for a moment. Things that rise and fall like waves {fluctuate}.

scene.alt: A little boat rocks up and down on the waves beside a bobbing duck.

blocks.html: spontaneous is often good (a spontaneous smile); impetuous and impulsive usually warn. vacillate is about indecision; fluctuate is about changing amounts.

head: word
what changes
a typical subject
blocks.cap: Who or what is changing, and how.

blocks.html: spontaneous is usually praise (a spontaneous laugh, a spontaneous party), while impulsive and impetuous usually warn: they mean acting before thinking. And vacillate is about indecision in a mind; fluctuate is about numbers and amounts going up and down.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: This topic is the mirror image of Making Things Better. Some of these verbs describe making a bad situation worse (exacerbate, aggravate, compound); some describe slow weakening, often from below or out of sight (undermine, erode, deteriorate); and some describe damage or danger (debilitate, impair, jeopardize, sabotage).

Make a bad thing worse: exacerbate, aggravate, compound. Weaken slowly: undermine (from beneath, or in secret), erode (wear away), deteriorate (grow worse). Damage and danger: debilitate (weaken badly), impair (damage), jeopardize (put at risk), sabotage (wreck on purpose).

entry.def: to make a problem or pain worse
entry.ex: Scratching a mosquito bite only {exacerbates} the itch.
entry.ctx: The drought was bad enough, but the town {exacerbated} the problem by watering its golf course every afternoon while the reservoir dried up.
entry.etym: From Latin exacerbare, “to irritate, to make harsh”: ex (thoroughly) + acerbus (harsh, bitter).

mn.cue: ex-ACERB-ate: add more SOUR to the sour
mn.text: Kai is already puckering from one lemon, and his brother hands him another. Adding sour to sour is how you {exacerbate} a problem.

scene.alt: A boy makes a sour face from a lemon while his brother offers another.

entry.def: to make worse; also, in everyday speech, to annoy
entry.ex: Lifting heavy boxes {aggravated} the coach’s sore back.
entry.ctx: Instead of calming the argument, Pip {aggravated} it by reminding his sister of every unfair thing she had ever done.
entry.etym: From Latin aggravare, “to make heavier”: ad (to) + gravis (heavy).
entry.note: Careful writers use aggravate to mean make worse; the sense “annoy” is common in everyday speech.

mn.text: Sami’s backpack is already heavy, and then Jonah sneaks a big rock into it. Grav means heavy: to {aggravate} a problem is to make it heavier.

scene.alt: A sneaky teen slips a rock into a hiker’s already heavy backpack.

entry.def: to weaken gradually or secretly
entry.ex: Constant teasing can {undermine} a child’s confidence.
entry.ctx: Though he praised the plan in public, the manager quietly {undermined} it, canceling its meetings and moving its money to other projects.
entry.etym: From under + mine: to dig a tunnel beneath a wall so that it collapses.

mn.text: A rabbit tunnels under the sandcastle’s tallest tower, and day by day the tower leans a little more. Weakening something from underneath is to {undermine} it.

scene.alt: A rabbit digs under a sandcastle, which begins to lean, while a girl gasps.

entry.def: to wear away slowly
entry.ex: Waves {eroded} the cliff a little more each winter.
entry.ctx: Small broken promises {eroded} the team’s trust in its captain: no single one mattered much, but together they wore it away.
entry.etym: From Latin erodere, “to gnaw away”: e (away) + rodere (to gnaw), the root of rodent.

mn.cue: e-RODE: gnawed away, as by a RODent
mn.text: Night after night, a little mouse nibbles the big wheel of cheese until only a sliver is left. Rodere means to gnaw: water, wind and time {erode} things the same slow way.

labels.text: e-RODE: gnawed away, bit by bit

scene.alt: A mouse nibbles away at a big wedge of cheese on the kitchen table.

entry.def: to become worse
entry.ex: Left out in the rain, the old book {deteriorated} until its pages stuck together.
entry.ctx: The weather {deteriorated} as the hikers climbed: sunshine gave way to clouds, then sleet, and finally a blinding snowstorm.
entry.etym: From Latin deteriorare, “to make worse,” from deterior, worse.

mn.text: Kai’s old kite starts with one small tear; after a week of wind, it is more holes than kite. It has {deteriorated}.

scene.alt: A sad boy flies a battered, torn kite in the wind.

entry.def: to weaken severely
entry.ex: The long heat wave {debilitated} the garden’s tomato plants.
entry.ctx: The flu {debilitated} Sami for a week; he was so weak that a walk to the kitchen left him needing a nap.
entry.etym: From Latin debilitare, “to weaken,” from debilis, weak.

mn.text: Day after day of blazing heat drains every bit of strength from the sunflowers until they droop to the ground. A heat wave can {debilitate} a garden.

scene.alt: Under a blazing sun, sunflowers droop to the ground while a girl looks on, worried.

entry.def: to damage or weaken
entry.ex: Very loud music can {impair} your hearing over time.
entry.ctx: Thick fog {impaired} the drivers’ view so badly that the town closed the bridge until it lifted at noon.
entry.etym: From Old French empeirier, “to make worse,” based on Latin pejor, worse.

mn.cue: im-PAIR: a smudged PAIR of glasses
mn.text: Grandpa’s pair of glasses is smeared with jam, and now he can barely read the paper. The smudges {impair} his sight.

scene.alt: A grandfather squints at a newspaper through glasses smudged with jam.

entry.def: to put in danger or at risk
entry.ex: Skipping practice could {jeopardize} Rosa’s spot on the team.
entry.ctx: By sharing the secret password with a stranger, Kai {jeopardized} the club’s whole treasure hunt, and the other members had to rewrite every clue.
entry.etym: From jeopardy, Old French jeu parti, “a divided game”: a game whose outcome hangs in the balance.

mn.text: Ignoring the THIN ICE sign, Rex skates right out to the middle of the pond, and every crack puts him in jeopardy. He chose to {jeopardize} his own safety.

scene.alt: A man tiptoes on cracking pond ice past a thin-ice sign while a grandmother calls him back.

entry.def: to damage or ruin on purpose
entry.ex: Someone {sabotaged} the science-fair volcano by swapping the baking soda for flour.
entry.ctx: The rival team tried to {sabotage} the race by moving the course markers, but the runners noticed the trick and followed their maps instead.
entry.etym: From French saboter, “to botch, to bungle,” from sabot, a wooden shoe.

mn.text: Before the wagon race, Rex creeps over and loosens a wheel on his rival’s wagon. Wrecking something on purpose is to {sabotage} it.

scene.alt: A sneaky man loosens a wheel on a rival’s racing wagon.

entry.def: to make a problem worse by adding to it
entry.ex: Arriving late, Dev {compounded} the problem by forgetting his uniform.
entry.ctx: The town’s mistake in closing the bridge was {compounded} when it closed the ferry too, leaving the island with no way to reach the mainland.
entry.etym: From Latin componere, “to put together”: com (together) + ponere (to put).
entry.note: Compound also means to combine or mix (to compound a medicine), and interest that compounds grows on itself. As a noun, a compound is a mixture or a fenced group of buildings.

mn.cue: com-POUND: POUND more trouble on top
mn.text: Theo spills his milk, and then the puppy runs through the puddle and tracks white paw prints across the whole house. The puppy {compounded} the problem.

scene.alt: A toddler has spilled his milk, and a puppy runs through it, tracking prints across the floor.

blocks.html: compound as a verb means to make worse (compound an error), not only to combine. aggravate in careful use means to make worse; "to annoy" is a common everyday meaning.

head: how it gets worse
words
rows: weakened from below or in secret
blocks.cap: Five ways things get worse.

blocks.html: compound as a verb means to add to a problem (“he compounded the error by lying about it”), not only to combine things. aggravate in careful writing means to make worse; “it really aggravates me” (annoys) is everyday speech.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Clubs, schools, towns and kingdoms all need ways to make rules and to unmake them. This topic’s words describe each step: a rule is enacted or decreed, written as a statute, approved (ratified) or blocked (vetoed), and later perhaps repealed, rescinded, abolished or nullified. These words appear constantly in history passages.

Making rules: enact (make into law), statute (a written law), mandate (an official order; also, authority from voters), decree (a ruler’s order), ratify (formally approve). Blocking and unmaking: veto (a power to reject), abolish (end completely), repeal (cancel a law), rescind (take back an order or offer), nullify (make void).

entry.def: to make into law
entry.ex: The town council {enacted} a rule requiring dogs to be leashed in the park.
entry.ctx: After years of debate, the state finally {enacted} the safety law, and by the next spring every new school bus had seat belts.
entry.etym: From en (into) + act, a law passed by a lawmaking body: to put into an act.
entry.note: Enact can also mean to act out: “The class enacted the signing of the treaty.”

mn.cue: EN-ACT: turn a plan INTO an ACT (a law)
mn.text: The town council votes yes, and the mayor signs the new leash rule with a flourish: now it is an official act. To make a plan into law is to {enact} it.

scene.alt: A woman signs a new leash law into effect while a boy and his dog look on.

entry.def: a written law
entry.ex: A {statute} passed by the state lawmakers last spring bans fireworks after ten o’clock at night.
entry.ctx: The judge explained that she could not simply follow her own sense of fairness; she had to apply the {statute} exactly as the lawmakers had written it.
entry.etym: From Latin statutum, “something set up,” from statuere, “to set up, to decide.”
entry.note: A statute (a law) is not a statue (a sculpture) or stature (height, or standing).

mn.text: In front of the courthouse, a stone statue holds up a scroll: the town’s first written law. The statue is art; the scroll is a {statute}.

scene.alt: A woman points to a stone statue holding a scroll; the statue is labeled statue and the scroll statute.

entry.def: an official order; also, authority given by voters
entry.ex: The school board issued a {mandate}: every student must wear a helmet on the bike path.
entry.ctx: Having won the election with eighty percent of the vote, the new mayor believed she had a clear {mandate} to rebuild the old park.
entry.etym: From Latin mandatum, “something ordered,” from mandare, “to order, to entrust.”

mn.text: The principal posts the new command by the bike path: “Helmets required.” An official order like that is a {mandate}.

scene.alt: A principal points to a helmets-required sign as a boy with a helmet stands by his bike.

entry.def: an official order from a ruler or authority
entry.ex: By royal {decree}, the last Friday in June became a holiday.
entry.ctx: The king’s {decree} was read aloud in every village square: from that day on, no one could cut wood in the royal forest without permission.
entry.etym: From Latin decretum, “something decided,” from decernere, “to decide”: de (from) + cernere (to sift, to decide).

mn.cue: de-CREE: the king DECIDES, all AGREE
mn.text: The king raises his scepter: “From now on, every Friday is ice-cream day!” The king decides, and everyone must agree. A ruler’s official order is a {decree}.

scene.alt: A king raises his scepter and declares ice-cream Fridays while children cheer.

entry.def: to formally approve an agreement or plan
entry.ex: The club members voted to {ratify} the new rules.
entry.ctx: The treaty was signed in the spring, but it did not take effect until each nation’s lawmakers had voted to {ratify} it that winter.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin ratificare, “to confirm,” from ratus, “fixed, settled.”

mn.cue: RAT-ify: every RAT’s paw says YES
mn.text: The rats hold a meeting on their new cheese-sharing rules, and every paw goes up. When a group formally approves an agreement, they {ratify} it.

scene.alt: Three rats leap up together to approve a scroll of rules, with cheese nearby.

entry.def: the power to reject a decision or law, or such a rejection
entry.ex: Mom used her {veto} on our plan to adopt a goat.
entry.ctx: The council voted to build the new road, but the mayor used her {veto}, and the project stopped until the council could gather enough votes to override it.
entry.etym: From Latin veto, “I forbid.”

mn.text: The kids vote three to nothing to adopt a goat, but Mom holds up one hand: “I forbid it.” That single blocking vote is a {veto}.

scene.alt: Children hold up a sign asking for a goat, and their mother blocks the plan.

entry.def: to end something officially, completely and for good
entry.ex: The school {abolished} its old rule against wearing hats in the hallway.
entry.ctx: The town {abolished} the toll on the old bridge, so drivers no longer had to stop and drop a quarter in the box every time they crossed the river.
entry.etym: From French abolir, from Latin abolere, “to destroy, to do away with.”

mn.text: The town bowls over the old toll gate on the bridge: no more stopping, no more paying, gone for good. To end something completely is to {abolish} it.

scene.alt: A giant bowling ball knocks over the old toll gate by the bridge while a man cheers.

entry.def: to cancel a law officially
entry.ex: The city {repealed} its old ban on skateboards in the park.
entry.ctx: The rule against bringing snacks into the library proved so unpopular that the board {repealed} it after just one month.
entry.etym: From Old French rapeler, “to call back”: re (back) + apeler (to call).

mn.cue: re-PEEL: PEEL the old rule off the wall
mn.text: A worker peels the old “NO SKATEBOARDS” sign right off the park wall, and the skaters cheer. To officially cancel a law is to {repeal} it.

scene.alt: A worker pulls down a no-skateboards sign in the park as a skater cheers.

entry.def: to take back or cancel an order, offer or decision
entry.ex: The coach {rescinded} the extra laps after the team apologized.
entry.ctx: The company offered Jamal the job, then {rescinded} the offer a week later when it discovered it could not afford to hire anyone new.
entry.etym: From Latin rescindere, “to cut off, to annul”: re (back) + scindere (to cut).

mn.cue: re-SCIND: CUT the order back off
mn.text: Ms. Ada writes HOMEWORK on the board, then the class wins the spelling bee, and she crosses it right off. To take back an order is to {rescind} it.

scene.alt: A teacher crosses out a homework assignment while her students cheer.

entry.def: to make legally void; to cancel out
entry.ex: A missing signature {nullified} the contract.
entry.ctx: Dev scored twice, but a penalty {nullified} the second goal, and the game ended in a tie.
entry.etym: From Latin nullus, “none,” + -ify: to make into nothing.

mn.cue: NULL-ify: make it NULL, worth ZERO
mn.text: Dev’s goal flies in, but the referee blows her whistle and waves it off: offside. The goal now counts for zero; she has {nullified} it.

scene.alt: A referee waves off a goal; the shocked player sees the scoreboard stay at zero.

blocks.html: statute (a law) is not statue (a sculpture) or stature (height or standing). ratify approves; repeal and rescind undo.

head: step
words
rows: enact; the law is a statute
repeal (a law), rescind (an order or offer), nullify (make void), abolish (end entirely)
blocks.cap: The life of a rule.

blocks.html: Three look-alikes: a statute is a law, a statue is a sculpture, and stature is height or standing. And keep the direction straight: ratify approves; repeal and rescind undo.

blocks.html: Ordinary is not always bad: mundane chores and commonplace inventions keep life running. But when writing or speech is ordinary in a tired way, critics reach for sharper words: banal, trite, hackneyed, prosaic, pedestrian. Several of these words began as pictures: a worn coin, a hired horse, a printer’s plate, a flat plate, a walker on foot.

Ordinary: mundane (everyday), commonplace (not unusual), conventional (the usual way). Worn out by use: banal, trite, hackneyed (adjectives); cliché (an overused phrase), platitude (a flat remark offered as wisdom) (nouns). Dull and unimaginative: prosaic, pedestrian.

entry.def: ordinary and everyday; dull
entry.ex: Folding laundry is a {mundane} chore, so Lin listens to music while she does it.
entry.ctx: The astronaut’s diary was surprisingly {mundane}: beside the views of Earth, she wrote mostly about brushing her teeth, changing air filters and what she ate for lunch.
entry.etym: From Latin mundanus, “of the world,” from mundus, world: the plain, everyday world.
entry.note: Mundane means ordinary, not bad: a mundane task can be pleasant enough.

mn.text: Every Monday it is the same: fold the laundry, take out the trash, wash the dishes. Plain, everyday chores like these are {mundane}.

scene.alt: A woman with headphones yawns over a basket of laundry on a Monday.

entry.def: ordinary; not unusual
entry.ex: Phones that take pictures, once a wonder, are now {commonplace}.
entry.ctx: A hundred years ago, flying across the ocean was a daring adventure; today it is so {commonplace} that passengers sleep through the whole trip.
entry.etym: A translation of Latin locus communis, “a common place”: a theme or saying everyone used.

mn.text: A plane roars over the river, and nobody fishing even looks up; you can see planes in common places everywhere. They are {commonplace} now.

scene.alt: A plane flies overhead while people by the river do not even look up.

entry.def: following what is usually done; traditional
entry.ex: Instead of a {conventional} birthday cake, Dev asked for a tower of pancakes.
entry.ctx: Most builders of the time made {conventional} brick houses, but she designed homes shaped like seashells, with curving walls and round windows.
entry.etym: From convention, Latin conventio, “a coming together, an agreement”: conventional ways are the ones people have agreed on.

mn.cue: CONVENTION-al: the way everyone agreed on
mn.text: At the business convention, every guest wears the same gray jacket and tie, the way everyone agreed long ago. Their style is {conventional}.

scene.alt: Three men stand in matching gray jackets and ties, while one girl in a cape stands out.

entry.def: dull and unoriginal because so common
entry.ex: The movie’s ending was {banal}: the hero won, the villain lost, and everyone cheered, just as we expected.
entry.ctx: Hoping for a fresh insight, the class was disappointed by the speaker’s {banal} advice: “Work hard, and follow your dreams.”
entry.etym: From French banal, “common to everyone,” first said of things like a village oven that everyone shared.

mn.text: Every single day, Kai’s lunch is one plain banana: no surprise, no change, nothing new. A lunch that dull and predictable is {banal}.

scene.alt: A bored boy holds up the same plain banana he has for lunch every day.

entry.def: used so often that it is no longer interesting
entry.ex: “Every cloud has a silver lining” felt {trite} to Maya right after she lost the match.
entry.ctx: Her early poems were full of {trite} images, roses as red as fire and eyes like stars, but her later work was fresh and surprising.
entry.etym: From Latin tritus, “worn,” from terere, “to rub”: a trite phrase has been rubbed smooth by use.

mn.cue: TRITE: TRIED and TRIED and TRIED
mn.text: Grandpa tells his favorite joke for the hundredth time, and the whole family groans: it has been tried too many times. The joke is {trite}.

cast.say: Ha! Did I ever tell you…

scene.alt: A grandfather tells his old joke again while the family groans.

entry.def: overused and unoriginal
entry.ex: The {hackneyed} plot, a lost dog finds its way home, had been filmed a dozen times.
entry.ctx: The judges rejected the slogan as {hackneyed}: “Better than ever” had already been printed on a thousand products.
entry.etym: From hackney, an ordinary horse for hire: ridden by everyone, it was worn out with use.

mn.cue: HACKNEY: a hired horse worn out by use
mn.text: The old hired horse has carried every tourist in town and now plods along, worn out by use. An idea worn out the same way is {hackneyed}.

scene.alt: A tired old horse for hire plods along while another child waits for a ride.

entry.def: an overused phrase or idea
entry.ex: “At the end of the day” is a {cliché} that adds nothing to most sentences.
entry.ctx: The story ended with a tired {cliché}: the hero woke up, and the whole adventure had been a dream.
entry.etym: From French cliché, a printer’s metal plate used to stamp the same words over and over.

mn.cue: CLICK-AY: CLICK, the same stamp again
mn.text: Click! Click! Click! The old printing plate stamps the very same phrase on page after page. A phrase repeated that often is a {cliché}.

scene.alt: A printing robot stamps out page after page of the same tired phrase while a girl yawns.

entry.def: a dull, obvious remark offered as if it were wise or new
entry.ex: “Everything happens for a reason” was the only {platitude} the coach could offer after the loss.
entry.ctx: Instead of real advice, the speaker offered {platitudes}: “Believe in yourself,” “Never give up” and “Tomorrow is another day.”
entry.etym: From French platitude, “flatness,” from plat, flat: a platitude is a flat, dull remark.

mn.text: Uncle Victor serves up an empty plate of wisdom: “Well, it is what it is.” A flat, obvious remark offered as if it were deep is a {platitude}.

scene.alt: A man proudly offers an empty plate along with an obvious saying; a teen is unimpressed.

entry.def: dull and unimaginative; lacking poetry
entry.ex: Asked what the clouds looked like, the {prosaic} boy said only, “Clouds.”
entry.ctx: Visitors expected the castle to hide secret passages and treasure, but its history was {prosaic}: for three hundred years it had mostly stored grain.
entry.etym: From Latin prosaicus, from prosa, prose: plain, ordinary writing, as opposed to poetry.

mn.text: Zoe looks up and sees a dragon, a castle and a ship in the clouds. Sami looks up and says, “Those are clouds.” His plain, unpoetic answer is {prosaic}.

scene.alt: A girl sees a dragon in the clouds; the boy beside her just sees clouds.

entry.def: ordinary and dull; lacking imagination
entry.ex: The band’s second album was {pedestrian} compared with its brilliant first one.
entry.ctx: The menu promised adventure, but the food was {pedestrian}: plain noodles, plain chicken and a salad anyone could make at home.
entry.etym: From Latin pedester, “on foot,” from pes, foot: writing that plods along on foot, never taking flight, is pedestrian.
entry.note: As a noun, a pedestrian is a person walking. As an adjective, pedestrian usually means dull, not “on foot.”

mn.cue: PED = FOOT: plods along, never flies
mn.text: Jonah’s story plods along like a tired walker, step, step, step, with a snail for company. Writing that never takes flight is {pedestrian}.

scene.alt: A bored teen plods down the sidewalk beside a slow snail.

blocks.html: pedestrian as an adjective means dull, not "on foot." mundane means ordinary, not bad.

blocks.html: Many of these words began as pictures: trite (rubbed smooth, like a worn coin), hackneyed (a hired horse), cliché (a printer’s stamp), platitude (flatness), pedestrian (on foot). Remembering the picture helps you remember the meaning.
