blocks.html: Two Latin verbs about the eyes stand behind this whole family. specere means to look (you hear it in inspect and spectator), and videre means to see (you hear it in video and vision). In English the first shows up as spec, spic or spect, and the second as vid or vis.
spec, spic, spect = look. vid, vis = see. Ask where the looking goes: around (circumspect), inward (introspective), back (retrospect), through (perspicacious), ahead (provident).
A root is a clue, not a rule: specious comes from the Latin word for appearance, so a specious claim only looks right. Check every root against the sentence the word sits in.

entry.def: careful to think about risks before acting
entry.ex: A {circumspect} hiker checks the weather twice before setting out.
entry.ctx: Unlike his brother, who signed whatever was put in front of him, Nate was {circumspect}: he read every line of the lease and asked about each fee.
entry.etym: From Latin circumspectus, “cautious, well considered,” from circumspicere, “to look around”: circum (around) + specere (to look).

mn.text: Before Pip crosses the busy street, he looks all around: left, right and left again. Looking all around before you act is being {circumspect}.

scene.alt: A boy at a street corner looks left and right before crossing, while a car comes down the road.

entry.def: looking inward at your own thoughts and feelings
entry.ex: After the game, the {introspective} pitcher sat alone, replaying every choice he had made.
entry.ctx: Maya was chatty at parties but {introspective} in her diary, where she asked herself why she felt the way she did and what she wanted to change.
entry.etym: From Latin introspicere, “to look into”: intro (inward) + specere (to look).

mn.text: Lila holds a magnifying glass up to her own heart: she is looking inside herself. A person who looks in like that is {introspective}.

scene.alt: A girl sits quietly holding a magnifying glass, thinking about her own feelings.

entry.def: a look back at things that have already happened
entry.ex: In {retrospect}, packing three sweaters for a beach trip was silly.
entry.ctx: At the time, the move to a new town felt like a disaster; in {retrospect}, it was the best thing that ever happened to the family, since it brought them good friends and a better school.
entry.etym: From Latin retrospicere, “to look back”: retro (back) + specere (to look).
entry.note: Usually heard in the phrase “in retrospect”: looking back now.

mn.cue: RETRO SPECS: glasses that look back
mn.text: Grandpa Gus puts on his old-fashioned specs and pages through photos from fifty years ago. Looking back like that is {retrospect}.

scene.alt: A grandfather in glasses smiles over an old photo album, remembering the past.

entry.def: easy to see or notice; standing out
entry.ex: Dad’s orange hat made him {conspicuous} in the crowd at the airport.
entry.ctx: Lena hoped to slip into class unnoticed, but her bright yellow raincoat made her {conspicuous}, and every head turned when she opened the door.
entry.etym: From Latin conspicuus, “in plain sight,” from conspicere, “to look at, notice.”

mn.text: Zoe hides behind a little bush, but her balloons and party hat stick out. “I can spy you!” Ivy calls. Zoe is {conspicuous}.

scene.alt: A girl hides behind a small bush, but her party hat and balloons give her away; her friend points and laughs.

entry.def: promising good things to come; favorable
entry.ex: A sunny sky on opening day was an {auspicious} start for the new farmers’ market.
entry.ctx: The team’s first season began on an {auspicious} note: they won their opening three games, and the coach began to hope for a championship.
entry.etym: From Latin auspicium, the reading of signs in the flight of birds, from auspex, “bird watcher”: avis (bird) + specere (to look).

mn.cue: AW, SPECIAL! a rainbow on race day
mn.text: On the morning of the big race, a rainbow arches over the track and Tia gasps, “Aw, special!” A sign that things will go well is {auspicious}.

scene.alt: A runner cheers at a rainbow over the track as a bright bird flies past.

entry.def: seeming true or right at first but false underneath
entry.ex: The ad’s {specious} promise that the shoes would make anyone run faster fooled no one on the track team.
entry.ctx: Dev’s argument sounded convincing at first, but it was {specious}: when his sister checked the numbers, every one of his facts turned out to be wrong.
entry.etym: From Latin speciosus, “good-looking, showy,” from species, “appearance,” from specere (to look). It once meant simply “fair to see.”
entry.note: Specious (only seeming true) is not spacious (roomy); it comes from species, “appearance.”

mn.text: “See? Shush, don’t check!” says the salesman, because his claim only sounds right until someone looks closely. It is {specious}.

scene.alt: A sly salesman hushes a boy who is inspecting his magic beans sign with a magnifying glass.

entry.def: quick to notice and understand things; sharp-minded
entry.ex: The {perspicacious} detective noticed that the muddy boots were two sizes too small.
entry.ctx: Most readers missed the clue on page ten, but the {perspicacious} few who caught it guessed the ending long before the last chapter.
entry.etym: From Latin perspicax, “sharp-sighted,” from perspicere, “to look through”: per (through) + specere (to look).
entry.note: Perspicacious describes a sharp mind; perspicuous, a different word, describes writing that is clear.

mn.cue: PURR-SPY-CAT: she sees through it all
mn.text: The Purr-Spy Cat spots the mouse hiding by the boot that everyone else walked right past. A sharp noticer like her is {perspicacious}.

scene.alt: A sharp-eyed cat spots a mouse hiding behind a boot.

entry.def: planning wisely for the future, especially by saving
entry.ex: The {provident} squirrel buried nuts all autumn and ate well all winter.
entry.ctx: Her grandfather had been {provident}, setting aside a little money every month for forty years, so the family did not panic when the factory closed.
entry.etym: From Latin providens, “foreseeing,” from providere, “to see ahead, provide for”: pro (ahead) + videre (to see).

mn.cue: PROVIDE-ent: see winter coming, PROVIDE for it
mn.text: The squirrel sees winter coming and provides for it, one basket of food at a time. Seeing ahead and saving is being {provident}.

scene.alt: A busy squirrel fills a basket of food for the winter beside a sign that says for winter.

entry.def: to picture something in the mind, especially something that could happen
entry.ex: Ada could {envision} the empty lot as a garden full of sunflowers.
entry.ctx: Where others saw only a dusty old barn, Rosa could {envision} a bright little theater, and she spent the summer turning that picture into a plan.
entry.etym: Made in English in the early 1900s from en- (into) + vision, from Latin videre (to see).

mn.cue: EN-VISION: see it IN your head
mn.text: Before Omar saws a single board, he can see the whole treehouse in his head. To {envision} is to see it in your mind first.

labels.text: EN-VISION: see it IN your mind

scene.alt: A man stands by a tree and a pile of boards, picturing the treehouse he will build.

entry.def: a person’s face, or the look on it
entry.ex: The old captain’s weathered {visage} broke into a wide grin.
entry.ctx: The portrait showed the queen’s stern {visage}, but her letters reveal a warm, funny woman behind that serious face.
entry.etym: From Old French visage, “face,” from vis (face), from Latin visus, “a look, sight,” from videre (to see).

mn.cue: VIS-AGE: the face shows your AGE
mn.text: Grandpa’s face in the mirror shows his age: every smile line from eighty happy years. That face is his {visage}.

labels.text: VIS-AGE: the face shows your AGE

scene.alt: An old man with a gray beard smiles at his face in a tall mirror.

blocks.html: specious sounds like "special" or "spacious" but means falsely convincing. perspicacious (sharp-minded) describes a person; perspicuous (clearly expressed) describes writing.

blocks.cap: The prefix tells you which way the eyes are turned.

blocks.html: Look-alikes: specious (falsely convincing) is not special or spacious. Perspicacious (sharp-minded, said of a person) is not perspicuous (clear, said of writing).

blocks.html: Half of these words praise courage and half describe fear. Each one has its own shade: a valiant person fights hard, an intrepid one explores without trembling, a plucky one stands up even when small. On the fearful side, a timid person is shy, an apprehensive one worries about what is coming, and a craven one runs away in shame.
Two Latin roots help. timere means to fear: timid, timorous. trepidus means trembling, alarmed: trepidation is trembling fear, and intrepid (in- = not) means not trembling.
Watch the tone. Audacious can be praise (an audacious rescue) or blame (an audacious lie). The sentence tells you which.

entry.def: brave and determined, especially in a hard fight
entry.ex: The {valiant} firefighters carried every last puppy out of the burning shelter.
entry.ctx: Though the little team was outnumbered and exhausted, it made a {valiant} stand in the final minutes and held the champions to a tie.
entry.etym: From Old French vaillant, “stalwart, brave,” from valoir (to be worthy), from Latin valere, “to be strong.”

mn.cue: VAL the ANT: small but VALIANT
mn.text: Val the ant plants her feet and faces the hungry crow to guard her hill. Tiny Val is {valiant}.

scene.alt: A tiny ant stands bravely in front of a big crow to protect its anthill.

entry.def: fearless and adventurous
entry.ex: The {intrepid} explorer paddled alone up the unmapped river.
entry.ctx: Most of the divers turned back at the mouth of the dark sea cave, but the {intrepid} pair swam on, eager to see what lay inside.
entry.etym: From Latin intrepidus, “unshaken, not alarmed”: in- (not) + trepidus (alarmed, trembling).
entry.note: Intrepid has nothing to do with trips: it means not trembling.

mn.text: Trepid means trembling, and in- means not. Tia steps into the dark cave with her lantern without a single shiver: she is {intrepid}.

scene.alt: An explorer with a lantern walks calmly into a dark cave as a bat flutters past.

entry.def: boldly daring, sometimes to the point of rudeness
entry.ex: Asking the famous chef for her secret recipe on live TV was an {audacious} move.
entry.ctx: The plan was {audacious}: the students would build a full-size rowboat in two weeks and sail it across the lake, though none of them had ever built anything bigger than a birdhouse.
entry.etym: From Latin audax, “bold, daring,” from audere, “to dare.”
entry.note: Audacious can be praise (an audacious rescue) or blame (an audacious lie); the context decides.

mn.cue: AWE-DACIOUS: so bold it leaves us in AWE
mn.text: Little Pip marches up to the king and asks to try on his crown. The whole court gasps in awe at such an {audacious} request.

scene.alt: A small boy points at the king’s crown and asks to try it on while the king looks shocked.

entry.def: not discouraged by danger or difficulty
entry.ex: The {dauntless} mail carrier delivered every letter through the blizzard.
entry.ctx: After three failed launches, a weaker team might have quit, but the {dauntless} engineers fixed the valve, checked every bolt and tried again the next morning.
entry.etym: Daunt comes from Old French danter, “to tame, subdue,” from Latin domitare (to tame); add -less, “without.”

mn.cue: DAWN-TLESS: out at DAWN in any storm
mn.text: Every day at dawn, through snow and howling wind, Greta delivers the mail. No storm can discourage her: she is {dauntless}.

scene.alt: A mail carrier marches through a snowstorm toward a mailbox with a letter.

entry.def: brave and spirited, especially against the odds
entry.ex: The {plucky} little goalie stopped shot after shot from the older team.
entry.ctx: The puppy was the smallest in the litter, but it was {plucky}: it marched right up to the big farm dogs and demanded a share of the bone.

mn.text: The smallest duckling plucks up her courage and leaps into the pond first, ahead of all the big ducks. That brave little bird is {plucky}.

scene.alt: The smallest duckling leaps into the water first while two big ducks hang back nervously.

entry.def: easily frightened; shy
entry.ex: The {timid} kitten hid under the bed whenever the doorbell rang.
entry.ctx: At first Sofia was too {timid} to raise her hand, but by spring she was leading the class debate.
entry.etym: From Latin timidus, “fearful,” from timere, “to fear.”

mn.text: When the friendly puppy trots up, little Tim hides behind his mom’s legs. Shy, easily frightened Tim is {timid}.

scene.alt: A toddler named Tim hides behind his mother as a friendly puppy says hello.

entry.def: fearful and nervous by nature
entry.ex: The {timorous} deer froze at the snap of a twig.
entry.ctx: Unlike his bold older sister, Leo was a {timorous} child who checked under the bed every night and never went near the creek alone.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin timorosus, “fearful,” from Latin timor (fear), from timere (to fear).

mn.cue: TIM-OR-MOUSE: a mouse full of fear
mn.text: Timmy the mouse trembles at every creak of the floor and every shadow on the wall. A creature that is always afraid is {timorous}.

scene.alt: A tiny mouse trembles with fear beside a piece of cheese.

entry.def: worried that something bad may happen
entry.ex: Jonah was {apprehensive} about his first day at the new school.
entry.ctx: The sailors grew {apprehensive} as the sky darkened and the wind picked up, and the captain ordered everyone to tie down the sails before the storm hit.
entry.etym: From Latin apprehendere, “to seize, grasp” (ad + prehendere); to apprehend a danger is to grasp in your mind that it may come.

mn.text: The hen spots a fox sniffing around the coop and cannot sleep all night, worrying about what he might do. She is {apprehensive}.

scene.alt: A worried hen watches a sneaky fox at the edge of the farm.

entry.def: nervous fear about something that is about to happen
entry.ex: With some {trepidation}, Kai stepped onto the stage for his first violin solo.
entry.ctx: The villagers watched the rising river with {trepidation}, knowing that one more night of rain could flood every street in town.
entry.etym: From Latin trepidatio, “alarm, trembling,” from trepidare, “to tremble.”

mn.text: Before his solo, Kai’s knees knock and his bow shakes. That trembling fear of what is about to happen is {trepidation}.

scene.alt: A boy with a violin trembles nervously on stage before his solo.

entry.def: shamefully cowardly
entry.ex: The {craven} guard dropped his post and ran at the first sound of trouble.
entry.ctx: Instead of admitting that he had broken the vase, the {craven} prince blamed a servant and hid in the tower until the fuss was over.

mn.text: When the cat creeps close, the raven flies off and leaves the little birds to fend for themselves. That shameful coward is a {craven} raven.

scene.alt: A raven flies off in a panic, leaving a small bird alone as a cat sneaks closer.

blocks.html: audacious can praise boldness or criticize rudeness; read the context. intrepid has nothing to do with trips: it comes from in- (not) and trepidus (alarmed).

head: word
brave or fearful?
its special shade
blocks.cap: Same field, different shades.

blocks.html: Craven is much harsher than timid. A timid person is shy and easily scared; a craven person abandons others to save himself. Calling someone craven is an insult.

blocks.html: Rules can be held tight or let loose. The first five words describe strictness, from the careful thoroughness of rigorous work to the cruel harshness of draconian laws. The next four describe going easy, from the mercy of a lenient judge to the carelessness of a lax guard. The last, forbearance, names the patience it takes to hold back.
Notice the tone. Rigorous and exacting usually praise; draconian always criticizes. Lenient can be kind; lax is a complaint.

entry.def: strict and exact about rules or standards
entry.ex: The pool has {stringent} rules: no running, no glass and no swimming without a lifeguard.
entry.ctx: The lab’s safety rules are {stringent}; a student who forgets goggles even once is sent out for the day.
entry.etym: From Latin stringens, “drawing tight,” from stringere, “to bind tight.”

mn.text: Coach Ada keeps her team rules pulled as tight as a string: no slack, no exceptions. Rules that tight are {stringent}.

scene.alt: A coach pulls a rope tight beside a sign that says team rules.

entry.def: extremely thorough and careful
entry.ex: After a {rigorous} search of the house, Mom found the missing key inside the cereal box.
entry.ctx: The bridge opened only after {rigorous} testing: loaded trucks rolled across it for a week, and engineers checked every bolt and every weld twice.
entry.etym: From Latin rigor, “stiffness, hardness,” from rigere (to be stiff).

mn.cue: check the RIG, ALL of US
mn.text: Before the sailboat race, all of us check every rope and knot of the rig, then check them again. An inspection that careful is {rigorous}.

scene.alt: Three teens inspect a sailboat with a magnifying glass, a checklist and a rope before a race.

entry.def: demanding great effort, care or skill
entry.ex: The {exacting} piano teacher made Rosa play the hard measure twenty times.
entry.ctx: Repairing old clocks is {exacting} work: a single bent spring or a speck of dust can stop the whole movement.
entry.etym: From the verb exact, “to demand,” from Latin exigere, “to drive out, demand”: ex (out) + agere (to drive).

mn.text: Chef Lin makes her new cook measure the sugar again and again until it is exact. A boss who demands that much care is {exacting}.

scene.alt: A chef points sternly while a nervous young cook measures sugar with a spoon beside a set of scales.

entry.def: serious and strict in manner
entry.ex: One {stern} look from the librarian quieted the whole table.
entry.ctx: Grandpa’s voice was {stern} when he found the open gate, but he was not cruel; he simply explained why the sheep must never be left loose again.
entry.note: A different word, the noun stern, is the back end of a ship.

mn.text: Principal Victor gives the noisy hallway one long stare, and everyone falls silent. A serious, strict look like that is {stern}.

scene.alt: A principal with crossed arms stares at two quiet, worried children.

entry.def: far too harsh and severe
entry.ex: Taking away recess for a whole month for one late homework is {draconian}.
entry.ctx: Under the old king’s {draconian} laws, stealing a single loaf of bread could cost a family its home, so the new queen’s first act was to soften them.
entry.etym: Named for Draco, a lawmaker of ancient Athens whose laws punished even small crimes with great severity.

mn.text: In the dragon’s castle the rule is: take one cookie and get no dessert for a whole year. Rules that harsh are {draconian}.

props.text: 1 COOKIE = NO DESSERT FOR A YEAR

scene.alt: A grumpy dragon stands under a banner with a very harsh rule while a boy holding one cookie looks shocked.

entry.def: merciful; less strict or harsh than expected
entry.ex: The {lenient} referee let the little kids redo their throw-ins.
entry.ctx: Most judges would have fined the young driver heavily, but this one was {lenient}: she let him off with a warning and a safety class.
entry.etym: From Latin leniens, “softening,” from lenire, “to soften, soothe,” from lenis (soft, mild).

mn.cue: LEAN-IENT: the judge LEANS toward mercy
mn.text: The judge leans down, smiles at the nervous boy who broke a window, and says, “Just fix it and say sorry.” She is {lenient}.

scene.alt: A smiling judge goes easy on a nervous boy.

entry.def: quick to give others what they want; not strict
entry.ex: The {indulgent} aunt let the twins eat birthday cake for breakfast.
entry.ctx: Their grandparents were so {indulgent} that the children came home from every visit expecting dessert before dinner and a bedtime of midnight.
entry.etym: From Latin indulgere, “to be kind to, give way to.”

mn.cue: IN-DULGE: Granny says yes to everything
mn.text: Granny Mae indulges every wish: cake for breakfast, a pony ride, staying up late. A granny who gives the kids whatever they want is {indulgent}.

scene.alt: A smiling grandmother hands a cake to two cheering children.

entry.def: allowing a great deal of freedom
entry.ex: The camp had a {permissive} bedtime: campers could stay up as long as they were quiet.
entry.ctx: The new school was far more {permissive} than her old one; students chose their own seats, ate snacks in class and could leave the room without asking.
entry.etym: From permit, from Latin permittere, “to let pass, allow”: per (through) + mittere (to let go).

mn.text: At Uncle Omar’s house you have permission for everything: pillow fights, pancakes at midnight, a fort in the living room. His house is {permissive}.

scene.alt: A relaxed uncle shrugs and smiles while children have a pillow fight in the living room.

entry.def: not strict or careful enough; loose
entry.ex: Security at the cookie jar was {lax}, and the dog took full advantage.
entry.ctx: The inspector blamed the leak on {lax} maintenance: no one had checked the pipes in years, and the warning light had been ignored for months.
entry.etym: From Latin laxus, “loose, slack,” the same root as relax.

mn.cue: reLAXed: too relaxed to do the job
mn.text: The guard is so relaxed that he naps in his chair while the dog helps himself to the cookies. That careless guard is {lax}.

scene.alt: A guard naps in his chair while a dog sneaks toward a cookie jar under a no dogs sign.

entry.def: patient self-control; holding back from anger or punishment
entry.ex: The babysitter showed great {forbearance} when the twins painted the kitchen door blue.
entry.ctx: The lender could have taken the farm after the bad harvest, but he showed {forbearance}, giving the family another year to pay.

mn.text: The cubs tug the big bear’s ears and climb on his back, but he never growls; he just waits. That patient holding back is {forbearance}.

scene.alt: A big calm bear lets two playful cubs climb on him and tug at him.

blocks.html: rigorous praises thoroughness; draconian criticizes harshness. lax is about loose rules; lenient is about mercy toward someone.

tone

blocks.html: Lax describes rules or care that are too loose (lax security). Lenient describes a person who goes easy on someone (a lenient judge). A judge can be lenient; a lock can only be lax.

blocks.html: All ten of these verbs mean speaking against someone, but they differ in three ways: how hard (a gentle warning or a furious scolding), how official (a friend’s comment or a vote by a council) and how (scolding, mocking or belittling).

From gentlest to harshest, roughly: admonish (warn gently) → reproach (show disappointment) → rebuke and reprimand (scold sharply or formally) → chastise and berate (scold severely, angrily, at length). Censure and denounce are formal and public; deride and disparage belittle with scorn.

entry.def: to criticize strongly and officially
entry.ex: The school board voted to {censure} the member who leaked the private report.
entry.ctx: The league did not suspend the coach, but it did {censure} him in a public statement, calling his behavior toward the referee unacceptable.
entry.etym: From Latin censura, the office of a Roman censor, an official who judged citizens’ conduct, from censere, “to assess.”
entry.note: Censure (to blame formally) is not censor (to cut out parts of a book, film or letter).

mn.cue: SEN-SURE: the council is SURE you were wrong
mn.text: The whole council stands up and votes together: they are sure their member broke the rules. To {censure} is to blame someone officially.

scene.alt: Two council members point at a man who broke the rules, under a banner.

entry.def: to scold someone sharply
entry.ex: The lifeguard {rebuked} the boys for running on the wet deck.
entry.ctx: Instead of praising her for finishing early, the teacher {rebuked} her for rushing, pointing to three careless mistakes on the first page.

mn.text: When Kai knocks the books off the shelf a second time, the librarian snaps, “Not again, young man!” She {rebukes} him sharply.

scene.alt: A librarian sharply scolds a boy who has knocked books onto the floor again.

entry.def: to tell someone you are disappointed in what they did
entry.ex: Grandma did not yell; she simply {reproached} him with a sad shake of her head.
entry.ctx: Lila {reproached} her brother for forgetting their mother’s birthday, not angrily but in a quiet voice that made him feel even worse.

mn.text: Mom approaches the broken lamp, sighs and says, “I expected better from you.” To {reproach} someone is to show your disappointment in them.

scene.alt: A disappointed mother looks at a knocked-over lamp while her son shrugs sheepishly beside a ball.

entry.def: to warn or scold gently but firmly
entry.ex: The coach {admonished} the players to drink water before practice.
entry.ctx: The librarian did not shout at the giggling students; she simply {admonished} them, with a finger to her lips, to keep their voices down.
entry.etym: From Latin admonere, “to remind, warn”: ad (to) + monere (to warn).
entry.note: Admonish is the gentlest word in this topic.

mn.text: “Helmet on, please,” says Mom, in her gentle but firm Mom-ish way. To {admonish} is to warn someone gently but firmly.

scene.alt: A mother gently reminds her daughter to put on her helmet before riding her bike.

entry.def: to scold formally, as a boss or official does
entry.ex: The manager {reprimanded} the clerk for leaving the register open.
entry.ctx: Because it was his third late arrival this month, the captain {reprimanded} the guard in writing, and a copy went into his file.
entry.etym: From French réprimande, from Latin reprimenda, “things to be held back,” from reprimere, “to press back, check.”

mn.cue: a RAP on the HAND from the boss
mn.text: The boss calls Dev into her office and gives him a formal rap on the hand for the late report. To {reprimand} is to scold officially.

scene.alt: A boss in her office formally scolds a young worker holding a late report.

entry.def: to scold or punish severely
entry.ex: The farmer {chastised} his son for leaving the barn door open all night.
entry.ctx: The critic {chastised} the city for letting the old theater fall apart, calling the neglect a disgrace to everyone who had ever loved the place.

mn.text: The farmer chases the goats out of his garden, scolding them hard the whole way. To {chastise} is to scold or punish severely.

scene.alt: An angry farmer chases two goats out of his garden, scolding them.

entry.def: to scold angrily and at length
entry.ex: The fan {berated} the umpire for ten straight minutes over one call.
entry.ctx: Rather than calmly explain the mistake, the chef {berated} the new cook in front of the whole kitchen, shouting about the burnt rice long after the pot was cleaned.

mn.text: Rex rants at the umpire for ten whole minutes over one call, shouting and stomping. To {berate} someone is to scold them angrily and at length.

scene.alt: A furious fan shouts on and on at a tired umpire.

entry.def: to mock and make fun of with scorn
entry.ex: Some kids {derided} her homemade costume, but it won first prize.
entry.ctx: Experts once {derided} the idea of a phone without buttons as a silly toy; within a few years, nearly everyone carried one.
entry.etym: From Latin deridere, “to laugh at, mock”: de (down) + ridere (to laugh), the root of ridiculous.

mn.text: The older kids point and laugh at Pip’s homemade cart: “Ha! You call that a ride?” To {deride} is to mock with scorn.

scene.alt: Two older boys point and laugh at a younger boy’s homemade wagon.

entry.def: to speak of something as if it had little worth
entry.ex: He {disparaged} his sister’s painting as “just a bunch of blobs.”
entry.ctx: It is easy to {disparage} a small library as old-fashioned, but for many families in town it is the only place with free books and computers.
entry.etym: From Old French desparagier, “to marry beneath one’s rank,” and so to lower or degrade.

mn.text: Victor stands at the curb and disses the whole parade: “Silly floats, tiny band, nothing special.” To {disparage} something is to talk about it as if it had little worth.

scene.alt: A sour man with crossed arms belittles a cheerful parade of teens with a drum and a flag.

entry.def: to declare publicly that something is wrong or evil
entry.ex: The mayor {denounced} the dumping of trash in the river.
entry.ctx: Within hours, every club in the league had {denounced} the vandalism, calling it a shameful attack on a field that children used every day.
entry.etym: From Latin denuntiare, “to announce officially, warn”: de + nuntiare (to announce).

mn.text: From the town hall steps, the mayor announces to everyone that dumping trash in the river is wrong and must stop. To {denounce} is to declare publicly that something is wrong.

scene.alt: A mayor with a megaphone publicly speaks out against dumping trash, beside a save our river sign.

blocks.html: censure (formal blame) is not censor (to remove material). admonish is the gentlest word here; berate is among the harshest.

blocks.cap: Three questions sort the ten words: how hard, how official, and how.

blocks.html: Censure and censor look alike. To censure is to blame formally (the senate censured him). To censor is to cut out material (the letter was censored).

blocks.html: Anger comes in many sizes and flavors. Some words tell how strong it is (vexed is mild; livid and irate are hot). Some tell why (indignant anger is about unfairness). Some describe a temper rather than a moment (irascible, petulant). And some name anger that has hardened over time into ill will (rancor, animosity, enmity).
Latin ira means anger: you can hear it in irate and irascible. A moment of anger: irate, livid, wrath. A temper: irascible, petulant. Long-lasting ill will: rancor, animosity, enmity.

entry.def: angry because something seems unfair
entry.ex: Ivy was {indignant} when she was blamed for the vase the cat had broken.
entry.ctx: The players were {indignant}, not because they lost, but because the referee had ignored three clear fouls against their goalie.
entry.etym: From Latin indignari, “to consider unworthy, be angry at”: in- (not) + dignus (worthy).
entry.note: Indignant anger is about unfairness, not just any annoyance.

mn.text: Ivy is blamed for the broken vase she never touched. “I did NOT!” she cries, angry at the unfairness. She is {indignant}.

scene.alt: A girl wrongly blamed for a broken vase protests angrily while the cat who did it sneaks away.

entry.def: very angry, often loudly so
entry.ex: Usually the calmest man on the street, Mr. Lee was {irate} when he found his garden trampled.
entry.ctx: After waiting four hours on the runway with no food or news, the passengers were {irate}, and several of them shouted at the crew.
entry.etym: From Latin iratus, “angry,” from ira (anger).

mn.text: Rex finds his soup stone cold, turns red and shouts, “I rate this place zero stars!” He is {irate}.

scene.alt: A furious customer shouts at a worried waiter holding a bowl of soup.

entry.def: furious; also, bluish-gray in color
entry.ex: Dad was {livid} when he saw the scratch on his new car.
entry.ctx: The coach was not merely annoyed but {livid}; his face turned red, and he kicked the water bucket across the field after the third missed goal.
entry.etym: From Latin lividus, “bluish, black and blue,” the color of a bruise; the sense “furious” came much later.
entry.note: In everyday use livid means furious. Its old meaning, bluish-gray like a bruise, still shows up in older books.

mn.text: When the goat eats his prize pie, Farmer Gus is so furious he flips his lid. He is {livid}.

scene.alt: A furious old farmer shouts at a happy goat that has eaten his pie.

entry.def: easily angered; quick-tempered
entry.ex: The {irascible} old cat hissed at anyone who came near its basket.
entry.ctx: The {irascible} editor would fly into a rage over a single misplaced comma, so new writers checked their work three times before handing it in.
entry.etym: From Latin irascibilis, from irasci, “to grow angry,” from ira (anger).

mn.cue: IRA-SCIBLE: IRA flares up at everything
mn.text: Old Ira snaps at the mail carrier, the wind and even the birds; the smallest thing sets him off. Ira is {irascible}.

scene.alt: A cranky man named Ira yells at a chirping bird while the startled mail carrier looks on.

entry.def: childishly sulky and bad-tempered
entry.ex: Told to turn off his game, the {petulant} boy pouted, sulked and stomped up the stairs.
entry.ctx: Instead of congratulating the winner, the {petulant} runner-up stomped off the court, refused to shake hands and sulked on the bus all the way home.

mn.cue: PET-ulant: sulks like a spoiled PET
mn.text: When he doesn’t get a second treat, Biscuit the puppy turns his back and sulks. What a {petulant} pet!

scene.alt: A puppy turns away and sulks because the girl will give him only one treat.

entry.def: to annoy, puzzle or frustrate
entry.ex: The squeaky door {vexed} Grandpa all winter.
entry.ctx: The math problem {vexed} the whole class for a week; every answer they tried came out a little wrong, and no one could see why.
entry.etym: From Latin vexare, “to shake, disturb.”

mn.text: Tap, tap, tap: every morning at five, a crow pecks at Grandpa’s window. Those pecks {vex} him no end.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather sits up in bed while a crow taps at his window at dawn.

entry.def: fierce anger
entry.ex: The cat’s {wrath} was terrible when it was lifted into the bathtub.
entry.ctx: Fearing the {wrath} of the head chef, the cooks scrubbed every pot until it shone before she came back from her break.

mn.text: Try to give the cat a bath and you will see true {wrath}: hissing, splashing, fur-on-end fury.

labels.text: WRATH = a cat in a BATH

scene.alt: A furious cat leaps hissing out of a bucket of bath water while a boy holding soap looks shocked.

entry.def: bitter resentment that lasts a long time
entry.ex: Years after the contest, he still spoke of the judges with {rancor}, a bitterness that never faded.
entry.ctx: Though the two neighbors had settled the fence dispute in court long ago, the {rancor} between them lingered, and they still refused to wave to each other.
entry.etym: From Latin rancor, “rankness, a grudge,” related to rancidus (stinking), the source of rancid.

mn.cue: r-ANCHOR: a grudge you drag for years
mn.text: Thirty years after losing the pie contest, Victor still drags his grudge around like a heavy anchor. Bitter resentment that lasts that long is {rancor}.

scene.alt: A grumpy man drags a heavy anchor on a chain, still brooding over an old grudge.

entry.def: strong dislike or hostility
entry.ex: There was no {animosity} between the rivals; they shook hands after every match.
entry.ctx: The {animosity} between the two clubs ran so deep that the league scheduled their games on different days to keep the fans apart.

roots.means: the quality of being full of

entry.etym: From Latin animositas, “boldness, high spirit,” from animus (spirit, mind); the sense of ill will came later.

mn.text: The cat and the dog next door hiss and growl at each other across the fence every single day. Their {animosity} is plain to see.

scene.alt: An angry dog and an angry cat glare at each other across a garden fence.

entry.def: deep, lasting hatred between enemies
entry.ex: The {enmity} between the two families lasted three generations.
entry.ctx: The old {enmity} between the river towns finally ended when a flood forced them to work side by side, and they found they liked each other.
entry.etym: From Old French enemistie, from Latin inimicus, “enemy”: in- (not) + amicus (friend).

mn.text: The kings of the two castles have been enemies for a hundred years, and neither will even nod to the other. Their {enmity} never fades.

scene.alt: Two kings with crossed arms glare at each other from opposite sides, each beside his own flag.

blocks.html: indignant anger is about unfairness, not about any annoyance. livid first meant bluish, like a bruise; in everyday use it means furious.

head: kind of anger
words
rows: a flash of anger right now
blocks.cap: Sort the words by what kind of anger they name.

blocks.html: Livid first meant bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Most readers now take it to mean furious, and that is the sense tests expect; the color sense survives in older writing (a livid sky).

Vocabulary.com Dictionary (definitions checked)

blocks.html: Some people notice everything; some notice nothing. These words describe both, and the steps in between: taking something in through the senses (perceive), telling things apart (discern), understanding something deep (fathom) and gathering facts a little at a time (glean). The adjectives describe watchful people (vigilant, wary), aware people (cognizant) and people who miss what is right in front of them (oblivious, heedless).
Paying attention: perceive, discern, vigilant, wary, cognizant. Not paying attention: oblivious, heedless. Hard to notice: subtle.

entry.def: to notice or become aware of, through the senses or the mind
entry.ex: Owls can {perceive} the tiny rustle of a mouse in the grass.
entry.ctx: At first the change was too small to {perceive}, but after a month everyone could see that the little tree had grown taller than the fence.
entry.etym: From Latin percipere, “to take hold of completely”: per (thoroughly) + capere (to take).

mn.text: Sami peers into the night sky and receives a tiny flash of light: a shooting star! To {perceive} is to take in something with your senses.

scene.alt: A boy with a telescope spots a shooting star in the night sky.

entry.def: to notice or tell apart, often with effort
entry.ex: In the fog, Dad could barely {discern} the outline of the barn.
entry.ctx: The twins look alike to strangers, but their friends can easily {discern} which is which: Mia always tilts her head when she listens.
entry.etym: From Latin discernere, “to separate, tell apart”: dis (apart) + cernere (to sift).

mn.text: Two gems look exactly alike, but Ada’s sharp eye can tell that this one is real and that one is glass. To {discern} is to tell things apart.

scene.alt: A woman studies two identical-looking gems with a magnifying glass to tell the real one from the fake.

entry.def: to understand something fully, after much thought
entry.ex: Pip could not {fathom} why anyone would put pineapple on a pancake.
entry.ctx: Scientists are still trying to {fathom} how the birds find their way home across thousands of miles of open ocean.
entry.etym: From Old English fæðm, “outstretched arms”; a fathom became a unit of six feet for measuring the depth of water, and to fathom came to mean to get to the bottom of something.
entry.note: Often used with “can’t”: I can’t fathom why he left.

mn.cue: FATHOM: get to the BOTTOM of it
mn.text: Sailors once lowered a weighted rope to find the depth of the sea in fathoms. To {fathom} a mystery is to get all the way to the bottom of it.

scene.alt: A sailor in a rowboat lowers a rope to measure the depth of the sea while a whale swims nearby.

entry.def: to gather information bit by bit
entry.ex: From the muddy paw prints, Lila {gleaned} that the dog had been in the garden.
entry.ctx: The reporter could not interview the mayor, so she {gleaned} what she could from old speeches, news clips and a few chats with neighbors.
entry.etym: From Old French glener, “to gather grain left behind after the harvest”; the sense of gathering facts came later.

mn.cue: GLEAN = CLEAN UP every last bit
mn.text: After the harvest, Nana Lou walks the field and picks up every last stalk the reapers missed. In the same way, a careful reader can {glean} facts bit by bit.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a straw hat gathers the last bits of the harvest into a basket.

entry.def: aware; knowing about something
entry.ex: The hikers were {cognizant} of the park’s bear rules because they had read every sign at the trailhead.
entry.ctx: The new principal was {cognizant} of the school’s problems before she arrived; she had read every report and talked with dozens of parents.
entry.etym: From cognizance, from Old French conoissance, “knowledge,” from Latin cognoscere, “to get to know.”
entry.note: Usually followed by “of”: cognizant of the risk.

mn.cue: reCOGNIZE-ant: you recognize what is going on
mn.text: Dev recognizes the cracked ice and the warning sign, so he stays on the shore. He is {cognizant} of the danger.

scene.alt: A teen in winter clothes points at a thin ice warning sign and stays off the frozen pond.

entry.def: watchful and alert for danger or trouble
entry.ex: The {vigilant} lifeguard never took her eyes off the water and spotted the struggling swimmer in seconds.
entry.ctx: During the dry summer, rangers stayed {vigilant}, climbing the fire tower every hour to scan the hills for the first wisp of smoke.
entry.etym: From Latin vigilare, “to stay awake, keep watch,” from vigil (awake).

mn.cue: a VIGIL: awake and watching all night
mn.text: All night long the old owl keeps a vigil over the henhouse, eyes wide open, watching for foxes. She is {vigilant}.

scene.alt: A wide-eyed owl on a fence keeps watch at night and spots a sneaking fox.

entry.def: cautious about possible danger or trickery
entry.ex: The stray cat was {wary} of strangers but loved the girl who fed it.
entry.ctx: Burned once by a deal that sounded too good to be true, Grandpa was {wary} of the smooth salesman and asked to see everything in writing.
entry.note: Wary (cautious) is not weary (tired). A weary hiker wants to rest; a wary hiker watches for bears.

mn.text: A sign says “Beware of the goose,” so Kai tiptoes past the pond, watching the goose every step. He is {wary}.

scene.alt: A boy tiptoes cautiously past an angry goose and a beware of goose sign.

entry.def: not aware of what is happening around you
entry.ex: Lost in her book, Maya was {oblivious} to the rain soaking her shoes.
entry.ctx: The tourists were so busy taking pictures that they were {oblivious} to the sign warning that the tide was coming in fast.
entry.etym: From Latin obliviosus, “forgetful,” from oblivisci, “to forget.”
entry.note: Followed by “to” or “of”: oblivious to the noise.

mn.text: Felix bobs his head to the songs in his headphones, “Oh, bliss!”, while the dog trots off with his sandwich. He is {oblivious}.

scene.alt: A man listening to music on a bench does not notice a dog running off with his sandwich.

entry.def: paying no attention to warnings or dangers; careless
entry.ex: {Heedless} of the wet-paint sign, Pip plopped down on the bench and ruined his shorts.
entry.ctx: The young pilot was not brave but {heedless}: he ignored every storm warning and flew straight into the thunderclouds.

mn.text: Pip pays no heed to the “Wet Paint” sign and sits right down on the bench. He is {heedless}.

scene.alt: A boy happily sits on a freshly painted bench, ignoring the wet paint sign.

entry.def: so slight or delicate that it is hard to notice
entry.ex: The soup had a {subtle} hint of lemon.
entry.ctx: The change in the painting was {subtle}; only an expert noticed that one tiny boat had been moved from the left side of the harbor to the right.
entry.etym: From Latin subtilis, “fine, thin, precise.” The b was added to the English spelling to match the Latin and was never pronounced.

mn.text: The b in subtle makes no sound at all, so you hardly notice it is there. A difference that slight is {subtle}.

scene.alt: An old professor peers through a magnifying glass, comparing two nearly identical paintings.

blocks.html: wary (cautious) is not weary (tired). oblivious is followed by "to" or "of": oblivious to the noise.

head: watchful
aware
unaware
blocks.cap: Watchful, aware and unaware.

blocks.html: Wary and weary differ by one letter. Wary means cautious; weary means tired. Oblivious takes “to” or “of”: oblivious to the noise, oblivious of the time.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories
Vocabulary.com Dictionary (definitions checked)

blocks.html: How often does it happen? These ten words answer that question in different ways. Some mean now and then, at no set time (sporadic, intermittent). Some mean again and again (recurrent, continual, habitual), and one means on a regular schedule (periodic). The rest mean without stopping (continuous, incessant, unremitting, persistent).
The famous pair: continual means again and again, with breaks (a dripping faucet); continuous means going on without a break (a flowing river).

entry.def: happening now and then, at irregular times
entry.ex: We heard only {sporadic} birdsong in the cold woods: a chirp here, then nothing for an hour.
entry.ctx: The town’s internet service was {sporadic}: it might work all morning, vanish for an hour, return for ten minutes and then fail again.
entry.etym: From Greek sporadikos, “scattered,” related to spora, “a sowing,” the source of spore.

mn.cue: SPORE-adic: popping up here and there
mn.text: After the rain, mushrooms pop up from scattered spores: one here, two there, none over there. They appear at {sporadic} spots and times.

scene.alt: A boy points at mushrooms that have popped up here and there in the forest.

entry.def: stopping and starting again, at irregular times
entry.ex: The forecast called for {intermittent} showers, stopping and starting all afternoon.
entry.ctx: The signal from the stranded ship was {intermittent}; it would crackle for a few seconds, go silent for minutes, then crackle again.
entry.etym: From Latin intermittere, “to leave off for a while”: inter (between) + mittere (to let go).

mn.text: The rain stops, starts and stops again, so Lila opens and shuts her umbrella all afternoon. The rain is {intermittent}.

scene.alt: A girl with an umbrella looks puzzled as a rain cloud and the sun take turns in the sky.

entry.def: never stopping, often to the point of annoyance
entry.ex: The puppy’s {incessant} barking went on all night without a single pause.
entry.ctx: After three days of {incessant} rain, without even an hour of sunshine, the creek rose over the road.
entry.etym: From Latin incessans, “unceasing”: in- (not) + cessare (to stop).

mn.text: The ants march across the picnic blanket all day long, never stopping for a moment. Their marching is {incessant}.

scene.alt: A line of ants marches nonstop toward a pie while a girl stands with her hands on her hips.

entry.def: done regularly, out of long practice; usual
entry.ex: Grandpa’s {habitual} morning walk, the same route every day for forty years, always ends at the bakery.
entry.ctx: Being late was not a one-time slip for Max but a {habitual} problem; he missed the first bell nearly every day of the term.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin habitualis, from Latin habitus, “condition, habit.”

mn.text: Every morning at seven, Grandpa Gus walks the dog, reads the paper and drinks one cup of tea, always in that order. It is his {habitual} routine.

scene.alt: A grandfather reads his morning paper beside a cup of tea and a sleeping dog, as he does every day.

entry.def: happening at regular intervals
entry.ex: The car needs {periodic} oil changes, one every five thousand miles, like clockwork.
entry.ctx: The comet makes {periodic} visits to our skies, returning roughly every seventy-six years, so most people see it only once in a lifetime.
entry.etym: From Greek periodos, “a going around, a cycle”: peri (around) + hodos (way).

mn.cue: PERIOD-ic: like the bell every PERIOD
mn.text: The school bell rings at the end of every class period, right on schedule. Its ringing is {periodic}.

scene.alt: The school bell rings on schedule as students head to their next class.

entry.def: happening again and again
entry.ex: Lost keys are a {recurrent} problem in our house; they go missing again every few weeks.
entry.ctx: Flooding is a {recurrent} danger in the valley; it has returned every few springs for as long as anyone can remember.
entry.etym: From Latin recurrere, “to run back, return”: re (back) + currere (to run).

mn.cue: RE-CURRENT: the current brings it back
mn.text: Kai tosses the beach ball out, and the waves carry it back to him, again and again and again. Its return is {recurrent}.

scene.alt: A wave carries a beach ball back to a laughing boy again and again.

entry.def: happening again and again, with short breaks between
entry.ex: The {continual} ringing of the phone, a new call every few minutes, made it hard to finish the report.
entry.ctx: His {continual} interruptions, a new question every few minutes, kept the class from finishing the story.
entry.etym: From Latin continuus, “hanging together, unbroken,” from continere (to hold together), the same source as continuous.
entry.note: Continual: again and again, with breaks (a dripping faucet). Continuous: without any break (a flowing river).

mn.cue: continu-AL: AL asks again, and again
mn.text: Al raises his hand, asks a question, waits a minute and asks another, all day long. His questions are {continual}: again and again, with short breaks.

scene.alt: A boy named Al raises his hand with yet another question while his teacher covers his eyes.

entry.def: going on without any break
entry.ex: At rush hour the highway is one {continuous} line of cars, bumper to bumper with no gaps.
entry.ctx: Unlike the old clock, which ticked forward in little jumps, the new clock’s second hand moved in one {continuous} sweep, never pausing.
entry.etym: From Latin continuus, “hanging together, unbroken,” from continere (to hold together).

mn.text: The river flows past Sven’s fishing spot day and night without stopping for even a second: One Unbroken Stream. Its flow is {continuous}.

scene.alt: A fisherman sits by a river that flows on and on without a break.

entry.def: refusing to give up; continuing for a long time
entry.ex: The {persistent} puppy scratched at the door again and again until someone finally let him in.
entry.ctx: The inventor’s first forty designs failed, but she was {persistent}, and the forty-first worked so well that she sold thousands.
entry.etym: From Latin persistere, “to continue steadfastly”: per (thoroughly) + sistere (to stand).

mn.cue: PER-SISTER-ent: little sister never gives up
mn.text: Ivy asks her big brother to play catch ten times, twenty times, fifty times, until he finally says yes. Ivy is {persistent}.

scene.alt: A little girl holding a ball keeps begging her teenage brother to play.

entry.def: never letting up or slackening
entry.ex: The hikers trudged on through the {unremitting} wind, which never eased for a moment.
entry.ctx: Her success came from years of {unremitting} practice: four hours at the piano every day, through holidays and summers alike.
entry.etym: From un- (not) + remit, “to slacken, ease off,” from Latin remittere, “to send back, let go.”

mn.text: Hour after hour, the desert sun blazes down on the travelers, with no cloud and no shade. The heat is {unremitting}.

scene.alt: A traveler and a camel trudge through the desert under a blazing sun.

blocks.html: continual means repeated with breaks; continuous means without a break. A dripping faucet is continual; a flowing river is continuous.

head: how often
words
blocks.cap: Sort the words by their pattern in time.

blocks.html: A dripping faucet is continual (drip, pause, drip). A flowing river is continuous (no pause at all). Memory trick: continu-ous = One Unbroken Stream.

blocks.html: There are many ways to help something along. You can make it easier (facilitate) or faster (expedite). You can help it grow, as a gardener helps a plant (foster, nurture, cultivate). You can stand up for it (champion), put your name behind it (endorse), keep it going (sustain) or jolt people into acting for it (galvanize).
One word in this family helps the wrong side: to abet is to help or encourage someone in doing wrong, as in the old legal phrase “aid and abet.”

entry.def: to make an action or process easier
entry.ex: A ramp {facilitated} moving the piano into the house.
entry.ctx: The new bridge will {facilitate} trade between the two towns; farmers who once spent a day driving around the lake will reach the market in an hour.
entry.etym: From French faciliter, from Latin facilis, “easy.”

mn.text: Instead of dragging the heavy piano up the steps, the movers roll it up a ramp. The ramp {facilitates} the job: it makes it easier.

scene.alt: A big man easily pushes a piano up a ramp.

entry.def: to speed up a process
entry.ex: Paying extra will {expedite} the delivery.
entry.ctx: To {expedite} the repairs, the city hired a second crew and kept the work going through the night, and the road reopened two weeks early.
entry.etym: From Latin expedire, “to free the feet” (as from a snare), and so to set free, make ready: ex (out) + pes, ped- (foot).

mn.text: Ped means foot. To get the package there today, the shop sends its fastest runner out the door. It {expedites} the delivery.

scene.alt: A delivery runner races down the street with a package.

entry.def: to encourage the growth or development of
entry.ex: The art club {fosters} young talent with free paint and lots of praise.
entry.ctx: The coach hoped to {foster} a sense of teamwork, so she paired older and younger players and had them practice every drill together.
entry.etym: From Old English fostrian, “to nourish, feed.”
entry.note: A foster family raises a child who is not its own by birth; the verb keeps that sense of helping something grow.

mn.text: With paint, space and praise, the art teacher helps her students improve faster than they ever could alone. She {fosters} their talent.

scene.alt: An art teacher claps as a proud boy paints at an easel.

entry.def: to care for and help grow
entry.ex: Lila {nurtured} the tiny seedlings with water and sunshine.
entry.ctx: A good teacher does more than correct mistakes; she {nurtures} a student’s curiosity, feeding every question with a book, a walk or a new experiment.
entry.etym: From Old French norriture, “food, upbringing,” from Latin nutrire, “to nourish.”

mn.cue: NURSE-ture: nurse it till it grows
mn.text: Granny Mae nurses the baby bird with drops of water until it is strong enough to fly. She {nurtures} it.

scene.alt: A grandmother gently feeds a baby bird in its nest with a spoon.

entry.def: to develop something by steady care and effort
entry.ex: Rosa {cultivated} a love of poetry by reading one poem every night.
entry.ctx: Over many years the shopkeeper {cultivated} loyal customers, remembering their names, their children’s birthdays and how they liked their coffee.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin cultivare, from Latin colere, “to till the soil, tend,” the same root as agriculture and culture.
entry.note: First used of fields and crops; now also of skills, friendships and tastes.

mn.text: Year after year, Omar tills, plants and weeds his garden until it blooms. In the same way, you can {cultivate} a skill with steady care.

scene.alt: A proud gardener with a rake stands beside a row of flowers that grow bigger and bigger.

entry.def: to fight for or speak up for a cause or person
entry.ex: Ms. Ortiz {championed} the idea of a school garden for years.
entry.ctx: Long before the trail was popular, a few hikers {championed} it, writing letters, clearing brush and leading free walks until the town agreed to protect it.
entry.note: As a noun, a champion is a winner, or a person who fights for a cause.

mn.cue: a CHAMP who fights FOR a cause
mn.text: Tia speaks up for the shelter dogs at every town meeting until the town builds them a new home. She {champions} their cause.

labels.text: a CHAMP fights FOR a cause

scene.alt: A woman holds up a sign for the shelter dogs at a town meeting, with a happy dog beside her.

entry.def: to publicly approve or support
entry.ex: Three local chefs {endorsed} the new cookbook.
entry.ctx: The doctors’ group did not merely allow the new playground rules; it {endorsed} them in a public letter, urging every school in the state to adopt them.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin indorsare, “to write on the back”: in (on) + dorsum (back). You endorse a check by signing its back.

mn.cue: EN-DORSE: sign your name on the BACK
mn.text: The chef signs the back cover of Lin’s cookbook and writes, “I recommend it!” She {endorses} it.

scene.alt: A chef signs the back of a cookbook while its delighted author cheers.

entry.def: to keep something going; to support it over time
entry.ex: Hot soup {sustained} the hikers on the long, cold climb.
entry.ctx: The little theater could not {sustain} itself on ticket sales alone, so neighbors held bake sales every month to keep its doors open.
entry.etym: From Latin sustinere, “to hold up from below”: sub (under) + tenere (to hold).

mn.cue: SOUP-STAIN: the soup keeps them going
mn.text: Their jackets have soup stains, but the hot soup keeps the hikers going all the way up the mountain. Food that keeps you going {sustains} you.

scene.alt: Two hikers with backpacks enjoy steaming bowls of soup on a mountain trail.

entry.def: to help or encourage someone, usually in doing wrong
entry.ex: The guard who looked the other way {abetted} the smugglers.
entry.ctx: Kai did not take the cookies himself, but he {abetted} his little brother by holding the ladder and keeping watch for Mom.
entry.note: Usually in the phrase “aid and abet,” which means to help someone commit a crime.

mn.cue: A BET: “I bet no one sees!”
mn.text: “Go on, I bet no one sees!” Rex whispers, holding the ladder steady while Pip reaches for the cookie jar. Rex {abets} the mischief.

scene.alt: A sneaky teen whispers encouragement as a boy on a stool reaches for the cookie jar.

entry.def: to shock or excite people into action
entry.ex: The coach’s speech {galvanized} the tired team.
entry.ctx: News that the old oak would be cut down {galvanized} the neighborhood; within a day, two hundred people had signed a petition and filled the town hall.
entry.etym: Named for Luigi Galvani, an Italian scientist of the 1700s who made frog muscles twitch with electric current; the word first meant to stimulate with electricity.
entry.note: Galvanize also means to coat iron with zinc to stop rust (a galvanized pail).

mn.cue: the GAL in the VAN jolts them awake
mn.text: The gal in the van blasts her horn, and the sleepy campers leap out of their tents, ready to go. She {galvanizes} them.

scene.alt: A woman with a megaphone wakes the campers, who leap up full of energy.

blocks.html: abet usually means helping wrongdoing (to aid and abet). galvanize means to jolt into action, not just to coat with zinc.

head: how it helps
words
blocks.cap: Ten ways to help, one of them shady.

blocks.html: Writers rarely use abet for good deeds. If a character abets someone, expect trouble: the getaway driver abets the robbers.

blocks.html: Who is in charge, and how? These words name kinds of power. Many of them are built from Greek parts: -archy and -cracy both mean rule, and the first part tells you who rules or how. auto- means self, olig- means few, and an- means without.
autocrat = self + power (one person rules alone). oligarchy = few + rule. anarchy = without + rule. bureaucracy = desk + rule (rule by offices and forms). hierarchy = a ranking from top to bottom.
These are words for history and the news, but the pictures here are fairy-tale kingdoms and clubhouses: the ideas are the same at any size.

entry.def: having supreme power; independent and self-governing
entry.ex: After a long struggle, the island became a {sovereign} nation with its own flag.
entry.ctx: The treaty recognized the little kingdom as {sovereign}: no larger country could tax its people or overrule its laws.
entry.etym: From Old French soverain, “highest, supreme,” from Latin super (above).
entry.note: As a noun, a sovereign is a king or queen.

mn.text: The little island kingdom reigns over itself and takes orders from no one. It is {sovereign}.

scene.alt: A proud queen raises her scepter on her own small island, beside its flag.

entry.def: the freedom to govern yourself or make your own choices
entry.ex: At college, Maya enjoyed the {autonomy} of planning her own days.
entry.ctx: The branch library was granted more {autonomy}; instead of waiting for orders from the main office, its staff could now choose their own books and hours.
entry.etym: From Greek autonomia, “independence”: autos (self) + nomos (law).

mn.cue: AUTO = SELF: you set your own rules
mn.text: On her birthday, Maya gets her own key and her own schedule: she decides where to go and when. She has {autonomy}.

scene.alt: A teen happily holds up her own key while her mother waves.

entry.def: a ruler who holds total power alone
entry.ex: The old czar was an {autocrat} who answered to no parliament.
entry.ctx: The club’s founder ran it like an {autocrat}, making every decision himself and never once asking the members to vote.
entry.etym: From Greek autokrates, “ruling by oneself”: autos (self) + kratos (power).

mn.text: King Victor signs every order himself and waves away his advisers: “I decide!” A ruler who holds all the power alone is an {autocrat}.

scene.alt: A king signs every order himself and ignores his worried adviser.

entry.def: a ruler who uses total power cruelly
entry.ex: In the legend, a {despot} took half of every farmer’s harvest.
entry.ctx: Unlike his fair-minded father, the young king became a {despot}, jailing anyone who complained and raising taxes whenever he liked.
entry.etym: From Greek despotes, “master, lord.”

mn.text: The cruel king marches into the village and takes every pot of soup for himself, leaving the people hungry. He is a {despot}.

scene.alt: A cruel king carries off the village soup pot while a grandmother and a boy look on sadly.

entry.def: cruel and unjust use of power
entry.ex: The rebels fought to free their land from {tyranny}.
entry.ctx: Under the old baron’s {tyranny}, villagers could be fined for singing in the street, and no one dared to complain.
entry.etym: From Greek tyrannos, “absolute ruler,” the same word that gave the dinosaur Tyrannosaurus its name.

mn.text: King Rex makes the townspeople bow every time he passes and punishes anyone who sneezes. His cruel, unjust rule is {tyranny}.

scene.alt: A cruel king in a crown orders frightened townspeople to bow.

entry.def: dominance of one group or nation over others
entry.ex: For centuries the city held {hegemony} over trade on the river.
entry.ctx: The kingdom never conquered its small neighbors, but its {hegemony} was clear: its coins, its laws and its fleet set the terms that everyone else had to follow.
entry.etym: From Greek hegemonia, “leadership,” from hegemon (leader).

mn.text: One giant hedge spreads over the whole street until every garden sits in its shade. That hedge’s {hegemony} is complete.

scene.alt: A giant hedge towers over the little gardens of a street while a neighbor stares in surprise.

entry.def: a system run by many officials and complicated rules
entry.ex: Getting a permit meant months of {bureaucracy} and forms.
entry.ctx: The new mayor promised to cut through the {bureaucracy}; instead of six offices and ten forms, a building permit would need one visit and one page.
entry.etym: From French bureaucratie: bureau (desk, office) + -cratie (rule).

mn.cue: BUREAU-CRACY: rule by desks and forms
mn.text: To get a library card, Pip fills out Form A, gets a stamp at Desk B, waits in Line C and is sent back to Form A. That maze of offices is {bureaucracy}.

scene.alt: A bored clerk at a desk sends a confused boy holding a pile of forms to the next window.

entry.def: a system that ranks people or things one above another
entry.ex: In the army’s {hierarchy}, a general outranks a colonel, and a colonel outranks a captain.
entry.ctx: The kitchen ran on a strict {hierarchy}: the head chef gave orders to the cooks, the cooks to the helpers, and the helpers to the new dishwasher.
entry.etym: From Greek hierarkhia, “rule of a high priest”: hieros (sacred) + arkhein (to rule); later, any ranking from top to bottom.

mn.text: At the castle the king stands highest, then the knight, then the cook. That ranking from higher to lower is a {hierarchy}.

scene.alt: A cook, a knight and a king stand on stacks of crates, each one higher than the last.

entry.def: rule by a small group of people
entry.ex: The city was run by an {oligarchy} of five wealthy merchant families.
entry.ctx: Although the club claimed to be open to all, it was really an {oligarchy}: three senior members made every decision and never put anything to a vote.
entry.etym: From Greek oligarkhia: oligos (few) + arkhein (to rule).
entry.note: Oligarchy is rule by a few; monarchy is rule by one.

mn.text: Ollie and his two best friends make every rule for the whole treehouse club; the other kids get no say. Rule by a few like that is an {oligarchy}.

labels.text: OLIG = FEW: rule by a FEW

scene.alt: Three boys in paper crowns stand on a bench making the rules while a girl crosses her arms.

entry.def: a lack of government or control; disorder
entry.ex: When the referee left, the game dissolved into {anarchy}.
entry.ctx: With no captain and no rules, the ship’s crew fell into {anarchy}: everyone gave orders, no one followed them, and the sails flapped loose for days.
entry.etym: From Greek anarkhia, “lack of a leader”: an (without) + arkhos (ruler).
entry.note: Strictly, anarchy means no ruler; in everyday use it means chaos.

mn.text: The teacher steps out for five minutes, and with no one in charge the room turns to chaos: paper planes, spilled paint, kids on desks. That is {anarchy}.

scene.alt: With no teacher in the room, children dance on desks and throw papers in a wild mess.

blocks.html: anarchy means "without a ruler"; in everyday use it means chaos. oligarchy (rule by a few) is not monarchy (rule by one).

head: word
who rules
parts
blocks.cap: The parts tell you who holds the power.

blocks.html: Sovereign and autonomy are about freedom from outside control: a sovereign nation answers to no other nation, and a person with autonomy makes her own choices. Hegemony is the opposite situation seen from above: one power dominating the rest.

blocks.html: Odd things come in many kinds, and English has a word for each. Some words describe how strange something is, from mildly peculiar to wildly bizarre and outlandish. Some describe people and methods that break the usual pattern (eccentric, unorthodox, idiosyncrasy). Some describe things that don’t fit or break the rule (incongruous, anomaly, aberration), and one describes the never-before-seen (unprecedented).
Roots help here: ec-centric = out of the center; ab-err-ation = wandering away; an-omaly = not even, not regular; un-pre-cedented = with nothing going before it.

entry.def: strange or odd; also, belonging only to one person or place
entry.ex: Grandpa has the {peculiar} habit of putting pickles on his ice cream.
entry.ctx: The fish is {peculiar} to this one lake; scientists have searched every other river and pond in the region and never found it anywhere else.
entry.etym: From Latin peculiaris, “of one’s own property,” from peculium (private property); the sense “strange” came later.
entry.note: In “peculiar to,” it means belonging only to: a custom peculiar to the island.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus orders a scoop of vanilla and asks for a pickle on top. Ivy stares. How {peculiar}!

scene.alt: A grandfather happily eats an ice cream cone with a pickle on top while a girl stares.

entry.def: odd in behavior in a harmless, quirky way
entry.ex: The {eccentric} inventor wore one red sock and one green sock every day.
entry.ctx: The neighbors thought old Mr. Pell was {eccentric}, since he walked his pet turtle on a leash, but they also thought he was the kindest man on the street.
entry.etym: From Greek ekkentros, “out of the center”: ek (out of) + kentron (center). It first described orbits that were off-center.

mn.text: Professor Edwin wears a wizard hat to the park and walks his turtle on a leash. He is a bit off-center but perfectly harmless: {eccentric}.

scene.alt: An old professor in a wizard hat happily walks a turtle on a leash in the park.

entry.def: very strange and surprising
entry.ex: Every morning, the cat performs a {bizarre} trick: riding the dog like a horse around the yard.
entry.ctx: At first the inventor’s machine looked {bizarre}, a tangle of pipes, bells and bicycle wheels, but it turned out to make perfect pancakes.
entry.note: Bizarre (very strange) is not bazaar (a market).

mn.text: At the bazaar, one stall sells socks for snakes. It is the most {bizarre} stall in the whole market.

scene.alt: At a market stall, a seller holds out a sock for a snake while a girl stares in shock.

entry.def: strikingly odd, almost unbelievable
entry.ex: As usual, Rex arrived at the picnic in an {outlandish} outfit: a rainbow cape and swim fins.
entry.ctx: The excuse was so {outlandish} that no one believed it: Max claimed a seagull had flown off with his homework and dropped it in the lake.
entry.etym: From Old English utlendisc, “foreign”: out + land. It once meant simply “from another country.”

mn.cue: OUT-LANDISH: from OUT of this LAND
mn.text: Rex strolls into the picnic in a rainbow cape, goggles and a big helmet, an outfit from some faraway land. It is {outlandish}.

scene.alt: A man in a pink cape, goggles and a helmet dances into a picnic while a grandmother gapes.

entry.def: not following the usual ways of doing things
entry.ex: For years the chef has used an {unorthodox} method: flipping pancakes with a tennis racket.
entry.ctx: Her teaching was {unorthodox}: instead of lectures and worksheets, the class learned fractions by baking bread and history by acting out old trials.
entry.etym: From un- (not) + orthodox, from Greek orthodoxos, “having the right opinion”: orthos (straight, correct) + doxa (opinion).

mn.cue: UN-ORTHO: NOT the usual straight way
mn.text: Chef Jamal flips his pancakes with a tennis racket, and every one lands perfectly in the pan. His method is {unorthodox}.

scene.alt: A chef flips a pancake high in the air with a tennis racket while a teen watches in surprise.

entry.def: out of place; not fitting in with its surroundings
entry.ex: Grandpa’s heavy wool coat looked {incongruous} on the sunny beach among all the swimsuits.
entry.ctx: The shiny glass tower looked {incongruous} beside the row of tiny, hundred-year-old wooden cottages, like a robot at a tea party.
entry.etym: From Latin incongruus, “not agreeing”: in- (not) + congruus (fitting, agreeing).

mn.cue: IN-CONGRUOUS: a penguin in the desert
mn.text: A penguin waddles across the hot desert sand past a puzzled camel. It is completely out of place: {incongruous}.

scene.alt: A sweating penguin stands in the hot desert as a camel stares at it.

entry.def: something that departs from what is normal or expected
entry.ex: A snowy day in Miami would be an {anomaly}.
entry.ctx: The scientists at first thought the strange reading was an {anomaly}, a glitch in one machine, but every instrument recorded the same signal again the next night.
entry.etym: From Greek anomalia, “unevenness”: an (not) + homalos (even).

mn.text: Sheep are not normally purple, so the one purple sheep in Omar’s flock is an {anomaly}.

scene.alt: A puzzled farmer scratches his head at one purple sheep among white sheep.

entry.def: a departure from what is normal or right, often a brief one
entry.ex: The team’s one loss was an {aberration} in an otherwise perfect season.
entry.ctx: Her grades had been excellent for years, so her teachers saw the failed quiz as an {aberration} rather than a sign that something was wrong.
entry.etym: From Latin aberrare, “to wander away”: ab (away) + errare (to wander, stray).

mn.text: The train that has arrived at eight o’clock sharp every day for ten years is two hours late today. That one late day is an {aberration}.

scene.alt: A shocked commuter with a briefcase reads a delayed sign at a train station that is always on time.

entry.def: a habit or way of behaving all your own
entry.ex: One of Uncle Felix’s {idiosyncrasies} is tapping his spoon three times before every meal.
entry.ctx: Each member of the band had an {idiosyncrasy}: the drummer wore two watches, and the singer would drink tea only from a chipped blue cup.
entry.etym: From Greek idiosynkrasia, “one’s own temperament”: idios (one’s own) + synkrasis (a mixing together).

mn.cue: IDIO = your OWN: a quirk all your own
mn.text: Uncle Felix taps his spoon on the bowl exactly three times before every meal: tap, tap, tap. It is his own little {idiosyncrasy}.

scene.alt: A man taps his spoon three times on his bowl before eating while a girl giggles.

entry.def: never done or known before
entry.ex: Snow on the beach in July was {unprecedented} in the town’s history.
entry.ctx: The young runner’s win was {unprecedented}: in the race’s hundred-year history, no one under fifteen had ever finished in the top ten, let alone first.
entry.etym: From un- (not) + precedented, from precedent, “an earlier example,” from Latin praecedere, “to go before.”
entry.note: Unprecedented means never happened before, not merely rare.

mn.text: Snow falls on the beach in July, something no one in town has ever seen before. The storm is {unprecedented}.

scene.alt: A boy in sunglasses gasps at a snowman on the beach in July.

blocks.html: bizarre (strange) is not bazaar (a market). unprecedented means never happened before, not merely rare.

what is odd about it

a method that breaks with custom
out of place where it is
a break from the normal pattern
blocks.cap: Ten ways to be unusual.

blocks.html: Bizarre (very strange) and bazaar (a market) sound alike. And unprecedented is stronger than rare: a rare event has happened before, but an unprecedented one never has.
