blocks.html: Two Latin verbs about speech build this family. loqui means to speak; it appears in English as loqu or locu (you may know ventriloquist, “belly speaker”). dicere means to say; it appears as dict (you know predict, “to say before,” and dictionary).

loqu, locut = speak. dict = say. The prefix tells you how: eloquent and elocution (speaking out), colloquial (speaking with others), soliloquy (speaking alone), circumlocution (speaking around the point), interlocutor (speaking between), edict (said out as an order).
One spelling trap: indict is pronounced in-DITE. The c is silent.

entry.def: speaking or writing in a fluent, moving way
entry.ex: Rosa gave an {eloquent} speech that left the whole gym in tears.
entry.ctx: The old fisherman was usually a man of few words, but when the town planned to close the harbor, he became {eloquent}, describing three generations of families who had lived from the sea.
entry.etym: From Latin eloquens, “speaking out,” from eloqui: e (out) + loqui (to speak).

mn.text: At graduation, Rosa’s words flow out so gracefully that the grandparents in the front row wipe their eyes. She is {eloquent}.

scene.alt: A graduate gives a moving speech at a podium while a grandmother wipes away happy tears.

entry.def: very talkative
entry.ex: Our {loquacious} cab driver told us his whole life story before we reached the hotel.
entry.ctx: Unlike her quiet twin, Bea was {loquacious}; she could chat for an hour with a stranger at the bus stop and still have more to say.
entry.etym: From Latin loquax, “talkative,” from loqui (to speak).

mn.cue: lo-QUACK-cious: a duck who never stops
mn.text: Daisy the duck quacks to everyone she meets, about the weather, the pond, the bread and the weather again. She is {loquacious}.

scene.alt: A chatty duck quacks on and on while a bored frog listens and a turtle falls asleep.

entry.def: used in ordinary, informal conversation
entry.ex: “Gonna” is a {colloquial} way of saying “going to.”
entry.ctx: The novel’s characters speak in a {colloquial} style, full of slang and half-finished sentences, just as real people talk at the kitchen table.
entry.etym: From Latin colloquium, “conversation”: com (together) + loqui (to speak).

mn.text: In class Dev says, “Good afternoon, Professor.” With his pals at the skate park, it’s “Hey, what’s up?” That everyday way of talking is {colloquial}.

scene.alt: Two teen friends greet each other casually at the playground.

entry.def: a speech in a play in which a character, alone, speaks thoughts aloud
entry.ex: In the second act, the prince delivers a long {soliloquy} about whether to leave home.
entry.ctx: The audience learned the villain’s plan through a {soliloquy}: alone on the dark stage, he told no one but himself exactly what he meant to do.
entry.etym: From Late Latin soliloquium, “talking to oneself”: solus (alone) + loqui (to speak).
entry.note: A soliloquy is spoken alone; a monologue may be spoken to other characters.

mn.cue: SOLO + LOQU: talking ALONE on stage
mn.text: Alone on the empty stage, the prince speaks his worried thoughts out loud to no one at all. His speech is a {soliloquy}.

scene.alt: A young actor dressed as a prince stands alone on stage, speaking his thoughts aloud.

entry.def: using many words to avoid saying something directly
entry.ex: Asked if he ate the last cookie, Pip answered with ten minutes of {circumlocution}.
entry.ctx: The letter was a masterpiece of {circumlocution}: three pages about “adjustments” and “new directions” that never once said the store was closing.
entry.etym: From Latin circumlocutio, “a speaking around”: circum (around) + loqui (to speak).

mn.text: Asked if he ate the last cookie, Pip talks about the weather, his homework and the dog, everything except yes or no. That is {circumlocution}.

scene.alt: A mother asks a simple question while her son talks in circles beside an empty cookie plate.

entry.def: the skill of pronouncing words clearly when speaking in public
entry.ex: Years of {elocution} lessons gave the actor a clear, ringing voice.
entry.ctx: In the old one-room schools, {elocution} was a subject of its own; pupils stood before the class to recite poems slowly, loudly and with every consonant crisp.
entry.etym: From Latin elocutio, “a speaking out,” from eloqui: e (out) + loqui (to speak).

mn.cue: E-LOCU-TION: speaking OUT, clear as a bell
mn.text: Professor Edwin rings a bell, and Maya repeats the tongue twister until every sound rings out clearly. She is practicing {elocution}.

scene.alt: A professor rings a bell while a teen practices saying a tongue twister clearly.

entry.def: the choice of words; also, how clearly words are spoken
entry.ex: The poet’s {diction} was simple: short, everyday words that hit hard.
entry.ctx: The essay’s ideas were fine, but its {diction} was wrong for a formal letter; words like “stuff” and “a bunch” made the writer sound careless.
entry.etym: From Latin dictio, “a saying, a way of speaking,” from dicere (to say).
entry.note: On the SAT, diction usually means word choice: a writer’s diction sets the tone.

mn.cue: DICTIONary: choosing the words you SAY
mn.text: Nell flips through her dictionary to pick the perfect word: not “shine” but “glimmer.” Her careful choice of words is her {diction}.

labels.text: DICT = SAY: the words you choose

scene.alt: A writer looks through a dictionary, choosing the perfect word.

entry.def: an official order from someone in authority
entry.ex: The queen’s {edict} declared every Friday a holiday.
entry.ctx: The principal’s new {edict}, posted on every classroom door, banned phones from the cafeteria starting Monday, and no one could argue with it.
entry.etym: From Latin edictum, “a proclamation,” from edicere, “to declare”: e (out) + dicere (to say).

mn.text: The royal herald unrolls a scroll and reads the queen’s new order aloud: every Friday is now pie day! That official order is an {edict}.

scene.alt: A herald reads a royal order from a scroll as a girl and a grandfather cheer.

entry.def: to formally charge someone with a crime
entry.ex: The grand jury voted to {indict} the banker for stealing from his clients.
entry.ctx: Because the evidence was strong, the grand jury {indicted} the shop owner, and a trial was set for the spring.
entry.etym: From Anglo-French enditer, “to accuse,” from Latin in + dictare (to declare); the c was added later to match the Latin.
entry.note: Pronounced in-DITE: the c is silent.

mn.cue: in-DITE: the INVITE no one wants
mn.text: The court’s letter is an invitation nobody wants: it formally charges the thief with stealing the town’s golden goose. To {indict} is to charge someone with a crime.

scene.alt: A judge hands a formal charge to a shocked thief, with a golden goose nearby.

entry.def: a person taking part in a conversation
entry.ex: Grandpa is a patient {interlocutor}; he lets you finish every sentence.
entry.ctx: The reporter was a skilled {interlocutor}: she listened closely, asked one short question at a time and let the long silences do the rest.
entry.etym: From Latin interloqui, “to speak between, interrupt”: inter (between) + loqui (to speak).

mn.cue: INTER-LOCU-TOR: the one you speak BETWEEN
mn.text: Across the café table, Lin and Omar trade ideas, each listening and answering in turn. Each is the other’s {interlocutor}.

scene.alt: Two friends sit across a café table, taking turns talking and listening.

blocks.html: Loquacious (very talkative) and eloquent (speaking beautifully) both come from loqui, but they are not the same: a loquacious person talks a lot; an eloquent one talks well.

blocks.html: Most of these words describe people who think too much of themselves, each in a different style: the arrogant person acts superior, the haughty one is cold and lofty, the condescending one talks down, the pompous one puffs up, the imperious one gives orders, and the supercilious one raises an eyebrow in scorn. Hubris is the kind of pride that leads to a fall.
On the other side stand three words of praise: modest, unassuming and self-effacing people don’t boast, don’t show off and don’t push themselves forward.

entry.def: acting as if you are more important than others
entry.ex: The {arrogant} new player refused to pass the ball to anyone.
entry.ctx: He was talented, but his {arrogant} habit of interrupting everyone and dismissing their ideas soon left him with no partners for the project.
entry.etym: From Latin arrogare, “to claim for oneself”: ad (to) + rogare (to ask).

mn.cue: AIR-OGANT: nose high in the AIR
mn.text: Victor struts down the street with his nose so high in the air that he never sees the people saying hello. He is {arrogant}.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat walks with his nose in the air, ignoring a boy who waves hello.

entry.def: proud in a cold way that looks down on others
entry.ex: The {haughty} duchess would not even glance at the servants.
entry.ctx: Her {haughty} reply, delivered with a cool stare and a turned shoulder, made it clear that she thought the question beneath her.
entry.etym: From haught, “high, proud,” from Old French haut (high), from Latin altus (high).

mn.text: Lady Greta stands on a box so she can look down on everyone, and she will not speak to anyone below her. She is {haughty}.

scene.alt: A haughty lady stands on a crate with her arms crossed, ignoring a girl who offers her a flower.

entry.def: talking down to others as if they were less smart or important
entry.ex: The salesman used a {condescending} tone, explaining what a “button” was.
entry.ctx: Grandma has driven a tractor for fifty years, so she laughed at the young mechanic’s {condescending} lecture on how to start an engine.
entry.etym: From Latin condescendere, “to stoop, come down”: con (with) + descendere (to come down).

mn.text: Rex bends way down to talk to the head chef as if she were a baby: “This is a SPOON.” His tone is {condescending}.

scene.alt: A man bends down to explain a spoon to an annoyed head chef.

entry.def: self-important and showy in speech or manner
entry.ex: The {pompous} duke gave a twenty-minute speech about himself at the ribbon cutting.
entry.ctx: Instead of simply saying the bus was late, the {pompous} official announced that “transit services are experiencing a temporary scheduling irregularity.”
entry.etym: From Late Latin pomposus, from pompa, “a procession, a grand display.”

mn.text: The duke arrives with a drumroll, a velvet cape and a speech all about how wonderful he is. He is {pompous}.

scene.alt: A duke in a cape and medals reads a long speech about himself while children yawn.

entry.def: commanding and bossy, expecting to be obeyed
entry.ex: With an {imperious} wave, the toddler sent his father back for more juice.
entry.ctx: The new manager’s {imperious} style, barking orders and never asking for opinions, made the staff nostalgic for her gentle predecessor.
entry.etym: From Latin imperiosus, “commanding,” from imperium (command, empire).

mn.text: From his high chair, little Theo points like an emperor: “Juice! Now!” And Dad runs to obey. Theo is {imperious}.

scene.alt: A toddler in a paper crown points and demands juice while his father rushes to bring it.

entry.def: scornfully superior; looking down your nose at others
entry.ex: The {supercilious} waiter raised an eyebrow at Pip’s muddy sneakers.
entry.ctx: The critic’s review was {supercilious}: rather than discuss the play, he sneered at the small theater, its folding chairs and its “charmingly amateur” actors.
entry.etym: From Latin supercilium, “eyebrow” (super, above + cilium, eyelid): the raised eyebrow of scorn.
entry.note: It comes from the Latin word for eyebrow, not from “silly.”

mn.text: The snooty waiter raises one eyebrow at Pip’s muddy sneakers: “Hmm. Are you lost?” His look is {supercilious}.

scene.alt: A snobbish waiter looks down his nose at a boy in muddy sneakers.

entry.def: too much pride, the kind that leads to a downfall
entry.ex: In the old myths, a hero’s {hubris} usually ends in disaster.
entry.ctx: The champion’s {hubris} cost him the title; sure that no one could beat him, he skipped training for a month and lost to an unknown in the first round.
entry.etym: From Greek hybris, “insolence, excessive pride”; in Greek tragedy, such pride often brings a hero down.
entry.note: Hubris is more than pride: it is pride that leads to a fall.

mn.cue: a HUGE BRAG before a fall
mn.text: “No wave can beat my castle!” Rex brags, building right at the water’s edge. The very next wave flattens it. His {hubris} brought him down.

labels.text: HU-BRAG-is: a HUGE BRAG, then a fall

scene.alt: A boastful man’s sandcastle is about to be swept away by a big wave.

entry.def: not boasting about your abilities or achievements
entry.ex: Though she had won the state prize, Kai’s sister was too {modest} to mention it.
entry.ctx: The scientist was {modest} about her discovery; in every interview she praised her students and called herself “just the one who wrote it down.”
entry.etym: From Latin modestus, “keeping due measure, moderate,” from modus (measure).
entry.note: Modest can also mean not large: a modest house, a modest salary.

mn.cue: MOD-EST: never says he’s the BEST
mn.text: Kai wins first prize at the science fair but just says, “My friends helped a lot.” He never calls himself the best. He is {modest}.

scene.alt: A boy holding a trophy shrugs shyly and gives credit to his friends while a girl claps.

entry.def: not drawing attention to yourself; quiet and humble
entry.ex: The {unassuming} man in the back row turned out to be the famous author.
entry.ctx: For a shop that sells the best bread in the state, it is surprisingly {unassuming}: no sign, no fancy windows, just a plain green door and a line of customers.

mn.text: The quiet woman in the plain sweater, reading in the back row, is the famous author everyone came to see. You’d never assume it: she is {unassuming}.

scene.alt: A plainly dressed woman reads quietly while a man looks around for the visiting author, not realizing it is her.

entry.def: keeping yourself in the background; humble
entry.ex: The {self-effacing} coach gave all the credit to her players.
entry.ctx: Although he had built most of the robot himself, the {self-effacing} engineer stood at the back of the photo and told reporters that the team deserved the praise.
entry.etym: From efface, “to rub out,” from French effacer: ex (out) + face (face, surface).

mn.text: When the team photo is taken, the coach steps to the very edge, nearly out of the picture, and says, “It was all them.” She is {self-effacing}.

scene.alt: Two teens cheer with a trophy while their coach stands far off at the edge of the picture.

blocks.html: hubris is more than pride: it is pride that leads to a fall. supercilious comes from the Latin word for eyebrow (raised in scorn), not from "silly."

blocks.cap: Seven shades of too much pride.

blocks.html: Modest, unassuming and self-effacing all praise humility. Self-effacing is the strongest: such a person actively steps out of the spotlight.

blocks.html: Writers judge conduct with these words. On the honorable side: ethical and virtuous people do right; probity and rectitude name their honesty and uprightness; propriety and decorum name good, fitting behavior. On the dishonorable side: corrupt and venal people can be bought, nefarious deeds are wicked, and reprehensible ones deserve blame.
Two pairs to sort: probity and rectitude are about honesty and goodness; propriety and decorum are about proper manners. Someone can have perfect decorum and still be corrupt.

entry.def: following principles of right conduct; morally right
entry.ex: An {ethical} reporter checks every fact before publishing a story.
entry.ctx: The company could have hidden the defect and saved millions, but its {ethical} founder insisted on recalling every toy and refunding every family.
entry.etym: From Greek ethikos, from ethos, “character, custom.”

mn.cue: EDITH-ICAL: Edith does the right thing
mn.text: When a customer pays twenty dollars too much, Edith runs down the street to give it back. Edith is {ethical}.

scene.alt: A shopkeeper named Edith runs after a customer to return money he overpaid.

entry.def: having high moral standards; good
entry.ex: The {virtuous} shopkeeper returned the lost wallet with every dollar still inside.
entry.ctx: The knight was {virtuous} in every way that mattered: he kept his promises, shared his food with strangers and never took credit for another’s deed.
entry.etym: From Latin virtus, “excellence, goodness, courage.”

mn.text: Sir Omar keeps every promise, shares his bread and never tells a lie: he is very true and very good. He is {virtuous}.

labels.text: VERY TRUE-ous: good to the core

scene.alt: A knight in armor gives bread to a grateful grandmother.

entry.def: correct, proper behavior
entry.ex: Out of {propriety}, the guests waited for the host to sit before they began eating.
entry.ctx: Grandmother valued {propriety} above all: thank-you notes within a week, no hats at the table and never a raised voice in company.
entry.etym: From Latin proprietas, “ownership, fitness,” from proprius (one’s own); the sense “proper behavior” came later.
entry.note: Propriety (proper behavior) is not proprietary (owned by someone, as a recipe a company keeps secret).

mn.text: At the fancy dinner, Ivy keeps her napkin on her lap, her elbows off the table and her “thank you” ready. She shows perfect {propriety}.

scene.alt: At a dinner table, a polite girl says thank you while a boy beside her eats messily.

entry.def: polite, dignified behavior that suits the occasion
entry.ex: The guests at the royal dinner behaved with perfect {decorum}.
entry.ctx: The debate began with {decorum}, each speaker waiting politely for a turn, but by the end the two sides were shouting over each other.
entry.etym: From Latin decorum, “that which is fitting,” from decor (beauty, grace), the same source as decorate.

mn.cue: DECOR-um: manners to match the fancy DECOR
mn.text: In the grand palace hall, guests bow, speak softly and wait their turn, matching the elegant decor. They show perfect {decorum}.

scene.alt: Two well-dressed guests bow politely before a king in his throne room.

entry.def: complete honesty and integrity
entry.ex: The judge was known for her {probity}; no one ever doubted her rulings.
entry.ctx: The town chose Mr. Ali to count the money from the fundraiser because of his {probity}: in forty years as the bank’s treasurer, he had never been off by a single penny.
entry.etym: From Latin probitas, “uprightness, honesty,” from probus (good, honest), the same root as prove.

mn.cue: PROBE-ITY: probe all you want, it’s honest
mn.text: The inspectors probe every page of Treasurer Lin’s books and find every penny in its place. Her {probity} is complete.

scene.alt: An inspector with a magnifying glass finds a treasurer’s account book perfectly honest.

entry.def: moral uprightness; strict honesty and goodness
entry.ex: Her {rectitude} made her the obvious choice to guard the prize money.
entry.ctx: Even his rivals admired the old captain’s {rectitude}; in fifty years at sea he had never broken a promise, hidden a gift or bent a rule for a friend.
entry.etym: From Late Latin rectitudo, “straightness,” from rectus (straight, right), the same root as rectangle.

mn.text: Judge Ada stands as straight as a ruler and lives the same way: she has never told a lie or taken a bribe. Her {rectitude} is famous.

scene.alt: A judge stands straight as a ruler beside the scales of justice.

entry.def: dishonest, especially in exchange for money or power
entry.ex: The {corrupt} referee was paid to call every play for one team.
entry.ctx: For years the {corrupt} inspector approved unsafe buildings in exchange for envelopes of cash, until a reporter followed the money.
entry.etym: From Latin corruptus, “spoiled, destroyed,” from corrumpere: com (thoroughly) + rumpere (to break).

mn.text: The referee pockets a bag of coins and calls every play for the team that paid him. Rotten to the core, he is {corrupt}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man slips a bag of money to a referee holding a whistle.

entry.def: willing to be bribed; open to doing wrong for money
entry.ex: The {venal} guard let anyone through the gate for a gold coin.
entry.ctx: The old courts were notoriously {venal}: a rich man could buy any verdict he liked, while a poor one could not even get a hearing.
entry.etym: From Latin venalis, “for sale,” from venum (sale), the same root as vend.
entry.note: Venal (open to bribes) is not venial (minor and easily forgiven, as a venial fault).

mn.cue: VEND-AL: pay him like a VENDING machine
mn.text: Drop a coin in his hand and the guard opens the gate for anyone, like a vending machine. He is {venal}.

scene.alt: A guard holds out his hand for a coin before letting a sneaky man through the castle gate.

entry.def: wicked or criminal
entry.ex: The villain’s {nefarious} plan was to steal the town’s clock so everyone would miss the fair.
entry.ctx: At first the stranger seemed charming, but his purpose was {nefarious}: he had come to swindle the widow out of her farm.
entry.etym: From Latin nefarius, from nefas, “a wrong, a crime”: ne (not) + fas (what is right).

mn.text: Late at night the villain sneaks off with the town clock so that everyone will miss the fair. His scheme is {nefarious}.

scene.alt: A masked villain sneaks through the village at night, carrying off the town clock.

entry.def: deserving strong blame
entry.ex: Rex behaved {reprehensibly} when he knocked down a little kid’s block tower on purpose.
entry.ctx: The coach called the players’ behavior {reprehensible}: they had mocked the losing team, thrown trash on the field and refused to shake hands.
entry.etym: From Late Latin reprehensibilis, from reprehendere, “to hold back, rebuke.”

mn.text: Rex knocks over little Theo’s block tower on purpose, and Tia scolds him sharply. Such behavior is {reprehensible}.

scene.alt: A teen knocks over a toddler’s block tower as a woman scolds him.

blocks.html: venal (open to bribes) is not venial (minor and easily forgiven). propriety (proper conduct) is not proprietary (owned).

blocks.html: An argument has moves, and each move has a word. You make a claim (assert, contend, or, without proof, allege). Your opponent answers it (rebut) and may even prove it wrong (refute). Someone may give in on a point (concede). You can argue for a cause (advocate) and urge others to act (exhort). The whole art of persuading is rhetoric, and a fierce attack on an idea is a polemic.
The key difference: to rebut is to argue against a claim, whether or not you win; to refute is to prove it wrong. Saying “that’s not true” is neither: it is just a denial.

entry.def: the art of persuasive speaking or writing; also, showy talk with little substance
entry.ex: The debate coach taught {rhetoric}: how to open strong, use examples and end with a question.
entry.ctx: The salesman’s pitch was all {rhetoric} and no facts: grand promises and stirring phrases, but not one word about the price or the warranty.
entry.etym: From Greek rhetorike, “the art of the public speaker,” from rhetor (speaker).
entry.note: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer: “Who doesn’t love a snow day?”

mn.cue: RHETOR = SPEAKER: the art of winning a crowd
mn.text: With a pause here and a question there, Jamal wins over the whole crowd using nothing but well-chosen words. He is a master of {rhetoric}.

scene.alt: A speaker at a podium wins over a cheering crowd with his words.

entry.def: to state something firmly and confidently
entry.ex: Zoe {asserted} that her cat could open doors, and then the cat did.
entry.ctx: The author does not merely suggest that sleep helps memory; she {asserts} it plainly in the first sentence and spends the chapter backing it up.
entry.etym: From Latin asserere, “to claim, declare”: ad (to) + serere (to join).

mn.cue: a SERGEANT doesn’t ask: he ASSERTS
mn.text: “We march at dawn!” the sergeant says, firm and sure, without a trace of doubt. He doesn’t ask; he {asserts}.

scene.alt: A man in a cap firmly announces the plan while two children salute.

entry.def: to argue that something is true; also, to compete
entry.ex: Maya {contends} that summer vacation should be a month longer.
entry.ctx: Some historians {contend} that the bridge was built by the Romans, but others point out that its stones were cut with tools invented centuries later.
entry.etym: From Latin contendere, “to strive, compete”: con (with) + tendere (to stretch).
entry.note: Contend also means to compete (to contend for the title) or to struggle (to contend with bad weather).

mn.text: In the class debate, Maya argues hard that summer should be longer, and she has three reasons ready. She {contends} it.

scene.alt: Two teens at podiums argue opposite sides in a class debate.

entry.def: to claim something, especially wrongdoing, without proof yet
entry.ex: Pip {alleged} that his sister ate the last cupcake, but he had no proof.
entry.ctx: The neighbors {allege} that the factory dumps waste into the creek at night, and they have asked the state to send inspectors to find out.
entry.note: News reports say “the alleged thief” because no one has proved the charge yet.

mn.cue: a-LEDGE: out on a LEDGE with no proof
mn.text: Pip says his sister ate his cupcake, but he has nothing to back it up, only a guess. He is out on a ledge: he {alleges} it.

scene.alt: A boy points at his sister and claims she ate his cupcake, while she shrugs in confusion.

entry.def: to prove that a claim is wrong
entry.ex: Sami {refuted} Rex’s claim by showing him a photo of a real moon rock.
entry.ctx: For years people believed the bridge was unsafe, but the engineer’s tests {refuted} that belief: it held three times the weight of the heaviest truck.
entry.etym: From Latin refutare, “to drive back, disprove.”
entry.note: To refute is to prove wrong, not just to deny or argue against.

mn.cue: RE-FUTE: PROOF puts the boot to it
mn.text: Rex claims the moon is made of cheese, so Sami shows him a moon rock in the science book. Sami {refutes} the claim: he proves it wrong.

scene.alt: A boy proves with a science book that the moon is rock, not cheese, while another looks shocked.

entry.def: to argue against a claim by giving an answer
entry.ex: Each speaker had two minutes to {rebut} the other side’s points.
entry.ctx: The lawyer rose to {rebut} the witness, pointing out that the street lamp had been broken that night; whether the jury believed her was another matter.
entry.etym: From Old French reboter, “to push back.”
entry.note: To rebut is to answer an argument; it does not mean you won. Winning with proof is refute.

mn.text: Each time Maya makes a point, Dev bounces an answer right back, like a ball off a wall. He {rebuts} every claim, though he may not win.

scene.alt: Two debaters bounce points back and forth like a ball.

entry.def: to admit that something is true, often unwillingly
entry.ex: After the long chess game, Grandpa {conceded} that Kai had won.
entry.ctx: Though she still disliked the plan, the team captain {conceded} that it would save time, and she agreed to try it for a week.
entry.etym: From Latin concedere, “to give way, yield”: con + cedere (to go, yield).

mn.text: After a long chess game, Grandpa tips over his own king and smiles: “You win.” He {concedes}.

scene.alt: A grandfather smiles and admits defeat at chess while his grandson cheers.

entry.def: to speak or argue in favor of
entry.ex: Rosa {advocated} for a crosswalk in front of the school.
entry.ctx: Doctors have long {advocated} washing hands before meals, explaining that this simple habit keeps many germs from spreading.
entry.etym: From Latin advocare, “to call to one’s aid”: ad (to) + vocare (to call).
entry.note: As a noun (AD-vuh-kit), an advocate is a person who speaks up for a cause or a person.

mn.cue: AD-VOC: add your VOICE for it
mn.text: Rosa adds her voice to the call for a crosswalk near the school, speaking up at every meeting. She {advocates} for it.

scene.alt: A teen calls out for a school crosswalk while a girl cheers beside a traffic cone.

entry.def: to urge strongly and earnestly
entry.ex: The coach {exhorted} her runners to give everything on the last lap.
entry.ctx: The old captain {exhorted} the crew not to give up, reminding them that the harbor lights were only a few miles away.
entry.etym: From Latin exhortari, “to encourage greatly”: ex (thoroughly) + hortari (to urge).

mn.text: On the last lap, the coach runs alongside the track, hollering, “Faster! You can do it!” She {exhorts} her runners.

scene.alt: A coach shouts encouragement as a runner speeds around the track.

entry.def: a strong written or spoken attack on an idea
entry.ex: His letter to the editor was a fiery {polemic} against the new parking rules.
entry.ctx: The book is less a balanced history than a {polemic}: every chapter attacks the old king and ignores anything good he did.
entry.etym: From Greek polemikos, “warlike,” from polemos (war).

mn.cue: POLE-MIC: grab the MIC and attack
mn.text: Victor grabs the mic and launches a fiery attack on the new school schedule, calling it the worst idea in history. His speech is a {polemic}.

scene.alt: A furious man with a microphone attacks the new school schedule.

blocks.html: refute means to prove wrong, not just to deny; rebut means to argue against, whether or not you win.

blocks.html: Test makers love refute. A writer who refutes a claim proves it false; a writer who merely rebuts or disputes it has only argued against it.

blocks.html: All ten words describe calm, but calm of different kinds. A serene face and a tranquil lake are peaceful. A composed, unflappable or imperturbable person stays steady when trouble comes, and keeps their equanimity. An impassive, stoic or phlegmatic person shows little feeling at all. A nonchalant person seems not to care.
Peaceful: serene, tranquil. Steady under stress: composed, unflappable, imperturbable, equanimity. Showing little feeling: impassive, stoic, phlegmatic. Unconcerned: nonchalant.
Careful: impassive (showing no feeling) and impassioned (full of feeling) look alike but mean opposite things.

entry.def: calm and peaceful; untroubled
entry.ex: At dawn the lake was {serene}, without a ripple or a sound.
entry.ctx: The city outside was loud and hurried, but the garden behind the old library was {serene}, with only birdsong and the trickle of a fountain.
entry.etym: From Latin serenus, “clear, calm, cloudless.”

mn.text: High on the mountain, Nana Lou sits on a rock and watches the sun go down over the quiet valley. It is a {serene} scene.

scene.alt: A grandmother sits peacefully on a mountain rock watching the sunset as a butterfly floats by.

entry.def: quiet and still; free from disturbance
entry.ex: By evening the stormy sea had turned {tranquil}.
entry.ctx: After a week in the noisy city, the family loved the {tranquil} cabin, where the only sounds at night were crickets and the wind in the pines.
entry.etym: From Latin tranquillus, “calm, quiet, still.”

mn.cue: a toy TRAIN and a QUILT: TRAN-QUIL
mn.text: Theo’s toy train sits still on the rug while he sleeps under his warm quilt. The whole room is quiet and {tranquil}.

scene.alt: A toddler sleeps peacefully in bed while a toy train and a teddy bear sit still on the floor.

entry.def: in control of your feelings; not flustered
entry.ex: Even when the lights went out, the pianist stayed {composed} and went on playing.
entry.ctx: Though she was nervous inside, Maya looked {composed} at the interview: she sat up straight, answered slowly and never once fidgeted.

mn.text: When the stage lights flicker during her recital, Lila keeps playing without missing a note. She stays {composed}.

scene.alt: A girl calmly plays the piano on stage while the lights flicker.

entry.def: casually unconcerned, as if nothing much matters
entry.ex: With a {nonchalant} shrug, Dev said he had probably won the contest.
entry.ctx: The rest of the family was frantic about the lost keys, but the cat was {nonchalant}, yawning and stretching in the sunny window as if nothing had happened.
entry.etym: From French nonchalant, “not caring”: non (not) + chaloir (to concern), from Latin calere, “to be warm.”
entry.note: Nonchalant can praise calm (a nonchalant hero) or criticize carelessness (nonchalant about homework).

mn.text: Everyone is hunting for the lost keys, but the cat just yawns in the sunny window: “I shall not care.” The cat is {nonchalant}.

scene.alt: A worried woman searches for her keys while the cat lounges calmly near them.

entry.def: staying calm even in a sudden crisis
entry.ex: The {unflappable} pilot landed the plane smoothly in the storm.
entry.ctx: When the oven caught fire during the big dinner, the {unflappable} chef simply put it out, opened a window and went on cooking as if nothing had happened.

mn.cue: UN-FLAP-able: never flaps like a chicken
mn.text: The chickens flap and squawk in a panic, but Nana Lou calmly scoops them up one by one. She is {unflappable}.

scene.alt: A calm grandmother gathers up chickens that are flapping around in a panic.

entry.def: enduring pain or hardship without complaining
entry.ex: The fisherman {stoically} hauled his nets through the freezing rain for hours, without one complaint.
entry.ctx: Though the march was long and the food was poor, the {stoic} travelers never grumbled; they simply put one foot in front of the other.
entry.etym: From the Stoics, Greek thinkers who taught that a wise person bears hardship calmly; they met in a painted porch called the Stoa.

mn.text: In freezing rain and howling wind, Sven hauls in his nets hour after hour without one complaint. He is {stoic}.

scene.alt: A fisherman in a raincoat steadily hauls in his net in the pouring rain.

entry.def: showing no feeling on your face
entry.ex: The palace guard stared {impassively} ahead while the children made silly faces at him.
entry.ctx: The judge listened to the dramatic story with an {impassive} face, so no one in the courtroom could guess what she was thinking.
entry.etym: From im- (not) + passive, in an old sense, “able to feel or suffer,” from Latin pati (to suffer).
entry.note: Impassive (showing no feeling) is the opposite of impassioned (full of feeling).

mn.text: The kids tell jokes and make silly faces, but the palace guard’s face does not move a bit. He is {impassive}.

scene.alt: A castle guard keeps a blank face while two children make silly faces at him.

entry.def: calmness and evenness of temper, especially under stress
entry.ex: Coach Ada met both the big win and the bad loss with {equanimity}.
entry.ctx: He accepted the news with {equanimity}; though the trip was canceled, he simply unpacked his bag and suggested a picnic in the park instead.
entry.etym: From Latin aequanimitas: aequus (even, equal) + animus (mind).

mn.text: Whether her team wins or loses, Coach Ada’s mood stays perfectly level, like a balanced scale. She meets both with {equanimity}.

scene.alt: A calm coach holding a trophy stands beside a perfectly balanced scale.

entry.def: so calm that nothing can upset you
entry.ex: Grandpa is {imperturbable}; he reads his paper calmly even in a thunderstorm.
entry.ctx: Reporters tried for an hour to rattle the {imperturbable} scientist, but she answered every rude question in the same quiet, even voice.
entry.etym: From Latin imperturbabilis: in- (not) + perturbare (to throw into confusion), from turba (turmoil).

mn.text: The wind howls, an umbrella flies past and hats blow away, but Grandpa calmly turns the page of his newspaper. He is {imperturbable}.

scene.alt: A grandfather calmly reads his newspaper on a park bench while a gale blows an umbrella and a hat away.

entry.def: calm and unexcitable by nature; slow to show feeling
entry.ex: Even as a baby, Sam was {phlegmatic}: he rarely cried, rarely squealed and hardly ever fussed.
entry.ctx: Her brother was excitable and loud, but she was {phlegmatic}; even on the day she won the scholarship, she only nodded and said, “Good.”

roots.means: one of the four “humors” of old medicine

entry.etym: From Greek phlegma, phlegm: old doctors believed too much of this body fluid made a person sluggish and calm.

mn.cue: a FROG on a MAT: fleg-MAT-ic
mn.text: While the ducks splash and squawk around him, the big frog sits on his lily pad, blinking slowly. Nothing excites him; he is {phlegmatic}.

scene.alt: A big frog sits calmly while two ducks splash and flap around it.

blocks.html: impassive (showing no feeling) is not impassioned (full of feeling); they are opposites. nonchalant can mean calm or too unconcerned.

head: kind of calm
words
blocks.cap: Calm, sorted by kind.

blocks.html: Stoic adds endurance: a stoic person bears pain or hardship without complaint. Phlegmatic describes a temperament: some people are simply born unexcitable.

Vocabulary.com Dictionary (definitions checked)

blocks.html: Writers compare constantly, and they need words for every kind of likeness and difference. Some words say two things are alike (akin, kindred) or explain one by another (analogy). Some say they differ: completely (disparate), as opposites (antithesis, dichotomy), where they should match (discrepancy) or just slightly (nuance). Juxtapose is what you do to compare: set things side by side. And a paradox seems to contradict itself.
Alike: akin, kindred, analogy. Different: disparate, discrepancy, dichotomy, antithesis, nuance (only slightly). Side by side: juxtapose. Seems impossible but may be true: paradox.

entry.def: a comparison that explains one thing by its likeness to another
entry.ex: The coach used an {analogy}: a team is like a clock, and every little gear matters.
entry.ctx: To explain how the computer’s memory works, the author drew an {analogy} to a library, with files as books and the processor as a busy librarian.
entry.etym: From Greek analogia, “proportion”: ana (according to) + logos (ratio, reason).

mn.text: To explain how the brain stores memories, Professor Edwin points from his head to his laptop: “It works like this!” That comparison is an {analogy}.

cast.say: The brain is LIKE a computer!

scene.alt: A professor compares the brain to the laptop on his desk while a student listens.

entry.def: similar or related
entry.ex: Her fear of heights is {akin} to her brother’s fear of deep water.
entry.ctx: The new game is {akin} to chess: both are played on a checkered board, both reward patience and both end when one king is trapped.
entry.note: Akin is usually followed by “to”: akin to a song.

mn.text: Kai’s puppy and Granny Mae’s old dog have the same spots, the same floppy ears and the same bark. They look like kin: they are {akin}.

scene.alt: A boy and a grandmother laugh at their two dogs, who look almost exactly alike.

entry.def: alike in nature or interests; related
entry.ex: Rosa and Nana Lou turned out to be {kindred} spirits, both crazy about mystery novels.
entry.ctx: Though they lived on opposite sides of the world, the two pen pals felt {kindred}: they loved the same music, feared the same spiders and laughed at the same jokes.

roots.means: condition (an old English ending, as in hatred)

entry.note: Often in the phrase “kindred spirits”: people who are alike at heart.

mn.text: Rosa and Nana Lou reach for the same old mystery novel and burst out laughing. They are like family at heart: {kindred} spirits.

scene.alt: A teen and a grandmother reach for the same book and smile, delighted to share a favorite.

entry.def: so different that they can hardly be compared
entry.ex: The club brought together {disparate} people: a pilot, a poet, a plumber and a pastry chef.
entry.ctx: The two reports were so {disparate}, one praising the new road and the other calling it a disaster, that readers wondered whether the writers had visited the same town.
entry.etym: From Latin disparatus, “separated,” from disparare, “to divide”; its meaning was colored by Latin dispar, “unequal.”
entry.note: Disparate means fundamentally unlike, not just a little different.

mn.text: A tiny feathered parrot and a huge swimming whale: they share almost nothing. They are {disparate}.

scene.alt: A small parrot on an island and a big whale in the sea, two creatures with almost nothing in common.

entry.def: a difference between things that should match
entry.ex: Lin noticed a {discrepancy} between the receipt and the number of crepes on her plate.
entry.ctx: The detective focused on one {discrepancy}: the butler said he had been asleep by ten, yet his tea was still warm at midnight.
entry.etym: From Latin discrepantia, from discrepare, “to sound differently, disagree”: dis (apart) + crepare (to rattle).

mn.text: The ticket says three crepes, but Lin’s plate holds only two. She spots the {discrepancy}.

scene.alt: A puzzled woman holds a ticket for three crepes but finds only two on the table.

entry.def: to place side by side, especially to compare or contrast
entry.ex: The photo {juxtaposes} the tallest player on the team with the tiny mascot.
entry.ctx: The museum {juxtaposed} an ancient clay pot with a modern plastic one, inviting visitors to notice how little the basic shape had changed in four thousand years.
entry.etym: From French juxtaposer: Latin juxta (beside) + French poser (to place).

mn.cue: JUXTA-POSE: POSE them side by side
mn.text: For the team photo, Rosa poses the giant center right beside the littlest fan. To {juxtapose} is to place things side by side.

scene.alt: A giant man and a tiny toddler pose side by side while a teen takes their photo.

entry.def: a split into two opposite parts or groups
entry.ex: The story sets up a sharp {dichotomy} between the noisy city and the quiet farm.
entry.ctx: The coach rejected the {dichotomy} between talent and hard work, insisting that every great player she had known needed plenty of both.
entry.etym: From Greek dikhotomia, “a cutting in two”: dikha (in two) + temnein (to cut).
entry.note: Strictly, a dichotomy has two opposite sides; using it for any difference stretches it.

mn.text: At summer camp, everyone is split into two opposite teams, Red and Blue, and every game is Red against Blue. That split is a {dichotomy}.

scene.alt: Two teams of children, one in red and one in blue, cheer on opposite sides of a line.

entry.def: the direct opposite
entry.ex: Pip’s messy room is the {antithesis} of his twin sister’s neat one.
entry.ctx: The quiet country inn was the {antithesis} of the loud city hotel where they had spent the week: no traffic, no crowds and not a single television.
entry.etym: From Greek antithesis, “opposition”: anti (against) + tithenai (to place).

mn.text: Pip loves noise, mess and speed; his twin, Lila, loves quiet, order and books. Lila is Pip’s {antithesis}.

scene.alt: A boy jumps around a messy room while his twin sister reads quietly in a tidy corner.

entry.def: a subtle difference in meaning, feeling or tone
entry.ex: A good actor can show a dozen {nuances} of sadness with just her eyes.
entry.ctx: The translation was accurate but flat; it lost every {nuance} of the poem, the gentle teasing and the sadness hidden in its last line.

roots.means: the state or quality of (a noun ending)

entry.etym: From French nuance, “a shade of color,” from nuer (to shade), related to Latin nubes (cloud).

mn.text: Nell mixes seven blues for the sky, each just one drop lighter than the last. Each tiny shade of difference is a {nuance}.

scene.alt: A painter at an easel carefully mixes slightly different shades of blue.

entry.def: a statement that seems to contradict itself but may be true
entry.ex: “The more you learn, the less you know” is a famous {paradox}.
entry.ctx: It is a {paradox} of travel that the longest trips can feel the shortest: when every day is new and full, the weeks fly by.
entry.etym: From Greek paradoxon, “contrary to expectation”: para (against) + doxa (opinion).

mn.text: A pair of wise ducks quack, “The more you learn, the less you know!” It sounds impossible but may be true: a {paradox}.

scene.alt: Two thoughtful ducks share a saying that seems to contradict itself.

blocks.html: A dichotomy is a split into two opposites; using it for any difference stretches it. disparate means fundamentally unlike, not just different.

how much
blocks.cap: From alike to opposite.

blocks.html: To juxtapose things is to put them side by side so that the reader compares them. Writers juxtapose to create contrast: a rich man’s feast next to a beggar at the gate.

Vocabulary.com Dictionary (definitions checked; origin of nuance)

blocks.html: Every story, storm and business has a start, and English has a crowd of words for it. Three are verbs for starting: commence, initiate and inaugurate. Three are nouns for the start itself: inception, genesis and onset. Four are adjectives for things that have only just begun: nascent, incipient, fledgling and rudimentary.

Listen for tone. Onset and incipient usually announce something unwelcome (the onset of a storm, an incipient leak). Nascent and fledgling are hopeful: something new is growing. Inaugurate means a formal ceremony.

entry.def: to begin, especially in a formal way
entry.ex: The concert will {commence} at seven o’clock sharp.
entry.ctx: Once the judge entered and everyone was seated, the trial could finally {commence}, three hours later than planned.
entry.etym: From Old French comencier, from Latin com- + initiare (to begin).
entry.note: A graduation is called a commencement because it begins the graduates’ new lives.

mn.cue: COMMENCEMENT: the day your new life BEGINS
mn.text: Graduation is called commencement because it is a beginning, not an end. On that day, the graduates {commence} their grown-up lives.

scene.alt: Two graduates in caps cheer under falling confetti on graduation day.

entry.def: to set something going; also, to admit a new member to a group
entry.ex: Zoe {initiated} the dancing by stepping onto the empty floor.
entry.ctx: No one wanted to be the first to apologize, so the twins sat in silence until their little brother {initiated} peace talks with a plate of cookies.
entry.etym: From Latin initiare, “to begin, admit,” from initium, “a beginning.”

mn.text: At the party everyone stands around shyly until Zoe takes the initial step onto the dance floor. She {initiates} the dancing.

scene.alt: A girl starts dancing first at a party while two shy friends watch.

entry.def: to open or begin with a formal ceremony; to install in office
entry.ex: The town {inaugurated} its new library with a ribbon, a band and a cake.
entry.ctx: The railway was {inaugurated} with great fanfare: flags flew, a band played and the first train carried two hundred cheering guests.
entry.etym: From Latin inaugurare, “to install after reading the omens,” from augur, a Roman official who read signs in the flight of birds.

mn.text: In August the town opens its new bridge with a band, balloons and a speech by Granny Mae. They {inaugurate} it.

scene.alt: A grandmother cheers under a grand opening banner as a boy drums beside the new bridge.

entry.def: the moment at which something is founded or begun
entry.ex: From its {inception}, the bakery was famous for its cinnamon rolls.
entry.ctx: The festival has grown enormously since its {inception} in 1990, when a dozen neighbors set up card tables in a parking lot.
entry.etym: From Latin inceptio, “a beginning,” from incipere, “to begin, take in hand”: in + capere (to take).

mn.cue: IN-CEPT-ion: the moment the idea is TAKEN IN
mn.text: Lin bites into her grandmother’s bread and cries, “I’ll open a bakery!” That moment was the bakery’s {inception}.

scene.alt: A woman tastes her grandmother’s bread and gets the idea to open a bakery.

entry.def: the origin or birth of something
entry.ex: The {genesis} of the giant oak was a single acorn.
entry.ctx: The {genesis} of the town’s famous fall fair was a single bake sale, held by three friends on a rainy afternoon fifty years ago.
entry.etym: From Greek genesis, “origin, birth,” related to gignesthai (to be born).

mn.text: Sami waters a tiny sprout beside the giant old oak. Every great tree has its {genesis}, its birth, in one small seed.

scene.alt: A boy kneels to water a tiny sprout that stands near a giant oak tree.

entry.def: the beginning of something, usually something unpleasant
entry.ex: At the {onset} of the storm, the picnickers grabbed their baskets and ran.
entry.ctx: With the {onset} of winter, the birds that had crowded the feeder all summer flew south, and the garden grew silent.

mn.text: The sky darkens and the first raindrops fall: the storm is setting on. At its {onset}, the picnickers grab their baskets and run.

scene.alt: Picnickers run with a basket and an umbrella as a storm begins.

entry.def: just born; only beginning to exist or grow
entry.ex: With six teams and one muddy field, the town’s {nascent} soccer league was only a few weeks old.
entry.ctx: The club was still {nascent}, with only six members and no meeting room, but its founders had big plans for the year ahead.
entry.etym: From Latin nascens, “being born,” from nasci (to be born), the same root as native and nature.

mn.text: The chick has just pecked its way out of the shell, and its life has only begun. Something that new is {nascent}.

scene.alt: A just-hatched chick peeps out of its nest as the mother hen looks on lovingly.

entry.def: just beginning to appear or develop, often as an early sign of trouble
entry.ex: Dad spotted the {incipient} leak while it was still a single drip.
entry.ctx: The dentist caught the {incipient} cavity early, when it was only a tiny gray spot, and filled it before it could ever hurt.
entry.etym: From Latin incipiens, “beginning,” from incipere (to begin): in + capere (to take).
entry.note: Close to nascent, but incipient often warns of something unwelcome: an incipient crack, an incipient cold.

mn.cue: IN-SIP-ient: the first little SIP of trouble
mn.text: A single drip from the ceiling is the first little sip of a leak. Fix it now, while the leak is still {incipient}, before the roof gives way.

scene.alt: A worried man points up at a drip from the ceiling falling into a bucket.

entry.def: new and inexperienced, like a young bird learning to fly
entry.ex: The {fledgling} pilot gripped the controls nervously on her very first solo flight.
entry.ctx: The {fledgling} theater company had no stage of its own yet, so its first play was performed in a borrowed barn with hay bales for seats.
entry.etym: From fledge, “to grow the feathers needed to fly,” + -ling, as in duckling.

mn.cue: a FLEDGLING bird: first wobbly flight
mn.text: Like a baby bird on its first wobbly flight, Kai’s brand-new lemonade stand is just getting started. It is a {fledgling} business.

scene.alt: A boy runs a new lemonade stand as a baby bird wobbles through its first flight overhead.

entry.def: basic and simple; not developed beyond the first stage
entry.ex: Pip’s first treehouse was {rudimentary}: four boards and a blanket for a roof.
entry.ctx: The travelers spoke only {rudimentary} French, enough to order bread and ask for the station, but not enough to follow the guide’s long stories.
entry.etym: From rudiment, from Latin rudimentum, “a first attempt,” from rudis (rough, unformed).

mn.text: Pip’s first treehouse is rough and simple: four boards, a rope and a blanket for a roof. It is {rudimentary}.

scene.alt: A proud boy stands by a tree with a single board nailed up as his simple treehouse.

blocks.html: nascent and incipient are close; incipient often warns of something unwelcome (an incipient problem). fledgling comes from a young bird learning to fly.

words
notes
rows: incipient often warns; fledgling = new and untested; rudimentary = basic

blocks.html: Fledgling comes from a young bird that has just grown the feathers to fly. A fledgling business, like the bird, is new, wobbly and still learning.

blocks.html: Ten verbs for getting in the way, from a little to a lot. Some only slow things down (hinder, hamper, impede, encumber). Some block them (obstruct, stymie) or defeat a plan (thwart). One holds back from inside (inhibit). Two stop things before they start (preclude, forestall).
Strength matters. Mud that impedes you slows you down; a locked door that precludes entry makes it impossible. Forestall means acting early, stepping in front of a problem before it arrives.

entry.def: to get in the way of; to slow down
entry.ex: The puppy tugging at her backpack {hindered} Ivy’s walk to the bus.
entry.ctx: Heavy snow {hindered} the rescue, but it did not stop it; the team simply moved more slowly and reached the cabin by dark.
entry.etym: From Old English hindrian, “to hold back,” related to hind and behind.

mn.text: Ivy tries to walk to the bus, but the puppy hangs onto her backpack from behind. The puppy {hinders} her.

scene.alt: A puppy tugs at a girl’s backpack from behind as she tries to walk to the bus.

entry.def: to hold back or slow down progress
entry.ex: The giant picnic basket {hampered} Dev’s climb up the hill.
entry.ctx: A shortage of buses {hampered} the school’s field trips all year; classes had to take turns, and some never left the building at all.
entry.note: A different word, the noun hamper, is a large basket for picnics or laundry.

mn.cue: a heavy HAMPER slows the hike
mn.text: Dev lugs the huge picnic hamper up the steep hill, one slow step at a time. The heavy basket {hampers} his climb.

scene.alt: A teen struggles uphill carrying an enormous picnic basket.

entry.def: to slow or block movement or progress
entry.ex: Thick mud {impeded} the hikers at every step.
entry.ctx: Fallen branches {impeded} the river’s flow, so the water rose behind them and spread across the meadow.
entry.etym: From Latin impedire, “to shackle the feet”: in + pes, ped- (foot).

mn.cue: IM-PED: FEET caught in the mud
mn.text: Pip’s boots sink deep into the mud, and every step is a struggle. The mud {impedes} him: it catches his feet.

scene.alt: A boy in a raincoat struggles to pull his feet out of deep mud.

entry.def: to block a path, passage or view
entry.ex: A fallen tree {obstructed} the road to the lake.
entry.ctx: The new billboard {obstructs} the view from the old inn; guests who once watched the sunset over the bay now stare at a giant sign.
entry.etym: From Latin obstruere, “to build against, block”: ob (against) + struere (to pile up, build).

mn.cue: OB-STRUCT: a STRUCTURE in the way
mn.text: A huge log lies across the road like a wall, and the bus cannot get past. The log {obstructs} the road.

scene.alt: A bus driver scratches his head at a huge log blocking the road.

entry.def: to stop someone from carrying out a plan
entry.ex: The goalie {thwarted} every shot in the second half.
entry.ctx: The squirrels’ plan to raid the bird feeder was {thwarted} by a slippery metal pole that none of them could climb.
entry.etym: From Old Norse thvert, “across”: to thwart is to cut across someone’s path.

mn.cue: THWACK! the goalie THWARTS the shot
mn.text: Dev winds up for the winning goal, but Maya leaps and thwacks the ball away. She {thwarts} his plan.

scene.alt: A goalie leaps and knocks away a shot as the shooter looks shocked.

entry.def: to hold back or restrain
entry.ex: Shyness {inhibited} Lila from raising her hand, though she knew the answer.
entry.ctx: Cold weather {inhibits} the growth of the vines; the grapes stay small and sour until the warm days of late summer.
entry.etym: From Latin inhibere, “to hold back”: in + habere (to hold).

mn.text: Lila knows the answer, but shyness holds her in, and her hand stays down. Shyness {inhibits} her.

scene.alt: A shy girl keeps her hand down, though she knows the answer, while classmates raise theirs.

entry.def: to weigh down with a burden
entry.ex: The hikers were {encumbered} by tents, pots and three days of food.
entry.ctx: The young couple’s plans were {encumbered} by debt; every dollar they earned went to old bills instead of the house they dreamed of.
entry.etym: From Old French encombrer, “to block up, burden.”

mn.text: Sven staggers home with a giant crate of a hundred cucumbers in his arms. He is {encumbered}: so weighed down he can barely move.

scene.alt: A big man staggers under the weight of a huge crate of cucumbers.

entry.def: to block completely; to leave stuck or stumped
entry.ex: The last riddle in the book {stymied} the whole family.
entry.ctx: Engineers were {stymied} for months: every design for the bridge failed the wind test, and no one could figure out why.
entry.etym: First a golf word of the 1800s: a stymie was a ball lying in the line between another ball and the hole.

mn.cue: STY-MIE: the pig blocks the STY
mn.text: The giant pig flops across the gate of its sty, and no matter what Farmer Omar tries, he cannot get in. He is {stymied}.

scene.alt: A big pig sleeps across the gate of its pen while a puzzled farmer scratches his head.

entry.def: to make impossible in advance; to rule out
entry.ex: The locked gate {precluded} any visit to the garden.
entry.ctx: Her broken wrist {precluded} playing in the final, so she spent the game on the bench, cheering louder than anyone.
entry.etym: From Latin praecludere, “to shut off”: prae (before) + claudere (to shut).
entry.note: Preclude is stronger than hinder: it rules something out completely, ahead of time.

mn.text: The museum door was locked before anyone arrived, so no one could get in at all. The locked door {precluded} any visit.

scene.alt: A boy and his grandmother sadly face a locked door with a closed sign.

entry.def: to prevent something by acting first
entry.ex: Mom {forestalled} a meltdown by handing out snacks before the kids got hungry.
entry.ctx: To {forestall} complaints about the noise, the band visited every neighbor a week before the party and invited them all to come.

mn.cue: FORE-STALL: stop it BEFORE it starts
mn.text: Just before the kids get hungry and cranky, Mom hands out sandwiches. She {forestalls} the meltdown.

scene.alt: A mother hands out sandwiches to two happy children just before snack time.

blocks.html: preclude rules something out ahead of time; it is stronger than hinder. forestall means acting early to prevent, like stepping in front of a problem.

words

heads it off by acting first

blocks.html: Two words have a Latin foot in them: impede (in + ped, foot: to tangle the feet) and its opposite expedite (ex + ped: to free the feet). One has a Latin door: preclude (pre + clud, shut).

Vocabulary.com Dictionary (definitions checked)

blocks.html: These are words of courtrooms and consciences. Two describe responsibility and blame (accountable, culpable). Five mean clearing someone of blame, each in its own way (exculpate, exonerate, acquit, absolve, vindicate). Condone means letting wrongdoing slide, punitive describes punishment, and clemency is mercy.
Listen for the Latin: culpa = fault (culpable, exculpate); onus = burden (exonerate: the burden of blame taken off); poena = punishment (punitive, like punish).

entry.def: responsible for your actions and expected to explain them
entry.ex: As class treasurer, Maya was {accountable} for every dollar of the trip fund.
entry.ctx: The new rules hold each driver {accountable}: if a package arrives damaged, the driver who carried it must explain what happened.

mn.cue: ACCOUNT-ABLE: able to give an ACCOUNT
mn.text: Maya, the class treasurer, can show where every dollar of the trip money went, down to the last receipt. She is {accountable}.

scene.alt: A student treasurer proudly shows her notebook of receipts to her teacher.

entry.def: deserving blame
entry.ex: The muddy paw prints showed that the dog was {culpable}.
entry.ctx: The report found the builder {culpable}: he had known the beams were cracked and had covered them with paint instead of replacing them.
entry.etym: From Latin culpabilis, “blameworthy,” from culpa (fault, blame).

mn.cue: CULP-able: the CULPRIT is to blame
mn.text: Muddy paw prints lead straight from the kitchen to the dog’s bed. The dog is the culprit: he is {culpable}.

scene.alt: A woman points at a guilty-looking dog sitting on its bed beside a trail of muddy paw prints.

entry.def: to show that someone is not guilty
entry.ex: The video from the hallway camera {exculpated} Ivy: it showed the cat knocking over the vase.
entry.ctx: New letters found in the archive {exculpate} the old mayor; they show that he had warned the council about the dam years before it broke.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin exculpare, “to free from blame”: ex (out of) + culpa (blame).

mn.text: The camera shows the cat, not Ivy, knocking over the vase. The video takes the blame right out of Ivy’s hands: it {exculpates} her.

scene.alt: A boy holds up a camera that shows the cat broke the vase, and his sister cheers.

entry.def: to clear completely of blame
entry.ex: When the real thief confessed, the police {exonerated} the gardener.
entry.ctx: After ten years in prison, the man was {exonerated} by new tests that proved someone else had committed the crime.
entry.etym: From Latin exonerare, “to unload, free from a burden”: ex (off) + onus (burden).

mn.cue: EX-ONUS: the load of blame lifted OFF
mn.text: When the real thief is caught, the heavy sack of blame falls off Jamal’s shoulders. He is {exonerated}.

scene.alt: A relieved man cheers as a heavy sack labeled blame falls away from him.

entry.def: to declare someone not guilty in a court
entry.ex: The jury {acquitted} the baker of stealing the prize-winning pie.
entry.ctx: Although the newspapers had already called her guilty, the jury {acquitted} her after one hour, finding that the evidence proved nothing.
entry.note: Acquit is a court word: a jury or judge acquits. Its opposite is convict.

mn.cue: AC-QUIT: you can QUIT worrying: not guilty!
mn.text: The jury foreman stands and reads, “Not guilty!” Rosa can quit worrying: the court has {acquitted} her.

scene.alt: In a courtroom, a juror reads “not guilty” and the young woman on trial cheers.

entry.def: to free someone from guilt, blame or a duty
entry.ex: Grandma {absolved} Pip of the broken teacup: “Accidents happen.”
entry.ctx: The team’s apology did not {absolve} it of responsibility; the club still had to pay to repair the field it had damaged.
entry.etym: From Latin absolvere, “to set free, loosen”: ab (from) + solvere (to loosen).

mn.text: Pip breaks Grandma’s teacup and expects a scolding, but she hugs him: “Accidents happen. You’re forgiven.” She {absolves} him.

scene.alt: A grandmother hugs her grandson and forgives him for breaking a teacup.

entry.def: to clear from blame or doubt; to prove right
entry.ex: When the old well gushed water, Sami felt {vindicated}.
entry.ctx: For years critics mocked her theory, but the new fossils {vindicated} her: the bird’s ancestors really had walked on two legs.
entry.etym: From Latin vindicare, “to claim, set free, defend.”
entry.note: Vindicate has nothing to do with revenge; that is vindictive.

mn.cue: VIN = WIN: proved RIGHT at last
mn.text: Everyone laughed at Sami for saying the old well still had water, until it gushed. He wins: the gushing well {vindicates} him.

scene.alt: A boy cheers as an old well he believed in gushes water, while a doubter stares.

entry.def: to accept or overlook wrongdoing
entry.ex: The school does not {condone} copying homework.
entry.ctx: By laughing along instead of stopping the teasing, the counselor seemed to {condone} it, and the campers took it as permission to continue.
entry.etym: From Latin condonare, “to give up, forgive”: con + donare (to give).
entry.note: Condone is nearly the opposite of condemn: to condone wrongdoing is to let it pass.

mn.cue: CON-DONE: “Eh, it’s DONE all the time”
mn.text: Pip peeks at the answer sheet, and the substitute just shrugs: “Eh, it’s done all the time.” By shrugging it off, he {condones} the cheating.

scene.alt: A boy peeks at an answer sheet while the substitute teacher just shrugs.

entry.def: meant as punishment
entry.ex: A five-hundred-dollar fine for one overdue library book would be {punitive}.
entry.ctx: The coach insisted the extra laps were not {punitive} but practical: the team simply needed to get in better shape before the season.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin punitivus, from Latin punire, “to punish.”

mn.text: The librarian posts a sign: one late book, a five-hundred-dollar fine! A fine like that is not a reminder; it is {punitive}.

scene.alt: A stern librarian points to a sign announcing a huge fine as a boy with a late book looks shocked.

entry.def: mercy, especially in punishing someone
entry.ex: The queen showed {clemency} to the hungry boy who had taken a loaf of bread.
entry.ctx: The judge could have given the maximum sentence, but she granted {clemency} because the young man had confessed and repaid every dollar.
entry.etym: From Latin clementia, “mildness, mercy.”

mn.text: Instead of punishing the hungry boy who took a loaf of bread, the queen hands him a basket of clementines. She shows {clemency}.

scene.alt: A kind queen gives a basket of fruit to a hungry boy holding a loaf of bread.

blocks.html: condone means to allow or overlook, not to condemn; they are near opposites. vindicate means to clear or prove right; it has nothing to do with revenge (vindictive).

blocks.html: Two famous mix-ups: condone (to overlook wrongdoing) is nearly the opposite of condemn (to declare it wrong); and vindicate (to prove right) has nothing to do with vindictive (seeking revenge).

blocks.html: Big and small are the first describing words children learn; these ten are their grown-up cousins. Five are for the enormous (immense, colossal, monumental, prodigious, gargantuan) and five for the tiny (minute, minuscule, diminutive, infinitesimal, negligible).
Each has a flavor. Monumental and prodigious often mean great in importance or skill, not just size. Diminutive usually describes a person. Negligible means so small it doesn’t matter.
Two traps: minuscule is spelled with a u (from minus), and minute the adjective is pronounced my-NOOT, not like the minute on a clock.

entry.def: extremely large or great
entry.ex: The blue whale is an {immense} animal, longer than two school buses.
entry.ctx: Looking out from the plane, she was struck by how {immense} the desert was: hour after hour, nothing but sand in every direction.
entry.etym: From Latin immensus, “immeasurable”: in- (not) + mensus (measured).

mn.text: Kai tries to measure the whale with his little ruler and gives up after the tail. It is {immense}: too big to measure.

scene.alt: A boy in a rowboat holds up a tiny ruler beside an enormous whale.

entry.def: enormous; huge enough to fill you with awe
entry.ex: A {colossal} statue towered over the harbor, dwarfing the ships below.
entry.ctx: The project was a {colossal} undertaking: three thousand workers, ten years and enough steel to build a small city.
entry.etym: From colossus, a gigantic statue, from Greek kolossos; the most famous was the huge bronze Colossus that stood at the harbor of Rhodes.

mn.cue: COLOSSUS: a statue so big it awes
mn.text: The giant statue at the harbor is so tall that the sailing ships look like toys at its feet. It is {colossal}.

scene.alt: A gigantic statue towers over a tiny girl and a small sailboat in the harbor.

entry.def: very great in size or importance
entry.ex: Finishing the five-thousand-piece puzzle was a {monumental} task.
entry.ctx: The discovery of the cure was a {monumental} achievement, one that historians still rank among the most important of the century.

roots.means: a means or result (a noun ending)

entry.etym: From monument, from Latin monumentum, “a reminder, a memorial,” from monere (to remind).

mn.cue: MONUMENT-al: as big as a MONUMENT
mn.text: After a whole summer, Lila fits the last of five thousand puzzle pieces into place. Finishing it was a {monumental} task.

scene.alt: A girl cheers as she finishes a giant five-thousand-piece puzzle.

entry.def: remarkably large or impressive
entry.ex: Professor Edwin owns a {prodigious} library, with books stacked to the ceiling.
entry.ctx: The young violinist had a {prodigious} memory: she could hear a long piece once and play it back the next day without a single wrong note.
entry.etym: From Latin prodigiosus, “wondrous,” from prodigium, “a wonder, an omen,” the source of prodigy.

mn.cue: PRODIGY-ous: a wonder of a size
mn.text: Professor Edwin’s books are stacked from the floor to the ceiling, so he needs a ladder to reach the top. His library is {prodigious}.

labels.text: PRODIGY-ous: a WONDER of a size

scene.alt: A professor on a ladder reaches for the top of towering stacks of books.

entry.def: enormous, especially in bulk or appetite
entry.ex: Omar grew a {gargantuan} watermelon that took four people to lift.
entry.ctx: The puppy’s appetite was {gargantuan}: it finished its own bowl, the cat’s bowl and half a loaf of bread before anyone noticed.
entry.etym: From Gargantua, a jolly giant with an enormous appetite in a French comic tale of the 1500s.

mn.text: Omar grows a watermelon so big that the whole family has to push to roll it out of the garden. It is {gargantuan}.

scene.alt: A man and a boy push an enormous watermelon across the garden.

entry.def: extremely small; also, very detailed
entry.ex: A {minute} speck of dust jammed the old watch.
entry.ctx: The scientist examined the leaf in {minute} detail, recording every tiny vein, spot and hair that most people would never notice.
entry.etym: From Latin minutus, “made small,” from minuere (to lessen).
entry.note: The adjective is pronounced my-NOOT. The noun minute (MIN-it), a sixtieth of an hour, comes from the same Latin word: a “small part.”

mn.text: Zoe’s pet newt is so tiny it fits on a fingertip; she needs a magnifying glass to see its toes. Her newt is {minute}.

scene.alt: A girl kneels with a magnifying glass to see a tiny newt on a leaf.

entry.def: extremely small
entry.ex: Split among ten friends, the last cookie became ten {minuscule} crumbs.
entry.ctx: The difference in price was {minuscule}, just two cents, so Grandma bought the pears from the farmer she liked best.
entry.etym: From Latin minuscula (littera), “rather small (letter),” from minus (less).
entry.note: Spelled with a u, from minus. “Miniscule” is a common misspelling.

mn.cue: MINUS-cule: so small it’s almost a MINUS
mn.text: The last cookie is shared with eight friends, and Ivy squints at her share: one crumb. It is {minuscule}.

scene.alt: A girl squints at the tiny crumb of cookie that is her share.

entry.def: very small, especially in height
entry.ex: The {diminutive} coach barely reached her players’ shoulders, but they hung on her every word.
entry.ctx: Though {diminutive} in size, the old pony was the boss of the barn; even the giant draft horses stepped aside for him.
entry.etym: From Latin diminutus, “made smaller,” from deminuere (to lessen), the same source as diminish.
entry.note: In grammar, a diminutive is a form that means “little”: duckling, booklet.

mn.text: Nana Lou, barely five feet tall, coaches a team of giants, and they all listen when she blows her whistle. She is {diminutive} but mighty.

scene.alt: A tiny grandmother coach with a whistle stands between two very tall players.

entry.def: too small to measure
entry.ex: Under the microscope, Sami found {infinitesimal} creatures swimming in a drop of pond water.
entry.ctx: The difference between the two scales was {infinitesimal}, less than the weight of a grain of sand, so the baker trusted either one.
entry.etym: From Modern Latin infinitesimus, “the infinitieth (part),” from infinitus (endless).

mn.text: Sami peers into the microscope at creatures so small that no ruler could ever measure them. They are {infinitesimal}.

scene.alt: A boy in a lab coat looks through a microscope at creatures too small to measure.

entry.def: so small or unimportant it can be ignored
entry.ex: Pouring one cup of water into the ocean has a {negligible} effect on its level.
entry.ctx: The repair added a {negligible} amount to the bill, only a dollar, so the shop owner simply didn’t charge for it.
entry.etym: From Latin negligere, “to neglect, disregard.”

mn.text: Pip pours one bucket of water into the ocean and checks whether the sea has risen. The difference is {negligible}: small enough to ignore.

scene.alt: A boy on the dock pours a bucket of water into the sea and wonders if it rose.

blocks.html: minuscule is spelled with a u (from minus), not "miniscule." minute the adjective is pronounced my-NOOT.

blocks.html: Minute has two pronunciations and two meanings. MIN-it is the sixty-second minute; my-NOOT means tiny, or carefully detailed (a minute examination). Both come from Latin minutus, “made small.”
