blocks.html: Three Latin roots do a great deal of work in English. vert (also spelled vers) means turn, as in reverse. ject means throw, as in reject. tract means pull or draw, as in tractor and attract. Put a prefix in front, and each root turns, throws or pulls in a new direction.

vert, vers = turn. ject = throw. tract = pull, draw. Find the root, then ask where the prefix sends it: a- away, ad- toward, sub- under, de- down, inter- between, con- together, pro- forward, in- not.

Each memory hook below acts out the parts. Say them out loud (de-JECT-ed: thrown down), look at the picture, then check the meaning against the sentences. The parts are a clue; the sentence has the last word.

entry.def: to turn away; to keep something bad from happening
entry.ex: Pip {averted} his eyes so he would not spoil the surprise in the gift bag.
entry.ctx: The crew worked through the night to patch the leaking dam, and their effort {averted} a flood that would have swamped the whole valley.
entry.etym: From Latin avertere, “to turn away”: ab (away) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: Captain Sven sees the rock ahead and turns the wheel hard; by turning away in time, he {averts} a crash.

scene.alt: A ship's captain turns the wheel hard to steer away from a rock in the sea.

entry.def: harmful or unfavorable; working against you
entry.ex: The soccer final was put off a week because of {adverse} weather: hail, lightning and high winds.
entry.ctx: Despite {adverse} conditions, including a broken-down bus and a cold, steady rain, the band reached the parade on time and played the whole route.
entry.etym: From Latin adversus, “turned toward, facing, opposed,” from advertere: ad (toward) + vertere (to turn).
entry.note: Adverse describes things and conditions (adverse weather, adverse effects). Don’t confuse it with averse, which describes a person’s dislike: averse to risk.

mn.cue: AD-VERSE: the wind TURNS against you
mn.text: Ivy runs east with her kite, but the wind turns and blows hard the other way; {adverse} winds work against her.

scene.alt: A girl struggles to hold her kite as a strong wind blows against her.

entry.def: able to do many different things, or to be used in many ways
entry.ex: A {versatile} player, Rosa can pitch, catch and cover first base.
entry.ctx: Unlike his brother, who could make only pancakes, Omar was a {versatile} cook: soup, curry, bread and birthday cakes all came out of his kitchen with equal skill.
entry.etym: From Latin versatilis, “able to turn; turning easily from one task to another,” from versare, “to keep turning.”

mn.cue: VERSE-atile: sings VERSES, plays it all
mn.text: Tia sings the verses, strums the guitar, beats the drum and plays the fiddle, turning easily from one to the next: she is {versatile}.

scene.alt: A smiling musician on a stage surrounded by a guitar, a drum, a violin and a microphone, ready to play them all.

entry.def: done by accident, without meaning to
entry.ex: One {inadvertent} tap on the screen sent Grandpa’s message to the whole family instead of just to Nana Lou.
entry.ctx: The spill was {inadvertent}; Dev had been watching the ball game on the screen, not his glass, when his elbow tipped it over.
entry.etym: From inadvertence, from Medieval Latin inadvertentia: in- (not) + Latin advertere, “to turn toward,” as in turning your mind toward something.
entry.note: An inadvertent mistake is not on purpose. It often comes from attention being somewhere else.

mn.cue: eyes IN the AD: a bump not meant
mn.text: Sami’s eyes are on the ad on the sign, not on the path, so he bumps a fruit cart. The bump is {inadvertent}: he did not mean it.

scene.alt: A boy reading a sign as he walks bumps into a fruit cart by accident, and lemons tumble.

entry.def: to secretly weaken or overturn something established
entry.ex: The sneaky player tried to {subvert} the rules by changing the score sheet when no one was looking.
entry.ctx: The spy did not fight the kingdom openly; instead he worked to {subvert} it from within, quietly turning the queen’s own advisers against her.
entry.etym: From Latin subvertere, “to turn from beneath, to overturn”: sub (under) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: Sneaky Rex crawls under the king’s banquet table and tips it over from beneath. To {subvert} is to overturn from underneath.

scene.alt: A sneaky man crawls under a king's table and tips it over while the king looks shocked.

entry.def: a guess made without enough proof
entry.ex: Whether the old map leads to anything at all is pure {conjecture}.
entry.ctx: With no fossils of its skin to study, the scientists could offer only {conjecture} about the creature’s color; their best guess was a dull green.
entry.etym: From Latin conjectura, from conicere, “to throw together”: com (together) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: Ada throws three clues together, a tipped vase, a paw print and a feather, and makes a guess: the cat chased a bird! Her {conjecture} may be wrong.

scene.alt: A woman with a magnifying glass looks at a tipped vase and a feather and guesses that the cat did it.

entry.def: sad and discouraged; low in spirits
entry.ex: After missing the bus to the big game, Kai sat on the curb looking {dejected}.
entry.ctx: The players had counted on a win, so they trudged off the muddy field {dejected}, heads down and hardly speaking.
entry.etym: From Latin deicere, “to throw down”: de (down) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: The wind throws Jonah’s new kite down into the mud, and his spirits fall with it: he sits slumped and {dejected}.

scene.alt: A teenage boy sits sadly on the ground beside his kite, which has crashed into a puddle.

entry.def: to break in with a remark while someone else is talking
entry.ex: Grandpa Gus likes to {interject} a joke in the middle of every story.
entry.ctx: Professor Edwin was halfway through his long explanation when a student {interjected} a quick question, and he paused to answer it before going on.
entry.etym: From Latin intericere, “to throw between”: inter (between) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: Mom and Dad are talking about dinner when Pip throws one word in between them: “Pizza!” He {interjects}.

scene.alt: A boy jumps between his talking parents and shouts his own idea for dinner.

entry.def: hard to manage, control or solve
entry.ex: The {intractable} goat refused to leave the porch, no matter how hard we pulled.
entry.ctx: Most leaks are quickly fixed, but the old barn roof proved {intractable}: every patch failed, and new drips appeared with each storm.
entry.etym: From Latin intractabilis: in (not) + tractabilis (manageable), from tractare, “to handle,” from trahere, “to pull.”

mn.text: Jamal pulls and pulls on the rope, but the donkey won’t move an inch. He can’t pull it or manage it: the donkey is {intractable}.

scene.alt: A farmer pulls hard on a rope, but a stubborn donkey refuses to move.

entry.def: lasting much longer than expected or usual
entry.ex: After a {protracted} search, Nana Lou found her glasses on top of her head.
entry.ctx: What was meant to be a quick ten-minute meeting became a {protracted} debate that ran past dinner and left everyone tired and hungry.
entry.etym: From Latin protrahere, “to drag forward, to draw out, to prolong”: pro (forward) + trahere (to pull).

mn.text: Professor Edwin’s “short” talk gets pulled out longer and longer, until his audience nods off. It is a {protracted} talk.

scene.alt: An old professor keeps talking at a podium while two students yawn and doze under a clock.

blocks.html: Two easy slips. Adverse describes conditions and effects (adverse weather, adverse side effects); averse describes a person who dislikes something (averse to risk). And an inadvertent mistake is an accident, not a choice: it happens without meaning to, often because attention was elsewhere.

opts.s: The hikers turned back an hour early to {avert} a soaking from the storm clouds rolling in.
opts.why: Turning back early kept the soaking from happening: they averted it.

blocks.html: Some people check every detail twice; others barely look. This topic gives you words for both. Six of them describe great care (one of them, fastidious, often pokes fun at too much of it), and four describe care that is missing.

Careful: meticulous, scrupulous, diligent, assiduous, fastidious, punctilious. Careless: negligent, remiss, cursory, perfunctory. The careless words differ in how they fall short: negligent and remiss fail a duty, cursory is hasty, and perfunctory is done without interest.

entry.def: very careful about every small detail
entry.ex: Lila keeps a {meticulous} record of every bird she sees, with the date, the time and the weather.
entry.ctx: Felix’s first sketches were messy, but his final map was {meticulous}: every street was labeled, every tree was drawn and not one line was out of place.
entry.etym: From Latin meticulosus, “timid, fearful,” from metus (fear). A meticulous worker is careful, as if afraid of the smallest mistake.

mn.cue: me-TICK-ulous: every box gets a TICK
mn.text: Maya puts a tick next to every item on her packing list, then checks each one twice: she is {meticulous}.

scene.alt: A teenage girl checks off every item on her packing list beside a neat suitcase.

entry.def: very careful to do what is right, or to get every detail exact
entry.ex: The {scrupulous} cashier ran after a customer to give back a dime of extra change.
entry.ctx: The judge at the baking contest was {scrupulous}: she would not taste her own niece’s pie, so that no one could ever say she had been unfair.
entry.etym: From Latin scrupulosus, from scrupulus, “a small sharp stone”: a worry that pricks the mind like a pebble in a shoe.

mn.text: Jamal checks every single screw on Kai’s bike, twice, before he says it is safe to ride: he is {scrupulous}.

scene.alt: A man kneels with a wrench, checking every screw on a bike while a boy in a helmet waits.

entry.def: working hard and steadily, with care
entry.ex: A {diligent} student, Sami reviews his notes every night, not just the night before a test.
entry.ctx: The garden thrived because Granny Mae was {diligent}: she weeded every morning, watered every evening and never skipped a day, even in the heat.
entry.etym: From Latin diligens, from diligere, “to value, to love”: a diligent worker cares about the work.

mn.text: Omar digs and plants all day, row after row, rain or shine. The hardworking gent is {diligent}.

scene.alt: A gardener in a straw hat digs hard in the sun beside a neat row of flowers he has planted.

entry.def: giving steady, careful attention to a task without letting up
entry.ex: Thanks to {assiduous} practice, Rosa finally played the whole piece without a single mistake.
entry.ctx: The puppy learned to sit in a week, but only because of Dev’s {assiduous} training: ten short lessons a day, with a treat for every success.
entry.etym: From Latin assiduus, from assidere, “to sit beside”: ad (near) + sedere (to sit). An assiduous worker stays seated at the task.

mn.text: Lin sits beside her thousand-piece puzzle hour after hour, fitting piece after piece, and never leaves her seat. Her work is {assiduous}.

scene.alt: A woman sits at a table working steadily on a big puzzle while the clock shows the hours passing.

entry.def: very fussy about details, neatness or cleanliness; hard to please
entry.ex: The {fastidious} cat refused to eat from a bowl with a single crumb in it.
entry.ctx: Most of the campers didn’t mind a little mud, but Victor was {fastidious}: he wiped his boots after every few steps and folded his sleeping bag into a perfect square.
entry.etym: From Latin fastidiosus, “squeamish, hard to please,” from fastidium, “disgust.”

mn.text: Victor tidies fast and often: one crumb on the café table, and out comes the broom. He is {fastidious}.

scene.alt: A fussy man rushes to sweep up a single crumb in a café while a woman laughs.

entry.def: very careful to follow the exact rules of proper behavior
entry.ex: The {punctilious} host greeted every guest by name and seated each one by the place card.
entry.ctx: Grandpa Gus is {punctilious} about manners: he stands when a guest comes in, writes a note for every gift and never starts eating before the cook sits down.
entry.etym: From punctilio, a fine point of manners, from Italian puntiglio and Spanish puntillo, “a small point,” from Latin punctum, “point.”

mn.text: Professor Edwin bows just so, pours the tea just so and sets each spoon just so: every small point of manners is right. He is {punctilious}.

scene.alt: An old professor in a bow tie bows politely to a grandmother over a neat tea table.

entry.def: failing to take the care you should
entry.ex: The {negligent} landlord ignored the broken stair for months.
entry.ctx: The night guard was found {negligent}: he had dozed through his whole shift while the alarm light on the back door blinked for three hours.
entry.etym: From Latin neglegens, from neglegere, “to disregard, to fail to care for,” the same source as neglect.

mn.text: The gent dozes on the park bench while his dog digs up the flower bed: he neglects the dog he should be watching. He is {negligent}.

scene.alt: A man dozes on a park bench while his dog digs up the flowers next to a No Digging sign.

entry.def: careless about a duty; failing to do what you should
entry.ex: I would be {remiss} if I didn’t thank the volunteers who set up all the chairs.
entry.ctx: The coach admitted that he had been {remiss}: he had forgotten to check the team’s helmets before the game, and two of them turned out to be cracked.
entry.etym: From Latin remissus, “slack, relaxed,” from remittere, “to send back, to let go, to ease off.”

mn.text: Taking out the trash is Dev’s job, but he missed it Monday and missed it again Tuesday. He has been {remiss}.

scene.alt: A teen shrugs beside an overflowing, smelly trash can while his mother scolds him for missing his chore.

entry.def: quick and not thorough; done in a hurry
entry.ex: A {cursory} glance at the menu told Kai there was no pizza.
entry.ctx: The inspector’s check was only {cursory}; she spent two minutes in a building that needed two hours, and she missed the cracked pipe in the basement.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin cursorius, “of running, swift,” from Latin cursor, “a runner.”
entry.note: Cursory has nothing to do with cursing. It comes from the Latin for running, like cursor and current.

mn.text: Pip runs past every painting in the museum, giving each one half a second: his look is {cursory}.

scene.alt: A boy races past the paintings in a museum while the guide calls for him to look.

entry.def: done only as a routine, with little care or interest
entry.ex: Jonah gave his aunt a {perfunctory} wave without looking up from his book.
entry.ctx: Her thank-you note was {perfunctory}: just “Thanks for the gift,” with no word about what the gift was or whether she liked it.
entry.etym: From Late Latin perfunctorius, from perfungi, “to get through with”: per (through) + fungi (to perform).

mn.cue: per-FUNK-tory: no FUN, just get THROUGH it
mn.text: Rosa plays “Happy Birthday” with a blank face, no fun and no feeling, only to get through it. Her playing is {perfunctory}.

scene.alt: A bored teen plays the piano with a blank face while a girl in a party hat looks let down.

blocks.html: scrupulous can mean careful about details or careful about right and wrong. cursory (hasty) has nothing to do with cursing: it comes from Latin for running.

head: word
what kind of care
you might hear
rows: care with details, or with right and wrong
not taking the care you owe
blocks.cap: Six kinds of care, and four ways to fall short.

blocks.html: Scrupulous has two sides. A scrupulous editor checks every comma (care with details); a scrupulous shopkeeper never cheats a customer (care about right and wrong). Its opposite, unscrupulous, almost always means dishonest. And cursory has nothing to do with cursing: it comes from Latin cursor, a runner, so a cursory look runs right past things.

opts.s: After a {cursory} glance at the instructions, Kai began building the shelf and soon had three pieces left over.
opts.why: A quick, careless glance explains the leftover pieces: it was cursory.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Is it the real thing? These ten words answer that question in different ways. Some promise that something is real, lawful or true to its name; others warn that it is fake, made up or a lie.
Real: authentic, bona fide, legitimate, veritable. Fake: spurious, bogus, counterfeit. Made up or untrue: apocryphal (a story that is probably not true), fictitious (invented) and mendacious (lying).

entry.def: real and not a copy; true to where it came from
entry.ex: The museum made sure the old letter was {authentic} before putting it on display.
entry.ctx: Visitors bought plastic copies at the gift shop, but the dinosaur tooth in the glass case was {authentic}: a real fossil dug from the cliffs nearby.
entry.etym: From Greek authentikos, “genuine, original,” from authentes, “a master, one who does a thing himself.”

mn.text: Nell’s book is signed by the author himself, right at the bookstore table: a real signature from the real writer. It is {authentic}.

scene.alt: An author signs books at a table while a happy reader holds up her signed copy.

entry.def: real; also, made or done in good faith, with no trickery
entry.ex: After years of lessons, Theo’s big sister is now a {bona fide} pilot.
entry.ctx: The letter looked like a trick, but it was a {bona fide} offer: the company really did want to buy Dev’s invention, and it sent a signed contract to prove it.
entry.etym: Latin for “in good faith”: bona (good) + fide (faith).

mn.text: Fido sniffs the two bones: one is plastic, but the other is the real thing, a {bona fide} bone!

scene.alt: A happy dog chooses a real bone over a pink plastic one.

entry.def: allowed by law or the rules; also, fair and reasonable
entry.ex: Being sick is a {legitimate} reason to miss practice.
entry.ctx: The referee ruled that the goal was {legitimate}, since no player had broken a rule, and all the booing from the stands could not change it.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin legitimatus, from Latin legitimus, “lawful,” from lex (law).

mn.cue: LEG-IT: the LEG kick was LEGAL
mn.text: The referee checks the rule book: Kai’s left-leg kick broke no rule. “Legit!” The goal is {legitimate}.

scene.alt: A referee reads the rule book and declares a boy's goal fair while he cheers.

entry.def: truly deserving the name; used to stress that a description fits
entry.ex: Granny Mae’s garden is a {veritable} jungle of tomatoes, beans and squash.
entry.ctx: The surprise party was no small get-together but a {veritable} crowd: more than a hundred neighbors packed the yard and spilled out onto the sidewalk.
entry.etym: From French véritable, “true,” from vérité, “truth,” from Latin veritas.
entry.note: Veritable stresses that a description fits (a veritable feast). It does not mean “literally”: Granny Mae’s garden is only like a jungle.

mn.text: Nana Lou’s dinner table is piled so high with food that feast is the only word for it: a {veritable} feast!

scene.alt: A grandmother proudly serves a table loaded with food while a teen cheers.

entry.def: false, though made to look true or real
entry.ex: The ad made {spurious} claims that the cream would make anyone look twenty years younger.
entry.ctx: Ivy’s argument sounded convincing at first, but its reasoning was {spurious}: she had picked out three rainy Mondays and claimed that it always rains on Mondays.
entry.etym: From Latin spurius, “false, not genuine.”

mn.cue: SPY-YOUR-ious: a SPY in a fake mustache
mn.text: The spy’s mustache looks real from far away, but up close it is glued on and false. His disguise is {spurious}.

scene.alt: A sneaky spy in a glued-on mustache and sunglasses is caught out by a girl who points at his fake disguise.

entry.def: fake; not genuine
entry.ex: The {bogus} ticket looked real until the usher held it up to the light.
entry.ctx: The email claimed that Nana Lou had won a free cruise, but the prize was {bogus}: there was no cruise, only a request for her bank number.
entry.etym: From old American slang of the 1800s, in which bogus meant counterfeit money.

mn.text: Kai sets plastic bugs on the picnic blanket to fool his sister. Lila laughs: the bugs are {bogus}, not real at all.

scene.alt: A boy tries to trick his sister with plastic bugs on a picnic blanket, and she laughs because they are fake.

entry.def: made to look real in order to fool people
entry.ex: The shopkeeper held the bill up to the light and saw that it was {counterfeit}.
entry.ctx: The handbags at the stall carried a famous label, but they were {counterfeit}: the stitching was crooked, and the “leather” peeled off in the first rain.
entry.etym: From Old French contrefait, “imitated,” from contrefaire, “to imitate”: contre (against, opposite) + faire (to make).

mn.cue: COUNTER-FEIT: FAKE money on the COUNTER
mn.text: Rex slaps shiny coins on the shop counter, but the clerk looks closely: they are painted wood! The coins are {counterfeit}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man tries to pay with fake coins, but the clerk spots them with a magnifying glass.

entry.def: widely told but probably not true
entry.ex: The {apocryphal} story says the town’s founder once out-ran a bear.
entry.ctx: Every student has heard about the teacher who never gave an A, but the tale is probably {apocryphal}; no one can name the teacher, the school or the year.
entry.etym: From apocrypha, old writings whose authors were doubtful, from Greek apokryphos, “hidden away.”
entry.note: An apocryphal story is doubtful, not proven false. It is widely repeated, but no one can show that it happened.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus has a pocket full of tall tales: the fish as big as a boat, the bear he out-ran. Fun stories, but probably not true: they are {apocryphal}.

scene.alt: A grandfather spreads his arms wide telling a tall tale by the campfire while two doubtful teens listen.

entry.def: made up; not real
entry.ex: The detective in the mystery lives at a {fictitious} address that no mail carrier could ever find.
entry.ctx: Although the town in the novel feels real, it is {fictitious}; the writer invented its streets, its shops and even its two-hundred-year history.
entry.etym: From Latin ficticius, “made up, artificial,” from fingere, “to shape, to invent,” the same source as fiction.

mn.text: A friendly dragon in Pip’s storybook flies over the castle. Fun to read about, but the dragon is {fictitious}: made up.

scene.alt: A boy reads a storybook while the friendly dragon from the story seems to fly beside him.

entry.def: lying; not telling the truth
entry.ex: The {mendacious} knight told the queen he had slain the dragon, though he had never left the castle.
entry.ctx: The witness seemed calm and sure, yet her story proved {mendacious}: the bus she said she took had not run that day, and the shop she named had closed years before.
entry.etym: From Latin mendax, “lying, false.”

mn.cue: MEND-acious: he MENDS his story with lies
mn.text: Caught beside the empty pie plate, Jonah mends his story again and again: “A dog ate it! No, a bird!” Every patch is a lie; he is {mendacious}.

scene.alt: A teen with pie crumbs throws up his hands and makes excuses while his mother stands with her hands on her hips.

blocks.html: apocryphal stories are doubtful, not proven false. veritable stresses that a description fits (a veritable feast); it does not mean "literally."

blocks.cap: From the real thing to an outright lie.

blocks.html: Two words people often stretch. An apocryphal story is doubtful, not proven false: it is told and retold, but no one can show that it happened. And veritable stresses that a description fits (a veritable feast, a veritable army of ants); it does not mean that something is literally true.

opts.s: Experts studied the brushstrokes for months before declaring the painting {authentic}, a real work by the old master and not a copy.
opts.why: A real work, not a copy, is authentic.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: These ten words come in five pairs that look or sound alike but mean different things. Mixing them up is one of the most common slips in writing, and test makers love to check for it. Learn each pair together, with a trick for telling the twins apart.

affect (to influence; a verb) and effect (the result; a noun). imply (the speaker hints) and infer (the listener figures out). elicit (to draw out) and illicit (not allowed). ingenious (clever) and ingenuous (innocent). eminent (famous) and imminent (about to happen).

entry.def: to have an influence on; to change
entry.ex: Lack of sleep can {affect} how well you do on a test.
entry.ctx: The long drought {affected} every farm in the valley: the corn grew short, the wells ran low and the cows had to be moved to greener pastures.
entry.etym: From Latin afficere, “to do something to, to act on”: ad (to) + facere (to do).
entry.note: Affect is almost always a verb. (In psychology, affect can also be a noun for the feelings a person shows.)

mn.cue: A is for ACTION: you AFFECT
mn.text: Pip taps the first block, and his one small action changes the whole row: his tap {affects} every block down the line.

scene.alt: A boy taps the first block in a row, starting a chain that will knock them all down.

entry.def: a result; a change that something causes
entry.ex: The new streetlights had a clear {effect}: far fewer people tripped on the dark corner.
entry.ctx: Planting trees along the street had a surprising {effect}; the block grew cooler in summer, and more neighbors came out to sit on their porches.
entry.etym: From Latin effectus, “a result,” from efficere, “to bring about, to work out”: ex (out) + facere (to do).
entry.note: Effect is usually a noun. As a verb it means “to bring about”: to effect a change is to make it happen.

mn.cue: E is for END: the EFFECT comes last
mn.text: Zoe waters her bean plant every day for a month. The end result, a plant taller than she is, is the {effect} of all that care.

scene.alt: A girl cheers beside a giant plant that grew because she watered it every day.

entry.def: to suggest something without saying it directly
entry.ex: By yawning loudly through the whole movie, Kai {implied} that it was boring.
entry.ctx: Mom never said that Dev’s room was messy, but she {implied} it: she handed him a trash bag and a laundry basket and smiled sweetly.
entry.etym: From Old French emplier, from Latin implicare, “to fold in, to entwine”: a meaning folded inside the words.
entry.note: The speaker implies; the listener infers.

mn.cue: IM-PLY: the hint goes IN the message
mn.text: The café is closing. Jamal yawns and points at the clock; without a word, he {implies} that it is time for the last customers to go.

scene.alt: A sleepy waiter points at the clock to hint that the café is closing, while two customers keep chatting.

entry.def: to figure out from clues or evidence
entry.ex: From the muddy paw prints on the rug, Lin {inferred} that the dog had come inside.
entry.ctx: The card did not say who had left the flowers, but Ada {inferred} that it was her neighbor: the roses matched the bush beside his front door.
entry.etym: From Latin inferre, “to bring in”: in (in) + ferre (to carry). You bring in a conclusion from the clues.

mn.cue: in-FUR: she INFERS from the FUR
mn.text: Lin spots brown fur all over the white sofa and figures it out: the dog has been napping there again. From the fur, she {infers} the truth.

scene.alt: A woman with a magnifying glass finds dog fur on the sofa and figures out that the dog has been napping there.

entry.def: to draw out a response, an answer or a feeling
entry.ex: The clown’s silly walk {elicited} giggles from every child in the room.
entry.ctx: The teacher’s question was meant to {elicit} more than a yes or a no; she wanted her students to explain their thinking out loud.
entry.etym: From Latin elicere, “to draw out, to lure out”: e (out) + lacere (to lure).

mn.text: Tia pulls a rabbit out of her hat, and the trick draws a gasp out of the crowd: it {elicits} a great big “Ooh!”

scene.alt: A magician lifts a rabbit up high, and the children in the audience gasp and clap.

entry.def: not allowed by law or by the rules
entry.ex: The camp counselors found an {illicit} stash of candy hidden under a bunk.
entry.ctx: The garage looked like an ordinary bike shop, but its back room hid an {illicit} business: stolen bikes were repainted there and sold in the next town.
entry.etym: From Latin illicitus, “not allowed”: in (not) + licitus (allowed), from licere, “to be allowed.”

mn.text: The sign says NO CATS ON THE TABLE, but Pepper sneaks up for the fish anyway. Her snack is {illicit}!

scene.alt: A sneaky cat climbs onto the kitchen table for a fish beside a sign that says no cats.

entry.def: very clever and inventive
entry.ex: Sami rigged an {ingenious} pulley that lowers snacks down to his bottom bunk.
entry.ctx: The flood had washed out the footbridge, but the villagers came up with an {ingenious} fix: they lashed empty barrels together into a floating walkway.
entry.etym: From Latin ingeniosus, from ingenium, “natural talent, cleverness,” the same source as engine and engineer.

mn.text: Dev’s robot sorts the laundry by color and folds every sock: an idea worthy of a genius. It is {ingenious}.

scene.alt: A proud teen with goggles shows off the clever sock-sorting robot he invented.

entry.def: innocent, trusting and open; with nothing to hide
entry.ex: With {ingenuous} delight, Theo told the whole family exactly what he had bought Mom for her birthday.
entry.ctx: The new student was {ingenuous}, not crafty: when the teacher asked whether she had read the book, she admitted at once that she had only watched the movie.
entry.etym: From Latin ingenuus, “freeborn; frank, open”: a person born free, with nothing to hide.
entry.note: Ingenuous (innocent, trusting) and ingenious (clever) differ by one letter. Disingenuous means only pretending to be innocent.

mn.text: When the teacher asks who forgot their homework, little Theo’s hand shoots up at once: he hides nothing. He is {ingenuous}.

scene.alt: A small boy cheerfully raises his hand to admit he forgot his homework while his teacher smiles.

entry.def: famous and respected in a field
entry.ex: An {eminent} scientist visited our school to talk about volcanoes.
entry.ctx: Although she had won every major prize in music, the {eminent} composer still taught a free piano class for beginners every Saturday morning.
entry.etym: From Latin eminere, “to stand out, to rise above”: e (out) + minere (to jut out).

mn.text: Professor Edwin stands out above everyone in his field, and the crowd rises to cheer him: he is {eminent}.

scene.alt: A famous old professor wearing a medal waves from a podium while teens cheer for him.

entry.def: about to happen, often something bad
entry.ex: With thunder rumbling closer, the lifeguard warned that a storm was {imminent}.
entry.ctx: Dark clouds piled up over the hills and the birds went quiet; everyone at the picnic could tell that rain was {imminent}, so they began packing up.
entry.etym: From Latin imminere, “to hang over, to threaten”: in (over) + minere (to jut out).

mn.text: A huge wave is rolling toward Lila’s sandcastle; it will hit in a minute. The crash is {imminent}!

scene.alt: A girl panics as a huge wave rolls toward her sandcastle.

blocks.html: Speakers imply; listeners infer. affect is usually the verb and effect the noun (though effect can be a verb meaning "to bring about"). ingenuous (innocent) and ingenious (clever) differ by one letter.

head: twins
the first one
the second one
a trick
rows: Affect is the Action; the Effect is the End result.
The speaker implies; the listener infers.
blocks.cap: Five pairs and a trick for each.

blocks.html: Two exceptions to the affect and effect rule. Effect can be a verb meaning “to bring about”: the new principal effected real change (she made it happen). And affect can be a noun in psychology, for the feelings a person shows. Everywhere else, affect is the verb and effect is the noun: the rain affected the game, and the rain had an effect on the game.

opts.s: The icy wind did not {affect} the penguins at all; they waddled happily across the snow.
opts.why: The blank needs a verb meaning “to influence”: affect.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories
Merriam-Webster, “Affect vs. Effect”

blocks.html: Fear comes in sizes. A qualm is a small twinge of doubt; dread is a heavy fear of something on its way; a phobia is a strong, lasting fear of one thing. This topic also gives you verbs for what frightening things do to us: they unnerve, daunt, intimidate and perturb.

Feelings (nouns): dread, qualm, misgiving, foreboding, phobia, consternation. What scares or worries us (verbs): unnerve, daunt, intimidate, perturb. Ask two questions: how strong is the fear, and is it about now or about what is coming?

entry.def: great fear of something that is coming
entry.ex: Kai felt a growing {dread} as the dentist’s door creaked open.
entry.ctx: The class had looked forward to the field trip for weeks, but as the bus crawled up the narrow cliff road, their excitement turned to {dread}.
entry.etym: From an Old English verb meaning “to fear.”

mn.cue: DREAD: the thing under the BED
mn.text: As bedtime nears, Pip is full of {dread}: he is sure something is hiding under his bed. (It is only the cat.)

labels.text: DREAD of what’s under the BED

scene.alt: A frightened boy stares at his bed, sure something is hiding under it; it is only a cat.

entry.def: a sudden uneasy feeling, especially a doubt about whether something is right
entry.ex: Rosa had no {qualms} about eating the last cookie; she had baked them all herself.
entry.ctx: Lila agreed to keep her friend’s secret, but later she felt a {qualm}: what if staying quiet meant that someone got hurt?
entry.note: A qualm is a twinge of doubt or conscience, not a full fear. People often say they have no qualms about doing something.

mn.cue: QU + CALM: calm, with a QUestion
mn.text: Zoe reaches calmly for the cookie jar before dinner, then pauses: “Should I?” That little twinge of doubt is a {qualm}.

scene.alt: A girl reaches for the cookie jar before dinner and stops, unsure whether she should.

entry.def: a feeling of doubt or worry about whether something will turn out well
entry.ex: Despite her {misgivings}, Ada let her son ride the giant roller coaster.
entry.ctx: The plan looked fine on paper, yet Omar had {misgivings}: the bridge was old, the river was high and the map was twenty years out of date.
entry.etym: From the old verb misgive, as in “my heart misgives me”: to fill with doubt.

mn.text: Marcus holds out the car keys to Jonah for his first drive alone, but his hand hesitates: he has a {misgiving} about giving them.

scene.alt: A worried father hesitates as he hands the car keys to his eager teenage son.

entry.def: to make someone lose courage or calm
entry.ex: The creaking floorboards {unnerved} the new babysitter.
entry.ctx: The goalie was usually steady, but the roaring crowd {unnerved} him; his hands shook, and he let in two easy goals.
entry.etym: From un- (taking away) + nerve, in its old sense of strength and courage.

mn.text: Dev boasted he would jump from the high rock into the river, but standing at the edge, he loses his nerve. The height {unnerves} him.

scene.alt: A teen with shaking knees stands on a high rock above a river, too scared to jump.

entry.def: to make someone feel discouraged or afraid to try
entry.ex: The steep trail did not {daunt} Granny Mae; she reached the top before anyone else.
entry.ctx: Most climbers would have turned back at the icy cliff, but the long drop did not {daunt} Tia, who checked her ropes and started up.
entry.etym: From Old French danter, from Latin domitare, “to tame.”
entry.note: Daunt (to discourage) is not taunt (to mock). Daunting is common as an adjective: a daunting task.

mn.cue: DAUNT = DON’T: the mountain says DON’T
mn.text: The giant mountain seems to say “Don’t!” to tiny Felix at its foot. Its size {daunts} him, and he almost turns back.

scene.alt: A small hiker with a backpack stares up at a huge mountain, discouraged.

entry.def: to frighten someone, often to make them do what you want
entry.ex: The big dog’s deep bark {intimidated} the mail carrier.
entry.ctx: Rex tried to {intimidate} the younger players by glaring and stomping, but they simply ignored him and went on with their game.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin intimidare, “to make afraid”: in (into) + timidus (fearful).

mn.text: The barn cat puffs up and hisses, and the little mouse turns timid and backs away from the cheese. The cat {intimidates} the mouse.

scene.alt: A puffed-up cat hisses at a little mouse, which backs away from a piece of cheese.

entry.def: a feeling that something bad is going to happen
entry.ex: Watching the black clouds gather, Sven had a {foreboding} that the fishing trip would end early.
entry.ctx: Nothing seemed wrong in the old house, yet Maya was filled with {foreboding}; the silence felt heavy, and she could not shake the sense that trouble was near.
entry.etym: From fore (ahead) + bode, an old word meaning “to announce or foretell.”

mn.cue: FORE-BOAT-ing: a bad feeling before the BOAT trip
mn.text: Before the boat trip, Sven sees black clouds rolling in and feels sure that trouble is coming. That feeling is a {foreboding}.

scene.alt: A fisherman on the dock looks worriedly at dark storm clouds rolling in over the sea.

entry.def: a strong, lasting fear of one thing, often far beyond any real danger
entry.ex: Felix has a {phobia} of elevators, so he always takes the stairs.
entry.ctx: Ivy’s {phobia} was out of all proportion to any real danger: even a photo of a tiny, harmless spider made her heart pound.
entry.etym: From Greek phobos, “fear, panic.” The ending -phobia names many fears: acrophobia is a fear of heights.

mn.cue: FOE-BEE-a: every BEE is her FOE
mn.text: To Greta, every bee is a foe: she has a {phobia} of bees and runs from even the smallest one.

labels.text: FOE-BEE-a: the BEE is her FOE

scene.alt: A woman runs in terror from a small, smiling bee in the garden.

entry.def: sudden alarm and confusion; shocked dismay
entry.ex: To the baker’s {consternation}, the wedding cake slid right off the cart.
entry.ctx: The lights went out just as the play reached its final scene, and {consternation} swept through the theater: people gasped, phones lit up and the actors froze.
entry.etym: From Latin consternatio, “dismay, alarm,” from consternare, “to throw into confusion.”

mn.cue: the whole NATION STARES in alarm
mn.text: At the town fair, the giant cake begins to topple, and the whole crowd stares and gasps in alarm: {consternation}!

scene.alt: A crowd at a fair gasps in alarm as a giant cake starts to topple off its table.

entry.def: to make someone worried or upset
entry.ex: It {perturbed} Grandpa Gus that the newspaper had not come by eight.
entry.ctx: The pilot’s calm voice usually soothed the passengers, so when he sounded rushed and tense, it {perturbed} them more than the bumpy air did.
entry.etym: From Latin perturbare, “to throw into confusion”: per (thoroughly) + turbare (to disturb), the root of disturb and turbulent.

mn.text: Sami’s drumming next door keeps disturbing Grandpa’s crossword until he can’t think straight. The noise {perturbs} him.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather tries to read his newspaper while a boy bangs loudly on a drum.

blocks.html: daunt (discourage) and taunt (mock) sound alike. A qualm is a twinge of doubt or conscience, not a full fear.

head: word
how strong
about what
rows: whether a plan will turn out well
trouble that is on its way
something that has just gone wrong
blocks.cap: Six fears, from a twinge to a shock.

blocks.html: The four verbs differ, too. To unnerve is to take away someone’s courage or calm; to daunt is to discourage someone from trying; to intimidate is to frighten someone, often to push them around; to perturb is to worry or upset. Don’t mix up daunt and taunt: to taunt is to mock. And a qualm is only a twinge of doubt, usually about whether something is right.

opts.s: Tia felt a {qualm} about reading her sister’s diary, so she closed it and put it back on the shelf.
opts.why: A small twinge of doubt about whether something is right is a qualm.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Learning comes with its own cast of characters: the beginner, the dabbler, the young wonder, the expert with fine taste, the master performer and the person who seems to know a little about everything. Two more words describe learning worn too heavily, and one describes teaching itself.

Beginners and dabblers: novice, dilettante. Young talent: prodigy, precocious. Experts: connoisseur (fine taste), virtuoso (performance), polymath (many subjects), erudite (deep reading). Learning overdone: pedantic (fussing over small rules) and didactic (teaching, often preachy).

entry.def: having or showing great knowledge from reading and study
entry.ex: The {erudite} librarian could answer questions about almost any book on the shelves.
entry.ctx: Though he never went to college, Grandpa Gus was {erudite}; he had read every history book in the town library and could talk about ancient Rome for hours.
entry.etym: From Latin eruditus, “instructed,” from erudire, “to polish, to teach”: e (out) + rudis (rough, untaught). Study takes the roughness out.

mn.cue: “READ IT!”: he has read them all
mn.text: Ask Professor Edwin about any book in the library and he smiles: “Read it!” He has read them all; he is {erudite}.

scene.alt: An old professor beside a tall stack of books tells a surprised teen that he has read the book she is holding.

entry.def: too concerned with small details and rules, often to show off learning
entry.ex: My {pedantic} cousin corrected my grammar in the middle of my birthday toast.
entry.ctx: The tour guide knew a great deal, but she was so {pedantic} that she spent ten minutes on the difference between two kinds of nails while the visitors fidgeted.
entry.etym: From pedant, from Italian pedante, “a schoolteacher.”

mn.text: Dan stops the soccer game to read out the rule about exactly how round the ball must be. Dan is {pedantic}.

scene.alt: A boy named Dan reads a rule book aloud in the middle of a soccer game while his bored friends wait.

entry.def: meant to teach a lesson, often in a preachy way
entry.ex: The picture book was so {didactic} that every page ended with a lesson about brushing your teeth.
entry.ctx: The film had fine actors, but it felt {didactic} rather than entertaining; every scene paused so that someone could deliver a little lecture on saving water.
entry.etym: From Greek didaktikos, “good at teaching,” from didaskein, “to teach.”

mn.cue: DID-ACT-ic: every ACT stops for a LESSON
mn.text: The class play did act out a story, but every scene stopped for a lecture: “And the lesson is…” The play is {didactic}.

scene.alt: A teen in a costume crown stops the class play to deliver a lesson while her classmates yawn.

entry.def: an expert judge of things that need fine taste, such as food, art or music
entry.ex: A cheese {connoisseur} can tell where a cheese was made from a single bite.
entry.ctx: Most visitors glanced at the paintings and moved on, but Felix was a {connoisseur}: he could name the painter, the year and even the kind of brush used.
entry.etym: From old French connoisseur, “one who knows,” from Latin cognoscere, “to come to know.”

mn.text: Victor takes one lick of each ice cream cone and names the flavor and the farm it came from. He is a {connoisseur}.

scene.alt: A man with a monocle tastes an ice cream cone and names its flavor while the shopkeeper claps.

entry.def: a person who dabbles in a subject or an art without serious study
entry.ex: He calls himself a painter, but he is a {dilettante} who finishes about one picture a year.
entry.ctx: Real gardeners spend years learning their soil, but Marcus was only a {dilettante}: he planted whatever looked pretty at the store and lost interest by July.
entry.etym: From Italian dilettante, “a lover of the arts,” from dilettare, “to delight.”

mn.text: Pip dillydallies: guitar on Monday, painting on Tuesday, chess on Wednesday. He dabbles in each and masters none: he is a {dilettante}.

scene.alt: A boy shrugs among a half-tried guitar, a painting, a chess piece and a tennis racket.

entry.def: a beginner; someone new to a skill or activity
entry.ex: As a {novice} skater, Lin spent more time on the ice than on her feet.
entry.ctx: The chess club welcomed everyone, from {novices} still learning how the knight moves to old masters who had played for fifty years.
entry.etym: From Latin novicius, “new,” from novus (new), the root of novel and renovate.

mn.text: Jamal is new on the ice: wobbly knees, waving arms, one big bump. He is a {novice} skater.

scene.alt: A man wobbles and falls on the ice for the first time while a teen skates easily nearby.

entry.def: a young person with an amazing talent
entry.ex: At six, the piano {prodigy} played a concert in a packed hall.
entry.ctx: Most children her age were learning to add, but Ivy was a math {prodigy}: at eight, she was solving puzzles that stumped her brother’s high school teacher.
entry.etym: From Latin prodigium, “a wonder, a sign of things to come.”

mn.cue: PRO-digy: a PRO, and only three
mn.text: Little Theo is only three, yet he plays the violin like a pro. The crowd can’t believe it: he is a {prodigy}!

scene.alt: A tiny boy holds up his violin on stage while a man in the audience claps in amazement.

entry.def: showing skills or behavior unusually early for one’s age
entry.ex: The {precocious} toddler could read the cereal box before she turned three.
entry.ctx: Most kindergartners just ask for juice, but {precocious} little Theo asked the waiter whether the orange juice was freshly squeezed.
entry.etym: From Latin praecox, “ripening early”: prae (before) + coquere (to cook, to ripen).
entry.note: Precocious can praise a child’s early skill, or tease a child for acting older than his years.

mn.text: Ivy is only four, yet she cooks a whole breakfast: pancakes, eggs and toast. She is {precocious}: ripe early.

scene.alt: A little girl in a chef's hat proudly serves breakfast in a pan while her astonished mother looks on.

entry.def: a person who knows a great deal about many different subjects
entry.ex: A true {polymath}, Professor Edwin has written books on birds, bridges and old poems.
entry.ctx: Ada was a {polymath}: she designed bridges by day, played the cello in the city orchestra by night and still found time to write a history of maps.
entry.etym: From Greek polymathes, “having learned much”: poly (much, many) + manthanein (to learn), the same root as mathematics.

mn.text: Ada knows math, music, maps, stars and many more subjects besides: she is a {polymath}.

scene.alt: A cheerful woman stands among a globe, a telescope, a violin, books and a blackboard of math.

entry.def: a person with outstanding skill, especially in playing music
entry.ex: The violin {virtuoso} played so fast that her bow seemed to blur.
entry.ctx: Many players can stumble through that hard passage, but only a {virtuoso} like Lin makes it sound easy, as if her fingers were simply dancing on the keys.
entry.etym: From Italian virtuoso, “skilled, excellent,” from Latin virtus, “excellence, worth.”

mn.text: Lin’s fingers race over the piano keys like a speeding train: choo-choo, oh so fast! She is a {virtuoso}.

scene.alt: A woman plays the piano at dazzling speed while a grandmother claps.

blocks.html: pedantic is a criticism; erudite is praise. precocious can praise a child's early skill or criticize a child for acting too old.

blocks.html: Watch the tone. Erudite praises deep learning, but pedantic criticizes someone who fusses over small points to show off. Didactic simply means meant to teach, though it often hints at preachiness. And precocious cuts both ways: it can praise a child’s early talent or tease a child for acting like a little grown-up.

opts.s: Dev had played the tuba for only a week, and like most {novices}, he squeaked more than he played.
opts.why: Someone a week into learning is a beginner: a novice.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Every story has a high point and an ending. These words name the top (zenith, apex, pinnacle), the bottom (nadir) and the moment a long effort reaches its peak (culminate). The rest describe the ways things end: they stop, they die out, or they simply fall out of use.

The top: zenith, apex, pinnacle. The bottom: nadir. Building to the peak: culminate. Ending: terminate, cessation, demise. Out of use: obsolete (out of date) and defunct (no longer existing or working).

entry.def: to reach the highest point or the final, biggest stage
entry.ex: A week of rehearsals {culminated} in a standing ovation on opening night.
entry.ctx: The long effort to save the old theater {culminated} in a grand reopening, with the whole town packed inside for the first show in twenty years.
entry.etym: From Late Latin culminare, “to crown, to reach the top,” from Latin culmen, “top, summit.”

mn.cue: CLIMB-inate: it CLIMBS to the big finish
mn.text: The fireworks show climbs higher and higher and ends with one giant golden burst: the show {culminates} in a grand finale.

scene.alt: Two children cheer as a fireworks show ends in a giant burst in the night sky.

entry.def: to bring to an end, or to come to an end
entry.ex: The bus line {terminates} at the edge of town, so we walked the last mile.
entry.ctx: After the third broken promise, the bakery decided to {terminate} its deal with the flour supplier and find a more reliable one.
entry.etym: From Latin terminare, “to set a limit, to end,” from terminus, “boundary, end.”

mn.cue: TERMIN-al: the END of the line
mn.text: The train pulls into the terminal, the very end of the line. “Everybody off!” The trip {terminates} here.

scene.alt: A train conductor waves at the last stop while a grandmother steps off with her suitcase.

entry.def: a stopping; the end of something
entry.ex: The {cessation} of the rain brought everyone out onto their porches.
entry.ctx: After months of construction next door, the sudden {cessation} of the hammering felt strange; the street was so quiet that the birds could be heard again.

roots.means: stop (from Latin cedere, to go, to yield)

entry.etym: From Latin cessatio, “a stopping,” from cessare, “to stop, to hold back,” the source of cease.

mn.text: The rain ceases, a rainbow appears, and Nell shakes out her umbrella. The {cessation} of the storm brings everyone outside.

scene.alt: When the rain stops, a woman lifts her umbrella and a toddler jumps in a puddle under a rainbow.

entry.def: the end of something; also, a death
entry.ex: The arrival of the big new mall led to the {demise} of the little corner bookshop.
entry.ctx: Once every family carried a phone in a pocket, the {demise} of the phone booth was only a matter of time; by the end, hardly anyone could find one.
entry.etym: From Anglo-French demis, “sent away, handed over,” from Latin dimittere, “to send away.”

mn.cue: DE-MIZE: his SIZE goes DOWN to nothing
mn.text: In the spring sun, the snowman’s size shrinks down, down, down, until only a puddle, a hat and a carrot are left. That is the snowman’s {demise}.

scene.alt: A girl kneels sadly beside a snowman that is melting into a puddle in the spring sun.

entry.def: no longer used or useful; out of date
entry.ex: Grandpa still keeps his {obsolete} typewriter on a shelf in the den.
entry.ctx: The old road map was {obsolete}; three highways had been built since it was printed, and the bridge it showed had been torn down years ago.
entry.etym: From Latin obsoletus, “worn out, grown old.”

mn.text: At the museum, Dev stares at a giant old radio the size of a fridge. Nobody uses one like that anymore: it is {obsolete}.

scene.alt: A teen with a phone stares, puzzled, at a huge old radio on display in a museum.

entry.def: no longer existing, working or in use
entry.ex: The {defunct} factory has been turned into apartments and a bakery.
entry.ctx: Weeds grew between the rails of the {defunct} railway line; no train had run there in thirty years, and the station clock had stopped at a quarter past four.
entry.etym: From Latin defunctus, “finished, dead,” from defungi, “to finish one’s work”: de (off) + fungi (to perform).

mn.text: The old robot in the alley no longer functions: no lights, no beeps, just a puff of dust. It is {defunct}.

scene.alt: A woman points at a broken old robot leaning in an alley, a puff of smoke rising from its head.

entry.def: the highest point; the time of greatest success or power
entry.ex: At its {zenith}, the little bakery sold a thousand loaves a day.
entry.ctx: The singer’s career reached its {zenith} in her forties, when every concert sold out within minutes; after that, she chose to sing only for small crowds.
entry.etym: From an Arabic phrase meaning “the path over the head,” which reached English through Old Spanish and Medieval Latin.
entry.note: In astronomy, the zenith is the point in the sky straight overhead; the nadir is the point straight below.

mn.text: From the very top of the peak, with the sun straight overhead, Maya can see everything beneath her. She has reached the {zenith}.

scene.alt: A hiker cheers on the very top of a mountain peak with the sun straight overhead.

entry.def: the top or highest point, often a pointed tip
entry.ex: The lion is called an {apex} predator because no other animal hunts it.
entry.ctx: The pyramid narrowed as it rose, and at its {apex}, the very tip, the builders set a single gleaming capstone.
entry.etym: From Latin apex, “tip, top.”

mn.cue: APE-X: the APE on the very tip
mn.text: A cheeky ape scrambles up to the pointed tip of the pyramid and waves: he has reached the {apex}.

labels.text: APE-X: the APE at the TIP

scene.alt: A monkey stands on the pointed tip of a pyramid in the desert.

entry.def: the highest point of success or achievement
entry.ex: Winning the state title was the {pinnacle} of Coach Omar’s career.
entry.ctx: For a young violinist, a solo with the city orchestra is the {pinnacle}; there is no higher honor in the whole state.
entry.etym: From Late Latin pinnaculum, a little peak or gable on a building.

mn.cue: a PIN and a CUP: the very top
mn.text: Rosa wins the gold pin and the giant cup at the national meet, the highest honor of all: the {pinnacle} of her career.

scene.alt: A champion with a gold medal holds up a trophy on the winner's stand while her friends clap.

entry.def: the lowest point
entry.ex: The team’s {nadir} came in October, when it lost five games in a row.
entry.ctx: After the flood, the town was at its {nadir}: shops were boarded up, roads were washed out and many families had moved away; yet within five years it had bounced back.
entry.etym: From an Arabic phrase meaning “opposite the zenith.”
entry.note: Nadir and zenith are opposites: the lowest point and the highest.

mn.text: Kai has spent every last coin. He shakes his piggy bank and gets nada, nothing at all: his savings have hit their {nadir}.

scene.alt: A sad boy sits on the floor shaking an empty piggy bank.

blocks.html: zenith and nadir are opposites: the highest and the lowest point. culminate means to reach a climax, not simply to end.

blocks.html: Zenith and nadir are opposites: the highest point and the lowest. Culminate does not simply mean to end; it means to reach the high point that a long effort has been building toward (the season culminated in a championship). And obsolete things still exist but are out of date, while defunct things no longer exist or work at all.

opts.s: Years of practice {culminated} in a gold medal at the national championship.
opts.why: The practice built up to its high point, the gold medal: it culminated.

blocks.html: When feelings run hot, these are the words for cooling them down. Some comfort a person who is hurting; some win over a person who is angry, often by giving something; some shrink a bad feeling; one stops trouble outright; and two settle a quarrel.

Comfort: soothe, console. Win over someone angry: appease, mollify, conciliate. Ease a feeling: assuage (pain, hunger, guilt), allay (fear, worry, doubt). Stop it: quell. Settle a conflict: reconcile, defuse.

entry.def: to calm or comfort, often gently; to ease pain
entry.ex: Priya hummed an old lullaby to {soothe} the fussy baby.
entry.ctx: Lila had tossed and turned for an hour, but the steady patter of rain on the roof {soothed} her, and soon her worries about the test faded into sleep.

mn.text: Priya sings a smooth, slow lullaby, and little Theo’s crying fades into sleepy sighs. Her song {soothes} him.

scene.alt: A mother sings softly beside her toddler, who drifts off to sleep in bed.

entry.def: to comfort someone who is sad or disappointed
entry.ex: Rosa {consoled} her little brother after his kite blew away.
entry.ctx: Losing the spelling bee by a single letter crushed Dev, so his grandmother {consoled} him with a hug and a reminder of how far he had come since last year.
entry.etym: From Latin consolari, “to comfort”: con (with) + solari (to comfort), the root of solace.
entry.note: The noun CON-sole (a cabinet or a control panel) is a different word with the stress on the first syllable.

mn.cue: a CONE for a SAD SOUL
mn.text: Pip comes in last in the race, so Nana Lou hands him an ice cream cone and a hug: “You ran your best.” She {consoles} him.

scene.alt: A grandmother offers an ice cream cone and kind words to a tearful boy who lost a race.

entry.def: to calm someone by giving them what they demand
entry.ex: To stop the twins’ chant of “Snacks! Snacks!”, Mom {appeased} them with a plate of crackers.
entry.ctx: The king tried to {appease} the angry dragon with a cartload of gold, hoping that once it got what it wanted, it would leave the village in peace.
entry.etym: From Old French apaisier, “to bring to peace”: a (to) + pais (peace), from Latin pax.
entry.note: Appease can carry a warning: giving in to demands may buy calm now but invite bigger demands later.

mn.text: The dragon roars for its dinner, so Sven slides it a giant bowl of peas. Full and happy, it settles down: Sven {appeases} the dragon.

scene.alt: A nervous man offers a big bowl of peas to a dragon, which calms down happily.

entry.def: to soften someone’s anger
entry.ex: A free dessert {mollified} the diner whose soup had come out cold.
entry.ctx: The neighbor was furious about the broken window until the boys offered to pay for it from their savings; the offer {mollified} him, and he even helped them find the ball.
entry.etym: From Late Latin mollificare, “to make soft”: mollis (soft) + facere (to make).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus is grumbling until little Molly brings him a warm cookie and a hug. His anger softens: Molly {mollifies} him.

scene.alt: A little girl named Molly gives her grandfather a cookie, and his grumpy face softens into a smile.

entry.def: to make a bad feeling, such as hunger, pain or guilt, less strong
entry.ex: A tall glass of lemonade {assuaged} our thirst after the long hike.
entry.ctx: Nothing could fully {assuage} Ada’s guilt about forgetting her best friend’s birthday, but the handmade card she sent the next morning helped a little.
entry.etym: From Old French assouagier, from Latin ad (to) + suavis (sweet, pleasant): to sweeten a bitter feeling.

mn.cue: A SAUSAGE to ASSUAGE his hunger
mn.text: After a long day of hiking, Jamal’s stomach growls. One hot sausage from the campfire {assuages} his hunger.

scene.alt: A hungry camper happily cooks a sausage in a pan over the campfire.

entry.def: to make fear, worry or doubt less strong
entry.ex: The pilot’s calm voice {allayed} the nervous passengers’ fears.
entry.ctx: Parents worried about the new playground, so the builders {allayed} their concerns by showing them the soft ground, the rounded corners and the safety report.
entry.etym: From Old English alecgan, “to lay down, to put aside.”
entry.note: You allay fears, worries and doubts. Don’t confuse it with alley (a narrow lane) or ally (a friend on your side).

mn.text: Before his checkup, Sami is scared, so Nurse Tia shows him each tool and lets him listen to his own heartbeat. Her kindness {allays} his fears.

scene.alt: A kind nurse explains her tools to a boy sitting on a hospital bed, and his worry fades.

entry.def: to put an end to something, such as a riot or a rumor, often by force
entry.ex: The teacher {quelled} the giggling with a single raised eyebrow.
entry.ctx: A rumor spread that the fair had been canceled, but the organizers quickly {quelled} it by posting photos of the rides already being set up.

mn.text: The lunchroom roars with yelling until Coach Omar blows one sharp whistle, and the noise stops at once. He {quells} the yell.

scene.alt: A coach blows a whistle, and two noisy children instantly fall silent.

entry.def: to win over someone who is angry, often by friendly acts
entry.ex: The hotel {conciliated} the upset guests with a free night’s stay.
entry.ctx: Instead of arguing back, the new manager tried to {conciliate} the angry workers: she listened to every complaint and had the broken heater fixed that same day.
entry.etym: From Latin conciliare, “to bring together, to win over,” from concilium, “a meeting,” the source of council.

mn.cue: CON-SILLY-ate: win him over with something SILLY
mn.text: Victor is angry about the ball in his garden, so Greta brings him a pie and sings a silly sorry song. His frown melts: she {conciliates} him.

scene.alt: A woman brings a pie and a silly apology song to her annoyed neighbor, whose frown begins to fade.

entry.def: to become friends again after a quarrel; also, to make two things agree
entry.ex: After a week of silence, the two friends finally {reconciled} over a shared pizza.
entry.ctx: The two stories of the accident seemed impossible to {reconcile}: one driver said the light was green, the other swore it was red, and both had witnesses.
entry.etym: From Latin reconciliare, “to bring together again”: re (again) + conciliare (to bring together).

mn.text: Lila and Maya had a wreck of a fight, but now they hug and smile, friends again: they {reconcile}.

scene.alt: Two girls who had quarreled hug and smile, friends again.

entry.def: to calm a tense or dangerous situation
entry.ex: Pip {defused} the argument at the dinner table by making everyone laugh.
entry.ctx: Tempers were rising at the neighborhood meeting until a calm voice {defused} the situation; she suggested a short break, and everyone came back ready to listen.

roots.means: the wick that sets something off

entry.etym: From de- (remove) + fuse: first, to take the fuse out of a bomb so it cannot go off; then, to calm a situation before it explodes.
entry.note: Defuse (calm a situation) is not diffuse (spread out).

mn.cue: DE-FUSE: put out the FUSE before the BOOM
mn.text: Kai and Dev are about to blow up at each other. Ada pours water on the sizzling fuse of their fight: she {defuses} it.

scene.alt: A calm woman pours water on a sizzling cartoon fuse between two angry boys.

blocks.html: defuse (calm a situation, as if removing a bomb's fuse) is not diffuse (spread out). You allay fears; you don't "alley" or "ally" them.

blocks.cap: Ten ways to cool things down.

blocks.html: Three look-alikes to keep apart. You defuse a tense situation (as if pulling the fuse from a bomb), but light, smells and ideas diffuse, or spread out. You allay fears; an alley is a lane and an ally is a friend on your side. And appease sometimes carries a warning: giving in to demands can buy calm now and invite bigger demands later.

opts.s: The coach’s calm pep talk {allayed} the team’s fears before the championship game.
opts.why: Fears are lessened, or allayed.

blocks.html: Some words describe people and creatures spoiling for a fight; others name the side we fight against and the ways fights end. Many come from Latin words for battle: bellum (war) in bellicose and belligerent, pugnus (fist) in pugnacious, and miles (soldier) in militant.

Ready to fight: hostile, belligerent, bellicose, pugnacious, truculent, militant. The other side: adversary. Ending the fight: truce (a pause), armistice (an end to the fighting) and diplomacy (talking it out).

entry.def: unfriendly; showing that you want to fight or oppose
entry.ex: The cat gave the new puppy a {hostile} stare and a low hiss.
entry.ctx: The visiting team expected a {hostile} crowd, but the home fans surprised them with polite applause and even a few friendly cheers.
entry.etym: From Latin hostilis, from hostis, “an enemy, a stranger.”

mn.cue: HOST-ILE: a HOST who wants a fight
mn.text: Felix answers his door with a scowl and crossed arms: “No visitors!” He is the most {hostile} host on the street.

scene.alt: A scowling man at his door shouts at two children who have come with a gift.

entry.def: acting angry and ready to fight
entry.ex: The {belligerent} customer shouted at the cashier over a ten-cent coupon.
entry.ctx: Instead of apologizing for the fender bender, the driver grew {belligerent}: he jumped out of his car, waved his arms and dared the other driver to do something about it.
entry.etym: From Latin belligerare, “to wage war”: bellum (war) + gerere (to carry on).

mn.cue: BELL-igerent: the goat with the BELL charges
mn.text: The goat with the bell around his neck lowers his horns and charges at anyone who comes near the barn. He is {belligerent}.

scene.alt: An angry goat wearing a bell charges at a farmer, who runs away.

entry.def: eager to fight or go to war; warlike by nature
entry.ex: The {bellicose} rooster picked a fight with every bird in the yard.
entry.ctx: The old general’s speeches grew more {bellicose} each year; he talked of nothing but battles, enemies and the glory of war.
entry.etym: From Latin bellicosus, “warlike,” from bellum (war).

mn.text: Every single morning, the rooster puffs up his chest and dares every animal in the yard to fight him. Fighting is his nature: he is {bellicose}.

scene.alt: A puffed-up rooster challenges a worried duck and a bored pig to a fight.

entry.def: quick to argue or fight
entry.ex: The {pugnacious} little terrier barked at dogs five times his size.
entry.ctx: Unlike his calm older sister, Dev was {pugnacious}; he would argue with anyone about anything, from baseball scores to the color of the sky.
entry.etym: From Latin pugnax, “fond of fighting,” from pugnare, “to fight,” from pugnus, “fist.”

mn.cue: PUG-NACIOUS: a PUG ready to fight
mn.text: The tiny pug plants his feet and growls at an elephant a hundred times his size: “Come on!” He is {pugnacious}.

scene.alt: A tiny pug growls at a huge, startled elephant.

entry.def: quick to argue or fight; fierce and defiant
entry.ex: The {truculent} toddler crossed his arms and refused to put on his shoes.
entry.ctx: Asked to explain why he was late, the {truculent} teenager only scowled, folded his arms and muttered that it was none of their business.
entry.etym: From Latin truculentus, “fierce, savage,” from trux, “wild, fierce.”

mn.text: Theo sits in his toy truck with his arms crossed and a fierce scowl: “Mine! Go away!” He is {truculent}.

scene.alt: A scowling toddler sits in his toy wagon, arms crossed, refusing to share with a girl.

entry.def: an opponent; someone you compete or fight against
entry.ex: In the chess final, Maya faced her toughest {adversary}: her own grandfather.
entry.ctx: The two lawyers were good friends outside the courtroom, but inside it they were {adversaries}, each working hard to win the case.
entry.etym: From Latin adversarius, “opponent,” from adversus, “turned against”: ad (toward) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: In the tug-of-war, it is Jonah versus Rosa, each pulling the other way: they are {adversaries}.

scene.alt: Two teens pull hard on opposite ends of a rope in a tug-of-war.

entry.def: fighting hard and aggressively for a cause
entry.ex: The {militant} members of the garden club demanded that every lawn in town become a vegetable patch.
entry.ctx: Most neighbors wanted to write polite letters about the park, but a {militant} few wanted to block the road and refuse to leave until the bulldozers were gone.
entry.etym: From Latin militare, “to serve as a soldier,” from miles, “soldier,” the root of military.

mn.cue: MILIT-ANT: an ANT army for a cause
mn.text: The ants march in a fierce line with tiny signs: SAVE OUR HILL! They will fight hard for their anthill: they are {militant}.

scene.alt: A line of determined ants marches with little signs that say Save Our Hill.

entry.def: an agreement to stop fighting for a while
entry.ex: The two brothers called a {truce} in their pillow fight so they could eat breakfast.
entry.ctx: The cats had battled over the sunny windowsill all week, but a {truce} held at dinnertime: side by side, they ate from their bowls without a single hiss.
entry.etym: From Middle English trewes, the plural of trewe, “a pledge,” a word related to true.

mn.cue: TRUCE: a TRUE pause, for now
mn.text: In the middle of their snowball fight, Kai waves a white flag: “Truce! Cocoa break!” For now, the fight is paused: it is a {truce}.

labels.text: TRUCE: a pause in the fight

scene.alt: In a snowy yard, one boy waves a white flag and another offers him hot cocoa, pausing their snowball fight.

entry.def: an agreement between two sides at war to stop fighting
entry.ex: The {armistice} was signed at dawn, and by noon the fighting had stopped all along the border.
entry.ctx: After four long years of war, the {armistice} finally brought the fighting to an end, though the two nations still needed months to work out a full peace treaty.
entry.etym: From Modern Latin armistitium: arma (weapons) + -stitium (a standing still), formed like solstice.
entry.note: A truce may be only a short pause; an armistice ends the fighting of a war, usually while a full peace treaty is worked out.

mn.text: The two kings shake hands over a signed scroll, and both armies put down their arms and stand still. The {armistice} ends the war.

scene.alt: Two kings reach toward each other over a peace scroll, each beside his own flag.

entry.def: the work of managing relations between nations; also, skill in handling people tactfully
entry.ex: With a little {diplomacy}, Lila got both brothers to share the last slice of cake.
entry.ctx: The border quarrel could have led to war, but patient {diplomacy} won out; after months of quiet talks, the two countries signed a treaty.
entry.etym: From French diplomatie, from diploma, an official paper, from Greek diploma, “a paper folded in two.”

mn.cue: DIPLOMA-cy: talk it out, then sign the paper
mn.text: Pip and Sami are fighting over the tree swing, so Lila sits them down, listens to each and gets them to sign a turn-taking deal. That is {diplomacy}.

scene.alt: A girl holds out a written deal for two boys, who agree to take turns on the swing.

blocks.html: belligerent and bellicose share bellum (war): bellicose describes a temperament, belligerent a behavior. A truce is a pause; an armistice ends the fighting of a war.

blocks.html: Bellicose and belligerent share Latin bellum, war. Bellicose usually describes a person’s nature (a bellicose ruler who loves war); belligerent describes how someone is acting (a belligerent customer shouting right now). A truce is a pause, while an armistice ends the fighting of a war.

opts.s: Even after losing the argument, Rex stayed {truculent}, scowling and refusing to shake hands.
opts.why: Scowling and refusing to shake hands is fierce and defiant: truculent.

blocks.html: Some things turn up wherever you look. These words describe how widely something is found (ubiquitous, prevalent, universal), how it spreads (pervasive, rampant, permeate, saturate, diffuse), which kind wins out (predominant) and something that belongs to one place (endemic).

Found everywhere: ubiquitous, universal. Common: prevalent; predominant (the most common or strongest). Spreading through: pervasive, permeate, saturate (to the very full), diffuse (spread out) and rampant (out of control). Always found in one place: endemic.

entry.def: found everywhere; seeming to be everywhere at once
entry.ex: Phones are so {ubiquitous} now that it is hard to find a bus rider without one.
entry.ctx: Twenty years ago only a few cafés offered free internet, but today it is {ubiquitous}: libraries, buses, parks and even some campgrounds have it.
entry.etym: From Latin ubique, “everywhere.”

mn.cue: YOU BIKE WITH US: bikes everywhere
mn.text: In this town, everyone calls out “You bike with us!” Bikes are on every path, every rack and every porch: they are {ubiquitous}.

scene.alt: Bicycles fill every corner of a park while two friends in helmets wave.

entry.def: spreading through every part of something
entry.ex: The {pervasive} smell of popcorn drifted through every corner of the theater.
entry.ctx: Worry about the coming storm was {pervasive}; it showed in the empty store shelves, the boarded-up windows and the anxious faces on every street.
entry.etym: From Latin pervadere, “to go through”: per (through) + vadere (to go).

mn.cue: per-VASE-ive: VASES all THROUGH the house
mn.text: Granny Mae loves flowers so much that there are vases on every table, shelf and windowsill in her house. Flowers are {pervasive} there.

scene.alt: A grandmother holds a bouquet in a room crowded with flower vases on every surface.

entry.def: widespread; common in a place or at a time
entry.ex: Colds are most {prevalent} in the winter months.
entry.ctx: Hats were once {prevalent}, so common that hardly anyone left home without one, but by the 1970s most people went out bareheaded.
entry.etym: From Latin praevalere, “to be stronger, to win out”: prae (before, above) + valere (to be strong).

mn.text: When it rains in our town, nearly all of us carry red umbrellas. Red umbrellas are {prevalent} here.

scene.alt: On a rainy city street, nearly everyone carries the same red umbrella.

entry.def: spreading or growing out of control
entry.ex: Weeds grew {rampant} in the empty lot behind the school.
entry.ctx: Before the new rules, cheating in the online game had been {rampant}; nearly every top score on the board turned out to be fake.
entry.etym: From Old French rampant, “climbing, rearing up,” from ramper, “to climb.” In old coats of arms, a lion rampant rears up on its hind legs.

mn.text: One ram jumps the fence, then ten more follow. Soon rams are running wild all over the farm: they are {rampant}!

scene.alt: A flock of rams leaps and runs wild across a farm while a grandfather shouts for them to stop.

entry.def: most common, strongest or most important
entry.ex: Blue is the {predominant} color in Kai’s room: blue walls, a blue rug and a blue bedspread.
entry.ctx: Many languages are spoken in the city, but English is {predominant}; it appears on nearly every sign and is taught in nearly every school.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin praedominari, “to rule over”: prae (before, above) + dominari (to rule).

mn.text: In Zoe’s garden, nearly every flower is yellow; only one is red. Yellow is the {predominant} color.

scene.alt: A girl in a yellow dress cheers in a garden of yellow flowers with just one red one.

entry.def: true of, used by or including everyone or everything
entry.ex: A smile is a {universal} sign of friendliness.
entry.ctx: The love of music seems almost {universal}: every culture that has ever been studied has had songs, from lullabies to work chants.
entry.etym: From Latin universalis, from universus, “all together, whole”: unus (one) + versus (turned).

mn.cue: UNIVERSE-al: true across the whole UNIVERSE
mn.text: Pip lands on a faraway planet, and the robot there waves hello, just like at home. Waving hello is {universal}!

scene.alt: A boy in a space helmet waves at a robot on another planet, and the robot waves back.

entry.def: regularly found in a particular place or among a particular group
entry.ex: The kiwi is {endemic} to New Zealand; in the wild, it lives nowhere else on Earth.
entry.ctx: Some problems come and go, but traffic jams are {endemic} to the city: they happen every single morning, as steady as the sunrise.
entry.etym: From Greek endemos, “native, belonging to a people”: en (in) + demos (people, district).
entry.note: Endemic (always present in one place) is not epidemic (a sudden outbreak that spreads widely and then fades).

mn.cue: EN = IN: found IN one place only
mn.text: The purple parrot lives on this one little island and nowhere else in the world. It is {endemic} to the island.

scene.alt: A purple parrot perches on a tiny island beside a sign that says Only Here.

entry.def: to spread through every part of something
entry.ex: The smell of fresh bread {permeated} the whole house.
entry.ctx: Excitement {permeated} the school in the week before the big game; even the cafeteria workers wore team colors, and every hallway rang with cheers.
entry.etym: From Latin permeare, “to pass through”: per (through) + meare (to go, to pass).

mn.cue: PER (through) + MEATE: spreads all the way THROUGH
mn.text: Nana Lou bakes bread, and the warm smell drifts through the window, down the street and into every house. It {permeates} the whole village.

scene.alt: A grandmother holds a fresh loaf, and its smell drifts down the street to two neighbors who sniff happily.

entry.def: to soak completely; to fill so full that no more can be added
entry.ex: The garden hose {saturated} the flower bed until water pooled on top.
entry.ctx: The sponge was so {saturated} that it could not hold another drop; every new splash simply ran off onto the counter.
entry.etym: From Latin saturare, “to fill full,” from satur, “full.”

mn.cue: SAT-u-RATE: he SAT in it, now SOAKED
mn.text: Sami sat right down in the biggest puddle on the playground, and his pants soaked up every drop they could hold. They are {saturated}!

scene.alt: A boy sits in a huge puddle, soaked through, while a teen laughs.

entry.def: to spread out over a wide area
entry.ex: A few drops of food coloring {diffused} slowly through the glass of water.
entry.ctx: The paper lampshade {diffused} the light, spreading a soft glow across the whole room instead of one harsh, bright spot.
entry.etym: From Latin diffundere, “to pour out, to spread”: dis (apart) + fundere (to pour).
entry.note: Diffuse (spread out) is not defuse (calm a tense situation). As an adjective, diffuse (dih-FYOOS) means spread out or wordy.

mn.text: Pop! Lila’s pillow bursts, and the feathers spread out over the whole room, every which way. They {diffuse}.

scene.alt: A girl's pillow bursts, and feathers spread out all over her bedroom.

blocks.html: endemic (always present in one place) differs from epidemic (a sudden spread). diffuse (spread out) is not defuse (calm a situation).

blocks.html: Two pairs to keep apart. Endemic means always present in one place or group, while an epidemic is a sudden outbreak that spreads widely and then fades. And diffuse (spread out) is not defuse (calm a tense situation): a lamp diffuses light; a friend defuses an argument.

opts.s: In our old neighborhood, red brick houses are {prevalent}; you can count the wooden ones on one hand.
opts.why: Something common and widespread in a place is prevalent.
