blocks.html: Two roots mean time. Greek chron gives us chronic and chronicle; Latin temp or tempor gives us temporary and tempo. A third Latin root, ann or enn, means year, as in annual and anniversary. Spot them, and a whole family of time words opens up.
chron (Greek) = time. temp, tempor (Latin) = time. ann, enn (Latin) = year. Then read the prefix: syn- together, ana- back or against, con- with, ex- out of, per- through.
Each hook below points at the root. Say the parts out loud (syn-CHRON-ize: same time), look at the picture, then check the meaning in the sentences.

entry.def: lasting a long time, or coming back again and again
entry.ex: Kai is a {chronic} latecomer: he has missed the first bell every day this month.
entry.ctx: The leaky faucet was not a one-time problem but a {chronic} one; no matter how often it was fixed, the dripping started again within a week.
entry.etym: From Greek chronikos, “having to do with time,” from chronos, “time.”
entry.note: Chronic means long-lasting or recurring, not “severe.” A chronic cough may be mild; it just keeps coming back.

mn.cue: CHRON = TIME: trouble that lasts a long TIME
mn.text: The kitchen faucet has dripped every day for a whole year: drip, drip, drip. The leak is {chronic}.

scene.alt: A man scratches his head beside a bucket catching a faucet drip that has gone on for a whole year.

entry.def: a record of events in the order they happened
entry.ex: Nana Lou keeps a {chronicle} of every family trip in a fat green notebook.
entry.ctx: The old ship’s log was a day-by-day {chronicle} of the voyage, recording every storm, every sighting of land and every supper of salted fish.
entry.etym: From Greek chronika, “records of the times,” from chronos, “time.”

mn.cue: CHRON-icle: a TIME record, day by day
mn.text: Sami writes down each day of the class trip in order, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, in his travel book: it is a {chronicle} of the trip.

scene.alt: A boy writes in a travel notebook under a banner listing the days of the week in order.

entry.def: arranged in the order in which things happened
entry.ex: Ivy lined up her baby pictures in {chronological} order, from her first day to her fifth birthday.
entry.ctx: The museum’s halls are {chronological}: you begin with ancient stone tools in the first room and finish with rockets and robots in the last.
entry.etym: From chronology, from Greek chronos (time) + logos (word, account).

mn.text: Ivy hangs her photos in order of time: baby, toddler, first grade, now. The row is {chronological}.

scene.alt: A girl points to a row of her photos hung in order from age one to now.

entry.def: something placed in the wrong time period
entry.ex: A knight checking his phone would be a funny {anachronism} in a movie about castles.
entry.ctx: The play was set in ancient Rome, so the audience giggled at the {anachronism} when an actor’s wristwatch flashed beneath his toga.
entry.etym: From Greek anachronismos: ana (back, against) + chronos (time).

mn.text: A knight in shining armor rolls up to the castle on a skateboard, chatting on his phone. Wrong time! He is an {anachronism}.

scene.alt: A knight in armor rides a skateboard past a castle while talking on a phone.

entry.def: to make things happen at the same time or at the same speed
entry.ex: Before the race, the timekeepers {synchronized} their stopwatches.
entry.ctx: The swimmers {synchronized} every move so perfectly that their legs rose from the water at the very same instant, like parts of a single machine.
entry.etym: From Greek synchronos, “happening at the same time”: syn (together) + chronos (time).

mn.text: Three dancers kick their legs at exactly the same moment, on the very same beat: they {synchronize} their moves.

scene.alt: Three dancers on a stage make the very same move at the very same moment.

entry.def: living or happening at the same time; also, modern
entry.ex: The museum’s new wing shows {contemporary} art, made in the last few years.
entry.ctx: Though the two writers never met, they were {contemporary}; both were born in the same year and published their first books within months of each other.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin contemporarius: com (together) + tempus (time).
entry.note: Contemporary can mean “of the same time as” (a contemporary of the author) or “modern” (contemporary furniture); context decides.

mn.text: Pip and Kai were born on the very same day and have shared every birthday since: they are {contemporary}, two kids of the same time.

scene.alt: Two boys in party hats cheer beside twin birthday cakes under a banner that says Same Birthday.

entry.def: having to do with time
entry.ex: The story jumps back and forth, so readers must follow its {temporal} clues: dates, seasons and ages.
entry.ctx: The detective studied the {temporal} details of the case: what time the lights went out, how long the dog barked and when the car finally drove off.
entry.etym: From Latin temporalis, from tempus, “time.”

mn.text: Detective Ada doesn’t ask where the thief went; she asks when. Clock, calendar, timetable: her questions are {temporal}.

scene.alt: A detective with a notebook thinks about when something happened, surrounded by an hourglass, a clock and a calendar.

entry.def: spoken or done without any preparation
entry.ex: Called on without warning, Dev gave an {extemporaneous} talk about his favorite book.
entry.ctx: Most of the toasts had been written weeks ahead, but the best one was {extemporaneous}: the bride’s grandfather simply stood up and spoke from the heart.
entry.etym: From Late Latin extemporaneus, from the Latin phrase ex tempore, “out of the moment.”

mn.cue: EX TEMPOR: OUT of the moment
mn.text: Asked to speak with no warning, Grandpa Gus stands right up and talks with no notes at all, straight out of the moment. His speech is {extemporaneous}.

labels.text: EX TEMPORE: NO NOTES, right now

scene.alt: A grandfather speaks into a microphone with no notes while a woman claps.

entry.note: Speech teachers use the word more narrowly: a talk planned ahead but given from brief notes, not read or memorized. For no preparation at all, they say impromptu.

entry.def: lasting or coming back year after year
entry.ex: Pizza is a {perennial} favorite in our school cafeteria.
entry.ctx: Weeds are a {perennial} problem in the garden; pull them up in June, and they are back again the next spring.
entry.etym: From Latin perennis, “lasting through the years”: per (through) + annus (year).
entry.note: Gardeners call a plant that comes back every year a perennial.

mn.text: Every spring, the same red tulips pop up in Nana Lou’s garden, year after year after year: they are {perennial}.

scene.alt: A grandmother kneels happily beside red tulips that bloom again every year.

entry.def: a year-by-year record of events; history
entry.ex: The great flood is still remembered in the town’s {annals}.
entry.ctx: The comeback was the greatest in the {annals} of the school; in a hundred years of yearbooks, no team had ever rallied from so far behind.
entry.etym: From Latin annales (libri), “yearly books,” from annus, “year.”
entry.note: Annals is nearly always plural: the annals of history.

mn.cue: ANN = YEAR: a book for every YEAR
mn.text: The town library keeps one big book for every year since long ago, shelf after shelf. Together they are the town’s {annals}.

labels.text: ANN-als: a record for each YEAR

scene.alt: An old professor points at big books labeled with years while a teen reads one.

blocks.html: Two words people stretch. Chronic means long-lasting or coming back again and again, not “very bad”: a chronic problem may be small; it just won’t go away. And contemporary has two senses: “of the same time as” (the painter and her contemporaries) and “modern” (contemporary furniture). Let the sentence decide.

opts.s: The band and the fireworks crew {synchronized} their watches so the music and the first rocket would start at the same moment.
opts.why: Making two things happen at the same time is synchronizing them.

blocks.html: People differ in how they meet the world. Some greet everyone with a smile, some light up a party, and some keep to themselves. This topic gives you seven words for warmth and three for keeping apart.

Friendly: amiable, affable (easy to talk to), genial (warm), jovial (jolly), convivial (lively in company), amicable (peaceful, without quarrels) and charismatic (with a charm that draws people in). Keeping apart: aloof (cool and distant), reticent (says little) and reclusive (lives apart).

entry.def: friendly and pleasant to be around
entry.ex: The {amiable} bus driver greeted every rider by name.
entry.ctx: Although the new neighbor looked stern in his dark suit, he turned out to be {amiable}, always ready with a wave, a joke and a helping hand.
entry.etym: From Old French amiable, “friendly,” from Late Latin amicabilis, from amicus, “friend.”

mn.text: Amy smiles and says hello to everyone she passes, from the mail carrier to the dog next door. Amy is {amiable}.

labels.text: AMI-able: AMY, a FRIEND to all

scene.alt: A smiling woman named Amy waves hello to the mail carrier and a happy dog.

entry.def: easy to talk to; friendly and good-natured
entry.ex: The {affable} chef chatted with every diner who stopped by the kitchen window.
entry.ctx: Despite his fame, the astronaut was {affable}; he answered every child’s question, posed for photos and laughed at even the silliest jokes.
entry.etym: From Latin affabilis, “easy to speak to,” from affari, “to speak to”: ad (to) + fari (to speak).

mn.cue: AF-FABLE: always has a FABLE for you
mn.text: Jamal always has a funny fable for anyone who sits beside him on the park bench. He is so easy to talk to: {affable}.

scene.alt: A smiling man on a park bench tells a story to two delighted children.

entry.def: friendly, warm and cheerful
entry.ex: Our {genial} host met us at the door with a big smile and mugs of hot cocoa.
entry.ctx: The night was cold, but the {genial} innkeeper made everyone feel at home: he lit a roaring fire, remembered every guest’s name and told cheerful stories over supper.
entry.etym: From Latin genialis, “festive, cheerful,” from genius, the guardian spirit once thought to watch over each person.

mn.cue: GENIE-al: as warm as a friendly GENIE
mn.text: Sven throws open his door with a grin as wide as a genie’s: “Come in! Cocoa’s hot!” He is {genial}.

scene.alt: A big, smiling man welcomes a girl in from the cold with a mug of cocoa.

entry.def: cheerful and full of good humor
entry.ex: The {jovial} mail carrier whistled and joked on every porch.
entry.ctx: Even after the long, rainy hike, Grandpa stayed {jovial}, singing silly songs and laughing so hard at his own jokes that everyone else started laughing too.
entry.etym: From Latin jovialis, “of Jupiter”: people born under the planet Jupiter were once said to be cheerful.

mn.text: Marcus laughs so hard at his own joke that his shoulders shake, and soon the whole café is laughing with him. He is {jovial}.

cast.say: Ho ho, that’s a good one!

scene.alt: A jolly man laughs so hard he shakes, and a teen at the café table laughs along.

entry.def: lively and friendly, enjoying feasts and good company
entry.ex: The {convivial} picnic went on long after the sun went down.
entry.ctx: The dinner was {convivial} rather than formal: neighbors passed dishes, swapped stories and laughed until the candles burned low.
entry.etym: From Latin convivium, “a feast,” from con (together) + vivere (to live).

mn.text: At the block party there’s food on every table, music in the air and laughter all around, with everyone living it up together. The party is {convivial}.

scene.alt: Neighbors dance, eat and laugh together at a lively block party.

entry.def: friendly and peaceful, without quarrels
entry.ex: After the game, the two teams shook hands and parted on {amicable} terms.
entry.ctx: Even after they decided to close their shop, the partners stayed on {amicable} terms; they split the tools fairly and still meet for lunch every Friday.
entry.etym: From Late Latin amicabilis, “friendly,” from amicus, “friend.”
entry.note: Amiable describes people (an amiable host); amicable usually describes relationships and agreements (an amicable settlement).

mn.cue: A-MIC-able: share the MIC, no fight
mn.text: Maya and Rosa both want to sing, so instead of quarreling, they share the microphone and sing together. Their deal is {amicable}.

scene.alt: Two teens share one microphone on stage, singing together happily.

entry.def: having a charm that draws people in
entry.ex: The {charismatic} coach could fire up the whole team with a single smile.
entry.ctx: The new student was not loud or flashy, yet she was {charismatic}; within a week, half the class wanted to sit with her at lunch.
entry.etym: From Greek charisma, “a gift, a favor,” from charis, “grace.”

mn.text: When Tia walks into the room, everyone turns and drifts toward her, as if she were holding a magnet. She is {charismatic}.

scene.alt: A smiling woman holds up a magnet, and two children drift happily toward her.

entry.def: cool and distant; not friendly or involved
entry.ex: The {aloof} cat watched the party from the top of the bookshelf.
entry.ctx: At the reunion, everyone hugged and chatted, but Victor stayed {aloof}, standing alone by the window and answering questions with a single word.
entry.etym: From an old sailors’ word meaning “to windward,” used of steering a ship away from something; aloof people keep their distance.

mn.cue: A-LOOF: alone up on the ROOF
mn.text: While the family plays in the yard below, the cat sits alone on the roof and won’t come down. The cat is {aloof}.

scene.alt: A bored cat sits alone on a rooftop while children below call for it to come play.

entry.def: not willing to say much or to share thoughts and feelings
entry.ex: Usually {reticent}, Sami surprised everyone with a long, funny speech at his sister’s graduation.
entry.ctx: Asked about the fire, the {reticent} witness said only “I saw smoke” and would not add a word, no matter how hard the reporters pressed.
entry.etym: From Latin reticere, “to keep silent”: re (back) + tacere (to be silent), the same root as tacit.
entry.note: Reticent means reluctant to speak or share, not reluctant in general. For “unwilling,” use reluctant.

mn.cue: RETI-CENT: not one CENT’s worth of words
mn.text: Ask Lin about her weekend, and you won’t get one cent’s worth of words: just a smile and a shrug. She is {reticent}.

labels.text: RETI-CENT: not a CENT of words

scene.alt: A teacher asks a shy woman to talk about herself, and she only puts a finger to her lips.

entry.def: avoiding the company of other people; living alone and apart
entry.ex: The {reclusive} painter rarely left her cabin in the woods.
entry.ctx: The famous author was so {reclusive} that he had not given an interview in forty years; letters went unanswered, and his gate stayed locked.
entry.etym: From Late Latin reclusus, “shut away,” from re- (back, away) + claudere (to shut).

mn.text: Omar lives alone in a cabin deep in the woods, with the door closed and a sign out front. He is {reclusive}.

scene.alt: A shy man hides beside his cabin deep in the forest, behind a sign that says Please Go Away.

blocks.html: reticent means reluctant to speak or share, not reluctant in general. amiable describes people; amicable describes relationships and agreements.

blocks.cap: Seven ways to be warm, and three ways to keep apart.

blocks.html: Two pairs to watch. Amiable describes people (an amiable host), while amicable usually describes relationships and agreements (an amicable settlement, amicable relations). And reticent means unwilling to speak or share, not unwilling in general: you can be reticent about your feelings, but you are reluctant, not reticent, to clean your room.

opts.s: Though the brothers disagreed about who should get the car, the talk stayed {amicable}, and they agreed to take turns.
opts.why: A talk without quarreling, ending in a fair deal, is amicable.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: When writers want to say “the best example” or “the model to follow,” they have many words to choose from. Seven of these name the model itself, one describes being the perfect example, and two are verbs for following a model or showing what a type is like.

The perfect example: paragon (of a good quality), epitome, quintessential. The model or pattern: paradigm, archetype (the original), prototype (the first trial version), exemplar, benchmark (a standard to measure by). Verbs: emulate (copy someone you admire, hoping to match them) and typify (be a typical example).

entry.def: a typical example or model; also, a widely accepted way of thinking
entry.ex: Her neat, colorful notes became the {paradigm} for the whole study group.
entry.ctx: For centuries, people accepted the old {paradigm} that the sun circled the earth; only careful measurements finally overturned that whole way of thinking.
entry.etym: From Greek paradeigma, “a pattern, an example”: para (beside) + deiknynai (to show).

mn.text: Jonah leads the parade with a high-stepping march, and every child behind him copies each step. His march is the {paradigm}.

scene.alt: A teen leads a parade, and the children behind him copy his marching steps.

entry.def: a model of excellence; a perfect example of a good quality
entry.ex: Granny Mae is a {paragon} of patience; no one has ever heard her raise her voice.
entry.ctx: The knight in the old tales was a {paragon} of courage and kindness: he never ran from danger and never turned away anyone in need.
entry.etym: From Old Italian paragone, “a touchstone,” a stone once used to test the purity of gold.

mn.cue: a PAIR of GOLD medals: a model of goodness
mn.text: Rosa wins a pair of gold medals at school, one for kindness and one for honesty. She is a {paragon} of good character.

scene.alt: A teen wins two gold medals, for kindness and honesty, while friends clap.

entry.def: a perfect example of a quality or a type
entry.ex: With his top hat and gold watch chain, Victor looked like the {epitome} of an old-fashioned gentleman.
entry.ctx: The cottage was the {epitome} of coziness: a crackling fire, a sleeping cat, a kettle humming on the stove and a quilt over every chair.
entry.etym: From Greek epitome, “a summary, a cutting short”: epi (upon) + temnein (to cut). The perfect example sums up a whole type in one.
entry.note: Say it ih-PIT-uh-mee, in four syllables, not “EP-ih-tome.”

mn.text: Curled on a soft rug by the warm fire, the cat purrs: “Look at me!” She is the {epitome} of coziness.

scene.alt: A cat curls up on a rug by a warm fire, the picture of coziness.

entry.def: an original model; a classic example of a type that others follow
entry.ex: The wise old wizard is an {archetype} found in stories all over the world.
entry.ctx: That first clumsy wooden bicycle was the {archetype} from which every later bike descended; its two wheels and handlebars are still the basic design today.
entry.etym: From Greek archetypon, “a first pattern”: arche (beginning) + typos (a mark, a model).

mn.cue: ARCHE-TYPE: the FIRST TYPE, copied in every tale
mn.text: Professor Edwin plays the wise old wizard in the school play, and every kid in a wizard hat copies him: the long beard, the staff, the deep voice. He is the {archetype}.

scene.alt: An old professor dressed as a wizard strikes a pose on stage while two children in wizard hats copy him.

entry.def: a first, trial version of something, built to test it
entry.ex: The engineers crashed the {prototype} on purpose to test its seat belts.
entry.ctx: Before building a hundred birdhouses for the fair, Dev made a single {prototype}, left it out in the rain, and then fixed the leaky roof on all the rest.
entry.etym: From Greek prototypon, “a first form”: protos (first) + typos (a model).

mn.text: Kai’s first paper plane flies three feet and nose-dives into the grass. It’s only the {prototype}; version two will fly farther.

scene.alt: A boy watches his first paper airplane nose-dive into the grass and plans a better one.

entry.def: a person or thing that serves as a model to copy
entry.ex: The teacher posted Lila’s essay as an {exemplar} of clear writing.
entry.ctx: The old mill is an {exemplar} of careful repair: other towns send their builders to study how its beams were replaced without changing its look.
entry.etym: From Latin exemplar, “a model,” from exemplum, “an example.”

mn.text: Ms. Tia pins Kai’s perfect poster on the board with a gold star: “Use this as your example!” His poster is the {exemplar}.

scene.alt: A teacher pins a student's poster with a gold star on the board as the example for the class.

entry.def: being the most perfect or typical example of something
entry.ex: A lemonade stand on a hot day is the {quintessential} summer business.
entry.ctx: With its red barn, white fence, grazing cows and a rooster crowing at dawn, the place was the {quintessential} farm, just like the pictures in a children’s book.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin quinta essentia, “the fifth essence,” a pure substance once thought to fill the heavens, beyond earth, air, fire and water.

mn.text: Sun, sand, waves, a bucket and an ice cream cone: Ivy’s beach day has all five essentials. It is the {quintessential} summer day.

scene.alt: A girl in sunglasses cheers with an ice cream cone on a sunny beach with a bucket, a sandcastle and a beach ball.

entry.def: to imitate someone you admire, hoping to match or surpass them
entry.ex: Little Theo {emulates} his big sister, practicing her cartwheels every afternoon.
entry.ctx: Jamal did not merely copy his grandmother’s recipes; he tried to {emulate} her, aiming to cook as well as she did and someday to invent dishes of his own.
entry.etym: From Latin aemulari, “to rival, to try to equal,” from aemulus, “a rival.”
entry.note: Emulate means more than copy: you emulate someone you admire, hoping to match or even beat them.

mn.cue: EM-U-LATE: “I’ll be like EM, you’ll see, LATEr!”
mn.text: Little Theo watches his big sister Em stretch up tall before her dance, then copies her move exactly: one day he’ll be as good as Em. He {emulates} her.

scene.alt: A small boy copies his big sister's dance stretch, hoping to be as good as she is someday.

entry.def: to be a typical example of; to show the usual features of
entry.ex: Long lines and loud music {typify} the first day of the county fair.
entry.ctx: Red brick houses with white porches {typify} the old neighborhood; walk down any of its streets, and you will see dozens of them.
entry.etym: From type (a model, a kind) + -ify (to make).

mn.text: A cactus, a camel and a blazing sun: these three {typify} the desert.

scene.alt: A camel and a cactus under a blazing sun show what a typical desert looks like.

entry.def: a standard that other things are measured against
entry.ex: Her record time became the {benchmark} for every runner on the team.
entry.ctx: The first phone that fit in a pocket set a new {benchmark}; after that, every company measured its phones against that one’s size and weight.
entry.etym: From surveying: a benchmark was a mark cut into stone where a surveyor set a bracket, or bench, to measure heights from.

mn.cue: BENCH-MARK: the MARK on the BENCH
mn.text: Every summer, Lila stands by the old park bench where Dad once marked her height. That mark is the {benchmark} she measures her growing against.

scene.alt: A girl stands by a park bench marked with last year's height while her father points to show how much she has grown.

blocks.html: epitome is pronounced ih-PIT-uh-mee. emulate means imitating out of admiration, hoping to match or surpass, not just copying.

a model of a good quality

blocks.html: Two traps. Epitome has four syllables: ih-PIT-uh-mee, not “EP-ih-tome.” And emulate is more than copying: you emulate someone you admire, hoping to match or even surpass them. A student who copies a neighbor’s answers is cheating, not emulating.

opts.s: Before making a hundred kites for the festival, the club built one {prototype} and tested it in a strong wind.
opts.why: A first trial version, built for testing, is a prototype.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some explanations make you nod; others make you squint. These words describe ideas, directions and writing on both sides of that line. Several began as words about light: lucid and elucidate hold Latin lux (light), while opaque and obscure first meant dark or shaded.

Clear: lucid, coherent (holds together), explicit (stated outright), incisive (sharp, to the point); to make clear is to elucidate. Unstated: implicit (suggested, not said). Unclear: opaque, obscure, nebulous (hazy), convoluted (twisted and tangled).

entry.def: clear and easy to understand
entry.ex: Ada gave a {lucid} explanation of how rainbows form.
entry.ctx: The instruction booklet was a jumble of tiny print, but Grandpa’s note was {lucid}: three short steps, each with a simple drawing.
entry.etym: From Latin lucidus, “bright, clear,” from lux (light).

mn.cue: LUCY-d: Lucy’s map is CLEAR as day
mn.text: Lucy’s map is so clear that anyone can follow it: one big arrow, three landmarks and an X. Her map is {lucid}.

scene.alt: A girl named Lucy holds up a clear, simple map, and a boy happily points the way.

entry.def: logical and consistent; holding together clearly
entry.ex: After a good night’s sleep, Dev rewrote his messy essay until it was finally {coherent}.
entry.ctx: Lila’s story was {coherent} from start to finish: each event led to the next, and the ending tied every loose thread together.
entry.etym: From Latin cohaerere, “to stick together”: co (together) + haerere (to stick).

mn.text: Every piece of Pip’s puzzle fits and sticks to the next, making one clear picture. Like his puzzle, his story is {coherent}.

scene.alt: A boy cheers beside a table where his puzzle pieces fit neatly together.

entry.def: stated clearly and fully, leaving nothing to guess
entry.ex: Mom’s rules were {explicit}: homework first, then one hour of games.
entry.ctx: The sign was {explicit}, “No dogs on the beach from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., no exceptions,” so no one could claim to have misunderstood.
entry.etym: From Latin explicitus, “unfolded, laid out,” from explicare: ex (out) + plicare (to fold).

mn.text: The beach sign spells it out in big letters, NO DOGS!, so Ivy and her pup turn around. The rule is {explicit}.

scene.alt: A girl and her dog stop in front of a large beach sign that says No Dogs.

entry.def: suggested but not said directly
entry.ex: Her smile carried an {implicit} invitation to join the game.
entry.ctx: No one said that the new kid could sit with them, but the invitation was {implicit} when Maya scooted over and patted the empty spot on the bench.
entry.etym: From Latin implicitus, “folded in, entwined,” from implicare: in (in) + plicare (to fold).
entry.note: Implicit means unstated, not “hidden on purpose.” It can also mean complete and unquestioning: implicit trust.

mn.text: Maya never says “Sit with me,” but she scoots over and pats the bench. The invitation is {implicit}.

scene.alt: A teen on a bench smiles and makes room for a shy boy holding his lunch, inviting him without a word.

entry.def: sharp and direct; going straight to the heart of the matter
entry.ex: The coach’s {incisive} comment fixed Kai’s swing in a single sentence.
entry.ctx: While the others rambled about the lunch menu, Rosa asked one {incisive} question, “Who is paying for it?”, and the whole debate came to a halt.
entry.etym: From Latin incisus, “cut into,” from incidere: in (into) + caedere (to cut).

mn.cue: IN-CIS-ive: CUTS right IN to the point
mn.text: The meeting is a tangle of talk until Rosa’s one sharp question cuts straight through it, like an arrow. She is {incisive}.

scene.alt: A teen asks one sharp question that cuts through a tangle of talk, and two men look surprised.

entry.def: to make clear; to explain
entry.ex: The museum guide {elucidated} how the ancient water clock kept time.
entry.ctx: Seeing the puzzled faces, the teacher paused to {elucidate}: she drew a diagram, gave two simple examples and then had the class try one together.
entry.etym: From Late Latin elucidare, “to make clear”: e (out) + lucidus (bright, clear).

mn.cue: E-LUC-idate: bring it OUT into the LIGHT
mn.text: Professor Edwin draws a simple picture on the board, and one by one the puzzled faces light up: “Oh, I see!” He {elucidates} the idea.

scene.alt: An old professor explains at the blackboard, and his students' faces light up with understanding.

entry.def: hard to understand; also, not letting light through
entry.ex: The {opaque} curtains kept the bedroom dark even at noon.
entry.ctx: The notice was so {opaque}, full of long words and endless sentences, that Dad had to call a lawyer just to find out what it meant.
entry.etym: From Latin opacus, “shaded, dark.”

mn.cue: oh-PAQUE: a box on your head: no seeing through
mn.text: For the costume party, Dev wears a cardboard box over his head. No light gets through; he can’t see out, and no one can see in. The box is {opaque}.

scene.alt: A teen with a cardboard box over his head gropes about, unable to see, while a woman laughs.

entry.def: not clear or easy to understand; also, not well known
entry.ex: The joke was too {obscure} for anyone at the table to get.
entry.ctx: The song was written by an {obscure} composer whom few people had ever heard of, yet once the radio played it, the whole town was humming along.
entry.etym: From Latin obscurus, “dark, dim, hidden.”
entry.note: Obscure has two senses: hard to understand (an obscure poem) and little known (an obscure village). As a verb, to obscure is to hide from view.

mn.cue: ob-SCURE: so dim, no one is SURE
mn.text: Through the thick fog, Sven can barely make out a shape on the water: a boat? a whale? No one is sure. It is {obscure}.

scene.alt: A man on the dock squints into thick fog, unsure what shape is out on the water.

entry.def: vague and unclear in form or meaning; hazy
entry.ex: Kai had only a {nebulous} plan for the weekend: “do something fun.”
entry.ctx: The club president’s promises were {nebulous}, all “better days ahead” and “a brighter future,” with no details about what she would actually do.
entry.etym: From Latin nebulosus, “misty, cloudy,” from nebula, “mist, cloud.”

mn.text: Ask Jonah what his new invention does, and his answer is as fuzzy as a cloud: “It… sort of… does stuff?” His idea is {nebulous}.

scene.alt: A teen shrugs, unsure what his invention does, while his idea floats in a fuzzy cloud.

entry.def: so twisted and complicated that it is hard to follow
entry.ex: The directions to the cabin were so {convoluted} that we got lost twice.
entry.ctx: The movie’s plot was {convoluted}: twins swapped places, a villain turned out to be a hero, and three different maps led to the same treasure.
entry.etym: From Latin convolutus, “rolled together,” from convolvere: con (together) + volvere (to roll).

mn.text: The signposts at the crossroads point every which way, and the directions twist around and back. Jamal gives up: the route is {convoluted}.

scene.alt: A dizzy man with a map stares at signposts pointing every which way.

blocks.html: implicit means unstated, not "hidden on purpose"; explicit and implicit are opposites. obscure has two meanings: hard to understand, and little known.

clear or not?
you might hear

blocks.cap: From crystal clear to hopelessly tangled.

blocks.html: Explicit and implicit are opposites: explicit is said outright; implicit is suggested without being said. Implicit does not mean hidden on purpose. (In “implicit trust,” it has a second sense: complete and unquestioning.) And obscure has two senses: hard to understand (an obscure poem) and little known (an obscure village).

opts.s: The rules of the game were {explicit}: printed in large letters right on the inside of the box lid.
opts.why: Rules printed out plainly are stated outright: explicit.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Six of these words are verbs for what puzzles do to us: they perplex, baffle, bewilder, confound, befuddle and flummox. The other four name the puzzles and the fixes we find ourselves in. Notice the difference: you are in a quandary, you face a dilemma, and you try to solve a conundrum or an enigma.

Verbs (to confuse): perplex, baffle, bewilder, confound, befuddle, flummox. Nouns: conundrum (the hard puzzle itself), quandary (your state of not knowing what to do), dilemma (a hard choice between two options) and enigma (a mystery, often a person).

entry.def: to confuse and trouble someone with something hard to understand
entry.ex: The strange thumping in the attic {perplexed} the whole family.
entry.ctx: The math problem {perplexed} even the teacher at first; she stared at it for a full minute before she spotted the trick hidden in the second line.
entry.etym: From Latin perplexus, “tangled, confused”: per (thoroughly) + plexus (woven, braided).

mn.text: Ivy finds a big X painted on the sidewalk, with no note and no arrow. It {perplexes} her all week.

scene.alt: A puzzled girl scratches her head over a big X painted on the sidewalk.

entry.def: to be too hard for someone to understand or solve
entry.ex: The locked-room mystery {baffled} every detective in the city.
entry.ctx: The magician’s last trick {baffled} the audience; though they watched his hands closely, no one could explain how the rabbit ended up in the front row.

mn.cue: BAF-FLE: the cookies FLEW out of a locked jar?
mn.text: The cookie jar is still locked, but every cookie is gone! The mystery {baffles} Dev and Lila. (The cat isn’t talking.)

labels.text: BAFFLE: HOW did they get out?

scene.alt: Two puzzled teens stare at an empty, locked cookie jar while a cat winks in the corner.

entry.def: to confuse completely, often with too many things at once
entry.ex: The huge airport, with its hundred gates and blinking signs, {bewildered} Granny Mae.
entry.ctx: The new phone’s menus {bewildered} Dad: every button opened three more choices, and soon he had no idea how to get back to the start.
entry.etym: From be- (thoroughly) + an old verb wilder, “to lead astray,” as if into a wilderness.

mn.text: Sami steps off the trail, and the jungle closes in around him: vines everywhere, paths in every direction. He is {bewildered}.

scene.alt: A dizzy boy with a backpack stands lost in the jungle as a monkey and a parrot look on.

entry.def: to confuse and surprise; also, to prove a prediction wrong
entry.ex: The tiny team {confounded} the experts by winning the whole tournament.
entry.ctx: The results {confounded} the scientists; the plants kept in the dark had somehow grown taller than the ones in the sun, the opposite of what everyone expected.
entry.etym: From Latin confundere, “to pour together, to mix up”: con (together) + fundere (to pour).
entry.note: Confound has two senses: to confuse (the riddle confounded us) and to prove wrong (the results confounded the experts).

mn.cue: con-FOUND: the experts FOUND they were wrong
mn.text: Everyone said the little team couldn’t win, but they did. The experts found they were wrong, and the surprise win {confounds} them.

scene.alt: Two small children hold up a trophy while two shocked experts who predicted they would lose stare in disbelief.

entry.def: to muddle someone’s thinking; to confuse
entry.ex: The long list of rules {befuddled} the new players.
entry.ctx: The riddle seemed simple, but its twist {befuddled} Kai; he said the answer was “Tuesday,” then “a candle,” then gave up and asked for a hint.
entry.etym: From be- (thoroughly) + fuddle, an old word meaning “to confuse.”

mn.text: Dev’s new video game has a hundred rules. His thoughts turn into a puddle of muddle, and his player keeps walking into walls. The game {befuddles} him.

scene.alt: A teen on the sofa stares at his game controller, confused by what the television is showing.

entry.def: to confuse someone so completely that they don’t know what to do
entry.ex: The self-checkout machine {flummoxed} Dad, who kept scanning the same banana.
entry.ctx: The tangle of pipes under the sink completely {flummoxed} the new plumber; he stared at it, scratched his head and finally called his boss for help.
entry.etym: An English dialect word of the 1800s whose origin is unknown.

mn.cue: FLUM-OX: the OX is totally STUMPED
mn.text: The ox stares and stares at the gate latch, nudges it, then stares some more. He has no idea what to do: it {flummoxes} him.

scene.alt: A confused ox stares at a closed farm gate, with no idea how to open it.

entry.def: a confusing and difficult problem; also, a riddle
entry.ex: How to fit six bikes into a tiny garage was a real {conundrum}.
entry.ctx: The town faced a {conundrum}: the old bridge was too weak for buses, yet tearing it down would cut the village off from the school for a whole year.
entry.etym: Of unknown origin; it first appears in English in the 1500s.

mn.cue: CONE + DRUM: how do they fit?
mn.text: Jamal has to fit a giant drum, a traffic cone and a tuba into one tiny car. It’s a real {conundrum}!

scene.alt: A puzzled man wonders how to fit a giant drum and a traffic cone into a tiny car.

entry.def: a state of not knowing what to do
entry.ex: Invited to two parties on the same night, Rosa was in a {quandary}.
entry.ctx: Lost on the trail as the sun went down, the hikers were in a {quandary}: should they keep walking in the dark or camp where they were and wait for morning?
entry.etym: Of uncertain origin; it first appears in English in the 1500s.
entry.note: A quandary is the uncertain state you are in; a conundrum is the puzzle itself.

mn.cue: QUAN-DARY: WANDERING, not knowing what to do
mn.text: Pip has one dollar to spend, and he wanders up and down the toy store, back and forth, unable to choose. He is in a {quandary}.

scene.alt: A worried boy with a dollar paces back and forth in a toy store, unable to choose.

entry.def: a hard choice between two options, often both unpleasant
entry.ex: Lila faced a {dilemma}: her best friend’s party and her cousin’s recital were both on Saturday at noon.
entry.ctx: The coach faced a {dilemma}; if she pitched her star player today, he would be too tired for the final, but if she rested him, the team might lose today’s game.
entry.etym: From Greek dilemma, “a double proposition”: di (two) + lemma (a premise, something taken for granted).
entry.note: A dilemma is a choice between two options, often both bad, not just any problem.

mn.text: Kai must eat one of two sour lemons; whichever he picks, he’ll pucker. Two choices, both sour: that is a {dilemma}.

scene.alt: A worried boy shrugs between two sour lemons, unhappy with either choice.

entry.def: a person or thing that is mysterious and hard to understand
entry.ex: The new neighbor was an {enigma}: no one ever saw him come or go, yet his garden was always perfect.
entry.ctx: To the scientists, the strange signal remained an {enigma}; it arrived every night at three o’clock, from no known star, and no one could explain it.
entry.etym: From Greek ainigma, “a riddle,” from ainissesthai, “to speak in riddles.”

mn.cue: a masked MYSTERY: who is it?
mn.text: Every evening a stranger in a mask leaves a single flower on the park bench and slips away. No one knows who it is: the stranger is an {enigma}.

scene.alt: At night, a masked stranger in a cape leaves a flower on a park bench while a teen watches, puzzled.

blocks.html: A dilemma is a hard choice between two options, not any problem. A quandary is the uncertain state you are in; a conundrum is the puzzle itself.

blocks.html: A dilemma is a hard choice between two options (di- means two), often both unpleasant; don’t use it for just any problem. The six verbs are close cousins, but confound has a second sense, to prove a prediction wrong, and bewilder often suggests being lost among too many things at once.

opts.s: The magician’s last trick {baffled} the audience; no one could explain how the rabbit ended up in the front row.
opts.why: The blank needs a verb: the trick was too hard to understand. It baffled them.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some people dream big; others get things done. The best plans need both. These words describe dreamers, playful imaginations and the hard-headed test that every dream must pass: is it practical, doable and able to last?

Dreamers: idealistic, visionary (sees what the future could be), utopian (a perfect society), quixotic (noble but hopeless). Playful imagination: whimsical, fanciful, reverie (a daydream). Doers: pragmatic (practical), feasible (doable), viable (able to work or last).

entry.def: guided by ideals of how things should be, rather than by what is practical
entry.ex: The {idealistic} young teacher believed that every student could learn to love poetry.
entry.ctx: Her plan to feed every hungry family in town by the end of summer was {idealistic}: the goal was beautiful, but she had no money, no truck and only three volunteers.
entry.etym: From ideal, from Late Latin idealis, from Greek idea, “form, pattern.”

mn.cue: IDEAL-istic: aiming for the IDEAL world
mn.text: Lila wants a world where everyone shares, no one is ever lonely and every day has cake. She is {idealistic}.

scene.alt: A girl standing on a crate cheers for a perfect world where everyone shares cake.

entry.def: thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom
entry.ex: The {visionary} inventor sketched flying machines long before anyone could build one.
entry.ctx: Most people saw only an empty lot full of weeds, but Tia was {visionary}: she pictured a garden where the whole neighborhood would grow vegetables, and five years later it was there.
entry.etym: From vision, from Latin visio, “a seeing,” from videre, “to see.”

mn.text: Tia looks at the weedy empty lot and sees what could be: rows of tomatoes and kids picking beans. She is {visionary}.

scene.alt: A woman points at an empty city lot and imagines the vegetable garden it could become.

entry.def: aiming for a perfect society; too ideal to be realistic
entry.ex: In their {utopian} town, no door had a lock and no neighbor ever argued.
entry.ctx: The club’s {utopian} plan, a school with no rules, no homework and no arguments, sounded wonderful, but no one could explain how it would actually work.
entry.etym: From Utopia, a perfect imaginary island in a book of 1516; the name means “no place” in Greek (ou, not + topos, place).

mn.cue: YOU-TOPIA: a perfect place that is NO place
mn.text: On Pip’s map of the perfect island, the rivers are lemonade and nobody ever argues. Lovely, but it’s no real place: a {utopian} dream.

scene.alt: A boy on a tiny island holds up a map of a perfect land under a rainbow.

entry.def: hopelessly idealistic and impractical, in a noble or romantic way
entry.ex: His {quixotic} plan was to clean every beach in the state by himself.
entry.ctx: Kai’s plan to buy a warm bed for every stray dog in the state with his lemonade money was {quixotic}: noble, determined and completely doomed.
entry.etym: From Don Quixote, the hero of a famous Spanish novel of the early 1600s, who rode out to fight windmills that he believed were giants.

mn.cue: QUICK-SHOT: a brave shot at the impossible
mn.text: Sami builds a cardboard rocket to fly to the moon by Friday. It’s a brave, noble shot at the impossible: his plan is {quixotic}.

scene.alt: A boy in goggles salutes beside the cardboard rocket he built to fly to the moon.

entry.def: playfully odd or fanciful; following sudden fancies
entry.ex: The café’s {whimsical} chairs were shaped like giant teacups.
entry.ctx: Nothing in the yard was ordinary: the birdbath was a boot, the gate was painted with dancing frogs and the scarecrow wore sunglasses; it was the most {whimsical} yard on the block.
entry.etym: From whimsy, a playful or odd notion, related to whim.

mn.text: On a whim, Nell plants daisies in an old boot, hangs teacups in a tree and gives her cat a party hat. Her garden is {whimsical}.

scene.alt: A woman in a party hat dances in a garden where flowers grow in an old boot.

entry.def: imaginative but not realistic; existing only in the imagination
entry.ex: Ivy drew a {fanciful} castle with candy towers and a moat of chocolate milk.
entry.ctx: The old sailor’s tales were {fanciful}; he swore he had ridden a whale and dined with a talking octopus, though everyone knew he had never left the harbor.
entry.etym: From fancy (a shortened form of fantasy) + -ful.

mn.text: Ivy paints a castle with candy towers, a lollipop bridge and a dragon who serves tea. Her picture is {fanciful}.

scene.alt: A girl paints a fairy-tale castle on an easel while a tiny dragon and a lollipop float nearby.

entry.def: a pleasant daydream; being lost in happy thoughts
entry.ex: The ringing phone snapped Grandpa out of his {reverie}.
entry.ctx: Gazing out the classroom window at the falling snow, Dev drifted into a {reverie} about sledding, so lost in it that he didn’t hear the teacher call his name twice.
entry.etym: From French rêverie, “dreaming,” from rêver, “to dream.”

mn.cue: RIVER-ie: drifting off by the RIVER
mn.text: Lying by the lazy river, Lin watches the clouds float by and drifts into happy thoughts of summer. She is lost in a {reverie}.

scene.alt: A woman lies on the grass by a river, smiling, lost in a happy daydream.

entry.def: dealing with things sensibly and practically
entry.ex: Rather than wait years for a new bridge, the {pragmatic} villagers built a ferry.
entry.ctx: While her friends argued over the perfect party theme, Maya took a {pragmatic} approach: she checked the budget, counted the chairs and ordered the pizza.
entry.etym: From Greek pragmatikos, “businesslike, practical,” from pragma, “a deed, a thing done.”

mn.cue: prag-MAT-ic: put down a MAT and get across
mn.text: The path to the barn is all mud, so Dev doesn’t wish it away; he lays down an old mat and walks right over. He is {pragmatic}.

scene.alt: A teen crosses a muddy path by laying a mat over it while his mother claps.

entry.def: possible to do; workable
entry.ex: With three more helpers, finishing the mural by Friday became {feasible}.
entry.ctx: Building a treehouse in a single afternoon was not {feasible}, so the friends split the job over five Saturdays and finished by the end of the month.
entry.etym: From Old French faisable, “doable,” from faire, “to do,” from Latin facere.
entry.note: Feasible means doable, not “likely.” A plan can be feasible and still never happen.

mn.cue: FEAST-ible: yes, we CAN make the feast
mn.text: Can two friends cook a feast for fifty? With three ovens, a list and a plan, yes: the feast is {feasible}.

scene.alt: Two friends with a plan and a pot cook a big feast, sure they can pull it off.

entry.def: able to work, live or succeed
entry.ex: Only one of the three seeds was {viable}, and it sprouted within a week.
entry.ctx: The lemonade stand turned out to be a {viable} business: after paying for lemons, sugar and cups, the twins still had twenty dollars left each Saturday.
entry.etym: From French viable, “able to live,” from vie, “life,” from Latin vita.

mn.cue: VI = LIFE: able to LIVE and grow
mn.text: Kai plants three seeds in three pots. Two stay bare, but one sprouts and keeps growing: that seed was {viable}.

scene.alt: A boy in a lab coat points to the one pot of three where a seed has sprouted.

blocks.html: quixotic comes from the hero of a famous novel who attacked windmills, thinking they were giants; it means admirably but impractically idealistic. feasible means doable, not "likely."

head: word
dreamer or doer?
you might hear
rows: doer: able to work or last
blocks.cap: Dreams, imagination and the practical test.

blocks.html: Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, the hero of a famous Spanish novel, who charged at windmills thinking they were giants; a quixotic plan is admirable but hopelessly impractical. And feasible means doable, not “likely”: it is feasible to bike across the country, but that doesn’t mean you will.

opts.s: Raising the money in a single week was not {feasible}, so the class planned two bake sales spread over a month.
opts.why: The question is whether it could be done: it was not feasible.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Things grow and things shrink. Gardens flourish, towns burgeon and rabbits proliferate; the moon wanes, the tide ebbs and storms abate. Each word tells you not just which way something is going but how: fast or slow, by multiplying, by sinking, by wasting away.

Growing: flourish and thrive (grow strong and healthy), burgeon (grow fast), proliferate (multiply). Shrinking or easing: wane and dwindle (little by little), ebb (flow back like the tide), abate (lessen; storms, noise, pain), subside (die down or sink lower) and atrophy (waste away from lack of use).

entry.def: to grow well and healthily; to do very well
entry.ex: Tomatoes {flourish} in Nana Lou’s sunny backyard.
entry.ctx: The little bakery {flourished} after the newspaper praised its bread; within a year it had doubled its staff and opened a second shop across town.
entry.etym: From Old French florir, from Latin florere, “to bloom,” from flos, “flower.”

mn.text: Nana Lou’s garden bursts with flowers of every color, taller and brighter every week. It {flourishes}.

scene.alt: A grandmother cheers beside a row of tall, bright flowers blooming in her garden.

entry.def: to grow strong and healthy; to do well
entry.ex: The rescued puppy {thrived} on long walks and lots of attention.
entry.ctx: Some plants wilt in deep shade, but ferns {thrive} there; they grow thick and green under the tall trees where little else will grow.
entry.etym: From Old Norse thrifask, “to grasp for oneself, to prosper.”

mn.cue: THRIVE rhymes with HIVE: a busy, growing HIVE
mn.text: Every week there are more bees and more honey; the busy hive grows and grows. It {thrives}!

scene.alt: A girl holds up a jar of honey beside a busy, growing beehive with happy bees.

entry.def: to grow or expand quickly
entry.ex: Weeds {burgeoned} in the empty lot after a week of rain.
entry.ctx: The town’s population {burgeoned} after the new factory opened; in just three years, two new schools were built and the old one doubled in size.
entry.etym: From Old French burjon, “a bud.”

mn.cue: BURGER-on: the BURGER stack grows FAST
mn.text: At the cookout, Sven’s stack of burgers grows fast: one, then three, then six, taller than his nose! The stack {burgeons}.

scene.alt: A laughing cook stands beside a towering stack of burgers that keeps growing.

entry.def: to increase quickly in number; to multiply
entry.ex: Rabbits {proliferated} in the meadow until there were hundreds.
entry.ctx: Food trucks have {proliferated} downtown; five years ago there were two, and now dozens line every street at lunchtime.
entry.etym: From proliferation, from French prolifère, “bearing offspring,” from Latin proles (offspring) + ferre (to bear).

mn.cue: PROLIFIC bunnies: LIFE makes more LIFE
mn.text: Two rabbits in spring, twenty by summer, two hundred by fall! The rabbits {proliferate}.

scene.alt: A farm field fills with more and more rabbits while a woman stares in shock.

entry.def: to grow smaller or weaker little by little
entry.ex: Interest in the new game {waned} after a few weeks.
entry.ctx: The moon waxes for two weeks and then {wanes}, shrinking a little each night until only a thin sliver is left.
entry.etym: From Old English wanian, “to lessen.”
entry.note: The moon waxes (grows) and wanes (shrinks).

mn.cue: WANE: a little LESS each night
mn.text: Each night Pip looks out his window, and each night the moon is a little thinner. The moon {wanes}.

scene.alt: A boy at night points at a row of moons that grow smaller from Monday to Thursday.

entry.def: to grow smaller little by little until little is left
entry.ex: Our supply of marshmallows {dwindled} as the campfire night went on.
entry.ctx: As the afternoon wore on, the crowd at the parade {dwindled}; by five o’clock, only a few families were left, folding up their chairs.
entry.etym: From dwine, an old word meaning “to waste away,” from Old English dwinan.

mn.cue: DWIN-DLE like a CAN-DLE: it shrinks down
mn.text: Maya reads late into the night, and her candle shrinks from tall to short to a tiny stub. It {dwindles}.

scene.alt: A sleepy teen reads beside three candles that shrink from tall to a tiny stub.

entry.def: to flow back out, like the tide; to fade away
entry.ex: As the tide {ebbed}, the children hunted for crabs in the pools left behind.
entry.ctx: Her anger {ebbed} slowly as she listened to her brother’s apology, and by the end she was laughing.
entry.etym: From Old English ebba, “low tide.”

mn.cue: EBB: the sea slides BACK, back, back
mn.text: The water slides back out to sea, and Sami finds starfish and shells left behind on the wet sand. The tide {ebbs}.

labels.text: EBB: the tide goes BACK OUT

scene.alt: At low tide, a boy kneels on the wet sand collecting starfish and shells the sea left behind.

entry.def: to become less strong or intense
entry.ex: We waited inside the barn until the storm {abated}.
entry.ctx: The noise from the street party finally {abated} after midnight, and the tired family could at last fall asleep.
entry.etym: From Old French abatre, “to beat down,” from batre, “to beat.”
entry.note: Abate is used for storms, noise, pain and anger that ease.

mn.cue: A-BAIT: the storm calms, so out comes the BAIT
mn.text: The wind drops, the rain slows, and the sun peeks out. The storm {abates}, so Omar grabs his bait and heads back to fishing.

scene.alt: A fisherman cheers on the dock as the storm eases and the sun comes out.

entry.def: to die down; also, to sink to a lower level
entry.ex: After the river flooded, it took a week for the water to {subside}.
entry.ctx: Kai’s giggles finally {subsided} when the teacher glanced his way, though they came right back the moment she turned to the board.
entry.etym: From Latin subsidere, “to settle down, to sink”: sub (under, down) + sidere (to settle).

mn.text: After the flood, the water in the park sinks down, lower and lower, until the bench appears again. The flood {subsides}.

scene.alt: A girl in a raincoat points as floodwater in the park sinks back down, uncovering a bench.

entry.def: to waste away or weaken from lack of use
entry.ex: After six weeks in a cast, the muscles in Dev’s arm had begun to {atrophy}.
entry.ctx: Skills you never practice can {atrophy}; after ten years without playing, Grandma found she could barely remember a single song on the piano.
entry.etym: From Greek atrophia, “lack of food, wasting away”: a (without) + trophe (nourishment).

mn.text: Grandpa Gus won a tennis trophy long ago, but he hasn’t touched a racket since. The trophy gathers dust, and his tennis skills {atrophy}.

scene.alt: A grandfather dozes on the sofa beside an old, dusty trophy and a racket he never uses.

blocks.html: The moon waxes and wanes: wane means shrink. abate is used for storms, noise and pain that ease.

which way

blocks.cap: Four ways to grow and six ways to shrink.

blocks.html: The moon waxes (grows) and wanes (shrinks); the tide flows in and ebbs out. Abate is the word for storms, noise, pain and anger that ease. And atrophy is shrinking for one reason only: lack of use.

opts.s: By the time the guests left, our tall pile of cookies had {dwindled} to three broken pieces.
opts.why: A pile that shrinks little by little until little is left has dwindled.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some words calm things down; these ten stir things up. They describe starting trouble, urging people on, waking them up and feeding feelings until they grow. Several are verbs of motion at heart: agitate means to shake, stoke means to feed a fire, and a goad and a spur were both pointed tools for driving animals forward.

Stirring up trouble: provoke, incite (urge people on), instigate (start it), foment (keep it brewing), agitate (shake up; upset). Urging on: goad (push, often by teasing), spur (urge to go faster or harder), rouse (wake or stir up). Feeding or causing: stoke (add fuel), engender (give rise to).

entry.def: to stir up a reaction, especially anger
entry.ex: Poking a sleeping cat is a sure way to {provoke} a hiss.
entry.ctx: The referee’s strange call {provoked} a storm of boos from the stands; fans who had been quiet all game were suddenly on their feet, shouting.
entry.etym: From Latin provocare, “to call forth, to challenge”: pro (forth) + vocare (to call).

mn.cue: pro-VOKE: POKE it and get a reaction
mn.text: Kai tickles the sleeping dragon’s nose with a feather, poke, poke, and he {provokes} a giant, smoky sneeze!

scene.alt: A sneaky boy tickles a sleeping dragon's nose with a feather, and the dragon wakes with a smoky sneeze.

entry.def: to urge people on, especially to trouble or violence
entry.ex: The prankster tried to {incite} a food fight in the cafeteria.
entry.ctx: Instead of calming the angry fans, the loudmouth in the front row tried to {incite} them, shouting that they should rush onto the field.
entry.etym: From Latin incitare, “to set in rapid motion, to urge on”: in (on) + citare (to set moving).
entry.note: Incite (urge on) is not insight (understanding), though they sound alike.

mn.cue: IN-CITE: urges everyone IN SIGHT on
mn.text: Rex jumps onto a lunch table and yells “Food fight!”, urging everyone in sight to start throwing. He {incites} trouble.

scene.alt: A troublemaker stands on a lunch table shouting for a food fight while two children look shocked.

entry.def: to start something, especially trouble; to bring it about
entry.ex: Dev {instigated} the snowball fight by tossing the first one at his sister.
entry.ctx: Nobody knew who had {instigated} the prank, but someone had started it: every chair in the classroom had been turned to face the back wall.
entry.etym: From Latin instigare, “to urge on, to goad.”

mn.cue: IN-STIG-ATE: in an INSTANT, it STARTS
mn.text: Dev throws the very first snowball, and in an instant everyone is throwing. He {instigates} the snowball fight.

scene.alt: A teen throws the first snowball of a snowball fight at a girl, who ducks.

entry.def: to stir up trouble or unrest
entry.ex: Rumors on the school bus {fomented} a feud between the two grades.
entry.ctx: The sly first mate spent weeks {fomenting} unrest among the crew, grumbling about the food and the pay until the sailors were ready to mutiny.
entry.etym: From Latin fomentum, “a warm compress,” from fovere, “to warm.” To foment was first to warm a sore; later, to heat up trouble.
entry.note: Foment (stir up trouble) is not ferment (to bubble the way yeast does), though both suggest something bubbling up.

mn.cue: FOAM-ENT: stir till trouble FOAMS over
mn.text: Victor stirs his pot of gossip faster and faster, adding a pinch of rumor here and a dash of grumbling there, until it foams over. He {foments} trouble.

scene.alt: A sneaky man stirs a bubbling pot as the word Trouble foams up out of it.

entry.def: to push or provoke someone into doing something
entry.ex: His teammates {goaded} Kai into singing at the talent show.
entry.ctx: Dev didn’t want to race, but his cousins {goaded} him with teasing until he finally lined up at the start, just to prove them wrong.
entry.etym: From Old English gad, a pointed stick for driving cattle forward.

mn.cue: GOAD: “GO! GO! GO!” until you do it
mn.text: Rosa’s friends chant “Go! Go! Go!” until she finally steps up to the microphone to sing. They {goad} her into it.

scene.alt: Friends chant and cheer to push a nervous teen toward the microphone on stage.

entry.def: to urge on; to push someone to act faster or harder
entry.ex: The cheering crowd {spurred} the tired runners toward the finish line.
entry.ctx: The news that the library might close {spurred} the neighbors to action; within a week they had raised enough money to keep its doors open.
entry.etym: From Old English spura, the pointed tool on a rider’s heel used to urge a horse on.

mn.cue: SPUR: cheers that PUSH you FASTER
mn.text: Jamal is tired in the last lap, but the crowd’s cheers push him to run faster and faster. The cheers {spur} him on.

scene.alt: A tired runner speeds up as children cheer him on from the side of the track.

entry.def: to wake someone up; to stir up feelings or action
entry.ex: The smell of pancakes {roused} Sami from a deep sleep.
entry.ctx: The coach’s speech {roused} the team; players who had been slumped on the bench at halftime leaped up, cheering and ready to play.

mn.cue: ROUSE the HOUSE: the rooster wakes everyone
mn.text: Cock-a-doodle-doo! The rooster crows right outside the window, and the whole house wakes up. He {rouses} everyone.

scene.alt: A rooster crows at the bedroom window, waking a sleepy boy, who stretches.

entry.def: to add fuel to a fire; to stir up strong feelings
entry.ex: Grandpa {stoked} the campfire until the flames leaped high.
entry.ctx: Every new rumor only {stoked} the town’s curiosity about the mysterious visitor, until people were lining up just to catch a glimpse of him.
entry.etym: From Dutch stoken, “to feed a fire.”

mn.cue: STOKE it and the flames SOAR
mn.text: Marcus adds another log to the campfire, and the flames leap high. He {stokes} the fire.

scene.alt: A man adds a log to a campfire, and the flames leap higher.

entry.def: to stir up or shake; to make someone anxious or upset
entry.ex: The washing machine {agitates} the clothes to shake the dirt loose.
entry.ctx: The long wait for news {agitated} the families in the hallway; they paced, checked their phones and asked for updates every few minutes.
entry.etym: From Latin agitare, “to drive about, to shake,” from agere, “to drive, to do.”
entry.note: Agitate can also mean to campaign hard for a change: to agitate for a new park.

mn.text: Theo shakes the snow globe hard, and the snow swirls wildly inside. He {agitates} it.

scene.alt: A toddler shakes a snow globe hard, sending the snow swirling.

entry.def: to cause something to exist; to give rise to
entry.ex: Her fair rules {engendered} trust among the players.
entry.ctx: The teacher’s patience {engendered} confidence in her shy students; by spring, kids who once whispered were reading aloud to the whole class.
entry.etym: From Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerare, “to bring to life, to produce”: in (in) + generare (to beget).

mn.text: Nell hands a neighbor a flower; he passes one to Ivy; she passes one to her grandpa. One kind act {engenders} many more.

scene.alt: Three neighbors pass flowers along, one kindness leading to the next.

blocks.html: foment (stir up trouble) is not ferment, though both suggest bubbling. incite (urge on) is not insight (understanding).

blocks.cap: Ten ways to stir things up.

blocks.html: Two sound-alike traps. Foment (stir up trouble) is not ferment (to bubble, as yeast does), though both suggest something bubbling up. And incite (urge on) is not insight (deep understanding). Notice, too, that engender and spur often describe good things: kindness engenders trust, and good news spurs people to act.

opts.s: The cheering crowd {spurred} the tired runners on toward the finish line.
opts.why: Cheers that urge runners to go faster spur them on.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Sooner or later, everyone gives in. These words tell how: by following a rule, by stepping aside, by softening after saying no, by quietly going along, by surrendering completely, or by bowing far too low.

Following a rule or request: comply, accede (agree). Giving way: yield, submit, relent (soften after refusing), succumb (give in to pressure or temptation). Giving something up: concession. Going along: acquiesce (quietly, often unwillingly). Surrendering: capitulate. Too humble: kowtow.

entry.def: to do what is asked, ordered or required
entry.ex: All visitors must {comply} with the museum’s no-flash rule.
entry.ctx: When the lifeguard blew her whistle and waved everyone out of the water, the swimmers {complied} at once, though a few grumbled as they climbed out.
entry.etym: From Italian complire, “to fulfill,” from Latin complere, “to fill up.”

mn.cue: COM-PLY: COME and PLAY by the rules
mn.text: The sign on the door says SHOES OFF, so Kai sits down and takes off his sneakers before he comes in to play. He {complies}.

scene.alt: A boy kneels to take off his sneakers beside a sign that says Shoes Off.

entry.def: to give way to pressure, to another person or to traffic
entry.ex: Drivers must {yield} to people in the crosswalk.
entry.ctx: For an hour the rusty gate held firm, but at last it {yielded} to the farmer’s shoulder and creaked open.
entry.etym: From Old English gieldan, “to pay, to give back.”
entry.note: Yield also means to produce: the orchard yielded a thousand bushels of fruit.

mn.text: Dev stops his bike and waits while a line of ducks waddles across the path. He {yields} to the ducks.

scene.alt: A teen stops his bike to let a line of ducks cross the path beside a Yield sign.

entry.def: to give in to someone’s authority or control
entry.ex: The players {submitted} to the referee’s decision without another word.
entry.ctx: After a long tug-of-war over bath time, the puppy finally {submitted}, standing still and dripping while Lila scrubbed behind his ears.
entry.etym: From Latin submittere, “to lower, to put under”: sub (under) + mittere (to send, to let go).
entry.note: Submit also means to hand something in: to submit an essay.

mn.cue: SUB-MIT: gives in and goes UNDER the suds
mn.text: After a long struggle, the muddy puppy gives up and sits still in the tub of suds. He {submits} to his bath.

scene.alt: A soapy puppy sits glumly in a tub of water, giving in to a bath, while a girl laughs.

entry.def: to become less strict or severe; to give in after refusing
entry.ex: Mom finally {relented} and let us stay up to watch the meteor shower.
entry.ctx: For weeks the coach refused to change the practice time, but when every family signed a letter asking her to, she {relented} and moved it to after dinner.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin relentare, “to soften,” from Latin lentus, “soft, bending.”

mn.text: Ivy begs to borrow her big sister’s bike. Maya says no, no and no again, then sighs and lends it after all. Maya {relents}.

scene.alt: A teen sighs and lends her bike to her delighted little sister.

entry.def: to give in to pressure, temptation or force
entry.ex: After an hour of staring at the cake, Jonah {succumbed} and ate a slice.
entry.ctx: The old oak had survived a hundred storms, but in last night’s wind it finally {succumbed}, crashing down across the empty road.
entry.etym: From Latin succumbere, “to sink down under”: sub (under) + cumbere (to lie down).

mn.cue: suc-CRUMB: gives in to the CRUMB
mn.text: Jonah promised himself no sweets, but the chocolate cake smells so good. He {succumbs} and takes a big bite.

labels.text: suc-CUMB: gives IN to the crumb

scene.alt: A teen gives in and takes a bite of chocolate cake despite his No Sweets sign.

entry.def: something given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement
entry.ex: As a {concession}, the coach let the team choose the music for practice.
entry.ctx: Neither side would budge until the landlord made a {concession}: she would fix the leaky roof if the tenants agreed to a slightly higher rent.
entry.etym: From Latin concessio, from concedere, “to give way”: con (thoroughly) + cedere (to yield).
entry.note: A concession stand sells snacks at a game; its owner has been granted, or conceded, the right to sell there.

mn.cue: a CONE-cession: give a CONE to make a deal
mn.text: Pip and Zoe both want the swing. Pip hands Zoe his ice cream cone, and she lets him swing first. The cone is his {concession}.

labels.text: a CONE-CESSION: a give-up for a deal

scene.alt: A boy offers his ice cream cone to a girl so that he can have the swing first.

entry.def: to accept or agree quietly, without protest, often unwillingly
entry.ex: Too tired to argue, Grandpa {acquiesced} to watching the cartoon movie one more time.
entry.ctx: Rosa had wanted pizza, but when the rest of the family voted for soup, she {acquiesced} with a small sigh and set the table without another word.
entry.etym: From Latin acquiescere, “to rest, to be at peace with”: ad (to) + quiescere (to be quiet).
entry.note: Acquiesce means quiet acceptance, often with a sigh, not eager agreement.

mn.text: The family votes for soup instead of pizza. Rosa sighs, says nothing and quietly sets out the bowls: she {acquiesces}.

scene.alt: A teen quietly carries a soup bowl while her father and little brother cheer for soup.

entry.def: to surrender or give in completely
entry.ex: After a long siege, the castle finally {capitulated}.
entry.ctx: The twins held out against bedtime for nearly an hour, bargaining and pleading, but at last they {capitulated} and climbed into bed.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin capitulare, “to draw up terms under headings,” from capitulum, “a chapter, a little head”; to capitulate was first to agree to terms of surrender.

mn.cue: CAP-itulate: off comes the CAP, up goes the white flag
mn.text: King Gus takes off his crown, raises both hands and waves a white flag from the castle: “We give up!” He {capitulates}.

scene.alt: A king with his crown on the ground raises his hands in surrender as a white flag flies from the castle.

entry.def: to agree to a request or demand
entry.ex: The principal {acceded} to the students’ request for a longer lunch.
entry.ctx: At first the town council refused, but after hundreds of letters it {acceded} to the neighbors’ demand and put a stop sign at the busy corner.
entry.etym: From Latin accedere, “to come near, to agree”: ad (to) + cedere (to go, to yield).
entry.note: Accede (agree) is not exceed (go beyond).

mn.cue: ac-SEED: says YES to more SEEDS
mn.text: The birds line up and squawk for more seeds, and Granny Mae says yes, tossing out another handful. She {accedes} to their demand.

scene.alt: A grandmother on a bench tosses more seeds to a row of squawking birds.

entry.def: to act too humbly and obediently in order to please someone powerful
entry.ex: The new player refused to {kowtow} to the bossy team captain.
entry.ctx: Instead of standing up for her own idea, Rosa’s partner {kowtowed} to the loudest kid in the group, agreeing with every word he said.
entry.etym: From Chinese kòutóu, “knock the head,” an old custom of kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground before a ruler.

mn.cue: KOW-TOW: bow down to your TOES
mn.text: Whatever bossy Pip in the paper crown says, Sami bows down to his toes: “Yes, boss! Anything, boss!” Sami {kowtows}.

labels.text: KOW-TOW: bow LOW to the boss

scene.alt: A boy bows low before a bossy boy wearing a paper crown and standing on a crate.

blocks.html: accede (agree) is not exceed (go beyond). acquiesce means quiet acceptance, not eager agreement.

blocks.cap: Ten ways to give in.

blocks.html: Two traps. Accede (agree) is not exceed (go beyond): the council acceded to our request, and the cost did not exceed our budget. And acquiesce means quiet acceptance, often with a sigh, not eager agreement. Notice, too, that kowtow is a criticism: it means being too humble, not simply polite.

opts.s: The twins begged for a puppy for a whole year before Dad finally {relented}.
opts.why: Giving in after refusing for a long time is relenting.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some things matter more than anything; others hardly matter at all. These words help you rank what is important, from the one thing everything depends on to the side issue that can wait.

Very important: crucial (it decides the outcome), pivotal (everything turns on it), paramount (above all else), preeminent (best of all), salient (stands out; most noticeable). Not important: trivial, trifling (small), frivolous (silly), peripheral (at the edge) and tangential (off the point).

entry.def: extremely important; deciding how things turn out
entry.ex: Getting enough sleep is {crucial} the night before a big test.
entry.ctx: The last-second catch was {crucial}: without it, the other team would have scored and won the championship.
entry.etym: From Latin crux, “cross,” through the idea of a crossroads, where a traveler must choose the right way.

mn.text: At the crossroads, one sign points home and the other points to the swamp. Choosing the right road is {crucial}!

scene.alt: A boy with a backpack stops at a forest signpost, choosing between the road home and the road to the swamp.

entry.def: of central importance; the point on which everything turns
entry.ex: Winning the coin toss turned out to be {pivotal} in the close game.
entry.ctx: Meeting her chemistry teacher was a {pivotal} moment in Ada’s life; before that, she had never thought about science, and afterward she could think of little else.
entry.etym: From pivot, the pin or point on which something turns.

mn.text: The whole seesaw tips up and down on one little pin in the middle. Without it, nothing moves: the pin is {pivotal}.

scene.alt: Two children play on a seesaw, with its middle pin, the pivot, circled.

entry.def: more important than anything else
entry.ex: On the field trip, safety was {paramount}.
entry.ctx: For the rescue team, speed was {paramount}; every minute counted, so they left their lunches behind and ran.
entry.etym: From Anglo-French paramont, “above, at the top,” going back to Latin ad montem, “to the mountain.”

mn.cue: PARA-MOUNT: high above the rest, like a MOUNTain
mn.text: On Tia’s hiking list, “Stay safe” towers above everything else, like a mountain over little hills. Safety is {paramount}.

scene.alt: A hiker points to a huge rock labeled Safety that towers over small rocks labeled snacks and speed.

entry.def: better or more famous than all others in a field
entry.ex: She is the {preeminent} expert on spiders in the whole country.
entry.ctx: Many bakers in the city made good bread, but Nell’s shop was {preeminent}: people crossed town and waited an hour in line just to buy her sourdough.
entry.etym: From Latin praeeminere, “to stand out above”: prae (before, above) + eminere (to stand out).

mn.cue: PRE-EMINENT: stands out above even the famous
mn.text: There are many famous bakers in town, but Nell stands out above them all; her line stretches around the block. She is {preeminent}.

scene.alt: A baker wearing a medal hands out bread to a long line of happy customers.

entry.def: most noticeable or important; standing out
entry.ex: The {salient} feature of the old house was its bright red door.
entry.ctx: The report was long, but Sami picked out its {salient} points: the bridge was unsafe, repairs would cost a million dollars, and work had to start before winter.
entry.etym: From Latin salire, “to leap”: a salient point leaps out at you.
entry.note: Salient means standing out, not salty.

mn.cue: SAIL-ient: the one red SAILboat that LEAPS out
mn.text: Among all the white sailboats on the bay, one is bright red. It leaps out at you: the red boat is the {salient} sight.

scene.alt: A boy points at the one red-sailed boat among many white ones.

entry.def: of little importance or value
entry.ex: Don’t worry about such a {trivial} mistake; it was only one comma.
entry.ctx: To Dev, the scratch on his bike seemed {trivial} next to the real problem: the front wheel was bent and would not turn at all.
entry.etym: From Latin trivialis, “commonplace,” from trivium, “a place where three roads meet.”

mn.cue: TRIVIA-l: a tiny fact that hardly matters
mn.text: Zoe frets that her left sock is one shade darker than her right. It’s a {trivial} difference; no one will ever notice.

scene.alt: A worried girl studies two almost identical socks with a magnifying glass while her cat looks bored.

entry.def: small and unimportant
entry.ex: The repair cost a {trifling} sum: just two dollars for a new screw.
entry.ctx: Compared with the flood that soaked the whole basement, the dripping faucet was a {trifling} problem, so Dad decided it could wait until spring.

mn.text: The ring toss costs one penny, and Ivy flips it into the jar without a second thought: a {trifling} sum.

scene.alt: A girl flips a single penny into a jar at a shop counter.

entry.def: not serious; silly or not worth taking seriously
entry.ex: Grandpa thought buying a hat for the dog was {frivolous}, but the dog loved it.
entry.ctx: With only twenty dollars left for groceries, Mom said that spending ten on balloons would be {frivolous}, so we drew decorations instead.
entry.etym: From Latin frivolus, “silly, worthless.”

mn.text: Victor buys his cat a tiny jeweled crown and a velvet throne. Frilly, silly and not needed at all: the purchases are {frivolous}.

scene.alt: A man bows to his cat, who sits on a velvet throne wearing a tiny crown.

entry.def: at the edge; of minor importance
entry.ex: The new bus line will reach even the {peripheral} neighborhoods at the edge of town.
entry.ctx: The main question was how to pay for the new library; the color of its carpet was a {peripheral} issue that could wait until later.
entry.etym: From Greek periphereia, “the line around a circle”: peri (around) + pherein (to carry).

mn.text: The soccer game rages in the middle of the field, but little Theo is out at the edge picking daisies. His part in the game is {peripheral}.

scene.alt: Two players race for the ball in the middle of the field while a toddler picks flowers at the edge.

entry.def: only slightly connected to the main point; going off the topic
entry.ex: The speaker’s {tangential} story about his cat had nothing to do with the budget.
entry.ctx: Asked about his science project, Kai gave a {tangential} answer: he started with the volcano model but soon wandered off into a story about his summer vacation.
entry.etym: From tangent, a line that touches a circle at one point and then goes off on its own, from Latin tangere, “to touch.”
entry.note: A tangential remark touches the topic and then heads off in another direction; to go off on a tangent is to wander from the subject.

mn.cue: TANGENT: touches the topic, then shoots OFF
mn.text: Professor Edwin starts the history lesson, then shoots off: “…which reminds me of my cat, who once…” His story is {tangential}.

scene.alt: An old professor wanders off the subject into a story about his cat while two students look puzzled and bored.

blocks.html: salient means standing out, not salty. A tangential remark touches the topic and then goes off in another direction.

head: word
how important?
you might hear
rows: best of all in a field
blocks.cap: From what matters most to what hardly matters.

blocks.html: Salient means standing out, not salty: it comes from Latin salire, to leap, so a salient point leaps out at you. And a tangential remark is like a tangent line in geometry: it touches the topic at one point and then heads off on its own.

opts.s: When a storm is coming, getting every boat into the harbor is {paramount}; nothing else matters until they are safe.
opts.why: Something that matters more than anything else is paramount.
