blocks.html: Put in- in front of a word and you often get its opposite: correct and incorrect, visible and invisible. All ten words in this topic are built that way. Each one is a no: impeccable is not able to go wrong, insatiable is not able to be filled up, irrevocable is not able to be called back.

in- = not. To be easier to say, it changes its last letter to match the sound after it: im- before b, m and p (impeccable), il- before l (illegal) and ir- before r (irrevocable). Many of these words end in -able or -ible, so they mean not able to be…

Peel off the in- and look at what is left. Sometimes it is a word you know (correct, apt); sometimes it is a Latin word worth learning (satis, enough; nocere, to harm). The memory hooks below lean on those parts.

entry.def: perfect; without a single flaw or fault
entry.ex: Her {impeccable} handwriting made the party invitations look printed.
entry.ctx: The young chef’s knife work was {impeccable}: every slice of carrot was the same thickness, and not one piece was wasted.
entry.etym: From Latin impeccabilis, “not able to sin”: in- (not) + peccare (to sin).

mn.cue: not a crumb to PECK: im-PECK-able
mn.text: The hen hunts all over Nana Lou’s kitchen floor and finds not one crumb to peck: the floor is {impeccable}.

scene.alt: A hen searches a spotless kitchen floor and finds nothing to peck, while a proud grandmother looks on.

entry.def: clumsy; lacking the skill to do something well
entry.ex: The {inept} referee kept losing track of the score.
entry.ctx: Although Marcus was a gifted singer, he was {inept} at dancing; he stepped on his partner’s feet twice in the first minute.
entry.etym: From Latin ineptus, “unsuited, foolish”: in- (not) + aptus (fit, apt).

mn.text: Felix is not apt at juggling: every ball he tosses ends up on the grass. He is {inept}.

scene.alt: A man tries to juggle and drops every ball while a girl laughs.

entry.def: not moving or acting; without energy or force
entry.ex: The cat lay {inert} on the warm windowsill all afternoon.
entry.ctx: The robot had worked for hours, but once its battery ran down it sat {inert} in the corner, not stirring even when the children called its name.
entry.etym: From Latin iners, “unskilled, idle”: in- (without) + ars (skill, art).
entry.note: Chemists call a substance inert when it does not react with others; helium is an inert gas.

mn.text: The puppy barks and barks at the big rock lying in the dirt, but the rock never moves: it is {inert}.

scene.alt: A puppy barks at a big rock in the dirt, but the rock does not move.

entry.def: impossible to defeat, tame or discourage
entry.ex: The {indomitable} little team kept playing hard even when it was losing by twenty points.
entry.ctx: Storms knocked down her fence three summers in a row, but Granny Mae’s spirit was {indomitable}; each time, she simply built it again, a little stronger.
entry.etym: From Late Latin indomitabilis, “not able to be tamed”: in- (not) + domitare (to tame).

mn.text: Big Sven pulls with all his might, but he can’t dominate little Zoe in tug-of-war; she won’t budge an inch. She is {indomitable}.

scene.alt: A small girl holds firm in a tug-of-war against a big man, who is sweating.

entry.def: impossible to stop or change; not moved by pleading
entry.ex: The {inexorable} tide crept up the beach and swallowed our sandcastle.
entry.ctx: We begged the clock to slow down before the last bell, but time was {inexorable}; the minutes ticked by at the same steady pace no matter what we wanted.
entry.etym: From Latin inexorabilis, “not to be moved by pleading”: in- (not) + exorare (to win over by pleading).

mn.text: Pip shouts “Stop!” at the sea, but the tide keeps coming in, no exceptions: it is {inexorable}.

scene.alt: A boy holds up his hands and shouts at a big wave rolling toward his sandcastle.

entry.def: impossible to satisfy; always wanting more
entry.ex: The puppy had an {insatiable} appetite for tennis balls.
entry.ctx: Lila’s curiosity was {insatiable}; after reading every book about volcanoes in the school library, she asked the librarian to order more.
entry.etym: From Latin insatiabilis: in- (not) + satiare (to fill, satisfy), from satis (enough).

mn.text: Ivy has eaten a whole stack of pancakes and still is not satisfied: “More!” Her appetite is {insatiable}.

scene.alt: A little girl beside a tall stack of empty plates cheers for more while the cook looks amazed.

entry.def: harmless; not likely to hurt or upset anyone
entry.ex: Her {innocuous} question about the weather somehow started a long argument.
entry.ctx: Mom worried that the new board game would start fights, but it proved {innocuous}: the worst thing that could happen was losing a turn and having to cluck like a chicken.
entry.etym: From Latin innocuus, “harmless”: in- (not) + nocere (to harm).

mn.cue: in-KNOCK-YOU-ous: it can’t KNOCK YOU over
mn.text: The huge beach ball bounces right into Theo, but it is so soft it can’t knock you over; it is {innocuous}.

scene.alt: A giant soft beach ball bounces into a toddler, who laughs.

entry.def: impossible to correct or reform; always misbehaving
entry.ex: Our {incorrigible} parrot still squawks at the mail carrier every single morning.
entry.ctx: Teachers had tried praise, extra chores and long talks, but the class clown remained {incorrigible}, cracking jokes all the way through every test.
entry.etym: From Late Latin incorrigibilis: in- (not) + corrigere (to correct).

mn.text: Farmer Jamal has told the goat “No!” a hundred times, but it still eats the socks off his line; it cannot be corrected. The goat is {incorrigible}.

scene.alt: A sneaky goat runs off with a sock while the farmer shouts at it once again.

entry.def: impossible to understand or read; mysterious
entry.ex: The cat stared at me with an {inscrutable} look, and I had no idea what it wanted.
entry.ctx: Most players grin when they draw a good card, but Grandpa Gus’s face stayed {inscrutable}, so no one at the table could guess whether he was about to win.
entry.etym: From Late Latin inscrutabilis: in- (not) + scrutari (to search, examine).

mn.text: Sami scrutinizes the cat’s face with a magnifying glass, but he still can’t tell what she is thinking: her face is {inscrutable}.

scene.alt: A boy studies a cat’s blank face through a magnifying glass and still looks puzzled.

entry.def: impossible to undo or take back
entry.ex: Pressing “send” felt {irrevocable}; the message was already on its way.
entry.ctx: The judges explained that their decision was {irrevocable}: once a skater’s score was posted, it could not be changed or taken back for any reason.
entry.etym: From Latin irrevocabilis, “not able to be called back”: in- (not) + revocare (to call back).

mn.text: Once Kai drops the letter into the mailbox, he can’t call it back, however loudly he shouts: mailing it was {irrevocable}.

scene.alt: A boy reaches toward a mailbox, shouting for the letter he just mailed to come back.

blocks.html: Not every in- means not: inflammable means easily set on fire, and invaluable means priceless. The in- that means not becomes im- before b, m and p, il- before l and ir- before r.

blocks.cap: Ten words, one prefix: take off the in- and you find the thing that cannot happen.

blocks.html: Watch the spelling change. Before p, in- becomes im- (impeccable, impossible); before r, it becomes ir- (irrevocable, irregular), which is why those words have a double r. Before l it becomes il- (illegal, illogical).

opts.s: However hard the coach argued, the referee’s call was {irrevocable}: the goal would not count.

blocks.cap: Which word fits? A call that cannot be taken back is irrevocable.

blocks.html: Some people hold their ground; some give way. English has a crowd of words for the first kind, and the trick is that they do not all mean the same thing about the person. Holding on to a goal through every setback is tenacious or steadfast, and we admire it. Refusing to budge when you are plainly wrong is obstinate or obdurate, and we don’t.

Ask two questions about each word: Is the person firm or yielding? and Does the writer approve? Resolute and steadfast praise firmness; intransigent and recalcitrant blame it. At the other end, docile and malleable describe someone (or something) easy to lead or shape.
Several of these words carry pictures inside them. Recalcitrant comes from a Latin verb for kicking back with the heels, obdurate from a verb for hardening, and malleable from the Latin for hammer.

entry.def: stubbornly refusing to change one’s mind or plan
entry.ex: The {obstinate} toddler refused to wear anything but her rain boots, even on a sunny day.
entry.ctx: Everyone else agreed the trail was washed out, but Uncle Victor was {obstinate}; he insisted on hiking it anyway and came back two hours later, muddy to the knees.
entry.etym: From Latin obstinatus, “determined,” from obstinare (to persist): ob- (in the way) + a part akin to stare (to stand).

mn.text: The donkey stands in the middle of the gate, and no amount of pushing will move it: it is {obstinate}.

scene.alt: A man pushes and pushes a grumpy donkey that will not move from the gate.

entry.def: holding on firmly; refusing to give up
entry.ex: The {tenacious} terrier would not let go of the rope toy.
entry.ctx: Most reporters gave up after the mayor’s office ignored their calls, but one {tenacious} young writer kept asking questions for months until she got answers.
entry.etym: From Latin tenax, “holding fast,” from tenere (to hold).

mn.cue: holds on with all TEN fingers
mn.text: The wind howls around the cliff, but Maya holds on with all ten fingers and keeps climbing: she is {tenacious}.

scene.alt: A climber clings to a big rock in the wind and keeps reaching higher.

entry.def: firm and loyal; not changing or giving way
entry.ex: Through every losing season, the team’s {steadfast} fans filled the bleachers.
entry.ctx: Friends came and went over the years, but Lila remained {steadfast}; whenever Rosa needed help, Lila was the first to show up.
entry.etym: From Old English stedefæst, “fixed in its place”: stede (place) + fæst (fixed, firm).

mn.cue: STEADY, held FAST in its place
mn.text: Every stormy night, keeper Tia stays at her post and keeps the lighthouse lamp burning for the boats: she is {steadfast}.

scene.alt: On a stormy night, a lighthouse keeper in a raincoat holds up a lantern, staying at her post.

entry.def: firmly insisting; refusing to be talked out of something
entry.ex: Grandpa was {adamant} that we wear our seat belts, even for a one-block drive.
entry.ctx: The class begged for one more week to finish their projects, but the teacher was {adamant}: the deadline was Friday, and no pleading would change it.
entry.etym: From an old noun adamant, a stone once believed to be unbreakable, from Greek adamas, “unconquerable.”

mn.cue: a NO as hard as a DIAMOND
mn.text: Pip begs to have cake for breakfast, but Granny Mae’s “no” is as hard as a diamond: she is {adamant}. (Diamond and adamant come from the same Greek word, adamas.)

scene.alt: A boy begs on his knees while his grandmother crosses her arms and says no; a hard diamond shines above her.

entry.def: firmly determined; set on a purpose
entry.ex: With a {resolute} face, Dev stepped up to take the last penalty kick.
entry.ctx: The flood had ruined half the town’s shops, yet the owners were {resolute}; within a month they had cleaned, repaired and reopened every door on Main Street.
entry.etym: From Latin resolutus, past participle of resolvere (to loosen, settle).

mn.cue: REZ-uh-LOOT: won’t quit till the LOOT
mn.text: Captain Ada has dug for three days, and she won’t stop until she finds the loot: she is {resolute}.

labels.text: RESO-LOOT: till I find the LOOT

scene.alt: A determined pirate digs on a sandy island toward a buried treasure chest.

entry.def: refusing to compromise or give way at all
entry.ex: The two {intransigent} cats each refused to give up the sunny spot on the porch.
entry.ctx: The talks failed because both sides were {intransigent}: neither would give up a single demand, so the meeting ended without even a partial deal.
entry.etym: From Spanish intransigente, “not coming to an agreement,” from Latin in- (not) + transigere (to come to terms).

mn.cue: the GENT who won’t make a deal: in-TRANS-i-GENT
mn.text: Pip offers nine coins for the hat, then nine and a half, but the seller is a gent who will not bend an inch: “Ten, or no deal.” He is {intransigent}.

scene.alt: A boy offers coins for a hat, but the seller crosses his arms and will not lower his price.

entry.def: stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate
entry.ex: The {recalcitrant} printer jammed every time we tried to print the poster.
entry.ctx: Most of the campers lined up when the whistle blew, but a few {recalcitrant} boys stayed on the dock and ignored every call to come in.
entry.etym: From Latin recalcitrare, “to kick back with the heels”: re- (back) + calx (heel).

mn.cue: KICKS BACK with his heels: re-CALC-itrant
mn.text: At bath time, Theo kicks his heels and shouts “No!” He fights every rule: he is {recalcitrant}.

scene.alt: A toddler sits on the floor kicking his heels and shouting no while his mother waits with the soap.

entry.def: hard-hearted and stubborn, especially when one should give way
entry.ex: Even the puppy’s sad eyes could not soften the {obdurate} landlord.
entry.ctx: The children explained, apologized and offered to pay for the window, but the neighbor remained {obdurate}, refusing even to listen.
entry.etym: From Latin obdurare, “to harden,” from durus (hard).

mn.text: However nicely the children ask, Rex won’t give back the ball that flew over his fence; his heart is as hard as durable stone. He is {obdurate}.

scene.alt: Two sad children ask for their ball back across a fence, but a grumpy man holds it up and refuses.

entry.def: calm and easy to teach, lead or control
entry.ex: The {docile} old horse let every child at the fair take a turn on its back.
entry.ctx: The trainer warned that the puppy would not stay {docile} forever; once it was bigger, it would pull hard on the leash unless it learned to heel now.
entry.etym: From Latin docilis, “easily taught,” from docere (to teach).

mn.cue: DOS-ul: it DOES ALL you ask
mn.text: Ask the pony to walk, stop or turn, and it does all you ask: it is {docile}.

scene.alt: A girl leads a calm, happy pony that follows her wherever she goes.

entry.def: easily shaped or bent; also, easily influenced
entry.ex: Warm wax is {malleable}, so the children pressed it into star shapes.
entry.ctx: Young children’s tastes are {malleable}; a toddler who hates peas this month may ask for seconds next month after seeing an older cousin enjoy them.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin malleabilis, from malleare (to hammer), from malleus (hammer).

mn.text: A few taps of the smith’s mallet and the soft gold bends into a ring: gold is {malleable}.

scene.alt: A smith taps soft gold with a mallet, shaping it into a ring.

blocks.html: tenacious and steadfast usually praise; obstinate and recalcitrant usually blame. The same firmness gets a kind word or an unkind one depending on the writer's view.

head: firm, and the writer approves
firm, and the writer disapproves
yielding
rows: tenacious: holds on, won’t give up
obstinate: won’t change a bad plan
malleable: easy to shape or sway
blocks.cap: The same firmness can be praise or blame. Look for the writer’s attitude in the sentence.

blocks.html: A writer who likes a stubborn character calls her tenacious or resolute; a writer who doesn’t calls her obstinate. On a test, read the sentence around the blank: if the stubbornness is causing trouble (“refused to listen,” “made things worse”), choose a word that blames.

blocks.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: Her {tenacious} effort finally paid off: after forty tries, the kite flew.

blocks.cap: The effort paid off, so the writer approves: tenacious.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Picture a long table full of good things. Some people take a little and stop; some people take everything in sight. This topic has five words for holding back and five for giving in to pleasure, and they come up often in history and fiction, where writers love to set a careful hero beside a greedy king.

Holding back: temperate (moderate), abstain (choose not to), abstemious (eating and drinking little), ascetic (giving up comforts on purpose), restraint (self-control). Giving in: hedonist (a person who lives for pleasure), sybarite (a lover of luxury), epicurean (devoted to fine food), decadent (soft with too much luxury), voracious (hungry for more).

Two of these words come from names. A sybarite is named for Sybaris, an ancient city famous for luxury, and epicurean comes from Epicurus, a Greek thinker whose name later came to stand for a love of fine food.

entry.def: moderate; showing self-control and avoiding extremes
entry.ex: Even when the team lost, Coach Ada gave a {temperate} answer instead of an angry one.
entry.ctx: Unlike his brother, who ate three desserts and stayed up until dawn, Omar was {temperate} in all things: one slice of pie, a short walk and early to bed.

roots.means: mix in the right measure, moderate

entry.etym: From Latin temperatus, past participle of temperare (to keep within limits, to moderate).
entry.note: A temperate climate is a mild one, with no extreme heat or cold.

mn.text: Nell’s habits are like a mild spring day, never too hot or too cold: one slice of cake, then “No more, thanks.” She is {temperate}.

scene.alt: A woman politely turns down a second slice of cake while a boy happily eats more.

entry.def: to choose not to do or have something
entry.ex: Grandpa {abstains} from coffee after lunch so he can sleep at night.
entry.ctx: Most of the club voted yes, two voted no, and Felix chose to {abstain}, saying he had not read the plan carefully enough to vote either way.
entry.etym: From Latin abstinere, “to hold back”: abs- (away) + tenere (to hold).
entry.note: In a vote, to abstain is to choose not to vote at all.

mn.cue: AB + STAIN: stay away from the STAIN
mn.text: At the party, Zoe keeps away from the chocolate fountain so nothing will stain her white dress: she {abstains}.

scene.alt: A girl in a clean white dress holds up her hands and turns down a chocolate cake.

entry.def: eating and drinking only a little; sparing
entry.ex: The {abstemious} hiker carried only a pear and a bottle of water for the whole day.
entry.ctx: At the wedding feast, while other guests went back for thirds, Professor Edwin stayed {abstemious}, taking a single plate of vegetables and a glass of water.

mn.text: At a table piled with food, Professor Edwin eats one stem of celery and calls it lunch: he is {abstemious}.

scene.alt: An old professor holds up a single vegetable beside a table piled high with food.

entry.def: giving up comforts and pleasures on purpose; very strict with oneself
entry.ex: The runner kept an {ascetic} schedule: early bed, plain food and no days off.
entry.ctx: The old sailor’s cabin was {ascetic}: a hard bunk, one blanket, a tin cup and nothing else, though he could easily have afforded more.
entry.etym: From Greek asketikos, “hardworking, disciplined,” from askein (to exercise, train).
entry.note: An ascetic can also be a person: one who lives this way.

mn.cue: a ROCK for a SEAT: uh-SEAT-ic
mn.text: The hermit on the mountain gave up his soft chair and uses a rock for a seat; he gives up every comfort on purpose. He lives an {ascetic} life.

scene.alt: A man in a plain robe sits calmly on a rock in the desert with only one bowl.

entry.def: control over one’s own actions or feelings; holding back
entry.ex: It took real {restraint} not to open the presents before Grandma arrived.
entry.ctx: The referee showed great {restraint}; though the player yelled at him for a full minute, he answered calmly and simply restarted the game.
entry.etym: From restrain, which comes through French from Latin restringere, “to draw back tightly”: re- (back) + stringere (to draw tight).

mn.text: The puppy strains and quivers, but it keeps the cookie balanced on its nose until Kai says “OK!” That is {restraint}.

scene.alt: A puppy holds very still with a cookie on its nose while a boy tells it to wait.

entry.def: a person who lives mainly for pleasure
entry.ex: On vacation, even sensible Aunt Lin turned into a {hedonist}, napping in the sun and ordering dessert first.
entry.ctx: Her brother saved and planned for the future, but she was a {hedonist} who spent every paycheck on concerts, fancy meals and trips the moment it arrived.
entry.etym: From Greek hedone, “pleasure.”

mn.text: Sven says he is done with chores forever; from now on it is ice cream, music and naps in the sun. He is a {hedonist}.

scene.alt: A big man in sunglasses lounges on the beach with ice cream and music, his briefcase tossed aside.

entry.def: spoiled by too much luxury and pleasure, and slipping downhill
entry.ex: The cake was so {decadent} that it had three kinds of chocolate and a layer of fudge.
entry.ctx: In its last years the old empire grew {decadent}: its nobles held endless banquets while roads crumbled, soldiers went unpaid and no one guarded the borders.
entry.etym: From French décadent, from décadence, from Medieval Latin decadentia: de- (down) + cadere (to fall).
entry.note: Today decadent is also used playfully for very rich food: a decadent dessert.

mn.text: The king lounges on his throne eating cake all day while the castle crumbles around him: his court has grown {decadent}.

scene.alt: A king munches cake on his throne while the columns of his castle crumble.

entry.def: a person devoted to luxury and comfort
entry.ex: A true {sybarite}, Victor would not sit on any chair without a velvet cushion.
entry.ctx: Her roommate was a {sybarite} who filled the apartment with silk pillows, scented candles and imported chocolates, so the student’s plain cot looked bare beside it all.
entry.etym: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southern Italy whose people were famous for their love of luxury.

mn.cue: SIBBY wants it all just RIGHT
mn.text: Sibby the cat sleeps only on silk pillows and sips cream from a golden bowl; everything must be just right for this little {sybarite}.

scene.alt: A proud cat lounges on a pile of silk pillows beside a golden bowl of cream.

entry.def: devoted to fine food and the pleasures of eating
entry.ex: Dad planned an {epicurean} birthday dinner with seven small courses.
entry.ctx: Tia’s tastes were {epicurean}; she would happily drive an hour to a tiny bakery for bread made with flour ground that morning.
entry.etym: Named for Epicurus, an ancient Greek thinker who taught that a calm, pleasant life is the goal; over time his name came to stand for a love of fine food.
entry.note: Epicurus himself praised simple pleasures, such as bread and water among friends.

mn.text: Chef Greta cooks an epic seven-course dinner and savors every bite: her tastes are {epicurean}.

scene.alt: A chef happily tastes a grand feast laid out on the table.

entry.def: wanting huge amounts of food, or of some activity
entry.ex: After swimming all morning, the {voracious} campers ate every pancake in sight.
entry.ctx: Sami is a {voracious} reader; he finishes a book every day and still asks the librarian what else he can borrow.
entry.etym: From Latin vorax, “greedy for food,” from vorare (to devour).

mn.text: Sami devours a book, then another, then another, and still wants more: he is a {voracious} reader.

scene.alt: A boy reads happily beside tall stacks of books he has already finished.

blocks.html: ascetic (self-denying) is not aesthetic (about beauty). epicurean today means fond of fine food, though the ancient philosopher it is named for taught simple pleasures.

head: holding back
giving in
rows: ascetic: gives up comforts on purpose
decadent: spoiled by luxury, slipping downhill
voracious: hungry for more and more
blocks.cap: Opposite ends of the table.

blocks.html: ascetic (uh-SET-ik), giving up comforts, is not aesthetic (es-THET-ik), having to do with beauty. An ascetic room is bare; an aesthetic room is beautiful.

blocks.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The hermit’s hut was {ascetic}: a bed of boards, one candle and a single shelf of books.

blocks.cap: A bare room with no comforts is ascetic.

blocks.html: Humor comes in many flavors. Some is warm and clever, some is dry and quiet, and some has teeth. Writers choose their humor words carefully, because the word tells you how the joke lands: a witty remark delights, a sarcastic one stings.

Gentle and clever: witty, wry, droll, levity. Out of place: facetious (joking when you should be serious). Sharp: sarcastic, sardonic. Kinds of mockery: a satire exposes foolishness, a parody imitates and exaggerates, and to lampoon is to make fun of someone in public.
When you meet one of these words in a passage, ask: Is the humor kind or cutting? Is it suited to the moment? Is it aimed at someone?

entry.def: cleverly funny, especially with quick remarks
entry.ex: Her {witty} reply made even the grumpy bus driver laugh.
entry.ctx: Grandpa’s toasts were never long or dull; they were {witty}, full of quick, clever lines that had the whole room laughing.
entry.etym: From Old English witig, “clever, wise,” from wit (mind, understanding).

mn.text: Rosa always has a quick, clever line ready, and her friends can’t stop laughing: she is {witty}.

scene.alt: A teen girl tells a clever joke and her friends burst out laughing.

entry.def: dryly funny, often with a touch of irony
entry.ex: Dad gave a {wry} smile when our “waterproof” tent leaked on the first night.
entry.ctx: Instead of complaining about the canceled flight, Aunt Lin made a {wry} joke: at least the airport chairs were teaching her patience.
entry.etym: From Old English wrigian, “to turn,” so first meaning twisted to one side, as in a crooked, wry smile.

mn.text: Rain pours on the picnic, and Grandpa Gus gives a crooked half smile: “Lovely day… for ducks.” His humor is {wry}.

scene.alt: In the pouring rain, a grandfather with an umbrella smiles a crooked smile while a duck splashes happily.

entry.def: funny in an odd, quiet or dry way
entry.ex: The old fisherman had a {droll} way of telling stories, never smiling while everyone else laughed.
entry.ctx: The comedian was not loud or silly but {droll}; he spoke in a flat, quiet voice and let the oddness of his remarks do the rest.
entry.etym: From French drôle, “funny, strange.”

mn.text: Baker Omar gives a bread roll a mustache and, with a perfectly straight face, bows: “Sir Roll, at your service.” His joke is {droll}.

scene.alt: A baker with a straight face presents a bread roll as if it were a knight, and a girl giggles.

entry.def: lightness of mood or humor, especially at a serious time
entry.ex: A little {levity} helped the nervous players relax before the final game.
entry.ctx: The ceremony was solemn, and the principal frowned at any {levity}; even a giggle from the back row earned a stern look.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin levitas, “lightness,” from levis (light in weight).
entry.note: Levity can be welcome (it eases a tense room) or unwelcome (it seems disrespectful); the sentence tells you which.

mn.cue: LEV = LIGHT: a joke that LEVitates
mn.text: The long meeting feels heavy until Dev’s joke floats up like a balloon and lifts everyone’s mood: a moment of {levity}.

scene.alt: In an office meeting, a young man’s joke floats up like a balloon and his coworkers laugh.

entry.def: joking at a time that calls for being serious
entry.ex: “Maybe we should all move to the moon,” Kai said, but he was only being {facetious}.
entry.ctx: When the coach asked how to fix the team’s defense, Jonah’s {facetious} answer, “Hire a dragon,” got laughs but no thanks; the coach wanted a real plan.
entry.etym: From French facétieux, from Latin facetia, “a jest, a witty saying.”

mn.cue: FACE-tious: a silly FACE at the wrong time
mn.text: When the teacher asks why his homework is late, Pip pulls a silly face and says, “My goldfish needed it.” He is being {facetious}.

scene.alt: A stern teacher asks for homework, and a boy makes a silly face and jokes.

entry.def: saying the opposite of what one means, to mock or show annoyance
entry.ex: “Oh, great, more homework,” Lila said in a {sarcastic} voice.
entry.ctx: When Dev called the three-hour traffic jam “a delightful little drive,” no one was fooled; his tone was {sarcastic}, and everyone knew he was miserable.
entry.etym: From sarcasm, from Greek sarkazein, “to tear flesh,” and so “to sneer, to speak bitterly,” from sarx (flesh).

mn.text: The bus splashes Kai with mud, and he says, “Oh, wonderful. Just what I wanted.” He means the opposite: he is being {sarcastic}.

scene.alt: A bus splashes a boy with puddle water, and he flatly says, “Oh, great.”

entry.def: grimly mocking; scornfully amused
entry.ex: The tired reporter gave a {sardonic} laugh when the “quick” meeting entered its third hour.
entry.ctx: After years of broken promises from the landlord about fixing the heat, Mr. Felix greeted the newest promise with a {sardonic} grin, as if to say he would believe it when he felt it.
entry.etym: From Greek sardonios, used of bitter, scornful laughter.

mn.cue: SARDINE-ic: a grim grin, packed like SARDINES
mn.text: Squashed into the train like a sardine in a can, Felix gives a grim grin: “Plenty of room, eh?” His humor is {sardonic}.

scene.alt: Four commuters are squashed together on a train platform; one gives a grim, mocking grin.

entry.def: humor that exposes foolishness or wrongdoing, often by exaggerating it
entry.ex: The comic strip is a gentle {satire} of office life, full of pointless meetings.
entry.ctx: The novel is more than a funny story; it is a {satire} that uses exaggeration to show how silly the town’s obsession with perfect lawns has become.
entry.etym: From Latin satura, “a mixture,” the name of a kind of Roman poem that made fun of people’s faults.

mn.cue: SAT + IRE: anger turned into laughs
mn.text: Tired of silly rules, the students put their ire into a play about a king who bans frowning; the whole school laughs and gets the point. The play is a {satire}.

scene.alt: On a stage, a boy dressed as a silly king orders “No frowning!” while two classmates laugh.

entry.def: a funny imitation that exaggerates the original
entry.ex: The class wrote a {parody} of a weather report, forecasting a ninety percent chance of homework.
entry.ctx: The song was not original; it was a {parody} of a well-known lullaby, with the same tune but new, silly words about a cat who refuses to go to sleep.
entry.etym: From Greek paroidia, “a song sung beside another”: para (beside) + oide (song).

mn.text: The parrot copies Grandpa’s sneeze, only louder and sillier: “AH-AH-AH-CHOOOO!” It is a {parody} of his sneeze.

scene.alt: A grandfather sneezes, and his parrot copies the sneeze much louder and sillier.

entry.def: to mock in public, often in writing or pictures
entry.ex: The comedy show {lampooned} the strangest fashion trends of the year.
entry.ctx: The cartoonist loved to {lampoon} show-offs; in her strips, anyone who bragged soon had a pigeon land on his hat in front of a crowd.

mn.cue: a joke poster under the LAMP
mn.text: The town is tired of Sir Rex’s bragging, so someone hangs a funny poster under the street lamp: “SIR BRAGS-A-LOT.” It {lampoons} him for all to see.

labels.text: a joke poster under the LAMP

scene.alt: Children laugh at a joke banner about a bragging knight hung under a street lamp, while the knight fumes.

blocks.html: sarcastic and sardonic both mock: sarcasm says the opposite of what it means, while sardonic humor is grim. A parody imitates something; a satire need not.

blocks.cap: From warm to cutting.

blocks.html: A parody always copies something: a song, a movie, a style. A satire may or may not copy anything; its aim is to show that some behavior is foolish. Many satires use parody as a tool. To lampoon is the action: to mock someone in public, often through satire or parody.

blocks.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The serious ceremony left no room for {levity}; even the youngest children sat silent.

blocks.cap: Lightness of mood at a serious time is levity; its opposite is gravity.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Some hours crawl and some fly. This topic gives you words for both ends: for the things that bore us and the moods boredom brings, and for the things that grab our attention and won’t let go.

Boring things: tedious (long and tiresome), monotonous (the same, over and over). Bored people: indifferent (not caring), jaded (worn out by too much), blasé (unimpressed), and the feeling itself, ennui. Interested people: engrossed, rapt, intrigued. And the verb that starts it all: to pique someone’s interest.
Notice the difference between a thing and a person. A lecture is tedious; the student listening to it is bored or indifferent. A story is fascinating; the listener is rapt.

entry.def: long, slow and tiresome
entry.ex: Sorting a thousand buttons by color was a {tedious} job.
entry.ctx: The first half of the movie was {tedious}, with long, slow scenes of people packing boxes, but the second half finally picked up speed.
entry.etym: From Late Latin taediosus, from taedium (weariness, boredom).

mn.text: Sorting a hundred teddy bears by size takes hours and hours: the job is {tedious}.

scene.alt: A bored boy sits on the floor facing a huge pile of teddy bears to sort.

entry.def: dull because it never changes; always the same
entry.ex: The {monotonous} hum of the fan put the baby to sleep.
entry.ctx: The speaker read every slide in the same flat, {monotonous} voice, never pausing or changing pitch, and half the audience was soon nodding off.
entry.etym: From Greek monotonos, “of one tone”: monos (single) + tonos (tone).

mn.cue: MONO-TONE: one note, again and again
mn.text: Felix plays the same single piano key for an hour: “Plink… plink… plink…” The sound is {monotonous}.

scene.alt: A man plays the same piano key over and over while a woman yawns.

entry.def: not caring or interested either way
entry.ex: The cat seemed completely {indifferent} to its expensive new toy.
entry.ctx: Most of the class cheered when the field trip was announced, but Dev seemed {indifferent}; he simply shrugged and went back to his drawing.
entry.etym: From Latin indifferens, “making no difference”: in- (not) + differre (to differ).
entry.note: Indifferent can also mean only average: an indifferent cook makes meals that are neither good nor bad.

mn.cue: it makes no DIFFERENCE to me
mn.text: Ask Uncle Marcus if he wants the red cup or the blue one, and he shrugs: it makes no difference to him. He is {indifferent}.

scene.alt: A girl offers a red cup or a blue one, and her uncle shrugs as if it makes no difference.

entry.def: tired and bored from having too much of something
entry.ex: After ten summers at the same beach, the {jaded} teenagers barely looked at the waves.
entry.ctx: Having eaten at every fancy restaurant in the city, the critic had grown {jaded}; dishes that thrilled other diners only made her yawn.
entry.etym: From jade, an old word for a worn-out horse.

mn.cue: a tired old JADE (a worn-out horse)
mn.text: An old word for a worn-out horse is a jade. Dusty has pulled the parade wagon a thousand times, and not even the brass band excites him now: he is {jaded}.

scene.alt: A bored old horse pulls a parade wagon past balloons and a drummer, not impressed at all.

entry.def: unimpressed, as if one has seen it all before
entry.ex: Kai acted {blasé} about meeting the star pitcher, but his hands were shaking.
entry.ctx: First-time visitors gasped at the giant waterfall, but the park ranger, who saw it every day, was {blasé} and kept checking her watch.
entry.etym: From French blasé, “worn out by too much pleasure,” from blaser (to wear out).

mn.text: The fireworks burst in every color, and little Ivy squeals, but her big sister just says, “Blah.” Rosa is {blasé}.

scene.alt: Under bursting fireworks, a little girl cheers while her teen sister crosses her arms and says, “Blah.”

entry.def: a weary, restless feeling of boredom
entry.ex: By the fourth rainy afternoon, a heavy {ennui} had settled over the cabin.
entry.ctx: Despite having every toy and game he could want, the young prince suffered from {ennui}; nothing excited him, and the long days dragged by.
entry.etym: From French ennui, “boredom, annoyance.”

mn.text: On the tenth rainy day of summer, the cousins sigh on the sofa: “What do WE do now?” They are full of {ennui}.

scene.alt: Two bored cousins slump in the living room on a rainy day, with nothing to do.

entry.def: so interested that one notices nothing else
entry.ex: Maya was so {engrossed} in her puzzle that she forgot to eat lunch.
entry.ctx: The scientist was {engrossed} in her experiment; she did not hear the phone, the doorbell or her assistant calling her name.

mn.cue: so lost in it, she misses the GROSS frog
mn.text: Lila is so deep in her book that she never notices the gross, slimy frog sitting on her head: she is {engrossed}.

scene.alt: A girl reads happily, not noticing the frog sitting on top of her head.

entry.def: completely fascinated; giving full attention
entry.ex: The children listened in {rapt} silence as Grandpa told the story of the winter the river froze solid.
entry.ctx: The audience sat {rapt} through the whole concert; no one coughed, whispered or checked a phone until the final note faded.
entry.etym: From Latin raptus, “seized, carried away,” from rapere (to seize).

mn.text: The children sit wrapped up in Professor Edwin’s tale, mouths open, not moving a muscle: they are {rapt}.

scene.alt: Three children sit on the floor, spellbound, as an old professor reads them a story.

entry.def: very curious and eager to know more
entry.ex: Lila was {intrigued} by the old map she found in the attic.
entry.ctx: At first the detective thought the case was simple, but the muddy footprints that led nowhere left her {intrigued}, and she spent all night studying them.
entry.etym: From French intriguer, “to puzzle,” from Italian intrigare (to tangle).

mn.text: A locked box sits high in the old oak tree. Who put it there, and what is inside? Kai can’t stop wondering: he is {intrigued}.

scene.alt: A boy points up at a mysterious locked chest wedged high in a tree.

entry.def: to stir up interest or curiosity
entry.ex: The movie trailer was made to {pique} your curiosity without giving away the ending.
entry.ctx: The museum hoped the giant dinosaur skeleton in the lobby would {pique} visitors’ interest and draw them deeper into the exhibits.
entry.etym: From French piquer, “to prick, sting.”
entry.note: As a noun, pique means a flash of hurt pride or annoyance: she left in a fit of pique.

mn.text: Through a knothole in the fence, Zoe takes one peek at the new neighbor’s puppy, and that peek {piques} her curiosity.

scene.alt: A girl on tiptoe peeks over a fence at a puppy, suddenly curious.

blocks.html: You pique interest (stir it), not "peak" or "peek" it. indifferent can mean uninterested or merely ordinary (an indifferent cook).

head: describes
bored side
interested side
blocks.cap: Match the word to what it describes: the thing, the person or the feeling.

blocks.html: You pique someone’s interest: you stir it up. You do not “peak” it (reach the top) or “peek” it (glance). The three words sound the same, which is why the hook above uses a peek to remember the spelling of the one that stirs.

blocks.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The mystery in chapter one was meant to {pique} the reader’s curiosity.

blocks.cap: To stir curiosity is to pique it.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Reading passages love arguments: a scientist defends a theory, a critic attacks a book, two historians disagree. To follow them you need words that rate an argument, from rock-solid to falling apart.

Strong: cogent (clear and convincing), trenchant (sharp and to the point), valid (logically sound), and three that mean no one can knock it down: irrefutable, incontrovertible, unassailable. Weak: tenuous (thin, slight), flimsy (easily broken), untenable (impossible to defend). And moot: open to debate, or no longer worth debating.
Look inside the long ones. Irrefutable is not able to be refuted; incontrovertible is not able to be turned against (contra + vert); untenable is not able to be held (ten, hold).

entry.def: clear, logical and convincing
entry.ex: Rosa made a {cogent} case for a longer lunch break, complete with charts.
entry.ctx: The lawyer’s argument was {cogent}: each point followed clearly from the last, and by the end even the doubtful jurors were nodding.
entry.etym: From Latin cogens, “compelling,” from cogere (to drive together): co- (together) + agere (to drive).

mn.text: In Ada’s argument every point fits the next like the cogs of a clock, so the whole thing turns smoothly: it is {cogent}.

scene.alt: A scientist points proudly at three gears that fit together perfectly.

entry.def: sharp, clear and forceful, cutting straight to the point
entry.ex: The coach’s {trenchant} comments at halftime showed the team exactly what was going wrong.
entry.ctx: Unlike the other reviewers, who praised the film vaguely, Ms. Lin wrote a {trenchant} critique that named its three biggest flaws in plain, sharp words.
entry.etym: From Old French trenchant, “cutting,” from trenchier (to cut), the same source as trench.

mn.cue: the TRENCH COAT detective: sharp and clear
mn.text: The detective in the trench coat sums up the case in one sharp, clear line: “The cake thief has frosting on his sleeve.” Her remark is {trenchant}.

scene.alt: A detective in a trench coat points her magnifying glass at a startled cake thief.

entry.def: logically correct or well grounded; also, officially accepted
entry.ex: Your library card is {valid} for one more year.
entry.ctx: The argument is {valid}, since its conclusion follows from its premises, but it is still wrong, because one of those premises is false.
entry.etym: From Latin validus, “strong,” from valere (to be strong).

mn.cue: VAL + ID: Val’s ID is accepted
mn.text: At the gate, Val shows her ID; it is real and up to date, so the guard waves her through. Her ID is {valid}.

scene.alt: A woman named Val shows her ID at a station gate, and the guard waves her through.

entry.def: impossible to prove wrong
entry.ex: The video replay was {irrefutable} proof that the ball crossed the line.
entry.ctx: Scientists once doubted that the continents move, but measurements from satellites now offer {irrefutable} evidence that they drift a few centimeters every year.
entry.etym: From in- (not) + refutable, from Latin refutare (to push back, prove wrong).

mn.text: Pip says he didn’t eat the cookies, but crumbs cover his face and his hand is still in the jar: the proof is {irrefutable}.

scene.alt: A boy with cookie crumbs all over his face insists it was not him, while his mother points.

entry.def: so certain that no one can dispute it
entry.ex: The photo finish was {incontrovertible}: the blue runner won by an inch.
entry.ctx: Historians had argued for years about when the old bridge was built, but the builder’s signed and dated plans, found in an attic, were {incontrovertible}.
entry.etym: From in- (not) + controvertible, from Latin controversus (turned against, disputed): contra (against) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: Sven and Tia argue over whose watermelon is heavier until the scale settles it: no controversy now. The answer is {incontrovertible}.

scene.alt: Two farmers stop arguing when a scale shows which watermelon is heavier.

entry.def: too strong to be attacked or questioned
entry.ex: With a twenty-point lead and two minutes left, the team’s position looked {unassailable}.
entry.ctx: Her reputation for honesty was {unassailable}; in forty years of running the store, she had never once shortchanged a customer.
entry.etym: From un- (not) + assailable, from assail (to attack), from Latin ad- (at) + salire (to leap).

mn.cue: un-a-SAIL-able: no ship can SAIL in
mn.text: The pirates sail at the island fort again and again, but its walls never give way: the fort is {unassailable}.

scene.alt: A pirate ship turns back from a strong fort high on a rocky island.

entry.def: very weak, thin or slight
entry.ex: The kitten kept a {tenuous} grip on the top of the curtain.
entry.ctx: The link between the two thefts was {tenuous}, resting only on the fact that both happened on a Tuesday, so the detective kept looking for stronger evidence.
entry.etym: From Latin tenuis, “thin.”

mn.text: The tent is held up by one thin, wobbly pole, and the next breeze could knock it down: its hold is {tenuous}.

scene.alt: A boy watches nervously as his tent leans in the wind, barely standing.

entry.def: weak and easily broken; also, hard to believe
entry.ex: The {flimsy} umbrella turned inside out at the first gust of wind.
entry.ctx: His excuse was {flimsy}: he said he missed practice because his shoelaces were untied, and no one believed him for a second.

mn.text: Kai’s kite is made of film-thin paper and two twigs, and the first gust rips it in half: it is {flimsy}.

scene.alt: A boy watches his thin paper kite tear apart in the wind.

entry.def: impossible to defend, keep or hold on to
entry.ex: With the river rising around the campsite, staying another night was {untenable}.
entry.ctx: Once an older map turned up, the claim that the village was founded in 1850 became {untenable}, because the map, dated 1820, already showed the village.
entry.etym: From un- (not) + tenable, from French tenir (to hold), from Latin tenere.

mn.cue: un-TEN-able: TEN = hold, so it can’t be HELD
mn.text: The sun is melting the snow fort, and Pip and Zoe can’t hold it much longer: their position is {untenable}.

scene.alt: Two children watch their snow fort melt in the sun, unable to save it.

entry.def: open to debate; also, no longer worth arguing about
entry.ex: Whether to hold the picnic indoors became {moot} when the rain stopped.
entry.ctx: The class argued for an hour about which bus to take on the field trip, but the question was {moot}: the trip had already been canceled because of the storm.
entry.etym: From Old English mot, a meeting where people gathered to debate questions.
entry.note: Moot first meant open to debate (a moot point); in American English it now often means no longer worth arguing about. Let the sentence decide. In law school, a moot court is a practice trial.

mn.cue: MOOT = MUTE: nothing left to argue
mn.text: Pip and Zoe argue over who gets the last cookie, until they see the dog already ate it. The argument goes mute: the question is {moot}.

scene.alt: Two children stop arguing over a cookie when they see the dog has already eaten it.

blocks.html: moot has two senses: open to debate (a moot point) and, in common American use, no longer mattering. In logic, valid describes reasoning that holds, whether or not its premises are true.

blocks.cap: A strong case and a weak one.

blocks.html: In logic, valid describes the shape of reasoning, not the truth of the facts. “All cats can fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom can fly” is valid (the conclusion follows) but not true, because the first premise is false. An argument that is valid and has true premises is called sound.

blocks.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The theory was {untenable}: every new experiment contradicted it.

blocks.cap: A theory that can no longer be defended is untenable.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: History, science and stories are full of order: what came first, what followed, what was coming next. This topic gathers the words that put things in time, and most of them are built from four Latin parts you can spot at a glance.

pre- and ante- = before (preliminary, predecessor, precursor, prescient, antecedent). post- = after (posterity, posthumous). sequ = follow (subsequent), and ced/cess = go (predecessor, successor, antecedent). The odd one out is harbinger, an old English word for someone sent ahead.

Two pairs are worth keeping straight: a predecessor held the job before you, and a successor holds it after you; something preliminary comes before the main event, and something subsequent comes after.

entry.def: coming before the main part, to prepare for it
entry.ex: The {preliminary} round of the spelling bee weeded out half the contestants.
entry.ctx: Before building the full bridge, the engineers ran {preliminary} tests on a small model to see how it would handle strong wind.
entry.etym: From Latin prae- (before) + limen (threshold): what comes before you step through the door.

mn.text: Before the big race, Dev stretches every limb, one by one: these are his {preliminary} exercises.

scene.alt: A runner in a headband stretches his arms before a race.

entry.def: coming after; following
entry.ex: The first storm knocked down a tree, and {subsequent} storms finished off the fence.
entry.ctx: Her first cake sank in the middle, but {subsequent} attempts, made after she fixed the oven temperature, rose perfectly.
entry.etym: From Latin subsequi, “to follow close after”: sub- (close to) + sequi (to follow).

mn.text: A sequel is the story that comes after the first one. Pip and Lila can’t wait for Part 2, due out the {subsequent} summer.

scene.alt: Two children cheer at a banner announcing Part 2 of a movie.

entry.def: a person who held a job or role before someone else
entry.ex: The new coach kept many of the drills from her {predecessor}.
entry.ctx: Unlike his {predecessor}, who rarely left the office, the new principal visited every classroom during his first week.
entry.etym: From Late Latin praedecessor: prae- (before) + decessor (one who has left an office), from decedere (to go away).

mn.cue: PRE-DESK-essor: at the DESK before you
mn.text: Edwin carries his box out the door, and Lin sits down at his old desk; the one who had the desk before her is her {predecessor}.

scene.alt: An old professor carries his box out of the office while a woman sits down at his old desk.

entry.def: a person or thing that follows another in a role or place
entry.ex: The old queen named her niece as her {successor}.
entry.ctx: The retiring baker trained Jamal for a full year so that her {successor} would know every recipe by heart when he took over the shop.
entry.etym: From Latin successor, from succedere (to come after): sub- (close after) + cedere (to go).

mn.text: In the relay, Dev hands the torch to Maya, who runs the next stretch: Maya is his {successor}.

scene.alt: A runner hands a torch to the next runner, who takes off.

entry.def: something that comes before and leads to something else
entry.ex: The old telegraph was an {antecedent} of today’s text message.
entry.ctx: In the sentence “Maya lost her scarf,” the {antecedent} of the pronoun her is Maya, the word that comes before it and that it points back to.

roots.means: being or doing (a noun or adjective ending)

entry.etym: From Latin antecedere, “to go before”: ante- (before) + cedere (to go).
entry.note: In grammar, the antecedent is the word a pronoun stands for.

mn.cue: the ANT-ecedent: the ANT that goes BEFORE
mn.text: The first ant marches ahead, and all the others follow behind it; the one that goes before is the {antecedent}.

scene.alt: A line of ants marches along, led by the first ant.

entry.def: something that came earlier and led the way to a later thing
entry.ex: The abacus was a {precursor} of the calculator.
entry.ctx: Long before the first airplane, the glider was its {precursor}, proving that a person could ride the air on fixed wings.
entry.etym: From Latin praecursor, “forerunner”: prae- (before) + currere (to run).

mn.text: Long before cars, horse-drawn carts rumbled down the roads; the cart ran ahead of the car in history. It was a {precursor}.

scene.alt: A horse-drawn cart on one side and a car on the other, with an arrow from the cart to the car.

entry.def: a sign or messenger of what is coming
entry.ex: The first crocus poking through the snow is a {harbinger} of spring.
entry.ctx: The sudden silence of the birds was a {harbinger} of the storm; within minutes, the sky turned dark and the rain began.
entry.etym: From Middle English herbergere, a person sent ahead to find lodgings for travelers.

mn.cue: HARK! A sign of what’s coming
mn.text: “Hark! Spring is on its way!” says the first butterfly over the melting snow; it is a {harbinger} of spring.

scene.alt: A butterfly flutters over the melting snow where the first flowers are coming up.

entry.def: knowing or sensing what will happen before it does
entry.ex: Her {prescient} warning about the leaky roof saved our books from the rain.
entry.ctx: Grandpa’s advice that everyone should learn to type seemed odd in 1975, but it proved {prescient}; within twenty years, nearly every office job required a keyboard.
entry.etym: From Latin praescire, “to know beforehand”: prae- (before) + scire (to know).

mn.text: On a cloudless morning, Granny Mae packs an umbrella; by noon it pours, and she is the only one dry. She was {prescient}.

scene.alt: A grandmother stays dry under her umbrella while a teen beside her is caught in the sudden rain.

entry.def: all the people of the future; later generations
entry.ex: Mom recorded Grandpa’s stories for {posterity}.
entry.ctx: The museum carefully preserves the old letters, not only for today’s visitors but for {posterity}, so that people a hundred years from now can read them too.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin posteritas, from posterus (coming after), from post (after).

mn.cue: a POSTER for the FUTURE: POSTER-ity
mn.text: The class seals a poster in a time capsule for the children of a hundred years from now: they are saving it for {posterity}.

scene.alt: Two children bury a time capsule holding a poster addressed to the future.

entry.def: happening or given after a person’s death
entry.ex: The poet’s best-known book was a {posthumous} collection, printed after she died.
entry.ctx: The painter sold only one picture in her lifetime; her fame was {posthumous}, growing only after her death, when museums began to collect her work.
entry.etym: From Latin postumus, “last, born after the father’s death”; the h was added later by people who linked it with humus (earth).
entry.note: Say POS-chuh-mus: the h is silent.

mn.cue: POST = after: praise that comes AFTER a life
mn.text: Great-Grandma Rose painted all her life, but her pictures won prizes only after she had passed away: her fame was {posthumous}.

scene.alt: A grandmother and a girl admire a prize-winning painting in a museum.

blocks.html: posthumous is pronounced POS-chuh-mus: the h is silent. prescient means foreseeing; it has nothing to do with "present."

blocks.html: prescient has nothing to do with present. It is pre- (before) + sci (know), the same sci as in science: a prescient person knows before. And posthumous is said POS-chuh-mus; the h is silent.

opts.s: The new mayor praised her {predecessor} for leaving the town’s budget in good shape.

blocks.cap: The one who held the job before her is her predecessor.

blocks.html: There are many ways to stop something. You can scare it off before it starts, talk someone out of it, hold it in check, cut it short, press it down or crush it flat. Each word in this topic names one of those ways.

Before it starts: deter (discourage, often by fear), dissuade (talk out of). Keeping it in check: curb (restrain), curtail (cut short). Pressing it down: repress, suppress, stifle. Crushing it: quash, squelch. Stopping a flow: stanch.
Three of these words share a Latin verb, premere, to press: re-press (press back), sup-press (press under) and, in a roundabout way, the everyday press itself.

entry.def: to discourage someone from acting, often through fear of what might happen
entry.ex: The barking dog {deters} anyone from climbing over the fence.
entry.ctx: The town hoped bright new streetlights would {deter} vandals, since people are less likely to cause trouble where they can easily be seen.
entry.etym: From Latin deterrere, “to frighten away”: de- (away) + terrere (to frighten).

mn.text: Felix dresses up as a scarecrow, and the crows flap off in terror; the scary sight {deters} them from the corn.

scene.alt: A man dressed as a scarecrow shouts “Boo!” and two crows fly away in fright.

entry.def: to talk someone out of doing something
entry.ex: Nothing could {dissuade} Maya from trying out for the team.
entry.ctx: Jonah planned to hike the trail alone after dark, but his sister {dissuaded} him by pointing out the steep cliffs and the lack of cell service.
entry.etym: From Latin dissuadere: dis- (away) + suadere (to urge).

mn.text: Dev wants to paint his room neon orange, but Dad talks him out of it: Dad {dissuades} him.

labels.text: DIS-SUADE: talk him OUT of it

scene.alt: A teen holds up a paintbrush over a bucket of orange paint while his father waves his hands, talking him out of it.

entry.def: to hold back or keep under control
entry.ex: The library posted a new rule to {curb} noise after six o’clock.
entry.ctx: To {curb} her spending, Lin left her credit card at home and carried only enough cash for the groceries on her list.
entry.etym: From French courbe, “curved,” first the curved strap or chain on a horse’s bit that holds the horse in check.

mn.text: Pip wants to dash after his ball, but Mom holds him back at the curb until the cars pass: she {curbs} his rush.

scene.alt: A mother holds her son back at the curb while a car passes and his ball sits in the street.

entry.def: to cut short or cut back
entry.ex: Rain {curtailed} the game after only three innings.
entry.ctx: Because the bridge was closed for repairs, the bus company had to {curtail} its route, ending at the river instead of crossing into town.
entry.etym: From an old word, curtal, “with a docked tail,” from French court (short); the spelling was later shaped by tail.

mn.text: Ten minutes into the picnic, a storm rolls in and snips the afternoon short like a tail: the rain {curtails} the picnic.

scene.alt: A storm cloud cuts a riverside picnic short as a man and a girl hurry to pack up.

entry.def: to hold back or keep down, especially a feeling
entry.ex: Dev had to {repress} a laugh when the principal’s microphone squeaked.
entry.ctx: For years she {repressed} her wish to become an artist, hiding her sketchbooks in a drawer, until a teacher saw them and urged her to apply to art school.
entry.etym: From Latin reprimere, “to press back”: re- (back) + premere (to press).

mn.text: Kai’s block tower crashes, and he feels the anger rising, but he presses it back down and takes a slow breath: he {represses} it.

scene.alt: A boy whose block tower has fallen holds his anger in, steaming but saying he is fine.

entry.def: to put down by force; to keep from being seen or known
entry.ex: The firefighters worked all night to {suppress} the brush fire.
entry.ctx: The company tried to {suppress} the report about its faulty toasters, but a worker shared it, and soon every customer knew.
entry.etym: From Latin supprimere, “to press under”: sub- (under) + premere (to press).

mn.text: Omar pours bucket after bucket until the campfire is pressed down to nothing: he {suppresses} the flames.

scene.alt: A man in a helmet pours a bucket of water on a campfire, putting it out.

entry.def: to hold back, as a yawn or a laugh; also, to smother
entry.ex: Grandpa {stifled} a yawn during the long speech.
entry.ctx: Too many strict rules can {stifle} creativity; when every drawing has to look the same, students stop trying new ideas.

mn.cue: a STIFF hand: STIF-le the yawn
mn.text: In the middle of the long concert, Professor Edwin clamps a stiff hand over his mouth to hold in a giant yawn: he {stifles} it.

scene.alt: An old professor presses a hand over his mouth to hold in a yawn while a violinist plays.

entry.def: to put a complete stop to; to cancel officially
entry.ex: The coach {quashed} the rumor that the team was moving to another city.
entry.ctx: The higher court {quashed} the earlier ruling, declaring it invalid, so the case had to be heard again from the very beginning.

mn.text: The judge brings her gavel down on the unfair rule and squashes it flat: she {quashes} it.

scene.alt: A judge raises her gavel to squash an unfair rule.

entry.def: to crush or silence completely
entry.ex: Mom {squelched} our plan to build a ramp off the garage roof.
entry.ctx: The manager’s harsh reply {squelched} any further questions; after that, no one at the meeting dared to raise a hand.

mn.cue: SQUELCH! like a boot in the mud
mn.text: Rex starts a silly rumor, and Lin stomps on it at once, squelch, like a boot in deep mud: she {squelches} it.

scene.alt: A woman stomps a rumor into the mud while the man who started it looks shocked.

entry.def: to stop the flow of a liquid
entry.ex: The plumber hurried to {stanch} the flood from the broken pipe.
entry.ctx: Volunteers piled sandbags along the riverbank to {stanch} the water pouring over the low wall, and by morning the flow had stopped.
entry.etym: From Old French estanchier, “to stop the flow of.”
entry.note: Also spelled staunch. As an adjective, staunch means loyal and firm: a staunch friend.

mn.text: Water gushes from a hole in the rain barrel, and Sven slaps his hand over it to stop the flow: he {stanches} the leak.

scene.alt: A big man presses his hand over a hole in a leaking barrel to stop the water.

blocks.html: dissuade is the opposite of persuade. stanch (stop a flow) is also spelled staunch, which also means loyal.

opts.s: Her friends tried to {dissuade} her from quitting the band, reminding her how much she loved the drums.

blocks.cap: Talking someone out of something is dissuading.

blocks.html: Every contest, court case and news story raises the same question: is the judgment fair? This topic gives you the words for a fair judge and for the things that spoil fairness, from a small leaning to a sour, suspicious eye.

Fair: impartial (takes no side), disinterested (has nothing to gain), objective (sticks to facts), equitable (fair to all), dispassionate (calm, not swayed by feelings). Unfair or shaky: subjective (based on personal taste), bias (a leaning), prejudice (judging before knowing), arbitrary (based on whim), jaundiced (soured by bitterness).
Watch for one famous trap: disinterested does not mean bored. It means having no personal stake, which is exactly what you want in a referee.

entry.def: treating all sides equally; not taking sides
entry.ex: A good referee stays {impartial}, even when her hometown team is playing.
entry.ctx: Because the judge had never met either family, she could be {impartial}, weighing only the facts each side presented.
entry.etym: From im- (not) + partial, “favoring one part or side.”

mn.cue: IM-PARTIAL: not PARTIAL to either side
mn.text: Nana Lou judges the pie contest wearing a blindfold, so she can’t favor her own grandson’s pie: she is {impartial}.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a blindfold tastes two pies while two children wait nervously.

entry.def: having nothing to gain or lose, and so able to judge fairly
entry.ex: We asked a {disinterested} neighbor to settle the argument, since she had no stake in it.
entry.ctx: The two bakeries agreed to let a {disinterested} expert choose the best bread; because she would earn nothing either way, both trusted her verdict.
entry.etym: From dis- (not) + interested, in its old sense of “having a stake or a share.”
entry.note: Careful: disinterested is not uninterested (bored). Many people now use it to mean bored, but careful writers and test makers keep the two apart. A disinterested judge is a fair one.

mn.cue: no INTEREST (no stake) in who wins
mn.text: Professor Edwin judges the pet show because he owns no pets: he gains nothing whoever wins. He is {disinterested}.

scene.alt: An old professor with no pets of his own judges a dog and a cat at a pet show.

entry.def: based on facts rather than personal feelings
entry.ex: A thermometer gives an {objective} reading of the temperature.
entry.ctx: Reviewers argue about whether the movie is good, but its length is an {objective} fact: it runs exactly two hours and ten minutes.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin objectivus, from objectum, “a thing put before the mind”: ob- (before) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: Dev and Jonah argue about whose fish is bigger, so Ada simply measures each one with a ruler: the answer is {objective}.

scene.alt: A woman settles an argument by measuring a fish with a ruler.

entry.def: based on personal feelings, tastes or opinions
entry.ex: Whether a song is beautiful is partly a {subjective} question.
entry.ctx: The judges tried to follow clear rules, but scoring a painting is partly {subjective}: one judge loved its bold colors while another found them far too loud.
entry.etym: From Latin subjectivus, from subicere (to place under): sub- (under) + jacere (to throw).

mn.cue: depends on the SUBJECT: the person
mn.text: Sami tastes the soup and gasps “Too spicy!”; Tia tastes the same soup and says “Not spicy enough!” Spiciness here is {subjective}.

scene.alt: Two people taste the same soup; one finds it far too spicy and the other too mild.

entry.def: a leaning for or against someone that gets in the way of fair judgment
entry.ex: The coach admitted a {bias} toward players who showed up early.
entry.ctx: Because the reviewer’s brother had made the film, readers suspected {bias} in her glowing review rather than fair judgment.
entry.etym: From French biais, “slant, sideways.”

mn.cue: BY US: he always picks ours
mn.text: In the art contest, Grandpa always picks the drawings made by us, his grandkids, whatever they look like: that is {bias}.

labels.text: BY US: he picks his own

scene.alt: A grandfather picks his grandson’s scribble as the winner while a girl with a fine painting looks sad.

entry.def: an opinion formed before knowing the facts, usually an unfair one
entry.ex: Lila tried to read the new book without {prejudice}, even though she had disliked the author’s first one.
entry.ctx: The coach admitted his {prejudice} against short players, formed before he had seen them play, until a five-foot guard led the team in steals.
entry.etym: From Latin praejudicium, “a judgment in advance”: prae- (before) + judicium (judgment).

mn.text: Dev decides he hates mushrooms before he has tasted a single bite: “Yuck!” He is judging ahead of time, out of {prejudice}.

scene.alt: A teen crosses his arms and says “Yuck!” at a plate of mushrooms he has never tasted.

entry.def: based on whim or chance rather than on reason
entry.ex: The order of the names on the list was {arbitrary}; it meant nothing at all.
entry.ctx: Students complained that the new dress code was {arbitrary}: no one could explain why green socks were allowed but blue ones were not.
entry.etym: From Latin arbitrarius, “depending on a judge’s choice,” from arbiter (judge).

mn.cue: the king rolls the dice: no reason at all
mn.text: King Victor rolls dice to decide each new rule: “Tuesday: no hats!” His rules are {arbitrary}.

scene.alt: A king tosses dice to make up a silly rule while a man in a hat scratches his head.

entry.def: fair and just to everyone involved
entry.ex: The sisters worked out an {equitable} plan for sharing the bike.
entry.ctx: The new carpool schedule was more {equitable} than the old one; instead of the same two families always driving, every family took a turn.
entry.etym: From French équitable, from équité (fairness), from Latin aequitas, from aequus (equal, fair).

mn.cue: EQUI-TABLE: EQUAL shares at the TABLE
mn.text: Nell cuts the pizza into equal slices so everyone at the table gets the same: her way of sharing is {equitable}.

scene.alt: A woman shares a pizza in equal slices among the children at the table.

entry.def: calm and fair; not swayed by strong feelings
entry.ex: The scientist gave a {dispassionate} report of the results, neither cheering nor complaining.
entry.ctx: While the fans screamed and argued, the referee remained {dispassionate}, calmly reviewing the replay before making her call.

mn.cue: DIS-PASSION: no PASSION, just a calm call
mn.text: The fans shout and stamp, but the referee calmly checks the line and makes her call: she is {dispassionate}.

scene.alt: A calm referee makes a call while one fan rages and another cheers.

entry.def: soured by bitterness, envy or distrust
entry.ex: After losing money once, Uncle Victor took a {jaundiced} view of every bargain.
entry.ctx: Years of broken promises had given the villagers a {jaundiced} view of the bridge plan; they assumed it would never be finished, whatever the builders said.
entry.etym: From jaundice, an illness that yellows the skin; people once believed it made everything look yellow to the sufferer, so a jaundiced eye sees the world in a sour light.

mn.text: Ivy offers Uncle Victor a free cookie, but he squints through his old yellow glasses: “What’s the catch?” His view of everything is {jaundiced}.

scene.alt: A girl offers a free cookie, and a man in yellowish goggles crosses his arms, suspicious.

blocks.html: disinterested means impartial (having nothing to gain), not uninterested (bored). A disinterested judge is a good thing.

head: fair
unfair or shaky
rows: bias: a leaning toward one side
blocks.cap: A fair judge and the things that get in the way.

blocks.html: disinterested = having no personal stake, so fair. uninterested = not interested, bored. “The disinterested judge listened closely” is high praise; “the uninterested judge yawned” is not.
Subjective is not always bad. Taste in music is subjective, and that is fine. It becomes a problem only when a judgment that should rest on facts rests on feelings instead.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: English has a whole toolbox of words for how hard something is, and each tool does a different job. A climb can be arduous, a duty onerous, a copying job laborious, a race grueling. A rival can be formidable, a box cumbersome, a ladder precarious. And some tasks are hopeless (futile) or much too easy (facile).

Hard work: arduous (steep, demanding), onerous (a heavy burden), laborious (slow and painstaking), grueling (exhausting). Hard to face or handle: formidable, cumbersome, precarious. No use: futile. Easy: effortless (praise) and facile (usually blame).
The Latin inside helps: arduus meant steep, onus a load, labor work, formido fear, and facilis easy.

entry.def: needing great effort; hard and tiring
entry.ex: The {arduous} climb took six hours, almost all of it uphill.
entry.ctx: Restoring the old ship was {arduous}: volunteers spent four winters scraping, sanding and replacing every rotten plank by hand.
entry.etym: From Latin arduus, “steep, high, difficult.”

mn.text: The trail rises like a wall, and Tia and Marcus puff up it one step at a time: the climb is {arduous}.

scene.alt: Two sweating hikers with backpacks trudge up a steep mountain trail.

entry.def: heavy and troublesome, like a burden
entry.ex: Caring for twelve goats turned out to be an {onerous} chore.
entry.ctx: The new rules were so {onerous} that small shops could barely follow them; each one demanded hours of extra paperwork every week.
entry.etym: From Latin onerosus, from onus (load, burden).
entry.note: Onerous has nothing to do with honor; think of onus, a load.

mn.text: Every box in the move lands on us: Sven staggers along under a tower of them. The job is {onerous}.

scene.alt: A big man staggers under a tall stack of heavy boxes.

entry.def: needing a lot of slow, careful work
entry.ex: Copying the old recipe book by hand was a {laborious} job.
entry.ctx: Before computers, making a dictionary was {laborious}; editors wrote each definition on a paper slip and sorted millions of slips by hand.
entry.etym: From Latin laboriosus, from labor (work, toil).

mn.text: Felix copies the whole thick book by hand with a feather pen, one slow letter at a time: the work is {laborious}.

scene.alt: A tired man copies a thick book by hand with a feather pen.

entry.def: extremely tiring and demanding
entry.ex: After a {grueling} practice in the heat, the team flopped onto the grass.
entry.ctx: The race was {grueling}: fifty miles over rocky trails, through rain and wind, with only two short stops for food.

mn.cue: too tired for anything but GRUEL
mn.text: After hiking up and down three mountains, Jonah is too tired to eat anything but a bowl of mush, called gruel: the hike was {grueling}.

scene.alt: An exhausted teen slumps by a campfire with a bowl of mush after a long hike.

entry.def: inspiring fear or respect through size, strength or difficulty
entry.ex: The chess champion was a {formidable} opponent.
entry.ctx: With its steep walls, deep moat and towering gate, the castle presented a {formidable} obstacle to anyone hoping to get inside.
entry.etym: From Latin formidabilis, from formidare (to fear), from formido (fear).

mn.cue: FORM-idable: a FORM so big you fear it
mn.text: The dragon guarding the gate is huge, fast and clever, and even brave Maya takes a deep breath: it is a {formidable} foe.

scene.alt: A girl in a helmet holds up a shield before a huge, smoking dragon guarding a castle.

entry.def: large and awkward to carry or use; also, slow and complicated
entry.ex: The {cumbersome} old suitcase had no wheels and kept banging into my knees.
entry.ctx: The sign-up process was {cumbersome}: families had to fill out four forms, mail them separately and then call to confirm each one.

mn.text: Pip tries to carry a huge piece of lumber home by himself, but it is so long and heavy that he can barely shuffle: it is {cumbersome}.

scene.alt: A boy staggers while carrying a huge, awkward log.

entry.def: unsteady and likely to fall or fail
entry.ex: The cat sat in a {precarious} spot on the very edge of the shelf.
entry.ctx: After the storm washed away half the trail, the hikers’ path along the cliff became {precarious}, with loose rocks sliding at every step.
entry.etym: From Latin precarius, “got by begging, uncertain,” from precari (to pray, beg): what you hold only by someone’s favor can be taken away at any moment.

mn.text: Dev carries a wobbling tower of twelve plates across the kitchen. Take care! It could crash at any moment: the stack is {precarious}.

scene.alt: A teen carries a tall, wobbling tower of plates that looks ready to fall.

entry.def: useless; having no chance of success
entry.ex: Trying to stay dry in that storm was {futile}.
entry.ctx: Every attempt to fix the old radio proved {futile}; no matter which part they replaced, it still made nothing but static.
entry.etym: From Latin futilis, “leaky,” and so “worthless.”

mn.cue: FUTILE = leaky: filling a bucket full of holes
mn.text: Grandpa Gus keeps pouring water into a bucket full of holes, and it runs out as fast as it goes in: his effort is {futile}.

scene.alt: A grandfather pours water into a bucket that leaks it all out again.

entry.def: too simple to be useful; shallow and easy
entry.ex: The essay offered a {facile} answer to a hard question.
entry.ctx: Her critics called the plan {facile}: it promised to fix the city’s traffic jams simply by painting new lines, ignoring every deeper problem.
entry.etym: From Latin facilis, “easy to do,” from facere (to do).
entry.note: Facile can also mean done with ease (a facile writer), but it is most often a criticism.

mn.text: Asked how to save the old theater, Rex says, “Just tell people to come!”, as if it were that simple. His answer is {facile}.

scene.alt: At a meeting, a man offers an oversimple answer while two others facepalm and frown.

entry.def: needing, or seeming to need, no effort at all
entry.ex: The dancer made the high leap look {effortless}.
entry.ctx: After years of practice, Maya’s piano playing seemed {effortless}, though anyone who had heard her first lessons knew how hard she had worked.

mn.text: Pip puffs halfway up the ladder, but the cat springs straight onto the top shelf in one smooth leap: for her it is {effortless}.

scene.alt: A boy struggles up a ladder while a cat leaps easily to the top of a bookshelf.

blocks.html: facile is usually a criticism (a facile answer), not praise. onerous means burdensome; it has nothing to do with honor.

what makes it hard
picture it
blocks.cap: Seven kinds of hard.

blocks.html: facile sounds like praise (it shares a root with facility, ease), but it is usually a criticism: a facile answer is too easy to be any good. If you mean easy in a good way, choose effortless. And onerous (a burden, from onus) has nothing to do with honor.

blocks.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The skater’s spins looked {effortless}, though she had practiced them every morning for six years.

blocks.cap: Easy in a good way, graceful: effortless.
