blocks.html: Three Greek parts build all ten words in this topic. path means feeling (or suffering), phil means love, and anthrop means human being. Add a prefix or a second part and you can read the word like a tiny sentence: phil + anthrop is “loves people,” and mis + anthrop is “hates people.”

path = feeling: apathy (a- = without: no feeling), empathy (em- = in: feeling with someone), antipathy (anti- = against: a feeling against), pathos (what stirs feeling), telepathy (tele- = far: feeling across a distance). phil = love: philanthropist, bibliophile. anthrop = human: philanthropist, misanthrope, anthropology, anthropomorphic.
Once you know these parts you can guess dozens of other words: sympathy, philosophy (love of wisdom), philharmonic (love of harmony), anthropoid (humanlike).

entry.def: lack of interest, feeling or concern
entry.ex: The team’s {apathy} was plain: no one even came to the last practice.
entry.ctx: The club failed not because anyone opposed it but because of {apathy}; hardly anyone cared enough to come to meetings or to vote.
entry.etym: From Greek apatheia, “freedom from feeling”: a- (without) + pathos (feeling).

mn.text: The class garden is wilting in the sun, but everyone just shrugs and walks past: nobody cares. That is {apathy}.

scene.alt: Two bored teens shrug and walk past drooping flowers that no one waters.

entry.def: the ability to understand and share another person’s feelings
entry.ex: Thanks to his {empathy}, Sami always knew when a friend needed cheering up.
entry.ctx: Instead of laughing when Kai dropped his lunch tray, Rosa showed {empathy}: she remembered how embarrassed she had felt last year and quietly helped him clean up.
entry.etym: From Greek em- (in) + pathos (feeling); English took the word up in the early 1900s.

mn.text: When Dev’s kite breaks, Lila feels his sadness as if it were her own and gives him a hug: she has {empathy}.

scene.alt: A girl hugs a crying boy whose kite lies broken on the grass.

entry.def: a strong, settled dislike
entry.ex: Grandpa’s {antipathy} toward loud music was no secret.
entry.ctx: Their {antipathy} began with a quarrel over a fence, and for twenty years the two neighbors refused even to say good morning to each other.
entry.etym: From Greek antipatheia: anti (against) + pathos (feeling).

mn.text: From the day they met, Whiskers the cat and Rufus the dog have glared and growled at each other: they share a deep {antipathy}.

scene.alt: A cat and a dog glare and growl at each other.

entry.def: a quality in a story, speech or scene that stirs pity or sadness
entry.ex: The movie’s last scene, with the old dog waiting by the door, is full of {pathos}.
entry.ctx: The speech was not clever or funny, but its {pathos} moved everyone; by the end, many listeners were quietly wiping their eyes.
entry.etym: From Greek pathos, “suffering, feeling.”

mn.text: In the school play, the lost puppy walks its lonely path home through the rain, and the audience reaches for tissues: the scene is full of {pathos}.

scene.alt: On a stage, a sad puppy walks under a rain cloud while audience members cry.

entry.def: the supposed sending of thoughts from one mind to another without words
entry.ex: The twins joked that they had {telepathy} because they always ordered the same sandwich.
entry.ctx: In the science-fiction novel, the two pilots talk by {telepathy}, sending thoughts silently across hundreds of miles without any radio.
entry.etym: Made up in English in the 1880s from Greek tele (far) + pathos (feeling).
entry.note: Telepathy is common in stories; there is no scientific evidence that it is real.

mn.text: Zoe is at one end of the town and Kai at the other, yet both suddenly think “Pizza!” at the same moment: they joke that it is {telepathy}.

scene.alt: Two children far apart think of the same pizza at the same moment.

entry.def: a person who gives money or time to help others
entry.ex: A local {philanthropist} paid for new books in every classroom.
entry.ctx: Though she had grown rich selling furniture, the {philanthropist} lived simply and gave most of her money to hospitals and schools.
entry.etym: From Greek philanthropos, “loving people”: philein (to love) + anthropos (human being).

mn.cue: PHIL loves ANTHROPOS: Phil loves people
mn.text: Phil loves people so much that he pays for a brand-new park where everyone in town can play: Phil is a {philanthropist}.

scene.alt: Children cheer a smiling man named Phil under a banner thanking him for a new playground.

entry.def: a person who loves books
entry.ex: The {bibliophile} had books stacked on every chair in his house.
entry.ctx: A true {bibliophile}, Granny Mae could not walk past a bookstore without going in, and she owned three copies of her favorite novel.
entry.etym: From French bibliophile, from Greek biblion (book) + philos (loving).

mn.text: Granny Mae hugs her newest book like an old friend, surrounded by towers of the ones she already loves: she is a {bibliophile}.

scene.alt: A grandmother hugs a book lovingly, surrounded by stacks of books.

entry.def: a person who dislikes people in general
entry.ex: The grumpy {misanthrope} in the story lives alone on a cliff and turns away every visitor.
entry.ctx: Though the old writer was called a {misanthrope} because he avoided parties and crowds, his letters show that he deeply loved a few close friends.
entry.etym: From Greek misanthropos, “hating people”: misein (to hate) + anthropos (human being).

mn.text: Rex lives alone at the top of the hill behind a sign that says GO AWAY, and he grumbles at every friendly visitor: he is a {misanthrope}.

scene.alt: A friendly neighbor waves with a pie, but a grump by his house and a GO AWAY sign just grumbles.

entry.def: the study of human beings and their ways of life
entry.ex: Maya plans to study {anthropology} to learn how people around the world celebrate the new year.
entry.ctx: Her work in {anthropology} took her to dozens of villages, where she recorded how families farmed, cooked, told stories and raised their children.
entry.etym: From Greek anthropos (human being) + -logia (study).

mn.cue: ANTHROPO + LOGY: the study of PEOPLE
mn.text: Ada spends a year in a mountain village, writing down how people cook, dance, farm and tell stories: she works in {anthropology}.

scene.alt: A woman takes notes as villagers dance and clap at a festival.

entry.def: giving human form or traits to animals or things
entry.ex: Fairy tales are full of {anthropomorphic} animals who talk and wear clothes.
entry.ctx: The cartoon gave the toaster {anthropomorphic} features, a smiling face and waving arms, so that it seemed like a cheerful friend.
entry.etym: From Greek anthropomorphos, “shaped like a human”: anthropos (human being) + morphe (form).

mn.text: In Lila’s picture book, the cat sits at the breakfast table, sips tea and says “Good morning!” just like a person: the cat is {anthropomorphic}.

scene.alt: A cat sits at the breakfast table with a cup of tea, saying good morning like a person.

blocks.html: empathy is feeling with someone, as if you were in their place. sympathy is feeling sorry for someone. You can sympathize with a friend whose team lost without sharing the feeling; empathy means you feel the loss too.

opts.s: The voters’ {apathy} was clear: only one person in ten showed up.

blocks.cap: Not caring at all is apathy; antipathy is a strong dislike.

blocks.html: Good sense comes in flavors. Some people are wise in the deep, slow way of long experience; some are quick and sharp; some are careful planners. And some, alas, are easy to fool or slow to catch on. This topic gives you a word for each.

Deep wisdom: sagacious, sage (a wise person). Sharp and practical: astute, shrewd, canny. Careful and sensible: judicious, prudent. Foolish: gullible (easily tricked), fatuous (smugly silly), obtuse (slow to understand).
Shrewd and canny can carry a hint of cleverness for one’s own benefit; judicious and prudent never do. They simply mean using good judgment.

entry.def: wise, with sound judgment drawn from experience
entry.ex: The {sagacious} old captain could read the coming weather in the clouds.
entry.ctx: Faced with a hard choice, the young queen turned to her most {sagacious} adviser, who had guided the kingdom wisely through forty years of trouble.
entry.etym: From Latin sagax, “keen, quick to notice,” first said of dogs with a sharp sense of smell.

mn.cue: SAGGY ears that know the way
mn.text: In the dry season, the old elephant with saggy, wrinkled ears leads the herd straight to the hidden water hole: she is {sagacious}.

scene.alt: A wise old elephant leads two young ones across the desert to a water hole.

entry.def: quick to see what matters and to use it well
entry.ex: An {astute} reader will notice the clue hidden in the first chapter.
entry.ctx: The {astute} shopkeeper noticed that umbrellas sold out on rainy mornings, so she began setting them by the door whenever rain was forecast.
entry.etym: From Latin astutus, “clever, crafty,” from astus (skill, cunning).

mn.cue: a STUDENT who spots it: a-STUTE
mn.text: The teacher’s riddle hides a trick, and Lila spots it in a second: “It’s a trick question!” She is {astute}.

scene.alt: A girl raises her hand, spotting the trick in the teacher’s riddle, while a classmate scratches his head.

entry.def: sharp and clever in practical matters
entry.ex: Grandma is a {shrewd} bargainer who never pays full price at the flea market.
entry.ctx: Selling lemonade at the top of the steep hill instead of at the bottom was a {shrewd} move: the tired hikers there would gladly pay for a cold drink.
entry.etym: From Middle English shrewe, “a nasty person,” the same word as the small animal; over time the meaning turned from nasty to sharp and clever.

mn.text: The little shrew sets up his lemonade stand at the top of the hill, right where the hikers are thirstiest: he is {shrewd}.

scene.alt: A clever little shrew sells cold drinks at the top of a hill to a hot, tired hiker.

entry.def: careful and shrewd, especially with money or business
entry.ex: The {canny} farmer sold her peaches in the city, where they fetched twice the price.
entry.ctx: A {canny} saver, Lou kept her money in three different places, so that no single mishap could ever wipe out everything she had.
entry.etym: From Scots, from can in its old sense of “to know how.”

mn.cue: she CAN’T lose it all: CAN-ny
mn.text: Nana Lou keeps her savings in three different piggy banks, so if one breaks, the rest are safe: she is {canny} with money.

scene.alt: A grandmother drops coins into three separate piggy banks.

entry.def: showing good, sensible judgment
entry.ex: A {judicious} pinch of salt turned the bland soup into a delicious one.
entry.ctx: The coach made {judicious} changes at halftime, resting her tired players and moving her fastest runner to defense, and the team held on to win.
entry.etym: From French judicieux, from Latin judicium (judgment).
entry.note: Judicious means wise in judgment, not quick to judge others.

mn.cue: JUDGE-icious: weigh it like a JUDGE
mn.text: Zoe weighs her choices like a fair judge before spending her birthday money, and picks the book she will read a hundred times: she is {judicious}.

scene.alt: A girl thinks carefully, weighing a book against a lollipop on a scale.

entry.def: careful and sensible, especially about the future
entry.ex: It is {prudent} to pack a flashlight before a camping trip.
entry.ctx: Rather than spend his whole paycheck, Jamal thought it {prudent} to save some for the winter, when work at the farm always slowed down.
entry.etym: From Latin prudens, a shortened form of providens, “seeing ahead.”

mn.cue: PRU-DENT: Pru’s car has no DENT
mn.text: Pru checks her mirrors, keeps her distance and slows down in the rain, so her old car has never had a single dent: she is {prudent}.

scene.alt: A careful driver named Pru stands proudly beside her shiny, dent-free old car.

entry.def: a very wise person, respected for good judgment
entry.ex: The village {sage} could settle any argument with a few calm words.
entry.ctx: Young players often sought out the old coach, a {sage} whose quiet advice had helped three generations of athletes.
entry.etym: From Old French sage, “wise,” from Latin sapere (to be wise).
entry.note: As an adjective, sage means wise: sage advice. The herb sage has a different origin.

mn.cue: the SAGE at the top: wise old head
mn.text: The children climb all the way up the hill to ask old Edwin their hardest question, because his answers are always wise: he is a {sage}.

scene.alt: A wise old man in a toga sits on a rock giving advice to two young listeners.

entry.def: easily fooled or tricked
entry.ex: The {gullible} tourist paid twenty dollars for a “solid gold” ring made of brass.
entry.ctx: Pip was so {gullible} that when his cousin told him the school had canceled Mondays, he stayed home and waited for Tuesday.
entry.etym: From gull, an old word meaning to trick, or a person who is easily tricked.

mn.text: Rex sells Pip a cone of “invisible ice cream” for two dollars, and Pip happily pays: he is {gullible}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man sells a boy an empty cone of “invisible ice cream,” and the boy happily pays.

entry.def: silly and pointless, in a smug way
entry.ex: The host kept making {fatuous} jokes about the weather that no one laughed at.
entry.ctx: Instead of answering the hard question, the speaker gave a {fatuous} reply about how everything would surely work out, smiling as though he had said something wise.
entry.etym: From Latin fatuus, “foolish.”

mn.cue: a smug grin and a silly idea
mn.text: Admiring himself in the mirror, Victor announces, “I am far too clever to need books!” His remark is {fatuous}: silly, and very pleased with itself.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat admires himself in a mirror and says something smug and silly.

entry.def: slow to understand or to notice
entry.ex: Sven was being {obtuse}; everyone else had guessed the surprise.
entry.ctx: Lila hinted a dozen times that she wanted to be left alone, but her brother was {obtuse} and kept asking her to play, never noticing her sighs.
entry.etym: From Latin obtusus, “blunt, dull,” from obtundere (to beat against, to blunt).
entry.note: In math, an obtuse angle is wider than a right angle: more than 90 degrees. Think blunt, not sharp.

mn.cue: an OBTUSE angle: blunt, not SHARP
mn.text: Everyone shouts “Surprise!” under a giant banner with Sven’s name on it, and he still asks whose birthday it is: he is being {obtuse}.

scene.alt: Under a birthday banner with his own name, a big man scratches his head and asks whose party it is.

blocks.html: judicious means wise in judgment, not "quick to judge others." obtuse (slow to understand) also names an angle over 90 degrees.

blocks.html: judicious means showing good judgment. It does not mean judging other people, and a judicious person is usually slow to criticize. obtuse also names an angle wider than 90 degrees: blunt, not sharp, which is a handy picture for a mind that is slow to catch on.

opts.s: It would be {prudent} to bring a jacket; the mountains get cold after dark.

blocks.cap: Careful planning for what might happen is prudent.

blocks.html: Writers need exact words for unkindness, so that readers can tell a sharp comment from a cruel one and a quiet snub from an open insult. This topic gives you those words. Knowing them helps you name what is happening, in a story or in real life, and choose better.

Making someone seem small: belittle, demean, denigrate. Words that look down: derogatory and pejorative (a word with a negative slant). Disapproving: deprecate. Kinds of insult: an affront (open), a slight (often quiet), an aspersion (an attack on someone’s good name). And invidious: likely to stir up envy or seem unfair.
Many of these begin with de-, meaning down: they push someone down. Pejorative comes from the Latin for worse, and aspersion from a verb meaning to sprinkle, as if splashing mud on a name.

entry.def: to make someone or something seem small or unimportant
entry.ex: Don’t {belittle} your little brother’s drawing; he worked hard on it.
entry.ctx: Rather than praise the team’s second-place finish, the coach chose to {belittle} it, calling it “just another loss” in front of the whole school.
entry.etym: First used in America in the 1780s: be- (make) + little.

mn.text: Rex sneers, “Baby stuff!” at Pip’s drawing, and Pip feels about two inches tall: Rex {belittles} it.

scene.alt: A sneering man points at a boy’s drawing, and the boy shrinks to a tiny size.

entry.def: to lower someone’s dignity or standing
entry.ex: The coach refused to {demean} his players by yelling insults at them.
entry.ctx: Forcing a worker to wear a sign reading “I was late” would {demean} anyone; the manager’s new rule was meant to embarrass, not to teach.

mn.text: Just to show who is boss, Victor makes the new worker scrub the whole floor with a toothbrush: the order is meant to {demean} him.

scene.alt: A smug boss points as a worker kneels to scrub the floor with a toothbrush.

entry.def: showing a low opinion; insulting
entry.ex: The referee warned the player to stop making {derogatory} comments about the other team.
entry.ctx: The review was not merely critical but {derogatory}; instead of discussing the book, it called the author lazy and foolish.
entry.etym: From Latin derogare, “to take away from, detract”: de- (away) + rogare (to ask).

mn.text: The rude frog croaks a nasty name at every snail that passes: “Slowpoke!” His remarks are {derogatory}.

scene.alt: A rude frog shouts “Slowpoke!” at a sad little snail.

entry.def: showing disapproval; giving a word a negative slant
entry.ex: “Cheap” is a {pejorative} way of saying “thrifty.”
entry.ctx: Calling the old car a “jalopy” is {pejorative}: the word makes the very same car sound shabby and worthless.
entry.etym: From Latin peior, “worse.”

mn.text: Lila calls the sniffing puppy “curious”; Aunt Greta calls it “nosy.” Same puppy, but nosy is the {pejorative} word: it makes things sound worse.

scene.alt: A girl calls a sniffing puppy curious while a grumpy woman calls it nosy.

entry.def: to criticize unfairly; to run down
entry.ex: It is unkind to {denigrate} other people’s work just to make your own look better.
entry.ctx: Instead of improving his own pies, the rival baker tried to {denigrate} hers, telling customers they were dry and stale, though they were nothing of the kind.

mn.text: Whatever the class paints, the jealous judge grades it down: “Ugly. Boring. F!” She {denigrates} their work.

scene.alt: A jealous judge holds up an F for a fine painting while the young painter looks hurt.

entry.def: to express disapproval of; also, to play down
entry.ex: The museum guide politely {deprecated} touching the paintings.
entry.ctx: Though Dev had scored the winning goal, he {deprecated} his own part in the game, insisting that his teammates had done all the hard work.
entry.etym: From Latin deprecari, “to pray against, to ward off”: de- (away) + precari (to pray).

mn.text: The cat sniffs the fancy new cushion, wrinkles her nose and stalks away: she {deprecates} it.

scene.alt: A cat turns up her nose at a new cushion and walks away.

entry.def: an open insult; something that offends
entry.ex: Arriving an hour late to his own party was an {affront} to his guests.
entry.ctx: The chef took the request for ketchup as an {affront}, since she had spent all day perfecting the sauce on that very dish.
entry.etym: From Old French afronter, “to strike in the face,” from Latin ad frontem (to the face).

mn.text: Right in front of everyone, Rex pushes away Nana Lou’s homemade pie and says, “Ew, no thanks!” It is an {affront}.

scene.alt: A man rudely refuses a grandmother’s homemade pie to her face, and she is shocked.

entry.def: an act that shows disrespect, often by ignoring or leaving someone out
entry.ex: Leaving Kai off the invitation list was a {slight} he never forgot.
entry.ctx: Grandma was hurt by the {slight}: everyone else at the table was served first, and no one even asked whether she wanted dessert.
entry.note: As an adjective, slight means small (a slight cold). The noun keeps the idea: a slight treats someone as small and unimportant.

mn.text: Ivy hands a party invitation to everyone in class except Kai; being left out on purpose makes him feel small. It is a {slight}.

labels.text: left OUT: made to feel SLIGHT

scene.alt: A girl hands out party invitations but skips one boy, who sits sadly alone.

entry.def: an attack on someone’s good name, usually unfair
entry.ex: Rex cast {aspersions} on Maya’s honesty without a shred of proof.
entry.ctx: The coach refused to cast {aspersions} on the referee; instead of blaming him for the loss, she said her team simply had not played well enough.
entry.etym: From Latin aspersio, “a sprinkling,” from aspergere (to sprinkle on): ad- (on) + spargere (to scatter).
entry.note: The word usually comes in the phrase cast aspersions on someone.

mn.cue: a-SPERS: SPRINKLING mud on a name
mn.text: Rex flicks muddy rumors at the poster with Maya’s name on it, splattering her good name: he casts {aspersions} on her.

scene.alt: A sneaky man flicks mud at a sign with a girl’s name on it while she watches sadly.

entry.def: likely to stir up envy or resentment; unfair
entry.ex: It is {invidious} to compare brothers’ report cards in front of the whole family.
entry.ctx: The principal refused to name a “best class,” saying such {invidious} rankings would only make the other classes feel resentful and unfairly judged.
entry.etym: From Latin invidiosus, “causing envy,” from invidia (envy), from invidere (to look at with envy).

mn.text: “Why can’t you be more like your sister?” Aunt Greta asks, pointing at Ivy’s trophy while Zoe looks on: the comparison is {invidious}.

scene.alt: A woman points at one girl’s trophy and tells the other girl to be more like her sister; the second girl looks hurt.

blocks.html: deprecate (disapprove) is often confused with depreciate (lose value). A slight can be quiet: leaving someone out on purpose is a slight even if nothing is said.

blocks.html: deprecate (disapprove of, play down) is often confused with depreciate (lose value). A car depreciates as it ages; a modest person deprecates her own success. A slight can also be quiet: leaving someone out on purpose is a slight even if nothing is said.

opts.s: “Stubborn” is the {pejorative} word; “determined” is the kind one.

blocks.cap: A word with a negative slant is pejorative.

blocks.html: Some speech is not just loud but angry, long and bitter. This topic gives you words for the kinds of angry speech, for the force behind them and for noise in general, from a crowd’s clamor to a band’s cacophony.

Angry speeches: a tirade (long and angry), a diatribe (a bitter attack), a harangue (a loud lecture). The words themselves: invective (abusive language), vitriolic (burning like acid). The force: vehement (intense), vociferous (loud about opinions), strident (harsh, grating). Noise: clamor (shouting), cacophony (clashing sounds).
Two Latin parts help: voc means voice (vociferous, vocal), and the Greek phon means sound (cacophony, telephone, symphony).

entry.def: a long, angry speech, often scolding someone
entry.ex: After the ball broke his window, the neighbor launched into a ten-minute {tirade} about careless children.
entry.ctx: Instead of calmly explaining the problem, the manager went on a {tirade}, shouting at the staff for half an hour about every mistake made that month.
entry.etym: From French tirade, “a long speech,” from Italian tirata (a pull, a volley), from tirare (to pull).

mn.cue: TIRE-ade: so long it TIRES you out
mn.text: Grandpa Gus rants about the ball in his tulips for so long that the children are worn out just listening: it is a {tirade}.

scene.alt: A grandfather rants on and on about a ball in his garden while two children grow sleepy.

entry.def: a bitter, sharply critical attack in speech or writing
entry.ex: His letter to the editor was a {diatribe} against the new parking rules.
entry.ctx: The review was less a careful critique than a {diatribe}: page after page of bitter attacks on the director, with hardly a word about the film itself.
entry.etym: From Greek diatribe, “a passing of time, a discussion,” from diatribein (to wear away): dia (through) + tribein (to rub).

mn.cue: DIA-TRIBE: words that RUB you raw
mn.text: The critic reads out his long, bitter scroll about the bakery: “Stale! Sour! Shameful!” His {diatribe} rubs poor Nell raw.

scene.alt: An angry critic reads a long, bitter attack on a bakery while the baker looks hurt.

entry.def: a long, loud lecture meant to scold or stir people up
entry.ex: The coach’s halftime {harangue} could be heard from the parking lot.
entry.ctx: Grandpa’s {harangue} about wasting electricity went on for twenty minutes, until everyone in the house had switched off every light they could find.
entry.etym: From French harangue, a speech to a crowd.

mn.cue: ha-RANG: it RANG in our ears
mn.text: Coach Ada lectures the team at the top of her lungs for twenty minutes, and her words rang in their ears all night: a real {harangue}.

labels.text: ha-RANG: it RANG in our ears

scene.alt: A fierce coach shouts a long lecture at two players, who cover their ears.

entry.def: insulting, abusive language
entry.ex: The two rival chefs traded {invective} across the crowded kitchen.
entry.ctx: The debate began politely, but it soon sank into {invective}, with both speakers calling each other names instead of discussing the question.
entry.etym: From Late Latin invectivus, “abusive,” from invehi (to attack with words), literally “to carry oneself against.”

mn.text: When his kite gets stuck in a tree, Rex lets fly a swarm of stinging insults at everyone nearby: his {invective} stings like a cloud of bees.

scene.alt: An angry man shouts insults that fly like stinging bees toward a man who hides his face.

entry.def: bitterly harsh and cruel in speech or writing
entry.ex: The {vitriolic} review hurt the young author’s feelings for weeks.
entry.ctx: The once-friendly letters between the two inventors turned {vitriolic}; each accused the other of stealing ideas and used the harshest words he could find.
entry.etym: From vitriol, an old name for a burning acid, from Latin vitrum (glass), because some of its crystals look like glass.

mn.text: The angry letter is so bitter that it seems to smoke on the page, like acid eating through paper: it is {vitriolic}.

scene.alt: A woman is shocked by a letter so bitter it seems to smoke in her hands.

entry.def: showing strong, intense feeling; forceful
entry.ex: Despite her {vehement} protests, Maya was given the early shift.
entry.ctx: The town’s reaction to the plan was {vehement}; hundreds of residents packed the meeting hall, many shouting that they would never let the park be paved.
entry.etym: From Latin vehemens, “eager, violent.”

mn.cue: VERY-MEANT: he VERY much MEANT it
mn.text: Asked whether he broke the lamp, Theo shakes his head so hard his hat flies off: “NO!” He very much means it; his denial is {vehement}.

scene.alt: A toddler shakes his head so hard his hat flies off, shouting no, next to a fallen lamp.

entry.def: loud and forceful in expressing opinions
entry.ex: The {vociferous} fans cheered every single point.
entry.ctx: The parents were {vociferous} in their support of the library, filling the meeting with loud speeches and signs demanding that it stay open.
entry.etym: From Latin vociferari, “to shout”: vox (voice) + ferre (to carry).
entry.note: Vociferous is about being loud, not about using many words; a wordy person is verbose.

mn.cue: VOC = VOICE: a VOICE that carries
mn.text: Nana Lou cheers so loudly at every game that the players can hear her from the far end of the field: she is a {vociferous} fan.

scene.alt: A grandmother shouts through a megaphone at a game while her embarrassed grandson hides his face.

entry.def: loud and harsh; forceful in a grating way
entry.ex: The {strident} car alarm went off at three in the morning.
entry.ctx: Her tone grew {strident} as the argument went on, her voice rising to a harsh, grating pitch that made everyone at the table wince.
entry.etym: From Latin stridere, “to creak, to shriek.”

mn.text: Sami saws away at his violin, and the strings shriek so harshly that the dog howls along: the sound is {strident}.

scene.alt: A boy scrapes harshly on a violin while the dog howls.

entry.def: a loud, confused noise, especially of people demanding something
entry.ex: The {clamor} of the crowd outside drowned out the speaker.
entry.ctx: When the store announced a half-price sale, the {clamor} at its doors grew so loud that the manager opened an hour early just to quiet the shouting shoppers.
entry.etym: From Latin clamor, “a shout,” from clamare (to cry out).

mn.text: At feeding time, the penguins crowd around the keeper, all squawking at once for clams and fish: what a {clamor}!

scene.alt: Three penguins squawk at once for fish while the keeper holds up his bucket.

entry.def: a harsh, jarring mix of sounds
entry.ex: Car horns, sirens and barking dogs made a {cacophony} outside my window.
entry.ctx: Unlike the sweet harmony of the choir, the first rehearsal of the beginner band was a {cacophony}, with every player honking a different note at a different speed.
entry.etym: From Greek kakophonia: kakos (bad) + phone (sound).

mn.text: On the first day of band practice, every beginner plays a different song at once, and Professor Edwin covers his ears: the result is a {cacophony}.

scene.alt: A beginner band plays a jumble of clashing notes while an old professor covers his ears, dizzy.

blocks.html: vociferous is about loud expression of opinion; it does not mean wordy. cacophony is harsh noise; euphony is its pleasant opposite.

blocks.html: vociferous means loud, not wordy: a vociferous fan shouts, while a verbose speaker simply uses too many words. cacophony (bad sound) has a pleasant opposite, euphony (good sound), from the Greek eu, good.

opts.s: The neighbors were {vociferous} in their complaints, shouting at the meeting until the plan was dropped.

blocks.cap: Loud and forceful about opinions: vociferous.

blocks.html: Low energy has many shades. Someone may be unwilling to work, too tired to try, slow and dreamy on a hot day, half asleep, or fast asleep. Writers use these words to set a mood (a languid summer afternoon) or to judge a person (an indolent worker).

Won’t make an effort: indolent. Low on energy: lethargic, languid, listless, torpid, and the feeling lassitude. Sleepy and asleep: somnolent (drowsy), soporific (causing sleep), dormant (sleeping for now), stupor (a dazed state).
Several come from Latin words for sleep: somn (somnolent, insomnia), sopor (soporific) and dorm (dormant, dormitory).

entry.def: lazy; unwilling to work or make an effort
entry.ex: The {indolent} cat watched the mouse run past without even lifting its head.
entry.ctx: Though he was clever, the {indolent} student never finished an assignment, preferring to nap in the library rather than do any work at all.
entry.etym: From Late Latin indolens, “feeling no pain”: in- (not) + dolere (to suffer); in English it came to mean “not troubling oneself,” and so lazy.

mn.text: The chore list grows longer every day, but Jonah stays sprawled on the sofa, too idle to lift a finger: he is {indolent}.

scene.alt: A teen lies on the sofa ignoring a sign that lists his chores and a broom left leaning nearby.

entry.def: sluggish and drowsy; lacking energy
entry.ex: The heat made everyone {lethargic}, and no one wanted to play outside.
entry.ctx: After the long overnight flight, the travelers were {lethargic}; they shuffled slowly through the airport, yawning and barely speaking.
entry.etym: From Greek lethargos, “forgetful, drowsy”: lethe (forgetting) + argos (idle).

mn.text: The monkey bounces around shouting “Come and play!”, but the sloth just groans, “Argh… later.” The sloth is {lethargic}.

scene.alt: A sleepy sloth hangs from a branch, groaning, while a lively monkey bounces nearby.

entry.def: slow, relaxed and without energy, often in a graceful way
entry.ex: We spent a {languid} afternoon floating on the lake.
entry.ctx: Unlike his brisk, busy sister, Felix moved with {languid} ease, strolling rather than walking and taking twice as long to do everything.
entry.etym: From Latin languidus, “faint, weak,” from languere (to be weak).

mn.text: On a hot afternoon, the cat stretches out long on the sunny bench and moves only to flick her tail: she is {languid}.

scene.alt: A cat stretches out lazily on a sunny park bench.

entry.def: without energy, interest or spirit
entry.ex: Without its morning walk, the dog lay {listless} by the door.
entry.ctx: The team looked {listless} in the second half, missing easy passes and barely chasing the ball, as if all their energy had drained away.
entry.etym: From list, an old word for desire or wish, + -less (without).

mn.cue: LIST-LESS: no wish to do a thing
mn.text: When the big game is called off, Lila slumps on the floor with her to-do list still blank; she has no wish to do anything at all. She is {listless}.

scene.alt: A girl slumps on her bedroom floor with a blank to-do list and an unused ball.

entry.def: slow and inactive, as if numb
entry.ex: In the cold, the {torpid} lizard barely moved.
entry.ctx: The village seemed {torpid} in the summer heat; shops closed at noon, dogs slept in the shade, and nothing stirred until evening.
entry.etym: From Latin torpidus, from torpere (to be numb).

mn.text: On a frosty morning, the tortoise hardly moves at all until the sun warms its shell: it is {torpid}.

scene.alt: A tortoise sits frozen still on a frosty morning, waiting for the sun to warm it.

entry.def: sleepy and drowsy; ready to doze off
entry.ex: The {somnolent} passengers dozed as the train rocked along.
entry.ctx: By the third hour of the meeting, the room had grown {somnolent}: heads drooped, eyes closed, and someone began, very softly, to snore.
entry.etym: From Latin somnolentus, from somnus (sleep).

mn.cue: SOMN = sleep: drowsy on the train
mn.text: On the long ride home, Rosa’s head keeps nodding toward her shoulder, and her eyes won’t stay open: she is {somnolent}.

scene.alt: Two travelers nod off on a station bench.

entry.def: causing sleep or drowsiness
entry.ex: The speaker’s {soporific} voice put half the class to sleep.
entry.ctx: The gentle rain on the roof had a {soporific} effect; within minutes of lying down, every camper in the tent was fast asleep.
entry.etym: From Latin sopor (deep sleep) + -fic (making).

mn.cue: SOUP-orific: soup that makes you SLEEPY
mn.text: Nana Lou’s warm soup is so soothing that after one bowl, Grandpa and Kai both nod off at the table: the soup is {soporific}.

scene.alt: A grandfather and a boy fall asleep at the table next to a pot of warm soup.

entry.def: asleep or inactive for a time, but able to wake again
entry.ex: The {dormant} volcano has not erupted for three hundred years.
entry.ctx: Seeds can stay {dormant} in the soil all winter, waiting until the warm spring rains wake them and they begin to sprout.
entry.etym: From French dormant, “sleeping,” from dormir (to sleep), from Latin dormire.
entry.note: Dormant means asleep for now, not dead: a dormant volcano can erupt again.

mn.cue: DORM-ant: asleep, but it will WAKE
mn.text: All winter the bear sleeps under the snow, quiet and still, but in spring it will wake up hungry: through the winter it is {dormant}.

scene.alt: A bear sleeps through the winter as snow falls around it.

entry.def: a heavy tiredness of body or mind
entry.ex: A strange {lassitude} came over him after the long trip.
entry.ctx: Weeks of hard work left Maya with a deep {lassitude}; even simple tasks like answering a letter felt like climbing a mountain.
entry.etym: From Latin lassitudo, from lassus (weary).

mn.text: After a week of exams and late nights, the lass drags her heavy backpack home, weary in every bone: she is full of {lassitude}.

scene.alt: A weary teen girl drags herself home under a heavy backpack.

entry.def: a dazed state in which one can hardly think or act
entry.ex: Woken at five in the morning, Dev stumbled around in a {stupor}.
entry.ctx: The news of the surprise win left the coach in a happy {stupor}; she stood on the sideline, blinking, unable to say a word.
entry.etym: From Latin stupor, “numbness, amazement,” from stupere (to be stunned).

mn.text: Half asleep at dawn, Dev stoops over the table and pours orange juice onto his cereal: he is in a {stupor}.

scene.alt: A sleepy teen in a daze pours orange juice into his cereal bowl.

blocks.html: soporific describes what causes sleep (a soporific lecture); somnolent describes the sleepy person. A dormant volcano can wake up again.

blocks.html: Where do our traits come from? Some we are born with; some are built into a thing’s nature; some we pick up by habit or from the outside world. Scientists, historians and novelists all lean on these words when they ask whether something is nature or nurture.

Born with it: innate, congenital, hereditary (passed down in the family), instinctive (done without learning). Part of a thing’s nature: inherent, intrinsic; its opposite is extrinsic (from outside). Knowing without reasoning: intuitive. Fixed by long habit: ingrained, inveterate.

Notice how many begin with in- meaning in (not not): in-nate (born in), in-herent (sticking in), in-grained (worked into the grain). And gen (birth) shows up in congenital, just as in genes and generation.

entry.def: present from birth; natural rather than learned
entry.ex: Some people seem to have an {innate} sense of direction.
entry.ctx: Her teachers wondered whether the girl’s musical gift was {innate} or learned, since she had hummed perfect tunes long before anyone taught her a note.
entry.etym: From Latin innatus, “inborn”: in- (in) + nasci (to be born).

mn.text: Before he can even talk, Theo taps a perfect beat on his high chair with two spoons; nobody taught him: his sense of rhythm is {innate}.

scene.alt: A toddler taps a perfect beat with two spoons while his amazed mother claps.

entry.def: existing as a natural, permanent part of something
entry.ex: A little mess is {inherent} in finger painting.
entry.ctx: Delay was {inherent} in sending letters by ship; no matter how hard the sailors worked, the crossing simply took weeks.
entry.etym: From Latin inhaerere, “to stick in”: in- (in) + haerere (to stick).

mn.text: Every lemon, big or small, is sour; the sourness is in here, part of what a lemon is: it is {inherent}.

scene.alt: A boy makes a sour face biting a lemon beside a pile of lemons.

entry.def: belonging to the basic nature of a thing; coming from within
entry.ex: Zoe practices piano for the {intrinsic} joy of making music.
entry.ctx: The old coin has little {intrinsic} value, since its metal is cheap, but collectors pay hundreds of dollars for it because it is so rare.
entry.etym: From Latin intrinsecus, “on the inside.”

mn.cue: IN-trinsic: the joy comes from INSIDE
mn.text: Zoe paints all afternoon with no prize and no audience, just for the happiness it gives her: her reason is {intrinsic}.

scene.alt: A girl happily paints at an easel, hearts glowing from inside her.

entry.def: coming from outside; not part of the thing itself
entry.ex: Prizes and grades are {extrinsic} rewards.
entry.ctx: The coach worried that her players cared only about {extrinsic} rewards, such as trophies and praise, rather than about the game itself.
entry.etym: From Latin extrinsecus, “on the outside.”

mn.cue: EX-trinsic: the reward comes from OUTSIDE
mn.text: Pip paints only because Victor is holding out a shiny medal for the winner; take the medal away and he stops. His reason is {extrinsic}.

scene.alt: A bored boy paints only because a man is holding up a shiny medal for the winner.

entry.def: done naturally, without learning or thinking
entry.ex: Pulling your hand back from a hot pan is {instinctive}.
entry.ctx: No one teaches a spider how to spin its first web; the skill is {instinctive}, built in from the moment it hatches.
entry.etym: From instinct, from Latin instinctus, “an urge, an impulse.”

mn.cue: in an INSTANT, no lessons needed
mn.text: The baby turtles hatch on the beach and, in an instant, head straight for the sea; no one shows them the way: the move is {instinctive}.

scene.alt: Baby turtles scurry across the sand straight toward the sea.

entry.def: known or understood without reasoning it out; also, easy to understand
entry.ex: The new phone was so {intuitive} that Grandma used it without reading the manual.
entry.ctx: Maya had an {intuitive} grasp of geometry; she often knew the answer to a problem before she could explain how she got it.
entry.etym: From Latin intueri, “to look at, consider”: in- (at) + tueri (to look).

mn.text: Rosa says “I’m fine!” with a smile, but Lila can tell at once that something is wrong; she just knows, without a single clue: Lila is {intuitive}.

scene.alt: A smiling girl with a little rain cloud over her head says she is fine, and her friend senses the truth and hugs her.

entry.def: present from birth; also, being so by nature, as if born that way
entry.ex: Uncle Felix is a {congenital} optimist who smiles even in a rainstorm.
entry.ctx: Her honesty seemed almost {congenital}: her parents said that even as a toddler she had owned up to every cookie she took.
entry.etym: From Latin congenitus, “born with”: con- (with) + genitus (born).

mn.cue: CON-GEN: there WITH him since BIRTH
mn.text: Felix has smiled at rainy days since he was a baby, and he still splashes in puddles, grinning: his cheerfulness is {congenital}.

scene.alt: A cheerful man in a raincoat jumps happily into a puddle in the rain.

entry.def: firmly fixed by long habit; deep-seated
entry.ex: Saying “please” and “thank you” was {ingrained} in us from an early age.
entry.ctx: The habit of rising at dawn was so {ingrained} in the old farmer that, years after he sold the farm, he still woke at five every morning.

roots.means: the grain of wood or cloth

mn.cue: IN the GRAIN: it won’t come out
mn.text: Nana Lou scrubs and scrubs, but the old jam stain has soaked deep into the wood grain and won’t come out. Like an old habit, it is {ingrained}.

labels.text: IN the GRAIN: won’t come out

scene.alt: A grandmother scrubs hard at a stain soaked into a wooden table.

entry.def: having a habit so long-standing that it is unlikely to change
entry.ex: My aunt is an {inveterate} traveler who has visited forty countries.
entry.ctx: An {inveterate} joker, Uncle Omar could not get through even a serious family meeting without at least one pun.
entry.etym: From Latin inveteratus, “grown old, long-established,” from vetus (old).

mn.cue: in-VETER-ate: a VETERan of the habit
mn.text: Professor Edwin has collected stamps every week for sixty years, a true veteran of the hobby: he is an {inveterate} collector.

scene.alt: An old professor lovingly studies his stamp album beside a tall stack of albums.

entry.def: passed down from parents to children
entry.ex: In the old kingdom, the title of duke was {hereditary}, passing from parent to eldest child.
entry.ctx: The family’s bright red hair is {hereditary}: Grandma had it, Mom has it, and now baby Rory has it too.
entry.etym: From Latin hereditarius, from hereditas (inheritance), from heres (heir).

mn.cue: HEIR-editary: passed DOWN to the HEIR
mn.text: Nell, her son Pip and baby Rory all have the same bright red hair, handed down from parent to child: it is {hereditary}.

scene.alt: A red-haired mother, her red-haired son and red-haired baby stand together.

blocks.html: inveterate (a long-held habit) is not invertebrate (an animal without a backbone). Intrinsic motivation comes from within; extrinsic motivation comes from rewards outside.

blocks.html: Time can be wasted, saved, stretched or rushed, and English has a word for each. This topic moves from the slow end (putting things off, dawdling, lingering) through pauses and rests to the fast end (hurrying, and hurrying too much).

Putting off: procrastinate, defer. Too slow: dawdle, linger, dilatory, belated. Pauses: a hiatus (a break in an activity), a respite (a rest from something hard). Fast: hasten (hurry) and precipitate (too hasty, without thinking).

Watch two words with double lives. defer means to put off, but also to give way to someone wiser (“I defer to the expert”). precipitate as an adjective means rash and hasty; as a verb it means to bring about suddenly.

entry.def: to keep putting off something one should do
entry.ex: If you {procrastinate} on your science project, you’ll be gluing it together at midnight.
entry.ctx: Maya knew the essay was due Monday, yet she continued to {procrastinate}, cleaning her room, sorting her books and baking cookies instead of writing a single word.
entry.etym: From Latin procrastinare, “to put off till tomorrow”: pro- (forward) + crastinus (of tomorrow), from cras (tomorrow).

mn.text: The homework pile grows taller, but Pip keeps playing and saying, “Tomorrow!” He pushes everything to tomorrow: he {procrastinates}.

scene.alt: A boy plays on a laptop, saying “Tomorrow!”, next to a big pile of homework and a calendar marked DUE.

entry.def: to put off until later; also, to give way to another’s judgment
entry.ex: The club agreed to {defer} the vote until everyone could attend.
entry.ctx: Though he had strong opinions about the garden, Kai chose to {defer} to his grandmother, who had grown tomatoes for fifty years and knew far more than he did.
entry.etym: Two Latin verbs met in this word: differre, “to put off,” and deferre, “to carry down, to yield.”
entry.note: To defer to someone is to give way to their judgment, out of respect: “I’ll defer to the coach.”

mn.cue: de-FER: carry it FAR off, to later
mn.text: Too busy today, Ada pushes the big cleanup box far off down the hall and writes “next week” on the calendar: she {defers} it.

scene.alt: A woman pushes a big box of work away toward next week on the calendar.

entry.def: to waste time; to move slowly and idly
entry.ex: Don’t {dawdle}; the bus leaves in five minutes!
entry.ctx: Instead of hurrying home as they had promised, the boys {dawdled}, skipping stones at the creek and watching ducks until the sun went down.

mn.text: On the way to school, Kai stops to poke every puddle, smell every flower and count every snail while Mom waits up ahead: he {dawdles}.

scene.alt: A boy kneels to look at a snail on the way to school while his mother waits impatiently.

entry.def: to stay longer than needed; to be slow to leave
entry.ex: The smell of fresh bread {lingered} in the kitchen all afternoon.
entry.ctx: Long after the concert ended, a few fans {lingered} by the stage door, unwilling to leave until they had seen the band one last time.

mn.text: The party ended at nine, but Uncle Omar stays at the door telling one more story, then another, longer and longer: he {lingers}.

scene.alt: At night, a guest keeps chatting at the doorway while his sleepy host yawns.

entry.def: slow to act; causing delay
entry.ex: The {dilatory} repair crew took three months to fix one pothole.
entry.ctx: The committee’s {dilatory} approach frustrated everyone; it held meeting after meeting, putting off the decision again and again, while the old bridge kept crumbling.
entry.etym: From Latin dilatorius, “delaying.”

mn.text: The waiter strolls, stops to read the paper, then dilly-dallies some more while the hungry diners watch the clock: he is {dilatory}.

scene.alt: A waiter reads the newspaper while a hungry customer waits and waits.

entry.def: coming late; overdue
entry.ex: Grandpa sent me a {belated} birthday card with an apology for being late.
entry.ctx: The thank-you note was {belated}, arriving a full two months after the party, but Aunt Lin was happy to get it all the same.

mn.cue: BE-LATE-d: LATE, but here at last
mn.text: A week after Zoe’s birthday, Pip runs up with a card: “Happy birthday… last week!” His wishes are {belated}.

scene.alt: A boy sheepishly hands a girl a birthday card a week late.

entry.def: a break or pause in an activity
entry.ex: The band went on {hiatus} for a year while its members traveled.
entry.ctx: After a two-year {hiatus}, during which the old theater was closed for repairs, the town’s summer plays finally returned.
entry.etym: From Latin hiatus, “an opening, a gap,” from hiare (to gape).

mn.cue: HI-ATUS: a GAP in the show
mn.text: The stage sits empty under a sign that says BACK IN JUNE, and only the theater cat is performing, by napping: the show is on {hiatus}.

scene.alt: An empty stage with a sign reading BACK IN JUNE and a cat napping in the spotlight.

entry.def: a short rest or relief from something hard
entry.ex: The shady oak offered a brief {respite} from the heat.
entry.ctx: The storm raged for three days, but on Tuesday afternoon there was a short {respite}: the rain stopped for an hour, and everyone rushed out to buy groceries.
entry.etym: From Old French respit, “delay,” from Latin respectus (a looking back).

mn.text: After three hot hours on the trail, the hikers flop down in the cool shade of a tree for a short rest: a welcome {respite}.

scene.alt: Two tired hikers rest happily in the cool shade of a tree on a hot day.

entry.def: to hurry; to make something happen sooner
entry.ex: We {hastened} home when we saw the dark clouds.
entry.ctx: Warm, sunny weather will {hasten} the tomatoes’ ripening, while a cold spell will slow it down.
entry.etym: From haste + -en (to make).

mn.text: The bus is pulling up, and Dev makes haste down the street with his backpack bouncing: he {hastens} to catch it.

scene.alt: A teen with a backpack runs fast to catch a bus.

entry.def: done suddenly and without careful thought; hasty
entry.ex: Selling the house after one bad day was a {precipitate} decision.
entry.ctx: The coach warned against any {precipitate} changes after a single loss; she wanted to study the game film carefully before deciding anything.
entry.etym: From Latin praecipitare, “to throw headlong,” from praeceps (headlong): prae- (forward) + caput (head).
entry.note: As a verb (prih-SIP-ih-tayt), precipitate means to bring about suddenly: the snub precipitated a quarrel.

mn.text: One raindrop lands on Grandpa’s nose, and he cancels the whole picnic at once without even looking at the sunny sky: his decision is {precipitate}.

scene.alt: On a sunny day, a grandfather feels one drop and shouts to cancel the picnic while a girl shrugs.

blocks.html: defer has two meanings: to postpone, and to yield respectfully (defer to an expert). precipitate as an adjective means hasty; as a verb it means to cause suddenly.

blocks.html: There are gentle ways and rough ways to get people to do what you want. This topic runs from the softest (a patient, kind word) through sweet talk and temptation to force and threats. Telling them apart helps you judge the characters you read about.

Gentle: coax. Sweet talk: cajole, wheedle. Temptation and charm: entice, lure, beguile. Force: compel (can be neutral), coerce (by threats), browbeat (by bullying), extort (getting money or favors by threats).
Two Latin roots sit inside the forceful ones: pel, drive or push (compel, propel, expel), and tort, twist (extort, contort, torture).

entry.def: to persuade gently and patiently
entry.ex: Lila {coaxed} the frightened kitten out from under the porch with a little tuna.
entry.ctx: The old engine would not start at first, but after twenty minutes of patient tinkering, the mechanic {coaxed} it back to life.

mn.text: The kitten is stuck high in the tree, so Lila holds up a treat and speaks softly, “Come on, sweetie,” until it creeps down: she {coaxes} it.

scene.alt: A girl gently holds up a treat to coax a frightened kitten down from a tree.

entry.def: to persuade with flattery or sweet talk
entry.ex: Dev {cajoled} his sister into lending him her bike by praising her cooking all week.
entry.ctx: When orders failed, the coach tried to {cajole} the team instead, telling them how talented they were and promising pizza if they ran just three more laps.

mn.text: Dev praises his sister’s cooking all week in his jolliest voice until she agrees to lend him her bike: he {cajoles} her.

scene.alt: A teen offers flowers and compliments to his sister, who suspects he wants her bike.

entry.def: to get something by flattery or sweet talk
entry.ex: The puppy {wheedled} a bite of toast from everyone at the table.
entry.ctx: Instead of asking directly, Pip tried to {wheedle} a later bedtime out of his parents, praising their cooking and offering to fold the laundry first.

mn.text: “You’re the best grandpa in the whole world,” Ivy sighs. “Pleeease, may I have another ice cream?” She is trying to {wheedle} one out of him.

scene.alt: A little girl sweet-talks her grandfather for another ice cream, and he melts.

entry.def: to attract or tempt by offering something pleasant
entry.ex: The smell of popcorn {enticed} us into the theater lobby.
entry.ctx: To {entice} new members, the chess club offered free lessons and hot cocoa at every meeting, and soon three times as many students showed up.

mn.cue: en-TICE: ICE cream draws you IN
mn.text: A big sign for cold ice cream hangs over the shop on a hot day, and everyone walking by turns and heads inside: the sign {entices} them.

labels.text: en-TICE: ICE cream pulls you IN

scene.alt: On a hot day, two children are drawn toward a big ice cream sign.

entry.def: to charm, sometimes in order to trick
entry.ex: The singer’s lovely voice {beguiled} the whole audience.
entry.ctx: The salesman’s friendly stories {beguiled} a young couple into buying a car they did not need; only later did they realize they had been tricked.
entry.etym: From be- + guile (cunning, trickery).
entry.note: Beguile can be pure praise (a beguiling smile) or a warning (beguiled by a con man); read the context.

mn.cue: BE-GUILE: charm full of GUILE (sly tricks)
mn.text: Rex bows low and showers Nana Lou with flowers and compliments, and while she blushes, he slips her pie behind his back: he {beguiles} her.

scene.alt: A smooth-talking man bows with flowers to a blushing grandmother while her pie sneaks away behind him.

entry.def: to tempt someone to go somewhere or do something
entry.ex: Bright porch lights {lure} moths on summer nights.
entry.ctx: The town hoped that a new park and lower rents would {lure} young families away from the crowded city and into its quiet streets.
entry.etym: From Old French loire, a bundle of feathers swung on a cord to call a hunting falcon back.

mn.text: The shiny lure wiggles and sparkles in the water, and the curious fish swims closer and closer: the shine {lures} it in.

scene.alt: A shiny fishing lure sparkles in the water, and a curious fish swims toward it.

entry.def: to force someone to act by using threats or pressure
entry.ex: No one should be {coerced} into joining a club.
entry.ctx: The pirate captain tried to {coerce} the townspeople into handing over their gold, threatening to block the harbor until they gave in.
entry.etym: From Latin coercere, “to hold in, restrain”: co- (together) + arcere (to shut in).

mn.text: Captain Rex points his finger and roars, “Scrub the deck, or no supper!” He doesn’t ask; he {coerces} the crew.

scene.alt: On a ship, a pirate captain shouts a threat at a frightened boy scrubbing the deck.

entry.def: to force or require someone to do something
entry.ex: The heavy rain {compelled} us to cancel the game.
entry.ctx: Though she wanted to keep reading, hunger finally {compelled} Maya to close her book and go downstairs for dinner.
entry.etym: From Latin compellere, “to drive together”: com- (together) + pellere (to drive).
entry.note: Compel can be neutral: the law compels drivers to stop at red lights.

mn.cue: com-PEL: the BELL pushes you up
mn.text: At six o’clock the alarm bell rings and rings, and Dev has no choice but to drag himself out of bed: the bell {compels} him.

scene.alt: A ringing alarm clock forces a sleepy teen to get out of bed.

entry.def: to bully someone with stern words and looks
entry.ex: The bossy captain tried to {browbeat} his crew into working through the night.
entry.ctx: Rather than persuade the committee with facts, the chairman {browbeat} its members, glaring and shouting until they agreed just to make him stop.

mn.cue: a frowning BROW beats you DOWN
mn.text: Marcus lowers his bushy brows, glares and thunders until Sami gives up his turn at chess: Marcus {browbeats} him.

labels.text: a frowning BROW beats you DOWN

scene.alt: A big man glares and shouts at a nervous boy across a chess table.

entry.def: to get money or something else by force or threats
entry.ex: In the old tale, the pirates {extorted} gold from every ship that passed.
entry.ctx: The scammer tried to {extort} money from the shop owner, threatening to post false reviews unless she paid him, but she called the police instead.
entry.etym: From Latin extorquere, “to twist out”: ex- (out) + torquere (to twist).

mn.cue: EX-TORT: TWIST it OUT of you
mn.text: Rex blocks the little bridge and growls that no one may cross unless they hand over a coin: he {extorts} money from every traveler.

scene.alt: A sneaky man blocks a bridge and makes a sad boy hand over a coin to cross.

blocks.html: beguile can mean charm or deceive; read the context. coerce uses pressure or threats; compel can be neutral (the law compels drivers to stop at red lights).

blocks.html: beguile can praise (a beguiling melody) or warn (beguiled by a swindler), so read the sentence. coerce always means pressure or threats, while compel can be neutral: the law compels drivers to stop at red lights.

opts.s: With soft words and a bit of cheese, Zoe managed to {coax} the shy mouse out of its hole.

blocks.html: Groups can welcome people or shut them out, and they can look outward at the wide world or turn inward. This topic gives you verbs for pushing people away and adjectives for narrow and wide horizons.

Keeping away or rejecting: shun (avoid), spurn (reject with scorn), snub (ignore coldly). Pushing out or down: ostracize (exclude from a group), banish (send away), alienate (drive away, make unfriendly), relegate (move to a lower place). Horizons: insular and parochial (narrow) versus cosmopolitan (worldly).

Some come with history. Insular comes from the Latin for island; ostracize from the pieces of broken pottery on which the citizens of ancient Athens wrote the name of someone to be sent away; cosmopolitan means “citizen of the world.”

entry.def: to avoid on purpose, again and again
entry.ex: After the food fight, the twins {shunned} the cafeteria for a week.
entry.ctx: Though the old house was perfectly safe, the children {shunned} it, crossing the street rather than walk past its creaky gate.

mn.cue: SHOO and RUN: keep far away
mn.text: Every cat in the neighborhood takes the long way around grumpy Rufus’s yard: they {shun} it.

scene.alt: Two cats steer well clear of a yard where a grumpy dog sits behind the fence.

entry.def: to reject with scorn
entry.ex: She {spurned} his offer of help and fixed the flat tire herself.
entry.ctx: The proud inventor {spurned} every offer to buy his idea, insisting that no amount of money could tempt him to give it up.

mn.text: Ivy offers Aunt Tia a homemade cookie, but Tia sniffs, turns up her nose and turns away: “Too plain for me.” She {spurns} it.

scene.alt: A girl offers a woman a cookie, and the woman turns away with her nose in the air.

entry.def: to ignore or treat coldly on purpose
entry.ex: Lila felt hurt when her old friend {snubbed} her at the party.
entry.ctx: The new student greeted everyone warmly, so he was puzzled when the team captain {snubbed} him, turning away without a word.

mn.cue: a SNUB nose stuck in the air
mn.text: Jonah waves and calls, “Hi, Maya!” but she sticks her nose in the air and walks right past him: she {snubs} him.

scene.alt: A teen boy waves hello, but a girl walks past him with her nose in the air.

entry.def: to shut someone out of a group
entry.ex: No one should be {ostracized} for liking different music.
entry.ctx: After he told the coach about the cheating, the other players {ostracized} him; no one sat with him at lunch or answered his messages for weeks.
entry.etym: From Greek ostrakizein, from ostrakon (a piece of broken pottery): the citizens of ancient Athens voted to send someone away by writing the name on such pieces.

mn.cue: OSTRA-CIZE: shut OUT of the huddle
mn.text: The penguins huddle close together and turn their backs on little Pebble, who stands alone in the snow: they {ostracize} him.

scene.alt: Three penguins huddle with their backs turned while a small penguin stands alone and sad.

entry.def: to send someone away as a punishment
entry.ex: In the legend, the king {banished} the traitor to a faraway island.
entry.ctx: The cat was {banished} from the kitchen after she knocked the cake off the counter, and she now sulks in the hallway at every mealtime.
entry.etym: From Old French banir, “to proclaim, to outlaw,” related to ban.

mn.text: “You are banned from my kingdom!” the king declares, pointing at the gate, and the scheming Rex trudges off with his bag: the king {banishes} him.

scene.alt: A king points sternly toward the road as a man carrying a bag trudges away from the castle.

entry.def: to make someone feel unwelcome, or to turn them against you
entry.ex: His rude comments {alienated} his teammates.
entry.ctx: By changing the rules without asking anyone, the club president {alienated} her members; within a month, half of them had quit.
entry.etym: From Latin alienare, “to make another’s, to estrange,” from alienus (of another).

mn.text: Dev brags and interrupts so much that his friends drift away one by one, until they feel like strangers: he {alienates} them.

scene.alt: A teen brags through a megaphone while his friends walk away from him.

entry.def: to move to a lower place, rank or position
entry.ex: The broken lamp was {relegated} to the attic.
entry.ctx: After losing every game, the team was {relegated} to the lower league, where it would have to play weaker teams for a whole season.
entry.etym: From Latin relegare, “to send away”: re- (away) + legare (to send).

mn.text: When Pip gets a shiny new robot, his old teddy is moved to the dusty top shelf at the back: the teddy is {relegated}.

scene.alt: A boy cheers over a new robot while his old teddy bear sits forgotten on a high shelf.

entry.def: narrow in outlook; cut off from outside ideas
entry.ex: The {insular} little town rarely welcomed visitors.
entry.ctx: The club had grown {insular}; its members talked only to one another, ignored new ideas and hardly noticed when the rest of the school stopped coming.
entry.etym: From Latin insularis, from insula (island).

mn.cue: INSUL = ISLAND: cut off from the world
mn.text: Grandpa Gus lives on his own little island and waves away every boat bringing news and new ideas: “No thanks!” His outlook is {insular}.

scene.alt: A grumpy man on a tiny island waves away a boat carrying a banner that says NEW IDEAS.

entry.def: having a narrow, local outlook
entry.ex: My cousin’s {parochial} view was that nothing interesting ever happened outside our county.
entry.ctx: The newspaper’s coverage was {parochial}, filling page after page with local bake sales while ignoring important events in the rest of the world.
entry.etym: From Latin parochia, “parish,” a small local district.

mn.cue: can’t see past the village OAK: par-OAK-ial
mn.text: To Uncle Felix, the whole world stops at the old oak at the edge of the village; nothing beyond it interests him: his outlook is {parochial}.

scene.alt: A man points at the old oak at the edge of his village, sure there is nothing worth seeing beyond it.

entry.def: familiar with many countries and cultures; worldly
entry.ex: The {cosmopolitan} city had restaurants from forty countries on a single street.
entry.ctx: Having lived in six countries and learned four languages, Aunt Lin was truly {cosmopolitan}, at ease in any crowd anywhere in the world.

roots.means: one who, having to do with

entry.etym: From Greek kosmopolites, “citizen of the world”: kosmos (world) + polites (citizen).

mn.cue: COSMO = WORLD: a citizen of the world
mn.text: Aunt Lin’s suitcase is covered with stickers from a dozen countries, and she greets everyone in their own language: she is {cosmopolitan}.

scene.alt: A smiling traveler with a sticker-covered suitcase and a globe greets people in several languages.

blocks.html: parochial in this sense means narrow-minded; it can also simply mean "of a parish," as in a parochial school. insular comes from the Latin for island.

blocks.html: Insular and parochial both mean narrow in outlook; cosmopolitan is their opposite. Parochial can also simply mean “of a parish,” as in a parochial school, with no criticism at all, so read the context.

opts.s: Traveling to twelve countries made Rosa far more {cosmopolitan} than her stay-at-home cousins.

blocks.html: Too much can be too much of a thing (a surfeit of candy), too much in a price (exorbitant), too much for the job (superfluous), or too much in amount (excessive, inordinate). Some of these words also carry the idea of not needed or not belonging.

Too much in amount: excessive, inordinate, a surfeit, to inundate. Extra, left over: a surplus. Not needed: superfluous, redundant (repeated), gratuitous (uncalled for). Not belonging: extraneous. Too high a price: exorbitant.

Look for “over” and “out” inside them: super/sur (over) in superfluous, surplus and surfeit; ex and extra (out, outside) in excessive, exorbitant and extraneous; and the Latin unda (wave) in both inundate and redundant.

entry.def: more than is necessary, normal or reasonable
entry.ex: Ten straight minutes of honking seemed a bit {excessive}.
entry.ctx: The fine of five hundred dollars for an overdue library book struck everyone as {excessive}; it was far more than the book itself was worth.
entry.etym: From excess, from Latin excedere (to go beyond): ex- (out) + cedere (to go).

mn.text: Pip pours syrup on his pancakes until it floods the plate, drips off the table and puddles on the floor: the amount is {excessive}.

scene.alt: A boy pours so much syrup on his pancakes that it drips onto the floor while a woman gasps.

entry.def: an amount left over beyond what is needed
entry.ex: The bakery gave its {surplus} bread to the shelter each evening.
entry.ctx: Because the farm grew far more corn than it could sell, it sent the {surplus} to a neighboring town that had suffered a poor harvest.
entry.etym: From Old French surplus: sur (over) + plus (more).

mn.text: Nell’s garden grows so many watermelons that she sets the extras by the road with a FREE sign: they are her {surplus}.

scene.alt: A woman offers free watermelons from a big pile of extras by the road.

entry.def: more than is needed; unnecessary
entry.ex: With the sun shining all day, the umbrella turned out to be {superfluous}.
entry.ctx: The editor cut every {superfluous} word from the article, so that the final version said just as much in half the space.
entry.etym: From Latin superfluus, “overflowing”: super (over) + fluere (to flow).

mn.text: The snowman already has a carrot nose, but Pip keeps adding more until there are five: four of them are {superfluous}.

scene.alt: A boy sticks yet another carrot nose onto a snowman that already has four.

entry.def: unnecessary because it repeats something already there
entry.ex: “Free gift” is {redundant}, since every gift is free.
entry.ctx: Once the town built a new bridge, the old ferry became {redundant}; there was no longer any need for a boat to carry people across.
entry.etym: From Latin redundare, “to overflow”: re- (again) + undare (to rise in waves).

mn.text: The shop sign shouts, “FREE GIFT! NO CHARGE! COSTS NOTHING!” Saying the same thing three times is {redundant}.

scene.alt: A boy scratches his head at a shop banner that says the same thing twice: free gift, no charge.

entry.def: not belonging; unrelated to the matter at hand
entry.ex: Remove any {extraneous} details from your summary.
entry.ctx: The detective ignored the {extraneous} gossip about the neighbor’s new car and focused only on the facts that bore on the missing painting.
entry.etym: From Latin extraneus, “from outside,” from extra (outside).

mn.cue: EXTRA-neous: EXTRA stuff that doesn’t belong
mn.text: Pip’s poster about bees has a slice of pizza glued right in the middle: it has nothing to do with bees. The pizza is {extraneous}.

scene.alt: A teacher points at a slice of pizza stuck in the middle of a boy’s poster about bees.

entry.def: far too high, especially of a price
entry.ex: The airport charged an {exorbitant} price for a bottle of water.
entry.ctx: Though the concert was wonderful, many fans stayed home because of the {exorbitant} ticket prices, which had doubled since the year before.
entry.etym: From Late Latin exorbitare, “to go off the track”: ex- (out of) + orbita (track, rut).

mn.cue: EX-ORBIT: a price blasted OUT OF ORBIT
mn.text: One cupcake for five hundred dollars? The price has rocketed right out of orbit: it is {exorbitant}.

scene.alt: A teen gasps at a cupcake priced at five hundred dollars while a rocket blasts off nearby.

entry.def: far greater than is usual or reasonable
entry.ex: Pip spends an {inordinate} amount of time choosing his socks.
entry.ctx: The project took an {inordinate} amount of time; what should have been a weekend job stretched into four whole months.
entry.etym: From Latin inordinatus, “disordered”: in- (not) + ordinare (to put in order).

mn.text: From sunrise to sunset, Grandpa polishes his old car, again and again: he spends an {inordinate} amount of time on it.

scene.alt: A grandfather lovingly polishes his already gleaming car from sunrise to moonrise.

entry.def: done without good reason; uncalled for
entry.ex: The movie was spoiled by {gratuitous} explosions that had nothing to do with the story.
entry.ctx: Her criticism of his essay was fair, but the {gratuitous} remark about his handwriting was simply unkind and added nothing.
entry.etym: From Latin gratuitus, “free, done without pay,” from gratia (favor).
entry.note: Gratuitous can also mean given free, without charge, its older sense; a gratuity is a tip.

mn.cue: GRATIS = for free: and for NO reason
mn.text: Pip walks by minding his own business, and Rosa calls out “Silly hat!” for no reason at all: the remark is {gratuitous}.

scene.alt: A teen girl points and mocks a boy’s hat for no reason as he walks sadly by.

entry.def: an amount that is too much; an excess
entry.ex: After the holidays we had a {surfeit} of cookies.
entry.ctx: The town suffered not from a lack of parking but from a {surfeit} of it; huge empty lots covered land that could have been parks.
entry.etym: From Old French sorfait, “excess,” from sorfaire (to overdo): sor (over) + faire (to do).

mn.text: After the party, Kai and Zoe stare at a mountain of candy, far more than they could ever eat: a {surfeit} of sweets.

scene.alt: Two children face a heap of candy, far more than they can eat; one looks dizzy.

entry.def: to flood; to overwhelm with a huge amount
entry.ex: After the storm, the swollen river {inundated} the low fields.
entry.ctx: When the radio show praised her bakery, Lin was {inundated} with orders, so many that she had to hire three new bakers to keep up.
entry.etym: From Latin inundare, “to flood”: in- (onto) + unda (wave).

mn.cue: IN + UNDA (wave): a WAVE of letters rolls IN
mn.text: After the radio show, wave after wave of order letters pours into Lin’s little bakery until she can barely see over them: she is {inundated}.

labels.text: UNDA = WAVE: a flood of letters

scene.alt: A baker is swamped by a wave of order letters pouring into her office.

blocks.html: gratuitous means unnecessary as well as free of charge. redundant also means repeating: "free gift" is redundant.

blocks.html: gratuitous means uncalled for, but it can also mean free of charge (the same root as gratis and gratuity, a tip). redundant means unneeded because repeated: “free gift,” “past history” and “unexpected surprise” are all redundant.

opts.s: The phrase “past history” is {redundant}, because all history is past.

blocks.cap: Saying the same thing twice is redundant.
