blocks.html: Three small Latin parts run through this topic. greg means flock or herd, the way sheep crowd together. plac means please or calm, and pac means peace (you know it from Pacific, the ocean early sailors found calm).

greg = flock: gregarious people love the flock; crowds congregate (flock together); an aggregate adds everything to the flock; to segregate is to set apart from the flock; and an egregious mistake stands out from the flock. plac = please, calm, and pac = peace: placate, placid, implacable, complacent, pacify.
Watch the little prefix in front of each root: it tells you which way the flock moves, or whether the calm is there at all (im- in implacable means not).

entry.def: fond of company; happiest when with other people
entry.ex: Our {gregarious} neighbor knows the name of every family on the block and most of their dogs.
entry.ctx: Unlike her quiet brother, who could spend a whole weekend alone with a book, Tia was {gregarious}: she planned picnics, joined three clubs and talked to everyone at the bus stop.
entry.etym: From Latin gregarius, “belonging to a flock,” from grex (flock, herd).

mn.cue: GREG and his FLOCK of friends
mn.text: Wherever Greg walks, a whole flock of friends tags along, laughing and talking; a man who loves company that much is {gregarious}.

scene.alt: Greg waves as a happy crowd of friends, and even a sheep, follows him through the park.

entry.def: shockingly bad; standing out for being so wrong
entry.ex: Printing the wrong date on every wedding invitation was an {egregious} mistake.
entry.ctx: A small spelling slip can be forgiven, but the newspaper’s error was {egregious}: it named the wrong winner of the science fair in a headline across the whole front page.
entry.etym: From Latin egregius, “standing out from the flock”: e- (out of) + grex (flock). In English it first meant outstandingly good.

mn.cue: EGG-GREE-jus: eggs on the king’s rug
mn.text: The new cook trips and drops a whole crate of eggs on the king’s royal rug; a blunder that stands out that badly is {egregious}.

scene.alt: A young cook trips and spills a crate of eggs across the throne room as the king cries out.

entry.def: to gather together in a crowd
entry.ex: Every evening the ducks {congregate} near the bench where Granny Mae sits.
entry.ctx: On hot afternoons the town’s teenagers {congregate} at the public pool; by four o’clock there is hardly room to spread a towel.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin congregare, “to flock together”: com- (together) + grex (flock).

mn.cue: a CONGA line at the GATE
mn.text: When the band strikes up, the whole street forms a conga line at the garden gate; when people gather in a crowd like that, they {congregate}.

labels.text: CONGA at the GATE: all GATHER

scene.alt: Neighbors dance in a conga line, all crowding together at a garden gate.

entry.def: a whole made by adding many parts together; a total
entry.ex: The {aggregate} of all the class’s penny jars came to almost forty dollars.
entry.ctx: No single gift to the shelter was large, but the {aggregate} was impressive: hundreds of small donations added up to enough for a new roof.
entry.etym: From Latin aggregare, “to add to a flock, to join”: ad- (to) + grex (flock).
entry.note: As a verb (AG-rih-gayt), aggregate means to collect into one whole. “In the aggregate” means taken all together.

mn.cue: ADD the GREG (flock) through the GATE
mn.text: Farmer Lin counts the sheep from every field as they trot through one gate; the grand total of the whole flock is the {aggregate}.

scene.alt: Sheep file through a farm gate while the farmer holds up a sign with the total count.

entry.def: to set apart from the rest; to keep separate
entry.ex: At the recycling center, workers {segregate} glass from paper and plastic.
entry.ctx: To keep the cough from spreading, the farmer had to {segregate} the sick lambs, moving them to a pen far from the healthy flock until they recovered.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin segregare, “to set apart from the flock”: se- (apart) + grex (flock).
entry.note: In American history, segregation names the unjust laws and customs that kept people of different races apart; the civil rights movement fought to end them.

mn.cue: a SEParate GATE, apart from the flock
mn.text: The farmer leads the coughing lamb through a separate gate into its own pen until it is well; to keep it apart from the flock is to {segregate} it.

scene.alt: A farmer points a sick lamb through its own gate, away from the rest of the flock.

entry.def: to calm someone’s anger, often by giving them something
entry.ex: To {placate} the crying toddler, Dad offered him a ride on his shoulders.
entry.ctx: The manager tried to {placate} the angry diners with free desserts, but they still grumbled about waiting an hour for their meal.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin placare, “to calm, to soothe,” related to placere (to please).

mn.cue: a PLAte of CAKE: calm at last
mn.text: When Grandpa Gus grumbles about the rain, Nana Lou sets a plate of cake in front of him, and the frown melts; she knows how to {placate} him.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather sits at a table as his wife brings him a slice of cake to cheer him up.

entry.def: calm and peaceful; not easily stirred up
entry.ex: At dawn the {placid} lake held the mountains like a mirror.
entry.ctx: The old mare was {placid}, standing quietly through thunder and fireworks, while the young colt bolted at every bang.
entry.etym: From Latin placidus, “gentle, calm,” from placere (to please).

mn.cue: a PLACE to SIT: still water
mn.text: Grandpa’s favorite place to sit is the river at sunrise, where not a ripple moves and even the duck dozes; it is {placid}.

labels.text: a PLACE to SIT: so CALM

scene.alt: An old man sits peacefully fishing by a still river while a duck dozes on the water.

entry.def: impossible to calm, please or change
entry.ex: The {implacable} wind howled for three days without a pause.
entry.ctx: Apologies, gifts and promises all failed; the old rival remained {implacable}, refusing even to shake hands at the reunion.
entry.etym: From Latin implacabilis: in- (not) + placabilis (able to be calmed).

mn.text: The children offer the roaring dragon a cake, a song and a bunch of flowers, but it roars on; it is not placate-able, it is {implacable}.

scene.alt: Two children hold out a cake and flowers to a dragon that keeps roaring angrily.

entry.def: so pleased with oneself that one stops watching for danger or trying to improve
entry.ex: After ten wins in a row, the team grew {complacent} and skipped practice.
entry.ctx: Because the bakery had no rivals for years, its owners grew {complacent}; when a new shop opened with fresher bread, they lost half their customers in a month.
entry.etym: From Latin complacere, “to please greatly”: com- (thoroughly) + placere (to please).

mn.text: The shepherd gets so comfy in his place that he naps while the sheep wander off; too pleased with himself to keep watch, he is {complacent}.

scene.alt: A shepherd dozes in his chair while his sheep stroll out of the open gate.

entry.def: to calm someone down or bring peace to a place
entry.ex: Rocking the cradle slowly was the only way to {pacify} the fussy baby.
entry.ctx: When the two neighbors began shouting over the fallen tree, Mrs. Ruiz stepped in to {pacify} them, offering to split the cost of hauling it away.
entry.etym: From Latin pacificare, “to make peace,” from pax (peace).

mn.text: A baby’s pacifier is named for what it does: pop it in, the crying stops, and peace returns. It helps {pacify} the baby.

scene.alt: A toddler sits calmly hugging a teddy bear while his mother whispers that there is peace at last.

blocks.html: egregious once meant "standing out from the flock" in a good way; today it means shockingly bad. complacent (smug) is not complaisant (eager to please).

blocks.cap: One root, five directions: the prefix tells which way the flock moves.

blocks.html: Two look-alikes to keep apart: complacent means smug and too comfortable, while complaisant means eager to please others. And placid describes something already calm, while to placate or pacify is to make someone calm.

blocks.html: People handle money in very different ways, and English has a sharp word for each. Some save every penny, some spend as if the money will never run out, some give it away by the bagful, and some want it all for themselves.

Sort the ten words into four groups. Savers: frugal (wise), parsimonious (stingy), avaricious (greedy). Spenders: extravagant, prodigal, profligate (each more wasteful than the last). Givers: munificent, largesse. Rich and poor: affluent, destitute.
Notice which words praise and which ones criticize. Calling a friend frugal is a compliment; calling him parsimonious is not, even though both describe a person who spends little.

entry.def: careful not to waste money, food or other things; thrifty
entry.ex: Our {frugal} grandmother saves twist ties, rubber bands and every jar that still has a lid.
entry.ctx: Though the family had plenty of money, they stayed {frugal}: they mended old clothes, grew their own beans and rarely ate at restaurants.
entry.etym: From Latin frugalis, “thrifty, simple,” from frux (fruit, the produce of the land).

mn.text: Nana Lou saves every coin, even the one she found under the sofa cushion, and patches her coat instead of buying a new one; she is {frugal}.

scene.alt: Nana Lou holds up a coin she found by the sofa, ready to drop it into her piggy bank.

entry.def: so unwilling to spend money that one is stingy
entry.ex: The {parsimonious} landlord would not even replace the burned-out light in the stairwell.
entry.ctx: The club’s treasurer was so {parsimonious} that she refused to buy new soccer balls, even after the old ones had gone flat and split at the seams.
entry.etym: From parsimony, from Latin parsimonia, “thrift,” from parcere (to spare).

mn.text: Look inside the word and you will find Simon, who hugs his money bag and will not chip in even a penny for the class party; Simon is {parsimonious}.

scene.alt: A stingy man named Simon hugs his money bag and refuses to add a penny to a girl’s party jar.

entry.def: spending far more than is wise or needed; going beyond reason
entry.ex: For her dog’s birthday, Mrs. Hale threw an {extravagant} party with a three-layer cake and a hired band.
entry.ctx: Their first apartment was tiny and cheap, so a piano that cost more than a year’s rent seemed {extravagant} to everyone they knew.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin extravagans, “wandering beyond (the limits)”: extra- (beyond) + vagari (to wander).
entry.note: Extravagant can describe more than spending: extravagant praise or extravagant claims go far beyond what is reasonable.

mn.text: Mrs. Hale buys an extra cake, extra balloons and an extra band for her dog’s party, just because; spending that far beyond what makes sense is {extravagant}.

scene.alt: A woman in a party hat cheers at her dog’s birthday, surrounded by two cakes, balloons and gifts.

entry.def: carelessly wasteful with money or other resources
entry.ex: The {prodigal} young heir spent his whole fortune on racehorses in a single year.
entry.ctx: Having been {prodigal} with his allowance all summer, buying every comic and candy bar in sight, Jonah had nothing left when the county fair finally came to town.
entry.etym: From Latin prodigus, “wasteful,” from prodigere, “to drive away, to squander”: pro- (forth) + agere (to drive).
entry.note: Prodigal means wasteful. A famous story tells of a prodigal son who wasted his money and then came home, so people sometimes use the word for anyone returning, but returning is not its meaning.

mn.cue: PROD the GOLD out the door
mn.text: Rich Rosa prods her gold coins right out the door with a broom, spending on anything that glitters; anyone that wasteful is {prodigal}.

scene.alt: A young woman in a tiara laughs as she sweeps a pile of gold coins out the open door.

entry.def: wildly and recklessly wasteful
entry.ex: The {profligate} prince spent the royal treasury on golden fountains while the town’s roads crumbled.
entry.ctx: The company’s {profligate} spending, on private jets and lavish parties, left it unable to pay its workers when sales slowed.
entry.etym: From Latin profligatus, past participle of profligare (to strike down, to ruin).
entry.note: Profligate can also describe someone who lives wildly, with no self-control; as a noun, a profligate is a reckless spender.

mn.text: Rex flings handfuls of gold coins off the bridge just to hear them splash; spending money that recklessly is {profligate}.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat tosses gold coins off a bridge into the river while a duck stares in shock.

entry.def: extremely generous in giving
entry.ex: Thanks to a {munificent} gift from a former student, the school built a new music hall.
entry.ctx: Most guests brought a small present, but Aunt Rosa was {munificent}: she paid for the whole wedding dinner and the band as well.
entry.etym: From Latin munificus, “generous”: munus (gift) + -ficus (making).

mn.cue: MOON-IF-icent: he’d give you the MOON
mn.text: Uncle Omar would give you the moon if he could; he has already paid for the whole team’s trip. He is {munificent}.

scene.alt: A generous uncle holds up the moon itself as a gift while two children cheer.

entry.def: generous giving, or the gifts given
entry.ex: Every December the baker’s {largesse} filled the shelter’s tables with bread and pies.
entry.ctx: The tiny library survived on the {largesse} of one devoted reader, who paid for new books every year and asked for nothing in return.
entry.etym: From French largesse, from large (generous, open-handed).
entry.note: Also spelled largesse, the more common spelling today.

mn.text: From the castle wall, the queen tosses down a large sack of bread and coins for the whole village; generous giving that large is {largesse}.

scene.alt: A queen hands out a big sack of coins and bread to cheering villagers.

entry.def: greedy for money and possessions
entry.ex: The {avaricious} dragon slept on a mountain of gold and counted every coin each morning.
entry.ctx: Rex was so {avaricious} that he charged his own brother for a cup of water and hoarded his gold rather than buy himself a winter coat.
entry.etym: From avarice, from Latin avaritia (greed), from avarus (greedy).

mn.cue: HAVE-a-RICH-us: I must HAVE all the RICHES
mn.text: The dragon must have all the riches in the land and growls at anyone who comes near its pile; it is {avaricious}.

scene.alt: A greedy dragon guards a treasure chest, coins, gems and a crown in its cave.

entry.def: having plenty of money; wealthy
entry.ex: The {affluent} family spent every summer at their lake house.
entry.ctx: The fishing village was once poor, but after the harbor was rebuilt it grew {affluent}: new houses lined the hill and sailboats crowded the docks.
entry.etym: From Latin affluere, “to flow toward, to abound”: ad- (to) + fluere (to flow).

mn.text: For the Hills family, money flows in like a river; they are {affluent}.

scene.alt: A rich man in a top hat holds up a bucket as gold coins pour down from a cloud.

entry.def: without money, a home or the basic things needed to live
entry.ex: After the flood, many {destitute} families slept in the school gym until their homes could be rebuilt.
entry.ctx: Once a wealthy merchant, he lost all his ships in a single storm and was left {destitute}, with no house, no savings and only the coat on his back.
entry.etym: From Latin destitutus, “abandoned,” from destituere (to forsake, to leave without).

mn.text: After the storm sank his ship, the merchant had not a stitch to his name but the shirt he wore; he was {destitute}.

scene.alt: A shipwrecked merchant sits on the beach holding an empty wallet beside broken planks.

blocks.html: frugal is a compliment; parsimonious is a criticism. prodigal means wasteful, not "returning home," though a famous story about a prodigal son who came home made many people think so.

head: word
who it describes
praise or blame?
blocks.cap: Savers, spenders and givers: the same habit can earn praise or blame.

blocks.html: Largess (also spelled largesse) is the noun for what a munificent person gives. Affluent and destitute sit at the two ends of having: plenty and nothing.

sources.name: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), for word histories

blocks.html: Stories are full of tricksters: the fake doctor with a miracle tonic, the stranger who claims to be someone he is not, the schemer who plots in secret. This topic gives you exact words for each kind of trick and for the people who help.

Tricksters: a charlatan fakes a skill; an impostor fakes who he is; a wily person is good at tricks. Tricks: a ruse, subterfuge, chicanery, a machination. Partners in a wrong: collusion, complicit, connive.
Several of these words carry Latin pictures inside them: subterfuge is fleeing in secret, collusion is playing together, and connive is shutting your eyes.

entry.def: clever at tricking others; crafty
entry.ex: The {wily} fox waited until the farmer fell asleep, then slipped under the fence.
entry.ctx: The chess champion was {wily}: she pretended to make a careless move, then sprang a trap that won the game three turns later.
entry.etym: From wile, an old word for a sly trick.

mn.text: While the guard dog snores, the fox tiptoes off with an egg; he plans his tricks for just that moment, because he is {wily}.

labels.text: WHILE he sleeps: a WILY fox

scene.alt: A sly fox tiptoes off with an egg while the guard dog sleeps and a hen looks shocked.

entry.def: a fake who claims special knowledge or skill in order to fool people
entry.ex: The {charlatan} sold bottles of colored water as a cure for baldness.
entry.ctx: He called himself a famous healer, but he was a {charlatan}: he had never studied medicine, and his “miracle tonic” was only sugar water.
entry.etym: From Italian ciarlatano, “a quack,” a seller of fake cures.

mn.text: Charlie sells a “magic tonic” from his cart that he swears will make you fly; a man who claims a skill he does not have is a {charlatan}.

scene.alt: A man in a top hat holds up a bottle of “magic tonic” while a doubtful old man and a girl look on.

entry.def: a person who pretends to be someone else to fool others
entry.ex: The man at the door claimed to be from the water company, but he was an {impostor} with a fake badge.
entry.ctx: Everyone believed the stranger was the old captain’s long-lost nephew until a neighbor who knew the family arrived and exposed him as an {impostor}.
entry.etym: From Late Latin impostor, “a deceiver,” from imponere, “to put upon, to impose on (someone).”
entry.note: Also spelled imposter.

mn.text: Rex puts on a chef’s hat and a fake mustache and poses as the famous Chef Sven, until the real Sven walks in; Rex is an {impostor}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man in a chef’s hat and fake mustache claims to be Chef Sven as the real chef points at him.

entry.def: a trick meant to fool someone
entry.ex: The phone call about a free cruise was a {ruse} to get our bank number.
entry.ctx: The “quick stop at the dentist” was only a {ruse}; when we pulled into the lot, all my friends jumped out from behind the cars to shout “Happy birthday!”
entry.etym: From French ruse, which first meant the doubling back of a hunted animal to throw off the hounds.

mn.text: Rex offers Pip a lovely rose, but it is a joke flower that squirts water in his face; the gift was a {ruse}.

scene.alt: A man offers a boy a flower that squirts water in his face.

entry.def: a sly trick used to hide something or to get out of something
entry.ex: Pretending to be asleep was the twins’ favorite {subterfuge} for skipping chores.
entry.ctx: Unable to leave the dull party openly, Felix turned to {subterfuge}: he had a friend call him with a made-up emergency so he could slip out early.
entry.etym: From Late Latin subterfugium, from subterfugere, “to escape secretly”: subter- (beneath, secretly) + fugere (to flee).

mn.text: Pip tucks a pillow under his blanket so it looks like he is asleep, then sneaks off to play; the pillow is his {subterfuge}.

scene.alt: A boy sneaks out the door with a ball while a pillow under his blanket pretends to be him asleep.

entry.def: clever, dishonest trickery, especially in business or law
entry.ex: The card game was pure {chicanery}; the dealer had marked every ace.
entry.ctx: The contract looked fair, but it was full of {chicanery}: tiny print on the last page let the company raise the price whenever it liked.
entry.etym: From French chicanerie, from chicaner (to quibble, to argue over small points).

mn.text: Sly Victor paints a plain hen gold and swears she lays golden eggs; that kind of dishonest selling is {chicanery}.

scene.alt: A sly seller points to a hen he has painted gold, while a doubtful buyer scratches his head.

entry.def: a secret, crafty plot, usually meant to do harm
entry.ex: Despite all her rival’s {machinations}, Lila won the spelling bee fair and square.
entry.ctx: The king’s adviser smiled at court every day, but behind closed doors his {machinations} never stopped: he forged letters, bribed guards and plotted to seize the throne.
entry.etym: From Latin machinatio, “a contrivance, a plot,” from machinari (to devise, to plot), from machina (machine).
entry.note: Say it with a hard k: mak-uh-NAY-shun, like the start of mackerel.

mn.text: In his secret lab, Rex builds a giant machine with gears and levers, all to steal the town’s pie-contest trophy; his crafty plot is a {machination}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man in a lab coat plots beside gears, a robot and a board that reads “steal trophy.”

entry.def: secret teamwork for a dishonest purpose
entry.ex: The two bakeries were caught in {collusion}, secretly agreeing to raise their prices on the same day.
entry.ctx: The referee’s strange calls were no accident; an inquiry found {collusion} between him and a coach who had promised him part of the prize money.
entry.etym: From Latin collusio, from colludere, “to play together, to be in secret league”: com- (together) + ludere (to play).

mn.cue: COL + LUD: PLAYING TOGETHER in secret
mn.text: Two players on rival teams secretly agree who will win and split the prize; their dishonest teamwork is {collusion}.

scene.alt: Two players from rival teams whisper and pass a secret deal on the field.

entry.def: taking part with others in doing something wrong
entry.ex: By hiding his friend’s copy of the stolen answers, Jonah became {complicit} in the cheating.
entry.ctx: The guard did not take the painting himself, but he was {complicit}: he left the back door unlocked and looked the other way.
entry.etym: From complicity, which goes back to Latin complicare, “to fold together.”

mn.text: Kai does not take the cookies himself, but he holds the ladder while Pip climbs to the jar; as Pip’s accomplice, Kai is {complicit}.

scene.alt: One boy holds a ladder steady while another climbs up toward the cookie jar.

entry.def: to plot secretly, or to let a wrong happen by looking away
entry.ex: The two brothers {connived} to sneak the stray puppy into the house without their parents noticing.
entry.ctx: The night guard {connived} at the theft: he watched the thieves on his camera screen, then shut his eyes and said nothing.
entry.etym: From Latin connivere, “to shut the eyes,” and so to pretend not to see.
entry.note: To connive at a wrong is to let it happen on purpose; to connive with someone is to plot together.

mn.cue: CON + NIVE: shut your eyes to a CON
mn.text: The museum guard covers his eyes while Rex tiptoes past with the jewel; by pretending not to see, the guard {connives} at the theft.

scene.alt: A guard covers his eyes on purpose while a thief tiptoes past with a jewel.

blocks.html: machination is pronounced mak-uh-NAY-shun, with a hard k. collusion is secret cooperation; a collision is a crash.

blocks.cap: Tricksters, their tricks, and the people who help them.

blocks.html: Two pairs to keep straight: collusion (secret teamwork) is not collision (a crash), and a charlatan fakes a skill, while an impostor fakes an identity.

blocks.html: Some speakers never quite tell a lie, yet you leave the conversation knowing less than when you started. They hint instead of saying, dodge instead of answering, and dress up weak reasons in fancy words. This topic names their moves.
Hinting: insinuate, innuendo. Dodging: evasive, equivocate, prevaricate. Hiding: dissemble (hide your feelings), obfuscate (make it murky). Fake cleverness: glib, sophistry, quibble.
When you read an argument, these words help you say exactly what is wrong with it: not just “I don’t trust him,” but “his answer was evasive, and his reasoning was sophistry.”

entry.def: smooth and quick with words but shallow or insincere
entry.ex: The salesman had a {glib} answer for every question but never once looked us in the eye.
entry.ctx: Her apology sounded {glib}: she rattled it off in two seconds, flashed a smile and went right back to her game.

mn.text: Victor’s words glide off his lips like skates on ice: fast, smooth and with nothing underneath. His talk is {glib}.

labels.text: GL-IB: words GLIDE off the LIPS

scene.alt: A smooth-talking man winks into a microphone on stage while a doubtful old man folds his arms.

entry.def: to hint at something unpleasant without saying it outright
entry.ex: Are you trying to {insinuate} that I ate the last cookie?
entry.ctx: Rex never said outright that Lila had copied her essay; instead he {insinuated} it, raising his eyebrows and asking how she had finished so fast.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin insinuare, “to wind one’s way in”: in- (in) + sinuare (to curve), from sinus (a curve).

mn.text: Pip looks at the empty cookie jar, then slowly at Kai, and says, “Hmm, someone ate them...” He does not accuse Kai directly; he {insinuates} it.

scene.alt: A boy eyes an empty cookie plate and then his nervous friend, hinting that the friend ate the cookies.

entry.def: a sly, indirect hint, usually an unkind one about someone
entry.ex: The gossip column was full of {innuendo} but had not a single fact.
entry.ctx: The rival bakery never accused Nell outright; it spread {innuendo} instead, wondering aloud why her kitchen was always closed on Mondays.
entry.etym: From Latin innuendo, “by nodding at,” from innuere (to nod to, to hint).
entry.note: The plural is innuendos or innuendoes.

mn.cue: a NOD and a WINK, not a word
mn.text: At the bake sale, Greta winks and murmurs, “Some people’s homemade pies come from a box, I hear...” That sly, unkind hint is {innuendo}.

labels.text: IN-NU-ENDO: a NOD and a WINK

scene.alt: At a bake sale, a woman winks and whispers an unkind hint about the baker, who looks annoyed.

entry.def: avoiding a direct answer or a clear statement
entry.ex: When asked where the cake had gone, the twins gave {evasive} answers about the weather.
entry.ctx: Usually Dev answered questions in detail, but about his report card he was strangely {evasive}, changing the subject every time his mother brought it up.
entry.etym: From evade, from Latin evadere, “to go out, to escape”: e- (out) + vadere (to go).

mn.cue: EVADE the question like a dodgeball
mn.text: Granny Mae asks who broke the lamp, and Pip ducks the question like a dodgeball: “Nice weather, huh?” His answer is {evasive}.

scene.alt: A grandmother asks who broke the lamp, and a boy dodges sideways, talking about the weather.

entry.def: to use vague or double-meaning words to avoid taking a clear position
entry.ex: Asked if he liked the new haircut, Dad {equivocated}: “Well, it’s certainly... different.”
entry.ctx: Instead of saying yes or no, the coach began to {equivocate}, talking about “options” and “seeing how things go” until the players gave up asking.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Late Latin aequivocus, “having the same sound, meaning two things”: aequi- (equal) + vox (voice).

mn.cue: EQUAL VOICES: yes AND no at once
mn.text: Asked if he likes Aunt Tia’s purple soup, Sami says, “Well, it’s... very purple!” His answer could mean yes or no; he {equivocates}.

scene.alt: An aunt offers a bowl of purple soup, and a boy shrugs, giving an answer that is neither yes nor no.

entry.def: to dodge the truth, often by speaking in a misleading way
entry.ex: When the teacher asked about the missing homework, Jonah began to {prevaricate}, spinning a long tale about a windstorm.
entry.ctx: The witness did not tell an outright lie, but she {prevaricated}, giving answers so slippery that the jury could not tell what she had really seen.
entry.etym: From Latin praevaricari, “to walk crookedly, to straddle,” and so to play false.

mn.text: Caught beside the broken vase, the cat varies its story every minute: first the wind did it, then the dog. That cat loves to {prevaricate}.

scene.alt: A cat beside a broken vase blames the dog, who looks shocked.

entry.def: to hide one’s true feelings or aims behind a false show
entry.ex: Though she was crushed by the news, Maya {dissembled} and smiled through the whole party.
entry.ctx: The spy had to {dissemble} for years, chatting cheerfully with the guards while secretly mapping every hallway of the fortress.
entry.etym: From Latin dissimulare, “to hide, to disguise”: dis- (not) + simulare (to make like, to pretend).
entry.note: Do not confuse dissemble (hide your feelings) with disassemble (take apart).

mn.cue: a mask that does NOT RESEMBLE you
mn.text: Maya is sad inside, but she holds up a smiling mask that does not resemble her real face at all; to hide your feelings that way is to {dissemble}.

scene.alt: A sad girl on a stage holds up a smiling mask to hide her true feelings.

entry.def: to make something confusing or unclear on purpose
entry.ex: The instructions were so full of jargon that they seemed meant to {obfuscate} rather than explain.
entry.ctx: Rather than admit the mistake, the company tried to {obfuscate} it, burying one honest sentence inside forty pages of technical language.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin obfuscare, “to darken”: ob- (over) + fuscus (dark).

mn.cue: OB-FUSC: make it DARK and murky
mn.text: To slip away, the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink until no one can see a thing; making things murky on purpose is to {obfuscate}.

scene.alt: An octopus squirts a dark cloud of ink while a confused fish cannot see through it.

entry.def: clever-sounding reasoning that is false or misleading
entry.ex: His argument that homework is bad because it wastes pencils was pure {sophistry}.
entry.ctx: The lawyer’s case sounded brilliant at first, but it was {sophistry}: each step seemed logical, yet together they proved something everyone knew was false.
entry.etym: From sophist, from Greek sophistes, “an expert, a wise man”; some teachers called sophists in ancient Greece became known for tricky arguments.

mn.text: Sami proves at the board that cats have four legs, his dog has four legs, so his dog must be a cat; it sounds clever, but it is {sophistry}.

scene.alt: A proud boy in a graduation cap “proves” on the board that his dog is a cat, while the dog looks puzzled.

entry.def: to argue or complain about small, unimportant points
entry.ex: Let’s not {quibble} over a nickel; just split the bill.
entry.ctx: Instead of fixing the big flaws in the plan, the committee spent an hour {quibbling} over whether the posters should be blue or teal.

mn.text: Pip and Lila argue for an hour over who gets the last tiny nibble of cookie; to argue over something that small is to {quibble}.

scene.alt: Two children point and argue across a table over a single tiny crumb of cookie.

blocks.html: dissemble (hide one's motives) is not disassemble (take apart). equivocate and prevaricate both dodge the truth; prevaricate leans toward lying.

words

rows: suggests something unkind without saying it
avoids a straight answer; prevaricate comes closest to lying
hides true feelings; makes things murky
smooth but shallow; false reasoning; fusses over trifles
blocks.cap: Four kinds of slippery speech.

blocks.html: Insinuate is the verb; innuendo is the noun for the hint itself. And dissemble (hide your feelings) is not disassemble (take apart).

blocks.html: Two uncomfortable feelings share this topic. Regret comes from knowing you did wrong: you feel sorry and want to make it right. Embarrassment comes from being seen doing something silly: your face goes red and you wish you could disappear.

Sorry for a wrong: remorse, contrite, penitent, compunction, rueful, and the verb atone (make up for it). Embarrassed: sheepish and abashed (mild), chagrin (embarrassed and annoyed), mortified (deeply embarrassed).
Several of these words hold sharp Latin pictures: remorse is a wrong that keeps biting you, contrite means crushed, and compunction is a prick of guilt, like a pin.

entry.def: deep, painful regret for having done wrong
entry.ex: Filled with {remorse}, Kai gave back the toy he had taken and apologized to his little brother.
entry.ctx: The vandal showed no {remorse} in court; he smirked through the whole hearing and never once apologized to the shop owner whose window he had smashed.
entry.etym: From Latin remordere, “to bite again”: re- (again) + mordere (to bite). Remorse is a wrong that keeps biting you.

mn.text: Kai broke his brother’s toy truck, and the guilt keeps biting at him all evening until he hands over his own teddy bear; that biting regret is {remorse}.

scene.alt: A sorry boy kneels and gives his teddy bear to his crying little brother beside a broken toy wagon.

entry.def: truly sorry for having done wrong
entry.ex: The {contrite} puppy crept out from under the table after chewing Dad’s slipper.
entry.ctx: At first Dev insisted the broken window was not his fault, but by dinner he was {contrite}, offering to pay for the glass from his own savings.
entry.etym: From Latin contritus, “crushed,” from conterere (to grind, to crush): a contrite person feels crushed by guilt.

mn.text: After chewing Dad’s slipper to bits, Rufus creeps over with his ears down and lays it at Dad’s feet; the crushed, sorry pup is {contrite}.

scene.alt: A sad puppy lies with its ears down beside a chewed slipper, apologizing to its owner.

entry.def: sorry for doing wrong and wanting to make up for it
entry.ex: The {penitent} boy swept up every bit of the vase he had knocked over.
entry.ctx: Unlike his brother, who shrugged off the scolding, Sam was {penitent}: he apologized to the neighbor and offered to mow her lawn for a month.
entry.etym: From Latin paenitens, “regretting,” from paenitere (to regret).

mn.text: After breaking Granny’s teapot, Pip takes a pen and writes “Sorry!” ten times on a big card, then offers to wash her dishes all week; he is {penitent}.

scene.alt: A sorry boy hands his grandmother a card that says sorry, next to the teapot he broke.

entry.def: showing regret, often with a sad or wry smile
entry.ex: With a {rueful} grin, Grandpa admitted he had locked the keys in the car again.
entry.ctx: Looking at the blackened cookies, Nell gave a {rueful} laugh: she had set the timer for twenty minutes instead of ten, and there was no one to blame but herself.
entry.etym: From Middle English rewful: rewe (sorrow, pity) + -ful.

mn.text: Pip kicks his new ball right onto the roof, then looks up with a sorry little half smile: “Oops.” That regretful look is {rueful}.

scene.alt: A boy scratches his head with a sorry half smile, looking up at the ball he kicked onto a roof.

entry.def: a twinge of guilt or doubt that stops or follows a wrong act
entry.ex: The raccoon ate the whole pie without the slightest {compunction}.
entry.ctx: Lila felt no {compunction} about pointing out the error on the board, but later she felt a pang of guilt when she saw how embarrassed her teacher looked.
entry.etym: From Latin compungere, “to prick hard, to sting”: com- (thoroughly) + pungere (to prick).
entry.note: It is most often used with no or without: “He took the last slice without compunction” means he felt no guilt at all.

mn.text: Reaching for her sister’s candy, Ivy feels a little prick of guilt, sharp as a cactus needle, and pulls her hand back; that twinge is {compunction}.

scene.alt: A girl reaches for her sister’s candy jar, then pauses with a twinge of guilt.

entry.def: to make up for a wrong one has done
entry.ex: To {atone} for forgetting her birthday, Sami baked his sister a three-layer cake.
entry.ctx: Having missed three practices, the goalie tried to {atone} for his absence by arriving early every day and staying late to pick up the cones.
entry.etym: From the phrase at one, “in harmony”: to atone first meant to become friends again.

mn.cue: AT ONE again: make it up
mn.text: Kai broke Lila’s kite, so he spends his whole Saturday building her a new one; he wants to {atone} for the wrong and be at one with her again.

cast.say: I made you a new one!

scene.alt: A boy gives a girl a new kite he built to make up for breaking hers, and she cheers.

entry.def: annoyance mixed with embarrassment, often after a failure
entry.ex: To his {chagrin}, Felix discovered he had worn mismatched shoes to the job interview.
entry.ctx: Much to the chef’s {chagrin}, the judges praised his rival’s simple soup and barely tasted the fancy dessert he had worked on all week.
entry.etym: From French chagrin, “sad, grief.”

mn.text: Felix slips in a puddle right in front of the whole bus stop, gets up red-faced and cross, and forces a shaky grin; that sour, embarrassed feeling is {chagrin}.

scene.alt: A man who just slipped in a puddle covers his eyes, red-faced and annoyed, as a girl laughs.

entry.def: deeply embarrassed or ashamed
entry.ex: Lin was {mortified} when her phone rang loudly in the middle of the school play.
entry.ctx: Jamal had bragged all week about his cooking, so he was {mortified} when his guests politely pushed the salty stew aside and asked if anyone wanted to order pizza.
entry.etym: From mortify, from Latin mortificare, “to put to death”: to be mortified is to feel you could die of embarrassment.

mn.cue: MORT = death: could DIE of shame
mn.text: When Lin’s phone blares a quacking ringtone in the silent theater, she wishes the floor would swallow her; she is {mortified}.

scene.alt: A woman blushes in horror as her phone rings in a quiet theater, while others glare and shush her.

entry.def: embarrassed and a little ashamed
entry.ex: Caught singing at the top of his lungs in the shower, Dev came out looking {abashed}.
entry.ctx: Jonah, usually so bold, stood {abashed} before the principal, staring at his shoes and mumbling that he had not meant to start the food fight.

mn.text: Caught with frosting on his nose after sneaking a taste of the birthday cake, Pip turns red and stares at his shoes, as bashful as can be; he is {abashed}.

scene.alt: A boy with frosting on his nose hides his face in embarrassment while his mother grins at him.

entry.def: embarrassed from knowing one has done something silly
entry.ex: Grandpa gave a {sheepish} smile when he found his glasses on top of his head.
entry.ctx: After insisting that the remote was broken, Dad wore a {sheepish} grin when we pointed out that he had forgotten to put the batteries in.
entry.etym: From sheep + -ish; at first it meant meek and timid, like a sheep.

mn.text: The sheep tries to jump the fence, lands in the pigs’ mud instead, and looks up with an embarrassed little grin; it looks {sheepish}.

scene.alt: A sheep with a muddy, embarrassed grin stands in a mud puddle while a pig laughs.

blocks.html: chagrin mixes embarrassment with annoyance. "Without compunction" means without any guilt.

head: word
feeling
strength
rows: embarrassed enough to want to vanish
sorry and ready to make up for it
guilt that will not stop biting
blocks.cap: Embarrassment and regret, from mild to strong.

blocks.html: You will often meet compunction in the negative: someone who acts without compunction or with no compunction feels no guilt at all. And to atone is what a penitent person does: make up for the wrong.

blocks.html: Some things are plain to see; others only seem true; and some are understood without anyone saying a word. Careful readers notice which is which, because writers use these words to tell you how much to trust a claim.

Plain to see: manifest, patent, unmistakable, palpable (you can almost touch it), overt (done in the open). Plain and shameless: blatant, flagrant. Only seeming: ostensible, purported. Unspoken: tacit.
When a passage says the ostensible reason or the purported letter, the writer is warning you: this is what was claimed, not necessarily what is true.

entry.def: clear and plain to see or understand
entry.ex: Her joy was {manifest} in the way she skipped all the way home.
entry.ctx: Though he said nothing, Gus’s disappointment was {manifest}: his shoulders slumped, his smile vanished and he left the party early.
entry.etym: From Latin manifestus, “caught in the act, plain to see.”
entry.note: As a verb, manifest means to show plainly: her worry manifested itself in sleepless nights.

mn.text: Pip swears he never touched the paint, but his hands and nose are bright blue; his guilt is {manifest}.

scene.alt: A boy with paint dripping from his hands insists he did not spill the blue paint as his mother points at him.

entry.def: so strong or clear that it can almost be touched
entry.ex: The tension in the room was {palpable} as the judges opened the envelope.
entry.ctx: As the last runner neared the finish line, the excitement in the stadium was {palpable}; strangers grabbed one another’s arms, and no one could sit still.
entry.etym: From Late Latin palpabilis, “able to be touched,” from palpare (to touch gently, to stroke).

mn.cue: PALP-ABLE: you could almost PAT it
mn.text: As the spelling bee reaches its last word, the nerves in the room are so thick that you could almost reach out and pat them; the tension is {palpable}.

scene.alt: Three nervous students at a spelling bee tremble; one reaches out as if the tension could be touched.

entry.def: done or shown openly, not hidden
entry.ex: Lila’s {overt} yawning during the long speech made the speaker frown.
entry.ctx: Unlike the sly hints her brother dropped, Ivy’s request was {overt}: she taped a picture of the bike she wanted right on the refrigerator door.
entry.etym: From Old French overt, “opened,” from ovrir (to open).

mn.cue: OVER-T: right out in the OPEN
mn.text: Ivy does not drop hints; she hangs a giant sign over the fridge that says “I WANT A BIKE!” Her wish is {overt}.

scene.alt: A girl points proudly at a huge banner that says she wants a bike, as her father laughs.

entry.def: completely obvious and done without shame
entry.ex: Copying your neighbor’s answers word for word is {blatant} cheating.
entry.ctx: Jonah’s excuse was a {blatant} lie; he claimed he had been home all evening, but half the class had seen him at the arcade.

mn.cue: BLAT-ant: as loud as a BLARING horn
mn.text: Rex copies Pip’s test while reading the answers out loud, as loud as a blaring horn; cheating that shameless and obvious is {blatant}.

scene.alt: A teen leans over a boy’s test and loudly reads the answers, cheating without hiding it.

entry.def: shockingly obvious and wrong
entry.ex: Picking up the soccer ball and running it into the goal was a {flagrant} break of the rules.
entry.ctx: Parking across three spaces in front of the hospital entrance was a {flagrant} violation, and the driver came back to find a ticket on his windshield.
entry.etym: From Latin flagrans, “burning, blazing,” from flagrare (to burn).
entry.note: Flagrant (shockingly obvious) is not fragrant (sweet-smelling). Flagrant suggests a wrong that blazes; blatant suggests one done without shame.

mn.cue: FLAG + RANT: a wrong that BLAZES
mn.text: Rex picks up the soccer ball and carries it into the goal; the referee waves her red flag and rants. A foul that glaringly wrong is {flagrant}.

scene.alt: A player runs off carrying the soccer ball in his hands while an angry referee waves a red flag.

entry.def: plain and obvious
entry.ex: His story about a dog eating his homework was a {patent} fib; he doesn’t even have a dog.
entry.ctx: The claim that the old bridge was safe was {patent} nonsense: anyone could see the cracks running through its stone arches.
entry.etym: From Latin patens, “lying open,” from patere (to be open).
entry.note: As a noun, a patent is the legal right to an invention. The adjective is most often met in the adverb patently: a patently false claim.

mn.cue: PAT’S TENT: as plain as can be
mn.text: Pat pitches a bright orange tent in the middle of the lawn and calls it her secret hideout; that hiding place is {patent} to everyone.

scene.alt: A girl named Pat waves from a big orange tent she calls a secret hideout while a boy laughs and points.

entry.def: stated or seeming to be true, but perhaps not the real thing
entry.ex: The {ostensible} reason for his visit was to return a book, but he stayed for three helpings of pie.
entry.ctx: Her {ostensible} purpose in calling was to ask about homework, but it soon became clear that she really wanted to know who was going to the dance.
entry.etym: From Latin ostendere, “to show, to hold out for view”: the ostensible reason is the one held up for show.

mn.text: Dev says he is visiting Nana Lou to fix her clock, which sounds sensible, but his eyes are on her cookies; fixing the clock is his {ostensible} reason.

scene.alt: A teen with a toolbox says he came to fix his grandmother’s clock, but he is really eyeing her cookies.

entry.def: claimed or said to be, but not proven
entry.ex: The museum showed a {purported} dinosaur egg that turned out to be a smooth river stone.
entry.ctx: The {purported} treasure map was a fake; experts showed that its “ancient” paper was only a few years old.
entry.etym: From purport, from Old French purporter, “to carry, to convey”: pur- (forth) + porter (to carry).

mn.text: The seller swears his purring cat once belonged to a king, but he has no proof at all; it is only the {purported} royal cat.

scene.alt: A seller claims his purring cat in a tiny crown belonged to a king, while a doubtful teen asks for proof.

entry.def: understood without being said out loud
entry.ex: With a {tacit} nod, the twins agreed to keep the surprise party a secret.
entry.ctx: No one ever announced the rule, but there was a {tacit} agreement in the house: whoever cooked dinner did not have to wash the dishes.
entry.etym: From Latin tacitus, “silent,” from tacere (to be silent). Taciturn comes from the same root.

mn.cue: TAC = SILENT: a deal with no words
mn.text: Across the dinner table, Zoe winks and Kai nods; without a word, they agree to swap peas for carrots. Their deal is {tacit}.

scene.alt: Two children wink at each other across a table, agreeing without a word.

entry.def: impossible to mistake for anything else; very clear
entry.ex: The {unmistakable} smell of fresh bread drifted down the street from the bakery.
entry.ctx: Even in the crowded station, Grandpa’s laugh was {unmistakable}; we simply followed the booming sound and found him by the ticket window.

mn.cue: UN-MISTAKE-ABLE: a giraffe in a crowd
mn.text: Grandpa brings his pet giraffe to the busy station; in a crowd of a hundred people, no one could mistake where he is. The giraffe is {unmistakable}.

scene.alt: A grandfather waves from a crowded station beside his very tall pet giraffe.

blocks.html: flagrant (shockingly obvious) is not fragrant. ostensible means "apparent, but maybe not real": the ostensible reason may hide the real one.

blocks.html: Flagrant (from Latin for blazing) is not fragrant (sweet-smelling). And when you see ostensibly, expect a twist: “Ostensibly, he came to help; in fact, he came to eat.”

blocks.html: Some things happen because people plan them; others happen by chance. English has a whole family of words for chance, from happy surprises to small accidents to full-scale disasters.

Chance itself: fortuitous, happenstance, fluke. Good luck: serendipity (lucky finds), windfall (unexpected gain), propitious (favorable signs). Bad luck: hapless (unlucky), mishap (a small accident), calamity (a disaster), debacle (a total failure).
Look for the old word hap, which meant luck or chance: it hides in happen, happy, perhaps, hapless, mishap and happenstance.

entry.def: happening by chance, often by lucky chance
entry.ex: Our meeting at the airport was {fortuitous}: neither of us knew the other was flying that day.
entry.ctx: The discovery was {fortuitous} rather than planned; the scientist had been studying something else entirely when she noticed the strange glow in her dish.
entry.etym: From Latin fortuitus, “happening by chance,” from fors (chance).
entry.note: Fortuitous first meant only “by chance,” lucky or not. Today it often means “happening by lucky chance,” and dictionaries accept both.

mn.text: Caught in the rain, Lila ducks under a shop awning and finds her old best friend sheltering there too; the meeting, pure chance and good fortune, is {fortuitous}.

scene.alt: Two old friends who met by chance in the rain hug under an umbrella.

entry.def: the luck of finding good things without looking for them
entry.ex: By pure {serendipity}, Sami found his favorite book at a yard sale for a dime.
entry.ctx: Searching the attic for a flashlight, Grandma found her mother’s long-lost diary instead; she called it {serendipity}, since she had given up hope of ever seeing it again.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: Coined in 1754 from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka, after a Persian fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept finding things they were not looking for.

mn.cue: a SERENE DIP finds a treasure
mn.text: Taking a serene dip in the lake, Omar feels something under his toes: a lost gold ring. Finding something wonderful without looking for it is {serendipity}.

scene.alt: A man wading at the beach holds up a gold ring he found by chance under his toes.

entry.def: favorable; likely to lead to success
entry.ex: Clear skies and a steady breeze made it a {propitious} day for the kite festival.
entry.ctx: With customers lining up out the door every morning, the owners decided it was a {propitious} moment to open a second bakery across town.
entry.etym: From Latin propitius, “favorable, well-disposed.”

mn.cue: a PRO-FISH day: every sign says GO
mn.text: The old fisherman sees calm water, a rainbow and fish leaping all around his boat; every sign is good, so it is a {propitious} day to fish.

scene.alt: A happy fisherman in a rowboat points at leaping fish under a rainbow.

entry.def: a lucky or unlikely chance happening
entry.ex: Her first basket from half court was a {fluke}; she missed the next twenty.
entry.ctx: Some called the underdogs’ win a {fluke}, but when the team won its next three games as well, the doubters went quiet.
entry.note: A fluke is also a kind of flatfish and one of the two halves of a whale’s tail; the “lucky chance” fluke is a separate word.

mn.text: Pip tosses a paper ball over his shoulder without even looking, and it flies straight into the trash can across the room; a lucky shot like that is a {fluke}.

scene.alt: A boy is amazed as a paper ball he tossed without looking flies into a far-off trash can.

entry.def: a chance happening; a coincidence
entry.ex: By {happenstance}, the two cousins ended up in the same college dorm.
entry.ctx: Their friendship began through {happenstance}, not planning: both had grabbed the same umbrella from the lost-and-found box on the same rainy afternoon.
entry.etym: A blend of happen and circumstance.

mn.text: Two strangers reach for the very last loaf of bread at the same moment and end up sharing a picnic; their meeting just happened, by {happenstance}.

scene.alt: A man and a woman reach for the same last loaf of bread at the same moment and laugh.

entry.def: an unexpected gain, such as money one did not work for
entry.ex: A {windfall} from a forgotten savings account paid for the family’s trip to the coast.
entry.ctx: The town had no money for a new library; the funds came as a {windfall} when a dusty painting in the town hall attic turned out to be worth a fortune.
entry.etym: First meant fruit or trees blown down by the wind, free for anyone to gather.

mn.cue: the WIND makes the fruit FALL
mn.text: A gust of wind shakes the old tree, and a dozen ripe pieces of fruit tumble right into Ivy’s basket; a gift you did not work for is a {windfall}.

scene.alt: Wind blows fruit off a tree, and it falls straight into a delighted girl’s basket.

entry.def: unlucky; having one bad break after another
entry.ex: The {hapless} hiker lost his map, then his hat, then his left boot.
entry.ctx: The {hapless} goalie had a miserable afternoon: the sun was in his eyes, his glove tore, and the winning goal bounced in off his own knee.
entry.etym: From Middle English hap (luck) + -less: without luck.
entry.note: Hapless means unlucky, not helpless.

mn.text: Poor Felix: a crow steals his sandwich, a rain cloud follows only him, and his umbrella turns inside out. With no luck at all, he is {hapless}.

scene.alt: A rain cloud pours on a sad man while a crow flies off with his sandwich.

entry.def: a disaster that causes great loss or suffering
entry.ex: The flood was the worst {calamity} the valley had seen in a hundred years.
entry.ctx: What began as a small kitchen fire became a {calamity}: the flames spread down the whole block, and dozens of families lost their homes.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin calamitas, “disaster, misfortune.”

mn.cue: no CALM at all: a disaster
mn.text: A giant wave sweeps away the whole sandcastle city the children spent all day building; to them, it is a {calamity}.

scene.alt: Two children panic as a huge wave crashes over the sandcastle city they built.

entry.def: a small accident or bit of bad luck
entry.ex: Apart from one {mishap} with a spilled paint can, the mural went up without trouble.
entry.ctx: The camping trip had only one {mishap}: a raccoon stole our pancakes, but nobody was hurt, and we laughed about it for weeks.
entry.etym: From Middle English: mis- (bad) + hap (chance), the same hap found in happen and perhaps.

mn.cue: MIS + HAP: a little BAD LUCK
mn.text: Ivy trips, and her ice cream cone lands upside down on the dog’s head; it is only a small {mishap}, and the dog does not mind one bit.

scene.alt: A girl trips and her ice cream lands on a happy dog’s head.

entry.def: a sudden and complete failure
entry.ex: The school play was a {debacle}: the curtain fell, the lights went out and the lead forgot every line.
entry.ctx: The new phone’s launch was a {debacle}; the batteries overheated, the stores ran out of chargers, and the company had to take back every phone within a week.
entry.etym: From French débâcle, the breaking up of ice on a river, from débâcler (to unbolt, to set free).

mn.cue: de-BAKE-le: the bake-off that fell apart
mn.text: At the big bake-off, Nell’s tower cake wobbles, tilts and crashes onto the judges’ table; the whole entry is a {debacle}.

scene.alt: A baker panics as her tall cake topples onto the judge’s table.

blocks.html: fortuitous first meant "by chance," good or bad; today it is often used to mean lucky. hapless means unlucky, not helpless.

rows: bad: a disaster; a total failure

blocks.html: The old word hap (luck) explains three of these words: hapless is luck-less, a mishap is bad luck, and happenstance is what just happens.

blocks.html: English has many words for destroying, and each one paints a slightly different picture: knocking down, laying waste, pulling up by the roots, wiping out every letter, or taking apart piece by piece.
Knocking down buildings: demolish, raze. Wide damage: devastate, ravage, decimate (a large part). Wiping out every trace: eradicate, annihilate, obliterate, expunge. Taking apart: dismantle.
Many of these words carry Latin pictures: eradicate holds radix (root), annihilate holds nihil (nothing), obliterate holds littera (letter), and decimate holds decimus (tenth).

entry.def: to knock down or destroy completely
entry.ex: The crew will {demolish} the old warehouse to make room for a park.
entry.ctx: The debate champion did more than disagree with her opponent’s claim; she {demolished} it, showing that every one of his facts was wrong.
entry.etym: From Latin demoliri, “to tear down”: de- (down) + moliri (to build, to heave a great mass).

mn.text: Theo spends one second looking at his sister’s tall block tower, then knocks the whole thing flat; he can {demolish} it faster than anyone can build it.

scene.alt: A laughing toddler knocks down a tall tower of blocks while his sister gasps.

entry.def: to destroy over a wide area; also, to overwhelm with grief or shock
entry.ex: The hailstorm {devastated} the farmer’s whole field of corn.
entry.ctx: The news {devastated} the team; after a season of hard work, they had been knocked out of the tournament because of a mistake on a single form.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin devastare, “to lay waste”: de- (completely) + vastare (to lay waste), from vastus (empty, vast).

mn.cue: DE-VAST-ATE: a VAST field laid waste
mn.text: A storm flattens a vast field of sunflowers in a single night, and the farmer drops to her knees; the storm has {devastated} her farm.

scene.alt: A farmer kneels in tears as a storm flattens her field of flowers.

entry.def: to damage badly and violently
entry.ex: Locusts {ravaged} the valley, stripping every field bare.
entry.ctx: The wildfire {ravaged} the hills for a week, leaving blackened trunks where green forest had stood.
entry.etym: From French ravager, from ravir (to seize, to carry off).
entry.note: The plural noun ravages means heavy damage: the ravages of time, the ravages of war.

mn.text: A herd of ravenous goats storms through Granny Mae’s garden and leaves nothing but stalks and torn petals; they {ravage} it.

scene.alt: Two goats tear through a garden, scattering leaves and flowers, as a grandmother cries out.

entry.def: to wipe out completely, as if pulling up by the roots
entry.ex: The town worked for years to {eradicate} the weeds choking the pond.
entry.ctx: Health workers set out to {eradicate} the disease entirely, vaccinating children in every village until not a single new case was reported.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin eradicare, “to pull out by the roots”: e- (out) + radix (root). Radish comes from radix too.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus does not just snip the weed; he yanks it out by the roots like a radish so it can never grow back. He wants to {eradicate} it.

scene.alt: A grandfather leans back and yanks a weed out of the ground, roots and all.

entry.def: to destroy completely; also, to defeat by a huge margin
entry.ex: In the board game final, Maya {annihilated} her brothers, winning by four hundred points.
entry.ctx: The volcano’s eruption {annihilated} the island’s forest; where thousands of trees had stood, there was nothing but gray ash.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Late Latin annihilare, “to bring to nothing”: ad- (to) + nihil (nothing).

mn.text: Zoe wins the checkers final 400 to nil; her brother is left with nothing at all. She {annihilates} him.

scene.alt: A girl cheers beside a scoreboard reading 400 to 0 while her brother covers his eyes.

entry.def: to wipe out so completely that no trace is left
entry.ex: The tide {obliterated} the names we had written in the sand.
entry.ctx: Years of wind and rain had {obliterated} the painted letters on the old barn, so no one remembered what the farm had once been called.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin obliterare, “to blot out, to make forgotten”: ob- (against) + littera (letter).

mn.text: Lila writes her name in huge letters on the sand, and one big wave wipes out every letter until no trace is left; the wave {obliterates} it.

scene.alt: A wave washes over a girl’s name written in the sand, wiping out the letters.

entry.def: to destroy a large part of something
entry.ex: A harsh winter {decimated} the deer herd, leaving only a few dozen animals.
entry.ctx: The new highway {decimated} the little town’s business: with drivers speeding past, most of its diners and gas stations closed within two years.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin decimare, from decimus (tenth). It first named a harsh Roman army punishment that struck one soldier in every ten.

mn.cue: DECI = TEN, but now MOST are gone
mn.text: Nell baked a hundred cookies; while she answered the door, the dog ate all but ten. He {decimated} the batch.

scene.alt: A happy dog sits by a nearly empty cookie plate while the baker cries out.

entry.def: to tear down completely, all the way to the ground
entry.ex: The city plans to {raze} the crumbling old mill next spring.
entry.ctx: Rather than repair the leaning barn, the farmers decided to {raze} it; by evening nothing was left but a flat patch of dirt where it had stood.
entry.etym: From older English rase, “to scrape, to shave off.”
entry.note: Raze sounds just like raise, but the two are opposites: to raise a barn is to build it; to raze it is to tear it down.

mn.cue: RAZE is the opposite of RAISE
mn.text: On one lot the crew raises a new house; on the next lot they tear the old one flat. To {raze} a building is the opposite of raising it.

scene.alt: On one side a builder stands by a new house; on the other, an old building lies flattened in a cloud of dust.

entry.def: to erase or remove completely
entry.ex: Once the mistake was found, the school {expunged} the late mark from her record.
entry.ctx: The judge agreed to {expunge} the old charge from his record, so it would no longer appear when employers checked his background.
entry.etym: From Latin expungere, “to mark for deletion with dots”: ex- (out) + pungere (to prick).

mn.text: Coach Omar takes a big wet sponge and wipes Kai’s name off the list of late players; the mark is gone, {expunged}.

scene.alt: A coach wipes a boy’s name off the late list with a sponge while the boy cheers.

entry.def: to take apart piece by piece
entry.ex: Dad had to {dismantle} the bunk bed to get it through the doorway.
entry.ctx: Rather than repair the broken clock, the curious student {dismantled} it, laying every gear and spring on the table in neat rows.
entry.etym: From Middle French desmanteler, “to strip of a cloak,” and so of a fort’s walls: des- (away) + mantel (cloak).

mn.cue: DIS-MAN-TLE: the robot MAN in pieces
mn.text: Sami unscrews the old robot man bolt by bolt and lines every piece up on the floor; he {dismantles} it to see how it works.

scene.alt: A boy in goggles kneels with a wrench, taking a robot apart and lining up its gears.

blocks.html: decimate once meant destroying one in ten; today it means destroying a large part, not all. raze (tear down) sounds like raise (build up).

blocks.html: Decimate once meant destroying exactly one in ten; today it means destroying a large part, but not all. If everything is gone, choose annihilate or obliterate.

blocks.html: Secrets come in many shapes: a plan kept quiet, a glance no one is meant to see, a talent no one has discovered yet, a message no one can read. This topic gives each its own word.

Secret actions: covert, clandestine, surreptitious, furtive, stealthy. Hidden meanings and motives: cryptic, veiled, ulterior. Hidden things: latent (there but not yet showing), elusive (hard to catch).

Notice the shades. Covert and clandestine describe whole plans; surreptitious, furtive and stealthy describe how a person moves or looks; and furtive adds a guilty air, since it comes from the Latin word for thief.

entry.def: secret; not openly shown or done
entry.ex: Lila shot a {covert} glance at the clock, hoping the teacher would not notice.
entry.ctx: The surprise party was a {covert} operation: invitations were passed in whispers, and the guest of honor never suspected a thing.
entry.etym: From Old French covert, “covered,” from covrir (to cover).

mn.text: Behind the sofa, under a blanket, the cousins whisper their plans for Mom’s surprise party; the whole plan is kept under cover, {covert}.

scene.alt: Two children hide behind a sofa, whispering surprise-party plans while their mother reads, unaware.

entry.def: done in secret, often because it is not allowed
entry.ex: The twins held a {clandestine} midnight feast in the attic.
entry.ctx: Because the old king had banned all music, the villagers held {clandestine} concerts in barns and cellars, with lookouts posted at every door.
entry.etym: From Latin clandestinus, “secret,” from clam (secretly).

mn.text: At midnight the cat clan meets on the rooftop by lantern light, so the dogs below never find out; their meeting is {clandestine}.

scene.alt: Three cats meet secretly by lantern light at night while a dog sleeps nearby.

entry.def: done secretly so as not to be noticed
entry.ex: Kai slipped a {surreptitious} carrot to the dog under the table.
entry.ctx: During the long speech, Rosa took a {surreptitious} look at her phone, tilting it below the table so the speaker would not notice.
entry.etym: From Latin surripere, “to snatch secretly”: sub- (under, secretly) + rapere (to seize).

mn.text: When Mom turns to the stove, Kai sneaks his carrots under the table to the dog; the quick, secret handoff is {surreptitious}.

scene.alt: A boy secretly passes a carrot to the dog under the table while his mother looks away.

entry.def: sly and secret, as if trying not to get caught
entry.ex: The raccoon cast a {furtive} look over its shoulder before diving into the trash can.
entry.ctx: His {furtive} manner gave him away: he kept glancing at the door, hiding his hands in his pockets and jumping whenever anyone spoke.
entry.etym: From Latin furtivus, “stolen, secret,” from fur (thief).

mn.cue: FUR = THIEF: a sly, guilty look
mn.text: The furry little thief tiptoes off with the fish, glancing back over its shoulder again and again; that sly, guilty look is {furtive}.

scene.alt: A cat sneaks away with a fish, glancing back guiltily, while the cook looks the other way.

entry.def: moving quietly and carefully so as not to be noticed
entry.ex: The {stealthy} cat crept up on the butterfly without rustling a single leaf.
entry.ctx: Unlike his noisy brother, who stomped up the stairs, Jonah was {stealthy}, slipping out the back door so quietly that even the dog did not wake.
entry.etym: From stealth, which comes from the same old English root as steal.

mn.cue: STEAL-THY: steal past without a sound
mn.text: Jonah tiptoes past the sleeping dog in his socks, carrying his shoes; he steals by so quietly that he is {stealthy}.

scene.alt: A teen tiptoes in his socks past a sleeping dog, carrying his shoes.

entry.def: present but hidden, or not yet active
entry.ex: Lin had a {latent} gift for singing that no one discovered until the school musical.
entry.ctx: The seeds lay {latent} in the dry desert soil for years; then a single heavy rain woke them, and the sand burst into bloom.
entry.etym: From Latin latens, “lying hidden,” from latere (to lie hidden).

mn.cue: LATE-nt: there all along, it shows up LATE
mn.text: Seeds sleep in the desert sand for years, then bloom late, after one rare rain; the flowers were {latent} there the whole time.

scene.alt: After a rare rain, flowers suddenly bloom from the desert sand while a girl cheers.

entry.def: mysterious and hard to understand
entry.ex: Grandpa left a {cryptic} note on the fridge: “Look where the moon sleeps.”
entry.ctx: The treasure map’s directions were {cryptic}; instead of plain steps, they gave riddles about crooked trees and a rock that “laughs at the sea.”
entry.etym: From Late Latin crypticus, from Greek kryptikos, “hidden,” from kryptein (to hide). A crypt is a hidden room.

mn.cue: CRYPT = hidden: a note in CODE
mn.text: Pip finds a note that says only “ZEBRA AT NOON, UNDER THE SECOND MOON,” and no one can work out what it means; it is {cryptic}.

scene.alt: A boy and an old professor puzzle over a mysterious coded note.

entry.def: partly hidden; hinted at but not said openly
entry.ex: Her remark about his “interesting” shoes was a {veiled} criticism.
entry.ctx: The coach never said outright that the team had played poorly, but his {veiled} comment about “players who think practice is optional” made everyone stare at the floor.
entry.etym: From veil, a thin cloth that covers the face: you can almost see what is behind it.

mn.text: Nana Lou smiles and says, “What lively music, dear!” but her hands are over her ears; her complaint is there, behind a thin veil. It is {veiled}.

labels.text: VEILED: a hint behind a curtain

scene.alt: A grandmother covers her ears while politely calling her grandson’s loud guitar playing lively.

entry.def: hard to find, catch or remember
entry.ex: The {elusive} snow leopard is rarely caught on camera.
entry.ctx: The answer stayed {elusive}: every time Maya thought she had remembered the word, it slipped away again like a fish between her fingers.
entry.etym: From Latin eludere, “to escape by a trick”: e- (out) + ludere (to play).
entry.note: Elusive (hard to catch) is not illusive (unreal, like an illusion).

mn.cue: e-LOOSE-ive: it gets LOOSE every time
mn.text: Every time Pip swings his net, the butterfly slips loose and flutters just out of reach; it is {elusive}.

scene.alt: A boy leaps with a net as a butterfly flutters just out of reach.

entry.def: hidden beyond what is openly said, as a secret reason
entry.ex: Was his offer to wash the dishes sincere, or did he have an {ulterior} motive?
entry.ctx: Dev’s sudden offer to walk the neighbor’s dog had an {ulterior} purpose: the neighbor baked the best brownies on the block and always paid in brownies.
entry.etym: From Latin ulterior, “farther, beyond.”
entry.note: Ulterior almost always describes a motive or a purpose.

mn.cue: ul-TERIOR: the real reason is in the inTERIOR
mn.text: Kai offers to vacuum Grandpa’s car, but his real reason is hidden in the car’s interior: the coins under the seats. His motive is {ulterior}.

scene.alt: A boy offers to clean a car while secretly thinking about the coins under its seats.

blocks.html: covert (secret) and overt (open) are opposites. elusive (hard to catch) is not illusive (unreal).

blocks.html: Two pairs to keep straight: covert (secret) and overt (open) are opposites, and elusive (hard to catch) is not illusive (unreal, like an illusion).

blocks.html: How do you describe the way something looks? A room can be beautiful, fancy, rich, flashy or bare, and each word tells the reader whether you admire it or wince at it.

Beauty: aesthetic (to do with beauty), exquisite (delicate and fine), sublime (awe-inspiring). Rich and fancy: ornate, opulent. Showing off: ostentatious, flamboyant. Too much: gaudy, garish. Bare: austere.
Pay attention to tone. Ornate and opulent can be praise or a gentle complaint; ostentatious, gaudy and garish always criticize; flamboyant can be either, depending on whether you enjoy the show.

entry.def: having to do with beauty or the enjoyment of beauty
entry.ex: The bridge is useful, but its {aesthetic} appeal is what draws the photographers.
entry.ctx: The engineers cared only whether the tower would stand; the architect worried about its {aesthetic} qualities, arguing for curves and colored glass that would make it beautiful.
entry.etym: From Greek aisthetikos, “having to do with the senses, with perception.”
entry.note: Aesthetic (about beauty) is not ascetic (living a strict, self-denying life). It is sometimes spelled esthetic.

mn.text: At the art show, Professor Edwin peers at each painting and asks, “Is that ick, or is that lovely?” He is judging its {aesthetic} value.

scene.alt: An old professor studies a painting on an easel through a magnifier while the nervous artist waits.

entry.def: extremely beautiful, fine and delicate
entry.ex: The tiny ship inside the bottle was {exquisite}, right down to its silk sails.
entry.ctx: Every detail of the music box was {exquisite}: the dancer’s painted face was no bigger than a grain of rice, yet you could see her smile.
entry.etym: From Latin exquisitus, “sought out, choice,” from exquirere: ex- (out) + quaerere (to seek).

mn.text: Lin searched every shop in the city for the finest teacup, and the one she finally found, painted with tiny gold birds, is {exquisite}.

scene.alt: A woman holds up a delicate, sparkling teacup she has finally found, gazing at it with delight.

entry.def: so grand or beautiful that it fills one with awe
entry.ex: From the mountaintop, the sunrise over the valley was {sublime}.
entry.ctx: Critics expected a pleasant concert, but the performance was {sublime}; when the last note faded, the audience sat in stunned silence before bursting into applause.
entry.etym: From Latin sublimis, “high, lifted up.”

mn.cue: SUB-LIME: climb up HIGH for a GRAND view
mn.text: After climbing all morning, Jamal reaches the summit and watches the sun rise over a sea of clouds; the view is so grand he cannot speak. It is {sublime}.

scene.alt: A hiker raises his arms in awe at the summit as the sun rises over a sea of clouds.

entry.def: covered with fancy, detailed decoration
entry.ex: The old theater had an {ornate} ceiling painted gold and carved with vines and birds.
entry.ctx: Grandma’s clock was {ornate}, with gilded vines curling around its face and tiny brass birds on top; the new clock beside it was a plain white circle.
entry.etym: From Latin ornatus, “decorated,” from ornare (to adorn, to furnish). Ornament comes from the same root.

mn.text: The king’s throne is covered in ornaments: golden curls, jewels, carved lions and a velvet cushion. It is {ornate}.

scene.alt: A proud king points to his golden, jewel-covered throne room.

entry.def: rich and luxurious
entry.ex: The hotel lobby was {opulent}, with marble floors and crystal chandeliers.
entry.ctx: After years in a tiny apartment, the family found the mansion almost too {opulent}: velvet curtains, golden faucets and a fountain in the front hall.
entry.etym: From Latin opulentus, “wealthy,” from ops (wealth, resources).

mn.text: The pampered cat naps on a velvet pillow, eats from a golden bowl and wears a tiny jeweled crown; visitors say “Ooh!” Its life is {opulent}.

scene.alt: A cat in a tiny crown lounges on a velvet pillow beside a golden bowl and a treasure chest.

entry.def: showy in order to impress others
entry.ex: He drove an {ostentatious} gold car with his name painted on both doors.
entry.ctx: Most guests wore simple clothes to the picnic, but Mr. Hale arrived looking {ostentatious}, in a white suit and three diamond rings, mentioning his yacht every five minutes.
entry.etym: From ostentation, from Latin ostentare, “to show off,” related to ostendere (to show).

mn.cue: os-TENT-atious: a GOLD TENT to show off
mn.text: At the campground, Victor pitches a golden tent with a flag and a sign bearing his name, just so everyone will look; that showing off is {ostentatious}.

scene.alt: A show-off in sunglasses and a top hat poses proudly beside his golden tent at a campsite.

entry.def: bold, colorful and showy in a way that draws attention
entry.ex: The {flamboyant} magician wore a purple cape covered in silver stars.
entry.ctx: Her quiet sister dressed in gray, but Rosa was {flamboyant}: she wore a feathered hat, sang on the bus and greeted everyone with a sweeping bow.
entry.etym: From French flamboyant, “flaming,” from flamboyer (to blaze).

mn.text: Jonah twirls into the party in a red-and-orange cape that ripples like fire, then takes a sweeping bow; he is {flamboyant}.

scene.alt: A teen in a flame-colored cape twirls on a stage in the spotlight.

entry.def: too bright or showy in a tasteless way
entry.ex: The {gaudy} sweater had blinking lights, sequins and a plastic snowman sewn on the front.
entry.ctx: The old diner had a simple charm until the new owner covered it in {gaudy} decorations: neon flamingos, flashing arrows and gold plastic palm trees.
entry.etym: From gaud, an old word for a showy trinket.

mn.text: Uncle Marcus wears a neon-pink tie, sparkly sunglasses, a party hat and six necklaces to the family picnic; everyone gawks, because his outfit is {gaudy}.

scene.alt: A man in a pink tie, party hat, sunglasses and jewelry poses while two teens stare in shock.

entry.def: so bright and showy that it is unpleasant
entry.ex: The {garish} orange paint made the little cottage look like a traffic cone.
entry.ctx: The soft candlelight of the café was replaced by {garish} neon signs that buzzed and flashed so brightly that diners squinted at their plates.

mn.text: Pip paints the doghouse lime green, hot pink and orange all at once; the colors glare so hard that Grandpa puts on sunglasses. They are {garish}.

scene.alt: A boy proudly shows off a doghouse painted in glaring colors while his grandfather shields his eyes.

entry.def: plain and without decoration; also, stern and strict
entry.ex: The cabin was {austere}: a cot, a wooden chair and a single lamp.
entry.ctx: Unlike his flashy brother, the old judge lived an {austere} life, eating simple meals, wearing the same gray coat for years and spending almost nothing on himself.
entry.etym: From Latin austerus, from Greek austeros, “harsh, severe.”
entry.note: Austere can also describe a stern, serious person: an austere headmaster.

mn.cue: AW, STARE at the bare walls
mn.text: Visitors to the old judge’s room can only say “Aw...” and stare: one stool, one candle, one plain table and nothing else. His room is {austere}.

scene.alt: An old man sits on a stool in a bare room with only a small table and a candle as a girl stares.

blocks.html: aesthetic (about beauty) is not ascetic (self-denying). gaudy and garish always criticize; ornate and opulent can praise.

an ornate ceiling; an opulent hotel
blocks.cap: From praise to blame, and from fancy to bare.

blocks.html: Aesthetic (about beauty) sounds like ascetic (living a strict, self-denying life), but the two are unrelated. And austere is the opposite of ornate and opulent.
