blocks.html: Five small Greek and Latin prefixes unlock this topic. Two mean all: Latin omni- and Greek pan-. Ambi- means both. Greek eu- means good or well (and its opposite, dys-, means bad). Hyper- means over or beyond.
omni- (all): omnipotent, omniscient. pan- (all): panacea, pandemonium. ambi- (both): ambivalent, ambiguous. eu- (good): euphemism, eulogy. hyper- (over): hyperbole. dys- (bad): dystopia.
You already know these prefixes from everyday words: omnivore (eats all), panorama (a view of all), ambidextrous (good with both hands), hyperactive (over-active).

entry.def: all-powerful; having unlimited power
entry.ex: In the fairy tale, the {omnipotent} wizard could turn mountains into marbles with a wave of his wand.
entry.ctx: The young king believed he was {omnipotent}, but the flood soon taught him that even a ruler cannot order the rain to stop.
entry.etym: From Latin omnipotens: omnis (all) + potens (able, powerful).

mn.text: In Pip’s daydream he lifts a whole house with one finger and waves away the rain clouds; he imagines he is {omnipotent}.

scene.alt: A boy in a cape holds a whole house up on one finger and blows the rain clouds away.

entry.def: knowing everything there is to know
entry.ex: The story is told by an {omniscient} narrator who knows every character’s secret thoughts.
entry.ctx: Grandma seemed {omniscient} to us kids: she always knew who had eaten the cookies, who had tracked in the mud and who had skipped brushing their teeth.
entry.etym: From Latin omnis (all) + sciens (knowing), the root of science.

mn.text: With her back to the room, Granny Mae says, “Pip, put that cookie back.” She knows everything that happens in her kitchen; she seems {omniscient}.

scene.alt: A grandmother with her back turned catches her grandson sneaking a cookie.

entry.def: a cure for all problems or illnesses
entry.ex: A new phone is no {panacea} for boredom.
entry.ctx: The new reading program helped many students, but the teachers warned that it was no {panacea}: some children still needed extra help with spelling, and others simply needed glasses.
entry.etym: From Greek panakeia, “cure-all”: pan (all) + akos (remedy).
entry.note: Panacea is most often used in the negative: “no panacea,” “not a panacea.”

mn.cue: PAN-ACEA: one PAN that cures ALL?
mn.text: A traveling seller swears his shiny frying pan cures colds, sadness and bad grades; nobody believes in a {panacea} like that.

scene.alt: A seller holds up a shiny frying pan under a sign claiming it cures everything, while a woman frowns.

entry.def: wild noise and confusion
entry.ex: When the mouse ran across the cafeteria, {pandemonium} broke out.
entry.ctx: The quiet library turned to {pandemonium} when the alarm went off: chairs scraped, books tumbled and everyone rushed for the doors at once.
entry.etym: Coined in 1667 by the poet John Milton as the name of the demons’ capital in his long poem: pan- (all) + Late Latin daemonium (evil spirit). The sense “wild uproar” came later.

mn.text: A mouse dashes across the kitchen; the cat leaps, every pan clatters to the floor, and everyone shrieks at once. The kitchen is {pandemonium}.

scene.alt: A mouse runs across a kitchen as a cat leaps, pans fly and people scream.

entry.def: having mixed feelings, pulled two ways at once
entry.ex: Lila felt {ambivalent} about moving: excited to see a new city but sad to leave her friends.
entry.ctx: He was {ambivalent} about the job offer; the pay was wonderful, but the long commute would mean seeing his children only on weekends.
entry.etym: Made from ambi- (both) + Latin valens (being strong): feelings that are strong in both directions.
entry.note: Ambivalent means pulled two ways at once, not uninterested. Someone who does not care either way is indifferent.

mn.text: Pip wants to go to the beach and wants to go to the movies just as much; pulled both ways at once, he is {ambivalent}.

scene.alt: A boy shrugs between a sign pointing to the beach and a sign pointing to the movies, pulled both ways.

entry.def: able to be understood in more than one way
entry.ex: Her {ambiguous} reply, “We’ll see,” could have meant yes or no.
entry.ctx: The note was {ambiguous}: “Meet me at the bank” could mean the bank on Main Street or the riverbank behind the school.
entry.etym: From Latin ambiguus, “uncertain,” from ambigere (to waver): ambi- (around, both ways) + agere (to drive).

mn.cue: the BANK? or the river BANK?
mn.text: Kai’s note says “Meet me at the bank,” so Lila waits at the riverbank while Kai waits at the money bank; the note was {ambiguous}.

labels.text: AMBI: TWO WAYS to read it

scene.alt: A girl waits at a riverbank reading a note that says bank, unsure whether it means the river or the city bank.

entry.def: a gentle word used in place of a harsh or blunt one
entry.ex: “Passed away” is a {euphemism} for “died.”
entry.ctx: The company called the layoffs “rightsizing,” a {euphemism} meant to make the loss of two hundred jobs sound like a sensible adjustment.

roots.means: a practice, a way of doing

entry.etym: From Greek euphemismos, from euphemos (speaking well): eu (well) + pheme (speech).

mn.cue: EU = GOOD: a nice word for a bad thing
mn.text: Grandpa Gus calls his rusty, smoking old car “a classic.” That kind word for a wreck is a {euphemism}.

scene.alt: A grandfather proudly calls his smoking, rusty old car a classic while a girl giggles.

entry.def: a speech or writing in praise of someone, especially someone who has died
entry.ex: Grandpa’s oldest friend gave a warm {eulogy}, full of funny stories, at his memorial.
entry.ctx: Rather than list the scientist’s awards, the {eulogy} described her kindness: the students she fed, the letters she answered and the neighbors she helped.
entry.etym: From Greek eulogia, “praise”: eu (well) + logos (word).
entry.note: A eulogy (praise) is not an elegy (a sad poem or song).

mn.cue: EU-LOGY: GOOD WORDS about a life
mn.text: At the memorial, Maya steps to the podium and shares warm, funny stories about her grandfather’s life; her speech of praise is a {eulogy}.

scene.alt: A teen at a podium shares kind memories of her grandfather beside flowers and a framed picture.

entry.def: deliberate exaggeration for effect
entry.ex: “I’ve told you a million times” is {hyperbole}.
entry.ctx: When Jonah said his backpack weighed a ton, he was using {hyperbole}; it was heavy, but he carried it the whole mile to school.
entry.etym: From Greek hyperbole, “excess,” from hyperballein (to throw beyond): hyper (beyond) + ballein (to throw).
entry.note: Say hye-PUR-buh-lee, not HYPE-er-bowl.

mn.cue: HYPER: words thrown way OVER the top
mn.text: Jonah staggers in with a small backpack, groaning, “This weighs a TON! I’m dying!” His over-the-top words are {hyperbole}.

scene.alt: A teen groans that his small backpack weighs a ton while his friend laughs.

entry.def: an imagined society where life is miserable and people are not free
entry.ex: The novel is set in a gray {dystopia} where no one is allowed to sing.
entry.ctx: Unlike the cheerful future in her first book, her new story imagines a {dystopia}: a crowded city where every word is recorded and no one dares to laugh.
entry.etym: Made from dys- (bad) + utopia, the name of an ideal land, from Greek ou (not) + topos (place).

mn.text: In the story, robots patrol gray streets under a sign that says NO SINGING, and nobody smiles; that miserable imagined world is a {dystopia}.

scene.alt: On a gray, rainy street, two sad people pass a patrolling robot and a sign that says no singing.

blocks.html: Keep the pairs apart: ambivalent (mixed feelings) is about how you feel; ambiguous (two possible meanings) is about what something says. And a eulogy praises, while an elegy mourns.

blocks.html: Some people bow too low; others stand too tall. This topic gives you words for both ends: the flatterers who will say anything to please someone powerful, and the bold ones who say whatever they like, no matter who is listening.

Bowing: deferential (politely respectful, a good thing), then obsequious, servile and fawning (too eager to please), and the sycophant who flatters to get ahead. Standing too tall: insolent, impudent, brazen, and the nouns temerity and effrontery (nerve).
Good manners sit in the middle. Being deferential to a grandparent is kind; being obsequious to a boss is embarrassing; being insolent to anyone is rude.

entry.def: showing polite respect and readiness to give way to others
entry.ex: The young players were {deferential} to their coach, listening closely and never interrupting.
entry.ctx: Though he outranked everyone on board, the new captain was {deferential}, asking the older sailors for advice before giving a single order.
entry.etym: From deference, from defer (to yield to another person’s wishes), from Latin deferre (to carry down, to hand over).

mn.text: At the door, Dev steps back, bows a little and lets Granny Mae go first; showing her that polite respect is being {deferential}.

scene.alt: A teen bows slightly and holds back so his grandmother can walk through the door first.

entry.def: too eager to please or obey someone
entry.ex: The {obsequious} waiter refilled our glasses every thirty seconds and laughed at every joke.
entry.ctx: A helpful assistant is a gift, but Victor was {obsequious}: he bowed whenever the boss walked by, agreed with everything she said and even held an umbrella over her on sunny days.
entry.etym: From Latin obsequiosus, “compliant,” from obsequi (to comply): ob- (toward) + sequi (to follow).

mn.text: Victor follows the queen everywhere, bowing low and crying, “Anything, Your Majesty! Anything!” That much eagerness to please is {obsequious}.

scene.alt: A man bows low and follows a bored queen, holding an umbrella over her indoors.

entry.def: a person who flatters powerful people to get ahead
entry.ex: The king’s court was crowded with {sycophants} who praised every word he said.
entry.ctx: Instead of warning the boss that her plan had serious problems, the {sycophant} praised it loudly, hoping to win the promotion.
entry.etym: From Greek sykophantes, literally “one who shows the fig”; no one is sure how it came to mean a flatterer.

mn.text: Rex follows the champion around shouting, “You’re the GREATEST! Can I carry your trophy?” He does it only to win favors; he is a {sycophant}.

scene.alt: A flatterer waves a sign and shouts praise at a champion holding a trophy.

entry.def: too willing to serve or obey others
entry.ex: The {servile} assistant agreed with every idea, even the ones he knew were wrong.
entry.ctx: The young prince wanted honest advisers, not {servile} ones; he grew tired of courtiers who said only what he wanted to hear.
entry.etym: From Latin servilis, “like a servant,” from servus (servant).

mn.text: Asked to pass the salt, Felix leaps up, polishes the shaker, bows and asks if he may also cut Ada’s food; that overeager serving is {servile}.

scene.alt: A man bows deeply while handing a salt shaker to a puzzled woman at a café table.

entry.def: flattering in an overeager, groveling way
entry.ex: The {fawning} fans crowded around the singer, praising even her sneezes.
entry.ctx: The review was not criticism but {fawning} praise: the writer called every scene a masterpiece and every actor a genius.
entry.note: To fawn (to flatter) is a different word from fawn (a baby deer).

mn.text: The puppy wags, rolls over and licks Sven’s boots, all for one biscuit; flattery that eager, from a person, is {fawning}.

scene.alt: A puppy leaps and wags, begging for a treat from a laughing man.

entry.def: boldly rude and disrespectful
entry.ex: The {insolent} student rolled his eyes and yawned loudly while the principal spoke.
entry.ctx: Asked politely to wait her turn, the customer was {insolent}: she snapped her fingers at the clerk and demanded the manager at once.
entry.etym: From Latin insolens, “unusual, overbearing”: in- (not) + solere (to be used to).

mn.text: Told to tidy his room, teenage Rex crosses his arms and says, “Make me!” Talking back that rudely is {insolent}.

scene.alt: A teen crosses his arms and refuses to clean his messy room as his mother points in shock.

entry.def: rudely bold, without shame; cheeky
entry.ex: The {impudent} parrot squawked “Bad haircut!” at every visitor.
entry.ctx: Rather than apologizing for being late, the {impudent} boy grinned and asked why the class had started without him.
entry.etym: From Latin impudens, “shameless”: in- (not) + pudens (feeling shame).

mn.text: Rosa’s parrot is a little imp: it squawks “Bad haircut!” at every guest who walks in. The bird is {impudent}.

scene.alt: A cheeky parrot squawks an insult at a bald grandfather, who looks shocked.

entry.def: bold and without any shame
entry.ex: In a {brazen} move, the squirrel climbed onto the picnic table and grabbed a whole sandwich.
entry.ctx: The thief was {brazen}: rather than sneaking in at night, he strolled through the front door at noon and waved at the security camera.
entry.etym: From Old English for “made of brass”: a brazen face is as hard and bold as brass.
entry.note: To brazen it out is to act boldly, as if one had done nothing wrong.

mn.text: In front of the whole family, the squirrel hops onto the picnic table, grabs a sandwich and stares right back at them; it is as bold as brass, {brazen}.

scene.alt: A bold squirrel stands on a picnic table with a sandwich while a family watches.

entry.def: reckless boldness; nerve
entry.ex: The rookie had the {temerity} to correct the famous coach in front of the whole team.
entry.ctx: Few people dared to argue with the stern old judge, so the courtroom gasped when a young clerk had the {temerity} to point out his mistake.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin temeritas, “rashness,” from temere (blindly, rashly).
entry.note: Temerity (nerve) is nearly the opposite of timidity (shyness), though they sound alike.

mn.cue: TEAM-erity: the rookie tells the TEAM captain
mn.text: On her first day, the smallest player on the team tells the giant captain, “You’re doing it wrong!” Everyone gasps at her {temerity}.

scene.alt: A small new player points up at the huge team captain and tells him he is wrong while a teammate gasps.

entry.def: shameless boldness; the nerve to do something rude
entry.ex: After breaking our window, he had the {effrontery} to ask for his ball back.
entry.ctx: The guest ate most of the cake before the birthday girl could blow out her candles, then had the {effrontery} to complain that it was too sweet.
entry.etym: From French effronterie, from Late Latin effrons, “shameless, barefaced”: ex- (out) + frons (forehead, face).

mn.text: Rex strolls past the long line, steps right to the front of it and tells the clerk to hurry up; that shameless nerve is {effrontery}.

scene.alt: A man cuts to the front of a long line and shouts at the clerk while the others glare.

blocks.html: deferential is polite; obsequious is too much. temerity (nerve) is not timidity (shyness): they are nearly opposites.

rows: too eager to please or obey
blocks.cap: Bowing and boldness, from polite to rude.

blocks.html: Temerity (nerve) and timidity (shyness) sound alike but are nearly opposites. And the verb fawn (to flatter) has nothing to do with a fawn, a baby deer.

blocks.html: Most people lean one way or another: toward music or math, toward cats or dogs, toward sleeping late or rising early. This topic gives you ten words for those leanings, from natural talents to favorite treats to everyday habits.

Tendencies: inclination, propensity, proclivity (often a bad habit), predisposed (leaning that way before you start). Likings: affinity, penchant, predilection. Nature and talent: disposition (usual mood), aptitude (natural ability). Habit: wont.
Look for the pictures of leaning and hanging inside them: inclination and proclivity come from Latin words for leaning and sloping, and propensity and penchant from words for hanging.

entry.def: a natural tendency or liking
entry.ex: Dev has an {inclination} to doodle in the margins of every notebook.
entry.ctx: Though her parents hoped she would study law, Rosa’s {inclination} was toward the sea; she spent every free hour on the docks, learning to sail.
entry.etym: From Latin inclinare, “to lean toward”: in- (toward) + clinare (to bend).

mn.text: Every morning the sunflowers lean toward the sun, and so does Rosa, who heads straight for the sunny dock; leaning toward what you like is an {inclination}.

scene.alt: A girl and two sunflowers all lean toward the bright sun.

entry.def: a person’s usual mood or nature
entry.ex: Our mail carrier has a sunny {disposition}; she whistles even in the pouring rain.
entry.ctx: The two puppies came from the same litter but had very different {dispositions}: one was calm and gentle, while the other barked at every leaf that moved.
entry.etym: From Latin dispositio, “arrangement,” from disponere (to arrange): dis- (apart) + ponere (to place).

mn.cue: a SUNNY DISPOSITION: the weather inside you
mn.text: Even in a rainstorm, Nell whistles and smiles as if a little sun followed her around; her usual mood, her {disposition}, is sunny.

scene.alt: A cheerful woman walks under her own little sun while a grumpy man stands under a rain cloud.

entry.def: a natural ability to learn or do something
entry.ex: Maya showed an early {aptitude} for languages and spoke three by age ten.
entry.ctx: Kai had never touched a piano before, but his {aptitude} was obvious: within a week he was playing songs by ear that took other students months to learn.
entry.etym: From Late Latin aptitudo, “fitness,” from aptus (fit, suited).

mn.text: The very first time Kai sits at a piano, he plays a whole song by ear; he has an {aptitude} for music.

scene.alt: A boy plays the piano on his first try while a woman claps in amazement.

entry.def: a natural liking for, or sense of connection with, someone or something
entry.ex: Ivy has always had an {affinity} for animals; stray cats follow her home.
entry.ctx: Though they had grown up on opposite sides of the world, the two cousins felt an instant {affinity}, finishing each other’s sentences within an hour of meeting.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin affinitas, “closeness, relationship,” from affinis (bordering on, related): ad- (to) + finis (border).

mn.cue: a FIN-ITY: the girl and the whale
mn.text: Every time Ivy visits the harbor, the same friendly whale swims up and waves a fin at her; the two share a natural {affinity}.

scene.alt: A girl on a dock waves to a friendly whale that swims up beside her.

entry.def: a strong liking for something
entry.ex: Grandpa has a {penchant} for loud plaid shirts.
entry.ctx: Her {penchant} for adventure showed early: by age ten she had climbed every tree on the block and tried to build a raft out of an old door.
entry.etym: From French penchant, “leaning,” from pencher (to lean).

mn.cue: PEN-CHANT: she can never pass up a PEN
mn.text: Lin cannot walk past a stationery shop without buying one more pen; she has a {penchant} for pens.

scene.alt: A woman lovingly holds up a new pen beside a box overflowing with pens.

entry.def: a natural tendency to act in a certain way
entry.ex: Our puppy has a {propensity} for chewing shoes.
entry.ctx: Given his {propensity} to exaggerate, nobody believed Jonah when he claimed to have seen a bear in the school parking lot.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin propensus, “inclined,” from propendere (to hang forward): pro- (forward) + pendere (to hang).

mn.text: Leave a shoe by the door and Rufus will find it within a minute; the puppy has a {propensity} for chewing shoes.

scene.alt: A happy puppy chews a shoe among other chewed shoes while its owner scolds.

entry.def: a tendency, often toward something one should not do
entry.ex: The raccoon’s {proclivity} for raiding trash cans did not make it popular with the neighbors.
entry.ctx: His {proclivity} for arguing with referees cost the team several penalties, and the coach finally benched him for the rest of the season.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

entry.etym: From Latin proclivitas, from proclivis (sloping forward): pro- (forward) + clivus (slope).
entry.note: Proclivity often hints at a bad habit; penchant and predilection are usually neutral or fond.

mn.text: No matter how many signs say NO CLIMBING, Pip always scrambles up the slide the wrong way; he has a {proclivity} for it.

scene.alt: A boy scrambles up a slide the wrong way past a sign that says no climbing.

entry.def: a special liking or preference
entry.ex: The cat has a {predilection} for napping in the laundry basket.
entry.ctx: At the dessert table, Grandma revealed her {predilection} at once, skipping the cakes and pies and heading straight for the lemon bars.
entry.etym: From Medieval Latin praedilectio, from praediligere (to prefer): prae- (before) + diligere (to love, to choose).

mn.text: At every party, Granny Mae walks right past the cakes and pies to the lemon bars; lemon is her {predilection}.

scene.alt: A grandmother walks past cakes and pies and reaches happily for a lemon treat.

entry.def: inclined ahead of time to act or think a certain way
entry.ex: Having grown up near the sea, Omar was {predisposed} to love sailing.
entry.ctx: The judges were {predisposed} to favor the hometown team, so the visitors knew they would have to play twice as well to win.
entry.etym: From pre- (before) + dispose (to incline, to arrange).

mn.cue: PRE-DISPOSED: leaning that way from the START
mn.text: Born into a family of bakers, little Theo seemed {predisposed} to love baking; his very first word was “Cake!”

scene.alt: A toddler in a chef’s hat says cake between his two baker parents.

entry.def: a habit or usual way of acting
entry.ex: As was his {wont}, Grandpa rose at dawn to feed the chickens.
entry.ctx: Rather than rush to work, as was her {wont}, Ada strolled slowly through the park that morning, stopping to watch the ducks.
entry.note: Wont is also an adjective: “he is wont to sing in the shower” means he usually does. Do not confuse it with won’t (will not).

mn.cue: WONT: what he always WANTS to do
mn.text: Every morning at six, as is his {wont}, Grandpa Gus feeds the chickens in his slippers.

scene.alt: A grandfather feeds his chickens at dawn, as he does every morning.

blocks.html: proclivity often hints at a bad habit; penchant and predilection are usually neutral or fond. wont (a habit) rhymes with "want" in most American speech but is a different word.

head: word
what kind of leaning
tone
rows: a tendency, often to something unwise
blocks.cap: Tendencies, likings, nature and habit.

blocks.html: Wont (a habit, said WAWNT, like want in many American accents) is a different word from won’t (will not). “As is her wont” means “as she usually does.”

blocks.html: You met the everyday words for praise and blame in earlier topics (commend, laud, rebuke, berate). These ten are rarer and stronger, the kind you find in reviews, speeches and history books.

High praise (nouns): encomium, panegyric, plaudit, paean. Harsh blame (verbs): excoriate, castigate, upbraid, lambaste. Attacking a person’s name: vilify (paint as evil), impugn (question their honesty).
A handy pattern: the four praise words are all nouns (you give a panegyric), and the six blame words are all verbs (you castigate someone).

entry.def: a speech or piece of writing full of high praise
entry.ex: The retiring coach received an {encomium} from every player on the team.
entry.ctx: Far from the lukewarm review she expected, the critic wrote an {encomium}, calling her first novel the most beautiful book of the year.
entry.etym: From Greek enkomion, a song of praise.

mn.cue: en-COME-ium: PRAISE as she COMES IN
mn.text: When Zoe comes in through the village gate with the spelling trophy, the whole town greets her with a song of high praise; that welcome is an {encomium}.

labels.text: en-COME-ium: PRAISE as she COMES IN

scene.alt: A girl walks in with a trophy under a banner as townspeople cheer her.

entry.def: a public speech or piece of writing of great praise
entry.ex: The principal’s {panegyric} for the retiring janitor brought the whole school to its feet.
entry.ctx: The biography reads less like history than a {panegyric}: it praises every decision its subject ever made and leaves out all of his mistakes.
entry.etym: From Greek panegyrikos, “for a festival of all the people,” from panegyris (a public gathering): pan- (all) + agyris (assembly).

mn.cue: PAN = ALL: praise in front of ALL
mn.text: At the school assembly, in front of everyone, the principal praises Mr. Marcus for forty years of fixing, sweeping and smiling; her speech is a {panegyric}.

scene.alt: A principal at a podium praises the shy, smiling school janitor in front of everyone.

entry.def: an expression of praise or approval (usually in the plural)
entry.ex: The young violinist won {plaudits} from critics across the country.
entry.ctx: The new bridge earned {plaudits} from engineers and artists alike, who praised both its strength and the graceful curve of its arch.
entry.etym: From Latin plaudite, “applaud!”, the word actors called out at the end of a play.
entry.note: Usually used in the plural, plaudits. Applaud comes from the same root.

mn.text: When Lila finishes her violin solo, the whole hall leaps up to applaud it; the cheers and praise she wins are {plaudits}.

scene.alt: A girl bows with her violin as the audience applauds.

entry.def: a song, speech or piece of writing full of joyful praise
entry.ex: The film is a {paean} to small-town life.
entry.ctx: After the long, dark winter, the first warm day inspired a {paean} from Grandpa, who stood on the porch and sang the praises of every crocus in the yard.
entry.etym: From Greek paian, a song of thanksgiving or triumph.
entry.note: Paean is said PEE-un, just like peon, but the two words have nothing in common.

mn.text: On the first warm day of spring, Grandpa Gus sits at the piano and sings a joyful song praising the sun, the robins and every new flower; it is a {paean} to spring.

scene.alt: A grandfather plays the piano and sings joyfully about spring flowers.

entry.def: to criticize very harshly
entry.ex: The review {excoriated} the restaurant for its cold soup and rude service.
entry.ctx: The coach did not simply point out the players’ mistakes; she {excoriated} them, listing every missed pass in a voice that carried across the whole field.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin excoriare, “to strip off the hide”: ex- (off) + corium (hide, leather).

mn.cue: EX-CORI: criticism that STINGS to the core
mn.text: The food critic tastes one spoonful of the chef’s soup and tears into it so harshly that the chef shrinks behind his ladle; she {excoriates} it.

scene.alt: A furious food critic shouts harsh words about a soup while the chef hides his face.

entry.def: to scold or criticize severely
entry.ex: The teacher {castigated} the class for leaving the art room a mess.
entry.ctx: The editor {castigated} the reporter in front of the whole newsroom for printing the story without checking a single fact.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin castigare, “to correct, to punish,” from castus (pure). Chastise comes from the same root.

mn.text: The queen meets the late knight at the castle gate and scolds him so sharply that his armor rattles; she {castigates} him.

scene.alt: A queen points and scolds a nervous knight in armor at the castle gate.

entry.def: to scold sharply
entry.ex: Mom {upbraided} us for tracking mud across the clean kitchen floor.
entry.ctx: Instead of thanking the volunteers, the manager {upbraided} them for arriving five minutes late, and half of them never came back.

mn.text: Tugging Lila’s tangled braids up tight, Aunt Tia scolds, “Do you EVER brush?” She {upbraids} her.

scene.alt: An aunt scolds a girl with tangled braids who sits looking unhappy.

entry.def: to criticize harshly
entry.ex: Critics {lambasted} the movie for its silly plot and wooden acting.
entry.ctx: Fans who had waited years for the new game {lambasted} it online, complaining that it crashed constantly and ended after just two hours.

mn.text: At the barnyard talent show, the lamb boos the rooster’s song so loudly that the rooster hides behind the hay; the lamb {lambastes} the act.

scene.alt: At a barnyard talent show, a lamb loudly boos while the rooster hides.

entry.def: to speak about someone as if they were evil
entry.ex: Old stories often {vilify} wolves, but real wolves rarely bother people.
entry.ctx: Instead of answering the new coach’s ideas, a few angry parents tried to {vilify} her, calling her selfish and dishonest without offering a shred of proof.
entry.etym: From Late Latin vilificare, “to make worthless,” from vilis (cheap, worthless).

mn.cue: VILE-ify: paint someone as a VILLAIN
mn.text: Rex hangs a poster calling the new kid a lunch-stealing villain, though it is not true at all; he is trying to {vilify} him.

labels.text: VILE-ify: paint them as a VILLAIN

scene.alt: A sneaky teen points to a sign falsely calling another boy a villain, while the boy looks hurt.

entry.def: to question someone’s honesty or the truth of a claim
entry.ex: The visiting coach {impugned} the referee’s fairness.
entry.ctx: Rather than argue with the scientist’s findings, the critic tried to {impugn} her motives, suggesting she had faked the results to win a prize.
entry.etym: From Latin impugnare, “to fight against, to attack”: in- (against) + pugnare (to fight).
entry.note: Impugn attacks someone’s honesty or a claim’s truth; it does not mean to punish.

mn.cue: im-PUG-n: the PUG fights your word
mn.text: Pip says he walked the dog twice today, but the pug barks, “Did NOT!” The pug {impugns} Pip’s story.

scene.alt: A boy claims he walked the dog twice while the dog barks back that he did not.

blocks.html: impugn attacks someone's honesty or a claim's truth; it does not mean to punish. paean is pronounced PEE-un, like "peon," but means a song of praise.

blocks.html: Impugn does not mean to punish: to impugn someone’s motives is to suggest they are dishonest. And paean is said PEE-un.

blocks.html: These ten words are traps. Each one looks or sounds as if it means something it does not: enervate sounds like energize, noisome sounds like noisy, restive sounds like restful. Test writers love them for exactly that reason.

The rule for this topic: never trust the sound. Enervate = weaken. Nonplussed and bemused = puzzled. Noisome = smelly. Restive = restless. Peruse = read closely. Belie = give a false picture of. Sanction and cleave each have two opposite meanings. Inflammable = burns easily.
When one of these words appears in a reading passage, slow down and let the sentence around it tell you which meaning fits.

entry.def: to weaken; to drain of energy
entry.ex: The long, humid afternoon {enervated} the hikers, and they barely made it back to camp.
entry.ctx: Far from energizing the team, the three-hour meeting {enervated} everyone; by the end, even the coach was slumped in his chair, too tired to speak.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin enervare, “to cut out the sinews”: e- (out) + nervus (sinew).
entry.note: Enervate means nearly the opposite of energize, though the two look alike.

mn.text: The heat wave drains every bit of nerve and strength out of Sven; he flops on the sand like a wet noodle. The heat {enervates} him.

scene.alt: A big man slumps on the hot sand, drained of energy, beside a nearly empty battery.

entry.def: so puzzled that one does not know what to say or do
entry.ex: When the parrot answered the phone, the caller was completely {nonplussed}.
entry.ctx: The magician’s final trick left the audience {nonplussed}; no one could explain how the elephant had vanished from the stage, and for a moment nobody even clapped.
entry.etym: From Latin non plus, “no more”: a point at which nothing more can be said or done.
entry.note: In careful writing, nonplussed means puzzled. A newer, informal American use means unbothered, nearly the opposite, so read it with care and use it for puzzled.

mn.text: Ms. Ada asks Kai, “What is forever plus one?” He opens his mouth, closes it, and just stares, with nothing more to say. He is {nonplussed}.

scene.alt: A teacher asks a tricky question and a boy stares back, too puzzled to answer.

entry.def: puzzled and confused
entry.ex: The tourists looked {bemused} by the street signs written in three languages.
entry.ctx: Kai stared at the rules for the new board game, {bemused} by all forty of them, and finally went back to his book.
entry.note: Bemused means puzzled, not amused. Some writers now use it for a puzzled sort of amusement, which is why careful readers check the context.

mn.text: Uncle Sven turns the new remote over and over, staring at its forty buttons; he is not amused, just confused: {bemused}.

scene.alt: A man stares, puzzled, at a remote control covered in buttons.

entry.def: having a very bad smell; also, harmful
entry.ex: A {noisome} odor drifted from the lunch box forgotten at the back of the closet.
entry.ctx: Despite what its name suggests, the swamp was not noisy at all; it was {noisome}, giving off a stench of rotting plants that made visitors hold their noses.
entry.etym: From Middle English noy (annoyance) + -some. It has nothing to do with noise.
entry.note: Noisome means smelly or harmful, not noisy.

mn.text: The tuna sandwich forgotten in Dev’s gym bag for a week smells so bad that the whole team holds its nose; the bag is {noisome}.

scene.alt: Two teens recoil from a gym bag giving off a terrible smell.

entry.def: restless and hard to control
entry.ex: The {restive} horse stamped and tossed its head at the starting gate.
entry.ctx: After two hours of waiting in the heat with no explanation, the crowd grew {restive}, shouting and pushing toward the locked gates.
entry.etym: From Anglo-French restif, “balky, refusing to move,” from rester (to stay, to resist).
entry.note: Restive means restless, not restful.

mn.text: Told to wait at the gate, the young horse stamps, snorts and tosses its head; it is anything but restful. It is {restive}.

scene.alt: A restless horse rears and stamps near a gate while its owner tries to calm it.

entry.def: to read carefully; also, often, to look over casually
entry.ex: Before signing, Dad {perused} every page of the lease.
entry.ctx: Rather than skim the contract, the lawyer {perused} it line by line, circling three clauses that would have cost her client thousands of dollars.
entry.note: Careful writers use peruse for reading closely, but many people now use it to mean browse or glance over. On a test, choose the careful sense unless the sentence clearly says otherwise.

mn.text: Professor Edwin reads the old treasure map with a magnifying glass, every tiny word and line, twice; he {peruses} it.

scene.alt: An old professor studies a map closely through a magnifying glass.

entry.def: to give a false picture of; also, to show to be false
entry.ex: Her calm smile {belied} how nervous she felt before the recital.
entry.ctx: The tiny restaurant’s plain front {belies} the feast inside; customers who wander in expecting a quick snack find a seven-course dinner waiting.
entry.etym: From Old English beleogan, “to deceive by lying”: be- + leogan (to lie).
entry.note: Belie has nothing to do with believe: if her smile belies her fear, the smile hides it.

mn.cue: BE-LIE: the LOOKS tell a LIE
mn.text: Grandma’s rusty little car looks as if it could barely roll, but at the go-kart track it zooms past everyone; its shabby looks {belie} its speed.

labels.text: BE-LIE: the LOOKS tell a LIE

scene.alt: A rusty little car zooms past at top speed while its grandmother driver cheers.

entry.def: official approval; also, a penalty for breaking a rule
entry.ex: The club cannot hold its bake sale without the principal’s {sanction}.
entry.ctx: The league imposed a harsh {sanction} on the team for cheating: it was banned from the playoffs and had to give back its trophy.
entry.etym: From Latin sanctio, “a decree, a binding law,” from sancire (to make sacred, to decree).
entry.note: Sanction can mean two nearly opposite things: approval (the school’s sanction) or a penalty (sanctions against a country). The verb to sanction usually means to approve. Let the sentence tell you which.

mn.cue: SANCTION: an OK... or a PENALTY
mn.text: Judge Edwin stamps OK on the parade plan, a {sanction} that lets it go ahead; then he fines the band that marched through the flower beds, a sanction of the other kind.

labels.text: SANCTION: an OK... or a PENALTY

scene.alt: A judge with a gavel stands between a sign reading approved and a sign announcing a fine.

entry.def: to split apart; also, to cling closely
entry.ex: With one swing of the axe, Grandpa {cleaved} the log in two.
entry.ctx: The bitter argument {cleaved} the club into two camps, and for months the members sat on opposite sides of the room.
entry.etym: Two Old English verbs fell together into one: cleofan (to split) and clifian (to stick, to cling).
entry.note: Cleave is its own opposite: to split apart, or to cling together (“the child cleaved to her mother”).

mn.cue: a CLEAVER SPLITS... a sloth CLINGS
mn.text: Grandpa’s axe splits the log in two, while in the tree above, a sloth clings tight to its branch; to {cleave} can mean either one.

scene.alt: A grandfather splits a log with an axe while a sloth clings to a branch above.

entry.def: easily set on fire; the same as flammable
entry.ex: Keep the {inflammable} paint thinner far away from the stove.
entry.ctx: Many people think the in- on the warning label means “not,” but the barrels marked {inflammable} were dangerous: a single spark could set them ablaze.
entry.etym: From Latin inflammare, “to set on fire”: in- (into) + flamma (flame).
entry.note: Inflammable and flammable mean the same thing. Because people mistook the in- for “not,” safety labels now usually say flammable.

mn.cue: IN-FLAME-able: can go up IN FLAMES
mn.text: One spark could send the barrel up in flames, so Marcus keeps the torch far away; the barrel is {inflammable}: it burns easily.

scene.alt: A worker in a hard hat holds up his hands to keep a burning torch away from a barrel marked with a fire warning.

blocks.html: enervate means to weaken, not to energize. bemused means puzzled, not amused. noisome means smelly or harmful, not noisy. restive means restless, not restful. inflammable means flammable, not fireproof. In careful writing nonplussed means puzzled; a newer, informal American use means unbothered, so read it with care.

sounds like it means

blocks.cap: Ten traps: what each word seems to mean, and what it does mean.

blocks.html: Sanction and cleave are called contronyms: words that are their own opposites. Only the sentence can tell you which meaning the writer wants.

blocks.html: Some thinking goes all the way down; some barely skims the surface. And some knowledge is so deep, or so specialized, that only a few people ever reach it. This topic gives you words for all three.

Deep or shallow: profound, superficial. Ways of thinking: cerebral (by the mind, not feelings), contemplate, ruminate (chew it over), pensive (quietly thoughtful). Knowledge few people share: abstruse, esoteric, arcane, recondite.

The four hard-knowledge words overlap, but each has its own picture: abstruse is pushed away out of reach, esoteric is for the inner circle, arcane is locked in a chest, and recondite is hidden away at the back.

entry.def: very deep in thought, feeling or effect
entry.ex: Grandma’s quiet advice had a {profound} effect on how I treat my friends.
entry.ctx: Though the child spoke in simple words, her answer was {profound}; the room fell silent as the grown-ups realized she had seen to the heart of the problem.
entry.etym: From Latin profundus, “deep”: pro- (forward, down) + fundus (bottom).

mn.cue: PRO-FOUND: FOUND at the very bottom
mn.text: Professor Edwin climbs down to the deepest part of the cave and finds a glowing gem no one else ever reached; a thought that comes from that deep is {profound}.

labels.text: PRO-FOUND: FOUND at the DEEPEST bottom

scene.alt: An old professor with a lantern kneels deep in a cave beside a glowing gem.

entry.def: on the surface only; not deep or thorough
entry.ex: Luckily, the scratch on the car door was only {superficial}.
entry.ctx: His knowledge of the subject was {superficial}: he could repeat a few famous names and dates, but he could not explain why any of it mattered.
entry.etym: From Latin superficialis, from superficies (surface): super (above) + facies (face).

mn.text: The little fish skims the top of the sea all day and never looks below, missing the treasure on the bottom; its view of the sea is {superficial}.

scene.alt: A fish swims at the top of the water, never noticing the treasure chest on the sea floor below.

entry.def: having to do with careful thinking rather than feelings
entry.ex: Chess is a {cerebral} game, all planning and no luck.
entry.ctx: Her brother loved action movies full of car chases, but Ada preferred {cerebral} films, where the excitement came from puzzles and clever conversation.
entry.etym: From Latin cerebrum (brain).
entry.note: Also said SAIR-uh-brul.

mn.text: While the other kids race around the field, Sami sits under a tree working out a chess puzzle; he likes the {cerebral} kind of fun.

scene.alt: A boy thinks hard over a chess piece while other children run and play in the background.

entry.def: to think long and carefully about something, or to look at it thoughtfully
entry.ex: Rosa sat on the dock to {contemplate} the sunset.
entry.ctx: Before accepting the job overseas, Jamal took a week to {contemplate} the choice, weighing what he would gain against everything he would leave behind.

roots.means: an open space marked out for watching
to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin contemplari, “to observe carefully,” from templum, an open space marked out for watching the sky.

mn.cue: con-tem-PLATE: staring at the PLATE, thinking
mn.text: Dev stares at the last slice of pizza on the plate for a long time: eat it or save it for his sister? He {contemplates} the question.

scene.alt: A teen stares thoughtfully at the last slice of pizza on a plate, deciding whether to eat it.

entry.def: quietly and deeply thoughtful, often a little sad
entry.ex: On the last day of camp, the {pensive} campers watched the lake in silence.
entry.ctx: Usually chatty at dinner, Grandpa was {pensive} that night, gazing out the window and answering every question with a faraway smile.
entry.etym: From French pensif, from penser (to think), from Latin pensare (to weigh, to ponder).

mn.cue: PEN-SIVE: chewing the PEN, lost in thought
mn.text: Lila sits by the rainy window chewing on her pen, thinking about the friend who moved away; she is quiet and {pensive}.

scene.alt: A girl rests her chin on her hand, holding a pencil, lost in sad thought by the window.

entry.def: to think something over again and again
entry.ex: Kai lay awake, {ruminating} about the easy goal he had missed.
entry.ctx: Rather than decide quickly, the judge preferred to {ruminate}, turning the case over in her mind for days before she wrote a single word.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin ruminari, “to chew the cud,” from rumen (throat).
entry.note: Cows, sheep and goats are ruminants: they chew their food, swallow it and bring it back up to chew again.

mn.cue: a COW chewing it over and over
mn.text: Daisy the cow chews the same mouthful of grass for an hour, round and round; to chew a thought over like that is to {ruminate}.

scene.alt: A cow chews slowly with a thoughtful look, thinking something over.

entry.def: very hard to understand
entry.ex: The professor’s {abstruse} lecture lost half the class in the first ten minutes.
entry.ctx: The instruction manual was {abstruse}, full of technical terms and tangled diagrams that even the engineer struggled to follow.
entry.etym: From Latin abstrusus, “hidden,” from abstrudere (to push away, to conceal): abs- (away) + trudere (to push).

mn.cue: AB-STRUSE: pushed AWAY out of reach
mn.text: Professor Edwin fills the board with symbols so tangled that every student’s head spins; the meaning is pushed far out of reach. His lecture is {abstruse}.

scene.alt: A professor points to a board of tangled symbols while a dizzy student cannot follow.

entry.def: understood or enjoyed by only a small group
entry.ex: The club’s {esoteric} jokes about antique buttons made no sense to newcomers.
entry.ctx: Most visitors hurried past the exhibit, but a few experts lingered for hours; its subject, the history of buttons, was too {esoteric} for the general public.
entry.etym: From Greek esoterikos, “belonging to an inner circle,” from a word meaning “within.”
entry.note: Esoteric means for insiders, not simply strange. Its opposite is exoteric, meant for outsiders too.

mn.text: Inside the Button Club, three members laugh at a joke about four-hole buttons that no outsider understands; their humor is {esoteric}.

scene.alt: Three club members laugh at an inside joke while an outsider scratches his head.

entry.def: known or understood by only a few; mysterious
entry.ex: The old book was full of {arcane} rules for a card game no one plays anymore.
entry.ctx: Only the oldest clerk understood the town’s {arcane} filing system, in which every folder was sorted by the color of its ink rather than by name or date.
entry.etym: From Latin arcanus, “secret, hidden,” from arca (chest, box).

mn.text: The old wizard keeps his strangest spells locked in a chest, written in a script only he can read; they are {arcane}.

scene.alt: An old wizard reads a scroll beside a glowing chest of secret spells.

entry.def: little known and hard to understand
entry.ex: The quiz bowl team studied {recondite} facts about ancient coins and rare beetles.
entry.ctx: Most readers found the essay {recondite}, packed with references to forgotten poets and obscure scientific papers that only a specialist would recognize.
entry.etym: From Latin reconditus, “hidden away,” from recondere (to put away, to conceal).
entry.note: Also said rih-KON-dite.

mn.text: Ada climbs to the dustiest shelf at the back of the library for a book on the moths of a single mountain; knowledge hidden that far back is {recondite}.

scene.alt: A woman on a ladder reaches for a dusty book on the highest shelf at the back of a library.

blocks.html: ruminate also describes a cow chewing its cud, so to ruminate is to chew over a thought. esoteric means for insiders, not "strange" in general.

blocks.cap: Deep, shallow and hidden: the pictures inside the words.

blocks.html: Three verbs and adjectives for thinking: to contemplate is to think long and carefully; to ruminate is to chew a thought over and over (like a cow with its cud); a pensive person is quietly, often sadly, thoughtful.

blocks.html: Writers describe the old and the new with surprising precision. A thing can be ancient and admired, or old and laughed at, or simply out of date; something new can be fresh, clever or startlingly experimental.

Very old: primeval (from the first ages), archaic (no longer used), hoary (gray with age), antiquated and antediluvian (out of date, often a joke). Unspoiled: pristine. Missing the old days: nostalgia. New: novel, innovative, avant-garde.
Two Latin roots do most of the work: nov means new (novel, innovative, renovate), and antiqu and ante point back to old and before.

entry.def: very old, or no longer in everyday use
entry.ex: “Thou” and “thee” are {archaic} words for “you.”
entry.ctx: The town still settled its disputes with a set of {archaic} rules written in 1790, long after every other town had updated theirs.
entry.etym: From Greek archaikos, “old-fashioned,” from archaios (ancient), from arche (beginning).

mn.cue: ARCH-aic: as old as a crumbling ARCH
mn.text: Among the broken columns, Professor Edwin reads aloud from a crumbling scroll: “Hark! Thou art welcome!” Words that old, no longer used, are {archaic}.

scene.alt: Among ancient ruins, an old professor reads old-fashioned words from a scroll while a boy looks puzzled.

entry.def: old-fashioned and out of date
entry.ex: The office still used an {antiquated} fax machine that jammed every afternoon.
entry.ctx: Compared with the bright new library across town, the old building, with its {antiquated} card catalog and flickering lamps, felt like a museum.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin antiquus (old, ancient), the source of antique.

mn.cue: ANTIQUE-ATED: belongs in an ANTIQUE shop
mn.text: Uncle Marcus still listens to the news on a radio the size of a suitcase that crackles more than it talks; it belongs in an antique shop. It is {antiquated}.

scene.alt: A man listens happily to a huge old radio while a teen holding a phone laughs.

entry.def: extremely old or old-fashioned (often said as a joke)
entry.ex: My uncle’s {antediluvian} computer takes ten minutes to start.
entry.ctx: The students giggled at the teacher’s {antediluvian} slides, full of cartoons and fonts that had gone out of style before any of them were born.
entry.etym: From Latin ante (before) + diluvium (flood): literally, from before the great flood of ancient stories.

mn.text: Uncle Victor rides to town in a creaky wooden cart pulled by an old horse, while the kids zoom past on skateboards; his ride seems to date from before the great flood. It is {antediluvian}.

scene.alt: A man rides a creaky wooden cart pulled by a sleepy horse while a teen on a skateboard laughs.

entry.def: very old; gray or white with age
entry.ex: The {hoary} old oak had stood in the village square for three hundred years.
entry.ctx: The comedian’s act was full of {hoary} jokes that audiences had been groaning at since their grandparents’ day.
entry.etym: From hoar, an old word for gray or white, as in hoarfrost.
entry.note: Hoary can describe gray hair or an idea worn out by long use: a hoary old joke.

mn.text: Professor Edwin’s beard is so long and white that it looks dusted with frost; he is {hoary} with age.

scene.alt: An old professor with a long white beard waves in the falling snow.

entry.def: belonging to the earliest ages of the world
entry.ex: The explorers hiked through a {primeval} forest of giant ferns and moss-covered trees.
entry.ctx: The cave paintings date from a {primeval} time, thousands of years before anyone had built a city or written a single word.
entry.etym: From Latin primaevus, “in the first age”: primus (first) + aevum (age).

mn.text: Deep in the jungle, Sami finds a valley where giant plants tower overhead and a dragon-sized lizard dozes, as if the world’s first age had never ended; the place is {primeval}.

scene.alt: An explorer points at a giant sleeping lizard in a jungle that looks untouched since the first ages.

entry.def: in its original condition; unspoiled
entry.ex: The old comic book was in {pristine} condition, without a single crease.
entry.ctx: Before the resort was built, the beach was {pristine}: no footprints, no litter, just smooth sand and clear water.
entry.etym: From Latin pristinus, “original, former.”
entry.note: Pristine means unspoiled, as it was at first, not merely clean.

mn.cue: PRIS-TINE: fresh snow no one has touched
mn.text: Ivy steps outside at dawn and finds the field covered in smooth new snow, without a single footprint; she can hardly bear to walk on it, because it is {pristine}.

scene.alt: A girl tiptoes at the edge of a sparkling field of fresh, untouched snow.

entry.def: a fond, wistful longing for the past
entry.ex: The smell of popcorn filled Grandpa with {nostalgia} for the movie theater of his childhood.
entry.ctx: Paging through the old photo album, Mom felt a wave of {nostalgia}: the treehouse, the bicycle with streamers, the summer evenings that seemed to last forever.
entry.etym: From Greek nostos (a return home) + algos (pain): it first named homesickness.

mn.cue: NOST-ALGIA: a sweet ACHE for the past
mn.text: Granny Mae turns the pages of her old photo album and smiles at her first bicycle and her childhood dog; the sweet ache she feels is {nostalgia}.

labels.text: NOST-ALGIA: a sweet ACHE for the PAST

scene.alt: A grandmother smiles fondly over an old photo album, remembering her childhood.

entry.def: new and unusual
entry.ex: Using a kite to deliver the birthday card was a {novel} idea.
entry.ctx: The inventor’s solution was {novel}: instead of building a bigger dam, she planted thousands of trees upstream to slow the floodwater.
entry.etym: From Latin novellus, “new,” from novus (new).
entry.note: As a noun, a novel is a long story. As an adjective, novel means new and different.

mn.text: Sami builds a little robot that walks the dog for him, leash and all; no one in town has seen anything like it. The idea is {novel}.

scene.alt: A proud boy watches the little robot he built walk his dog through the park.

entry.def: bringing in new ideas or ways of doing things
entry.ex: The school’s {innovative} garden program teaches math through planting.
entry.ctx: Rather than copy the other bakeries, Nell was {innovative}, inventing flavors no one had ever tried, like lemon-basil scones and pepper-honey cookies.
entry.etym: From Latin innovare, “to renew, to make new”: in- (into) + novare (to make new), from novus (new).

mn.text: Nell bakes cookies no one has ever tasted, pepper-honey and lemon-basil, and hangs a sign saying NEW FLAVORS; she is {innovative}.

scene.alt: A baker with a bright idea offers a new kind of cookie under a sign announcing new flavors.

entry.def: new and experimental, especially in the arts
entry.ex: The museum’s new wing shows {avant-garde} paintings that look nothing like traditional art.
entry.ctx: In its day the composer’s music was {avant-garde}, full of clashing sounds that shocked audiences; today the same pieces are played at school concerts.
entry.etym: From French avant (before, ahead) + garde (guard): the vanguard, the front part of an army that marches ahead of the rest.

mn.text: Nell paints with her feet, her elbows and a dripping mop, far ahead of what anyone else is trying; her art is {avant-garde}.

scene.alt: An artist in a beret dances wildly before her experimental painting while an old man scratches his head.

blocks.html: pristine means unspoiled, not just clean. hoary can describe gray hair or an idea worn out by long use (a hoary joke); antiquated and antediluvian poke fun at the old.

blocks.html: Pristine does not just mean clean: a pristine forest is untouched by people, and a pristine old book is still as it was when new. A hoary joke is not white-haired; it is just very old.

blocks.html: Half of these words are about grabbing, and half are about letting go. Kings and crowns appear often, because power changing hands is where English needed the most exact words.

Taking: usurp (without the right), confiscate (by authority), appropriate (for your own use), commandeer (for urgent official use), wrest (by force or effort). Giving up: relinquish (let go), renounce (formally give up), repudiate (reject, disown), forfeit (lose as a penalty), abdicate (give up a throne or duty).
Ask two questions about each word: who has the right to the thing, and is it taken by force, by authority or by choice? The answers sort the words.

entry.def: to take a position or power without the right to it
entry.ex: The scheming duke tried to {usurp} the throne while the young queen was away.
entry.ctx: The assistant coach began to {usurp} the head coach’s role, calling plays and giving speeches until no one knew who was really in charge.
entry.etym: From Latin usurpare, “to take into use, to seize”: usus (use) + rapere (to seize).

mn.cue: you SLURP my soup, you SIT on my throne?
mn.text: While the king naps, the cat climbs onto his throne, puts on his crown and slurps his soup; it has no right to rule, but it {usurps} the throne.

scene.alt: A cat in a crown sits on the king’s throne beside his soup while the king points in fury.

entry.def: to take something away by authority
entry.ex: The teacher {confiscated} the phones and kept them in a drawer until the end of class.
entry.ctx: At the border, officers {confiscated} the fruit from every traveler’s bag, since bringing it into the country could spread plant pests.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin confiscare, “to put into the treasury”: com- (together) + fiscus (basket, treasury).

mn.cue: CON-FISH-CATE: the CAT loses the FISH
mn.text: The fish seller catches the cat with a stolen fish and, as boss of the stall, takes it right back and locks it in the cooler; he {confiscates} it.

scene.alt: A fish seller holds up a fish he has taken back from a sad cat.

entry.def: to take something for one’s own use, often without permission
entry.ex: My little brother {appropriated} my best pillow and refused to give it back.
entry.ctx: Rather than come up with her own idea, Tia {appropriated} her friend’s design for the poster contest and entered it under her own name.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Late Latin appropriare, “to make one’s own”: ad- (to) + proprius (one’s own).
entry.note: As a verb it is said uh-PROH-pree-ayt. The adjective, uh-PROH-pree-it, means suitable: appropriate clothes.

mn.text: Pip plops down on Lila’s comfy beanbag, sticks a sign on it that says “PIP’S PROPERTY” and will not budge; he has {appropriated} it.

scene.alt: A boy sits smugly on his sister’s beanbag next to a sign claiming it as his property while she protests.

entry.def: to take over something for official or urgent use
entry.ex: The firefighters {commandeered} a neighbor’s garden hose to soak the burning shed.
entry.ctx: When the bridge washed out, the sheriff {commandeered} every rowboat on the lake to ferry stranded families across the river.
entry.etym: From Afrikaans kommandeer, from French commander (to command).

mn.cue: COMMAND HERE: this boat is needed!
mn.text: The flood captain points at the fisherman’s rowboat and calls out, “I need this boat for the rescue, right here, right now!” She {commandeers} it.

scene.alt: A rescue captain in a raincoat points at a fisherman’s rowboat and orders it into service.

entry.def: to pull or take away by force or great effort
entry.ex: Lila finally {wrested} the stuck lid off the pickle jar.
entry.ctx: After years of losing, the underdogs {wrested} the championship from the team that had won it six seasons in a row.
entry.etym: From Old English wraestan, “to twist.” Wrestle comes from the same word.

mn.text: Pip and the goat both grab the same rope; after a long tug and twist, Pip wrestles it free. He {wrests} it from the goat.

scene.alt: A boy and a goat play tug-of-war with a rope as the boy pulls hard to win it.

entry.def: to give up or let go of something
entry.ex: The toddler refused to {relinquish} the television remote.
entry.ctx: After forty years running the bakery, Mr. Ortiz finally {relinquished} control to his daughter, though he still came in every morning to taste the bread.
entry.etym: From Latin relinquere, “to leave behind”: re- (behind) + linquere (to leave).

mn.cue: re-LINQU: LEAVE it behind, hand it OVER
mn.text: After forty years at sea, the old captain hands the ship’s wheel to the new young captain and steps back; he {relinquishes} command.

labels.text: re-LINQU-ish: LEAVE it, hand it OVER

scene.alt: An old sea captain hands the ship’s wheel to a young captain.

entry.def: to formally give up a claim, right or habit
entry.ex: The prince {renounced} his right to the throne so he could become a painter.
entry.ctx: After years of eating sweets at every meal, Grandpa {renounced} sugar entirely, announcing at dinner that he would never touch another cookie.
entry.etym: From Latin renuntiare, “to report back, to give up”: re- (back) + nuntiare (to announce).

mn.cue: re-NOUNCE: ANNOUNCE you GIVE IT UP
mn.text: Standing on a chair at dinner, Grandpa Gus announces to the whole family, “I give up cookies forever!” He {renounces} sweets.

scene.alt: A grandfather stands on a stool and announces he is giving up cookies while his granddaughter gasps.

entry.def: to refuse to accept or be connected with
entry.ex: The scientist {repudiated} her earlier claim after new tests proved it wrong.
entry.ctx: The club publicly {repudiated} the rude flyer that had been posted in its name, explaining that none of its members had written it.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin repudiare, “to reject, to cast off.”

mn.cue: re-PUDDLE-ate: toss it in the PUDDLE
mn.text: Someone hands Dev a rude note signed with his name; he crumples it and tosses it into a puddle, shouting, “Not mine!” He {repudiates} it.

scene.alt: A teen points at a crumpled note he has thrown into a puddle, angrily rejecting it.

entry.def: to lose something as a penalty
entry.ex: The team {forfeited} the game when only six players showed up.
entry.ctx: Because she returned the library book a full year late, Maya {forfeited} her borrowing privileges for the rest of the summer.
entry.etym: From Old French forfait, “a crime,” from forfaire (to do wrong): fors (outside) + faire (to do).

mn.text: Only three players show up for the big final, so the team must give up the game and the trophy without playing; they {forfeit}.

scene.alt: Three sad players stand beside a sign reading no game because too few of them came to play.

entry.def: to give up a throne, an office or a responsibility
entry.ex: The old king {abdicated} in favor of his daughter.
entry.ctx: When the twins left the dishes for their mother night after night, she accused them of {abdicating} their share of the chores.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

entry.etym: From Latin abdicare, “to renounce, to resign”: ab- (away) + dicare (to declare).

mn.cue: AB-DIC: SAY it AWAY: “No longer king!”
mn.text: The tired old king lifts off his crown, sets it on his daughter’s head and says, “It is yours now.” He {abdicates}.

scene.alt: An old king hands his crown to his delighted daughter.

blocks.html: appropriate as a verb (uh-PRO-pree-ate) means to take; as an adjective (uh-PRO-pree-it) it means suitable.

taking or giving up?
how
blocks.cap: Taking and giving up: who, how and by what right.

blocks.html: Appropriate has two pronunciations. The verb (uh-PROH-pree-ayt) means to take; the adjective (uh-PROH-pree-it) means suitable. “It is not appropriate to appropriate your sister’s pillow.”

blocks.html: History is full of people who broke from the group: lone thinkers, deserters, protesters, rebels at sea and in the hills. These words name them, and the uprisings and splits they caused.

People: dissident (speaks out), insurgent (fights), renegade (deserts), maverick (goes their own way), iconoclast (attacks cherished beliefs). Uprisings: mutiny (by sailors or soldiers), insurrection (a violent uprising), sedition (words that stir one up). Splits and sides: faction, partisan.
Notice the tone. A maverick or an iconoclast can be admired; a renegade or an insurgent usually is not. The same person may be a dissident to the government and a hero to the crowd.

entry.def: a person who openly disagrees with an official policy or ruling group
entry.ex: The old kingdom jailed any {dissident} who spoke out against the king’s harsh taxes.
entry.ctx: Most members of the club went along with the new rules, but one {dissident} stood up at every meeting to argue that they were unfair.
entry.etym: From Latin dissidere, “to sit apart, to disagree”: dis- (apart) + sedere (to sit).

mn.cue: DIS-SID: SITS APART from the crowd
mn.text: When the whole hall stands to cheer the king’s new tax, Lin stays in her seat with her arms crossed; she sits apart, a {dissident}.

scene.alt: In a hall where everyone stands and cheers, one woman stays seated holding a sign that says no.

entry.def: a rebel who fights against a government or those in power
entry.ex: In the old tale, the {insurgents} hid in the mountains and raided the baron’s supply wagons.
entry.ctx: The rebel band was small, but the {insurgents} knew every path through the hills, and the king’s soldiers could never catch them.
entry.etym: From Latin insurgere, “to rise up”: in- (against) + surgere (to rise).

mn.cue: IN-SURGE: SURGE UP against the rulers
mn.text: In the old story, the hill folk surge up the slope toward the cruel baron’s castle, waving their banner; each of them is an {insurgent}.

labels.text: IN-SURGE: RISE UP against the RULER

scene.alt: A determined band of villagers with a banner marches toward a castle.

entry.def: a rebellion, especially by sailors or soldiers against their officers
entry.ex: Tired of moldy biscuits, the sailors staged a {mutiny} and locked the captain in his cabin.
entry.ctx: The crew had sailed for months without pay, so when the captain ordered them around the stormy cape, they refused and seized the ship in a {mutiny}.
entry.etym: From French mutin, “rebellious.”

mn.cue: MUTE-iny: the crew won’t stay MUTE
mn.text: On the fishing boat, the ship’s cats, fed up with sardines, take over the wheel and steer for the cheese island while the captain splutters; it is a {mutiny}!

scene.alt: Two cats take over a ship’s wheel while the shocked captain shouts for order.

entry.def: a violent uprising against a government or authority
entry.ex: The governor sent troops to put down the {insurrection} in the northern provinces.
entry.ctx: What began as a peaceful march over the price of bread grew into an armed {insurrection}, and for a month the rebels held the capital.
entry.etym: From Late Latin insurrectio, from insurgere (to rise up).

mn.text: In Pip’s dream, the little chess pawns rise up all at once and chase the king right off the board; it is an {insurrection}.

labels.text: IN-SURRECT: RISE UP against the KING

scene.alt: A row of small chess pawns charges at a big chess king wearing a crown, while a boy watches in surprise.

entry.def: speech or action that stirs people to rebel against a government
entry.ex: The printer was arrested for {sedition} after publishing pamphlets urging people to overthrow the king.
entry.ctx: In the old kingdom, even a joke about the queen could be punished as {sedition}, so people learned to whisper their complaints.
entry.etym: From Latin seditio, “a going apart, a revolt”: sed- (apart) + itio (a going).

mn.cue: SAID-ition: words SAID to stir a revolt
mn.text: Standing on a crate in the market, Rex shouts for the crowd to rise up against the queen; words like that are {sedition}.

scene.alt: A man on a crate shouts through a megaphone for the crowd to rise up against the queen.

entry.def: a person who deserts a group or cause, or who breaks the rules
entry.ex: The {renegade} knight left the king’s army and joined the outlaws in the forest.
entry.ctx: Once the team’s star, he became a {renegade} in the fans’ eyes when he quit in the middle of the season to play for their fiercest rival.
entry.etym: From Spanish renegado, from Medieval Latin renegatus (one who has denied): re- + negare (to deny).

mn.text: In the night, Sir Dev slips out through the castle gate and runs to join the outlaws in the woods; he is a {renegade}.

labels.text: RAN from the GATE: a DESERTER

scene.alt: At night, a young knight sneaks out of the castle gate and runs toward the forest.

entry.def: an independent person who does not go along with the group
entry.ex: A {maverick} among bakers, Nell puts pickles in her chocolate cake.
entry.ctx: While every other architect was designing glass towers, Ada was a {maverick}, building homes of mud brick and straw that stayed cool without air conditioning.
entry.etym: From the name of a Texas rancher of the 1800s who did not brand his calves; an unbranded calf came to be called a maverick.

mn.cue: the CALF that goes its OWN WAY
mn.text: Every cow in the herd plods toward the barn, but one young calf trots off the other way to explore the hill; it is a {maverick}.

scene.alt: Three cows walk toward the barn while one small calf happily heads the other way.

entry.def: a person who attacks cherished beliefs or traditions
entry.ex: The young chef was an {iconoclast} who served dessert first and breakfast for dinner.
entry.ctx: In a field that treated tradition as sacred, the scientist was an {iconoclast}, publicly questioning ideas her own teachers had called beyond doubt.
entry.etym: From Greek eikon (image) + klastes (breaker): it first named people who broke religious images.

mn.text: While the whole town bows to the old statue, Lila holds up a sign asking why, and says the town’s favorite traditions are silly; she is an {iconoclast}.

scene.alt: A teen holds up a sign asking why beside a town statue that an old man bows to.

entry.def: a small group within a larger one, often at odds with the rest
entry.ex: The chess club split into two {factions}: those who wanted a tournament and those who wanted pizza nights.
entry.ctx: Within the town council, a small {faction} refused to approve the budget, and its stubbornness delayed the new bridge by a whole year.
entry.etym: From Latin factio, “a group acting together,” from facere (to do).

mn.cue: FACTION: a group that splits OFF
mn.text: At the bake-sale meeting, two kids march to their own corner, insisting on cookies while everyone else wants cupcakes; they are a {faction}.

labels.text: FACTION: a group WITHIN a group

scene.alt: Three children cheer for cupcakes while two others stand apart with arms crossed, insisting on cookies.

entry.def: strongly supporting one side, often without fairness
entry.ex: The {partisan} crowd booed every call that went against the home team.
entry.ctx: A fair referee must never be {partisan}; if she favors one team, the whole game becomes meaningless.
entry.etym: From French partisan, from Italian partigiano, from parte (part, side).
entry.note: Bipartisan means involving both major political parties. As a noun, a partisan is a strong supporter of one side, or a fighter in a resistance group.

mn.text: Grandpa wears his team’s colors from hat to socks, cheers every play for his side and boos every call against it; he is {partisan}.

scene.alt: A grandfather in his team’s red colors boos the referee, who shrugs.

blocks.html: maverick and iconoclast can be praise; renegade and insurgent usually are not. partisan means taking one side; bipartisan means involving both major parties.

blocks.html: Partisan means strongly for one side; bipartisan means involving both major parties, and nonpartisan means taking no side at all.

blocks.html: Writers about science, health and history need exact words for harm: harm that is quick or slow, open or hidden, to the body or to a plan. They also need a few words for the opposite, the things that do us good.

Harmful in general: detrimental, deleterious. Poison and fumes: toxic, noxious. Hidden or slow harm: pernicious, insidious. Fierce harm: virulent. Unfriendly: inimical. Good for you: salutary (a helpful effect), salubrious (healthful).
Two Latin roots help: salus means health (salutary, salubrious), and amicus means friend, so inimical (in- + amicus) means unfriendly.

entry.def: causing harm or damage
entry.ex: Staying up all night is {detrimental} to your grades.
entry.ctx: The new parking lot proved {detrimental} to the pond: oil washed off the pavement with every rain, and within two years the frogs had disappeared.
entry.etym: From Latin detrimentum, “loss, damage,” from deterere (to rub away, to wear down).

mn.cue: de-TRIM-ental: too much TRIM does HARM
mn.text: Pip trims Grandpa’s little bush, then trims some more, and more, until only a bare stick is left; all that trimming is {detrimental} to the bush.

scene.alt: A boy proudly holds a saw beside a stump that used to be a bush while his grandfather gasps.

entry.def: poisonous; harmful to living things
entry.ex: Some common garden flowers are {toxic} to cats.
entry.ctx: The old paint in the house was {toxic}: it contained lead, which can make children seriously ill if they swallow even tiny chips.
entry.etym: From Late Latin toxicus, from Greek toxikon, poison smeared on arrows (from toxon, a bow).
entry.note: Today toxic is also used for anything that harms people slowly, like a toxic friendship.

mn.text: The bottle under the sink has a big warning label and a skull on it; what is inside is {toxic}, so the cat backs away.

scene.alt: A cat backs away from a green poison bottle as a woman warns that it is not for pets.

entry.def: harmful, especially to health; also, very unpleasant
entry.ex: The {noxious} fumes from the burning tires drove everyone indoors.
entry.ctx: Unlike the harmless steam from the kettle, the gas leaking from the old furnace was {noxious}, and the family had to leave the house until it was repaired.
entry.etym: From Latin noxius, “harmful,” from noxa (harm).
entry.note: Noxious fumes harm you; obnoxious people only annoy you.

mn.cue: KNOCKS-ious: fumes that KNOCK you back
mn.text: The old truck coughs out a black cloud so foul that it nearly knocks the jogger off his feet; its fumes are {noxious}.

scene.alt: A jogger staggers back from the thick black exhaust pouring from an old car.

entry.def: causing great harm, often slowly or in a way that is hard to see
entry.ex: Gossip can have a {pernicious} effect on a friendship.
entry.ctx: The habit seemed harmless at first, a few minutes of games before homework, but it proved {pernicious}, quietly eating up whole evenings until her grades began to slip.
entry.etym: From Latin perniciosus, “ruinous,” from pernicies (ruin, destruction).

mn.text: The pretty pink flowers spreading through Lin’s garden look nice, but week by week they choke out every bean and carrot; the weed is {pernicious}.

scene.alt: Pretty weeds have spread across a garden, crowding out the vegetables, while the gardener frowns.

entry.def: harmful, often in a way that is not obvious at first
entry.ex: Too much sun can have {deleterious} effects on your skin.
entry.ctx: The chemical seemed safe in short tests, but over the years it proved {deleterious}, slowly weakening the shells of the birds whose food it touched.
entry.etym: From Greek deleterios, “harmful,” from deleisthai (to hurt).

mn.text: A sneaky computer bug deletes one of Sami’s files every night, until his whole science project is nearly gone; the bug is {deleterious}.

scene.alt: A boy panics as a sneaky bug on his desk deletes the files on his laptop.

entry.def: spreading harm slowly and secretly
entry.ex: Rust is {insidious}: it eats away at a bridge long before anyone sees the damage.
entry.ctx: The rumor was {insidious}; no one noticed it spreading from table to table until, weeks later, half the class had stopped speaking to Dev.
entry.etym: From Latin insidiosus, “cunning,” from insidiae (an ambush), from insidere (to sit in, to lie in wait).

mn.text: A tiny leak drips inside the wall for months where no one can see it, until the ceiling sags; the damage is {insidious}.

scene.alt: Water drips from a hidden leak in the ceiling into a bucket as a grandmother looks up in shock.

entry.def: extremely harmful or severe; also, bitterly hostile
entry.ex: A {virulent} flu swept through the school, closing it for a week.
entry.ctx: The critic’s review was {virulent}: instead of simply disliking the play, she attacked the actors, the director and even the audience for clapping.
entry.etym: From Latin virulentus, “full of poison,” from virus (poison, venom).
entry.note: Also said VEER-uh-lunt, without the y sound.

mn.cue: VIRUS-lent: a VIRUS at full strength
mn.text: This flu spreads so fast and hits so hard that by Friday only one student is left in the classroom; it is {virulent}.

scene.alt: A worried teacher stands in a nearly empty classroom where one sick boy sneezes.

entry.def: harmful or unfriendly, like an enemy
entry.ex: Cold, salty air is {inimical} to most tropical plants.
entry.ctx: The desert’s scorching days and freezing nights are {inimical} to most living things, yet the tough little cactus thrives there.
entry.etym: From Late Latin inimicalis, from Latin inimicus (enemy): in- (not) + amicus (friend).

mn.cue: IN-IMIC: NOT AMICable, NOT a friend
mn.text: The snowman who wandered into the desert finds the blazing sun no friend at all; the heat is {inimical} to him.

scene.alt: A snowman melts into a puddle under the blazing desert sun.

entry.def: having a good effect, often after a hard lesson
entry.ex: Losing the first game had a {salutary} effect on the team: they practiced twice as hard.
entry.ctx: Though the low grade stung, it proved {salutary}; Kai began studying every night and finished the year near the top of his class.
entry.etym: From Latin salutaris, “healthful,” from salus (health, safety).
entry.note: Salutary has nothing to do with saluting today, though both go back to salus: a salute was once a wish for someone’s good health.

mn.text: After missing the bus once, Dev sets an alarm every night and never misses it again; he salutes the lesson, which was {salutary}.

scene.alt: A teen proudly salutes his alarm clock after learning not to miss the bus.

entry.def: good for one’s health
entry.ex: The village was known for its {salubrious} climate, with clean air and mild summers.
entry.ctx: After years in the smoky city, Grandma moved to a {salubrious} seaside town, where she walked the beach every morning and slept better than she had in decades.
entry.etym: From Latin salubris, “healthful,” related to salus (health).

mn.text: Every day Nana Lou eats a fresh salad in the cool sea breeze; her seaside town is {salubrious}.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a straw hat happily eats a salad in the sea breeze.

blocks.html: salutary (beneficial) has nothing to do with saluting; salubrious means healthful. noxious fumes harm; obnoxious people annoy.

head: word
kind of harm (or good)
rows: harmful in general (deleterious often not obvious at first)
slow, hidden harm (insidious creeps in secretly)
fierce and severe (a virulent disease, virulent words)
has a good effect, often a hard lesson
blocks.cap: Ten words for what harms and what helps.

blocks.html: Noxious fumes harm you; an obnoxious person only annoys you. And salutary (good for you) has nothing to do with saluting today.
